(A) is the dominant trap: it takes the mover data as proof that parks never matter, which is too strong, since a slow-acting effect, or effects on people who already live near a new park, aren't ruled out. (D) is one explanation the facts allow but don't support, (B) is an unsupported quantity, and (E) compares movers with non-movers, which the survey never does.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Adults near parks are far more likely to exercise regularly; 2. Adults who moved near a park in the last five years exercise no more than they did before the move.

breakdown.analysis: So what does the mover data show? Not that parks never matter; only that moving next to one didn't change anything within a few years. That leaves several possibilities: exercisers choose park-side homes, or parks work slowly, or parks matter mostly to people who grew up near them. We need the answer that commits to what all of those share. A conditional does that: if parks have an effect, it isn't a quick one. Most students pick (A) or (D). (A) overreaches from "no quick change for movers" to "no change ever, for anyone." (D) picks one explanation and treats it as shown. Hard-to-like answers like (C) win because they say only what the facts force.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the lesson of the movers. But it's too strong. The movers were tracked for at most five years, and a new park also changes things for people already living nearby. "Would not change" isn't supported.
We don't know how many adults live near parks. If few do, most exercisers could live elsewhere despite the higher rate.
CORRECT. It doesn't claim parks matter, and it doesn't claim they don't. It says only that any effect isn't quick, which is exactly what the unchanged movers show.

Tempting: self-selection fits the pattern. But the survey never compares movers' exercise habits with anyone else's, so it doesn't show exercisers are more likely to move near parks. It's one possible story.
The survey compares movers before and after their move, not movers with non-movers. Nothing here ranks them.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Most of the small businesses that received grants from the Strand Valley development fund last year are restaurants, and most restaurants in the province lose money. So most of the businesses that received the fund's grants last year are losing money.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Most of the volunteers at the Wexcombe animal shelter are college students, and every college student who volunteers there has completed the shelter's safety training. So most of the shelter's volunteers have completed that training.

Most of the members of the Arden Street choir are retired teachers, and most of the choir's members sing in its alto section. So at least some of the retired teachers in the choir sing in the alto section.
Most of the people who buy season tickets to the Rowan Theater live downtown. So most of the people who live downtown buy season tickets to the Rowan Theater.
A majority of the Quayside apartments' tenants must own a car, since most of them commute to jobs outside the city, and most of the region's out-of-city commuters own a car.
Most of the households in Ridgemont that installed solar panels last year have since seen their electricity bills fall. So the panels are what lowered most of those households' bills.
questions.explanation: The economist chains two 'most' claims: most grant recipients are restaurants, and most restaurants in the province lose money, so most recipients lose money; but the recipients could be among the profitable minority of restaurants. (D) repeats this most-plus-most chain with its conclusion first: most tenants commute out of the city, most such commuters own cars, so a majority of tenants own cars. (B) is the dominant trap: it also has two 'most' premises, but both are about the same group, so its modest conclusion is valid. (A) is a valid most-plus-every chain, (C) reverses a 'most' claim, and (E) infers a cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most grant recipients are losing money.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most recipients are restaurants; most restaurants in the province lose money.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B (in a larger population) are C; so most A are C.

breakdown.analysis: Most + most doesn't chain. The grant-winning restaurants could be the healthy ones; maybe the fund picks winners. It's like saying most of my friends are lawyers, most lawyers are unhappy, so most of my friends are unhappy. We need another argument that links two "most" claims through a middle group and concludes "most." Watch the decoy that has two "mosts" but about one group, which is valid, and the one with "every" in the second slot, also valid.

choices.note: Tempting, because its first premise has the same "most A are B" form. But the second premise is "every college student who volunteers there." Most + every → most is valid. A valid argument can't match a flawed one.
Tempting: two "most" premises, just like the original. But both are about the choir's members, so they must overlap, and the conclusion only claims "at least some." That's valid.
A different flaw: it flips "most A are B" into "most B are A." Most season-ticket buyers live downtown doesn't mean most downtown residents buy tickets.

CORRECT. Most tenants commute out (most A are B); most regional out-commuters own cars (most B are C); so most tenants own cars (most A are C). Same broken chain: the tenants might be the out-commuters without cars. The conclusion just comes first.
A causal flaw (bills fell after the panels, so the panels caused it), not a quantifier chain.
choices.example: Example of E's flaw: Most students who hired a tutor raised their grades, so the tutoring is what raised them.

questions.stimulus:
Dr. Osei: The new guideline telling doctors not to prescribe antibiotics for uncomplicated ear infections in children over two has worked. Prescriptions for such infections have fallen by a third since it took effect, and serious complications have not become any more common.

Dr. Lund: Those figures can't tell us that yet. Serious complications of ear infections are so rare that even a real increase would take several years to show up in the data.
questions.stem: Dr. Osei and Dr. Lund disagree over whether
choices: fewer antibiotics have been prescribed for uncomplicated ear infections in children over two since the guideline took effect
serious complications of ear infections are uncommon enough that a rise in them would be slow to appear in the data
doctors should prescribe antibiotics for children's ear infections less often than they did before the guideline
the complication figures gathered so far are adequate for judging whether the guideline has had harmful effects
the guideline should be suspended until several more years of data on complications have been collected
questions.explanation: Osei judges the guideline a success partly because complications haven't risen; Lund says the data are too thin to show that yet. So they disagree over whether the complication record so far is enough to judge the guideline's effects, which is (D). (A) is a fact Lund never disputes, (B) is Lund's claim alone, and (E) goes beyond Lund, who says only that it's too early to judge, not that the guideline should be suspended.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Osei: The guideline worked: prescriptions fell by a third and serious complications didn't rise.; Lund: The figures can't show that yet; complications are so rare that a real rise would take years to appear.

breakdown.analysis: Lund doesn't fight about the prescriptions. She fights about what the complication numbers prove. Osei treats "no rise so far" as evidence the guideline is safe. Lund says that with an outcome this rare, "no rise so far" is what you'd see whether or not there's a problem. So the clash is about the evidence, not the policy. Neither one says what doctors should do next. Prephrase: they disagree over whether the current complication data are good enough to judge the guideline.

choices.note: Lund grants this. Her objection starts after the prescription numbers: she disputes what the complication numbers show. Common ground, not a dispute.
Lund's claim only. Osei never says how rare complications are or how quickly a rise would show up.
Neither speaker says this. Osei says the guideline worked, not that prescribing less is right in general. Lund doesn't say anything about prescribing at all.

CORRECT. Osei relies on the absence of any rise in complications to call the guideline a success, so he treats the data as adequate. Lund: "Those figures can't tell us that yet." One says the data are enough to judge; the other says they aren't.

Tempting, because it sounds like what a cautious critic would want. But Lund says only that it's too soon to call the guideline a success. She never asks for it to be suspended, and Osei never addresses suspension either.

questions.stimulus:
Ruiz: The city should drop its proposal to cap annual rent increases. Under a cap, landlords could not recover what they spend maintaining their buildings, so they would let those buildings decay.

Baird: I oppose the cap too, but that worry is misplaced: the proposal lets landlords exceed the cap to cover documented repairs. My concern is that capped landlords grow pickier, shutting out applicants with thin credit histories.
questions.stem: Ruiz and Baird disagree over whether
choices: the proposed cap would leave landlords no means of passing the cost of upkeep on to their tenants
the city should decline to adopt the proposal to cap the annual rent increases that landlords in the city may impose
landlords whose rents are capped become more selective in choosing their tenants
rent caps tend to reduce the number of apartments that are available for rent in a city
landlords who cannot recover their maintenance costs tend to let their buildings decay
questions.explanation: Both oppose the cap, so (B) is common ground. They differ on the reason: Ruiz says landlords couldn't recover maintenance costs, and Baird says the proposal's repair exception lets them do exactly that. That's (A). (C) is Baird's claim alone; (E) is Ruiz's mechanism, which Baird never denies; he just says it won't be triggered here.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ruiz: Drop the rent cap; landlords couldn't recover maintenance costs and would let buildings decay.; Baird: Also opposes the cap, but the proposal allows increases for documented repairs; his worry is that landlords would shun applicants with thin credit.

breakdown.analysis: Here the two speakers share a conclusion. Baird says "I oppose the cap too." So the obvious answer, the one about whether to adopt the cap, is the trap. The disagreement is in the reasons. Ruiz: under the cap, landlords can't recover upkeep costs. Baird: yes they can, through the repair exception. Lesson: when the second speaker agrees with the bottom line, look for the premise he rejects.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ruiz says that under a cap landlords "could not recover" maintenance spending. Baird says the proposal lets them exceed the cap "to cover documented repairs." One says there's no way to pass upkeep costs on; the other says there is.
Tempting, because most disagreement questions turn on the recommendation. Not this one. Ruiz wants the proposal dropped, and Baird says "I oppose the cap too." They agree.
Baird's claim only. Ruiz never discusses how landlords pick tenants.
Neither speaker mentions how many apartments are available. Out of scope.

Ruiz assumes this, but Baird never denies it. He says the worry is misplaced because this proposal lets landlords recover repair costs, not because landlords who can't recover costs would keep up their buildings anyway.

questions.stimulus:
Bioethicist: The hospital should not let its researchers use stored blood samples in the new genetic study. Patients gave those samples to be tested for diagnosis, and using a person's tissue for a purpose he or she never agreed to violates that person's autonomy.

Hospital administrator: The consent form that each of those patients signed expressly permitted leftover samples to be used in research, genetic research included.
questions.stem: In responding to the bioethicist, the hospital administrator does which one of the following?
choices: rejects the principle that using a person's tissue for a purpose he or she never approved violates that person's autonomy
argues that the medical value of the genetic study outweighs any concern about the patients' autonomy
suggests that the bioethicist's objection would apply equally to the diagnostic testing the patients requested
questions whether patients understand what they are agreeing to when they sign a hospital's consent form
contests a factual premise of the bioethicist's objection while leaving its underlying principle unchallenged
questions.explanation: The bioethicist's objection rests on a principle (using tissue for an unapproved purpose violates autonomy) and a factual claim (these patients agreed only to diagnostic testing). The administrator attacks only the factual claim: the patients did agree to research use. That's (E). (A) is the near-miss: the administrator never challenges the principle; his point is that the case doesn't fall under it.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Bioethicist: Don't use stored samples for the genetic study; patients agreed only to diagnostic testing, and using tissue for an unapproved purpose violates autonomy.; Administrator: The consent form expressly allowed research use, including genetic research.

breakdown.analysis: Split the bioethicist's argument into its two parts: 1. Rule: using tissue for a purpose the person never agreed to violates autonomy. 2. Fact: these patients agreed only to diagnosis. Which part does the administrator hit? Only the fact. He says nothing about whether the rule is right. If anything, his reply works only if the rule is fine and the case simply doesn't meet it. Prephrase: he denies the factual premise but leaves the principle alone.

choices.note: Tempting, because the administrator is clearly on the other side. But he never says the principle is wrong. He says the patients DID agree, so the principle isn't triggered.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Using tissue without consent doesn't violate autonomy at all, since the patient no longer needs it."

choices.note: No weighing happens. The administrator never mentions the study's value.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Whatever the autonomy cost, the study could save thousands of lives."

choices.note: He never compares research use to diagnostic testing.
choices.example: Example of this method: "By your logic, even the diagnostic tests were a violation, since patients didn't approve each specific test."

choices.note: Opposite of his move. He relies on the consent form; questioning whether patients understood it would undercut his own reply.

CORRECT. The bioethicist's factual premise is that patients agreed only to diagnostic use. The administrator says the form "expressly permitted" research use. He targets that fact and never disputes the autonomy principle.

questions.stimulus:
Kerr: Suburban turnout in last month's referendum on the regional transit tax was the lowest in twenty years, even though suburban households would pay most of the tax. Suburban voters plainly didn't much care whether it passed.

Dunne: Every poll had predicted that the tax would pass easily. People who believe their votes can't change an outcome often stay home, however strongly they feel about it.
questions.stem: Kerr and Dunne disagree over whether
choices: suburban households would bear most of the cost of the regional transit tax
the suburbs' unusually low participation in the referendum reflected a lack of concern about its result
the polls taken before the referendum predicted that the transit tax would pass by a wide margin
people who think that their votes will not affect an outcome are less likely to vote than other people are
the transit tax would have been defeated if more suburban voters had gone to the polls
questions.explanation: Kerr reads low suburban turnout as indifference; Dunne offers another reading (voters thought the result was settled), which commits him to denying that the turnout shows indifference. That's (B). (A) is Kerr's premise, which Dunne leaves alone; (C) and (D) are Dunne's points only; and neither speaker says how the vote would have gone with higher turnout, so (E) is out.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Kerr: Suburban turnout was a 20-year low though suburbs pay most of the tax, so suburban voters didn't care.; Dunne: Polls said the tax would pass easily, and people who think their vote can't matter stay home however strongly they feel.

breakdown.analysis: Both speakers accept the turnout number. They fight over what it means. Kerr: low turnout means indifference. Dunne: low turnout means people thought the result was settled, "however strongly they feel." That last phrase commits Dunne to rejecting Kerr's reading. Prephrase: they disagree over whether the low turnout shows that suburban voters didn't care.

choices.note: Kerr's premise. Dunne doesn't challenge who pays the tax.

CORRECT. Kerr: suburban voters "plainly didn't much care." Dunne explains the low turnout by the polls and says people stay home "however strongly they feel." One reads the turnout as indifference; the other rejects that reading.
Dunne's claim only. Kerr never mentions the polls, so he takes no position.
Dunne's general claim. Kerr never discusses why people skip voting in general, so this isn't a point of disagreement.
Tempting, because it sounds like the stakes of the argument. But neither speaker predicts how a bigger suburban turnout would have voted. Kerr doesn't even say which way suburban voters leaned.

questions.stimulus:
Senator Ilic: Lobbyists should be barred from giving legislators gifts of any kind. Even a modest gift creates a sense of obligation, and voters have no way to tell which gifts have influenced a vote.

Senator Park: A total ban would make it illegal for a lobbyist to buy a legislator a cup of coffee during a meeting, which is absurd. What we should ban is any gift worth more than a modest meal.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Senator Ilic and Senator Park agree that
choices: a lobbyist should be prohibited from buying a legislator a cup of coffee during a meeting
even a gift of modest value creates in a legislator a sense of obligation to the giver
a lobbyist should not be permitted to pay for a legislator's week-long stay at a resort
voters cannot determine which of the gifts that lobbyists give have influenced legislators' votes
gifts worth more than a modest meal are more likely to influence a legislator's vote than smaller gifts are
questions.explanation: Ilic would ban every gift; Park would ban every gift worth more than a modest meal. A week at a resort falls under both bans, so both are committed to (C). (A) is Ilic's alone; Park calls banning coffee absurd. (B) and (D) are Ilic's reasons, which Park never addresses, and (E) is a rationale Park might hold but never states.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ilic: Ban all gifts from lobbyists; even modest gifts create obligation, and voters can't tell which gifts mattered.; Park: A total ban would outlaw a cup of coffee, which is absurd; ban gifts worth more than a modest meal.

breakdown.analysis: For agreement questions, find where the two positions overlap. Ilic: ban everything. Park: ban everything above a modest meal. Anything worth more than a modest meal sits inside both bans. Now look for an example that's clearly above that line. Nothing in the dialogue mentions resorts, so you have to apply both rules to a new case. That's the step that makes this harder than word-matching.

choices.note: Ilic yes, Park no. Park says making the coffee illegal would be "absurd." This is their clearest disagreement.
Ilic's reason. Park never says whether modest gifts create obligation; he objects to the ban's reach, not to this claim.
CORRECT. A week-long resort stay is worth far more than a modest meal, so Park's ban covers it, and Ilic's ban covers every gift. Both are committed to prohibiting it.
Ilic's claim only. Park doesn't discuss what voters can tell.

Tempting, because it sounds like the thinking behind Park's line. But Park never gives a reason for drawing the line where he does, and Ilic thinks even modest gifts are a problem, so she isn't committed to this comparison.

questions.stimulus:
Rae: The crater near Vosk was most likely formed by a meteorite impact. It is nearly circular and has a raised rim, both of which are typical of impact craters.

Toma: Some volcanic explosions also leave nearly circular craters with raised rims. So the features you cite would be present whether or not a meteorite struck there, and we should therefore conclude that no meteorite formed the crater.
questions.stem: Toma's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats evidence that does not favor a hypothesis over a rival as grounds for rejecting that hypothesis
overlooks the possibility that the crater was formed by some process other than an impact or a volcanic explosion
infers that most craters with raised rims are volcanic from the fact that some volcanic craters have raised rims
draws a general conclusion about the origins of craters from the features of a single crater
fails to consider that features shared by impact and volcanic craters might still differ in ways that reveal a crater's origin
questions.explanation: Toma shows that Rae's evidence fits a volcanic origin as well as an impact. That at most shows Rae's evidence doesn't settle the matter; Toma instead concludes that no meteorite was involved. (A) describes that move. (B) is a familiar flaw Toma doesn't commit, since he never concludes the crater is volcanic; (E) objects to Toma's premise rather than to how he reasons from it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No meteorite formed the crater.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rae's features (circular, raised rim) also occur in volcanic craters, so they'd be present either way.

breakdown.analysis: Grant Toma everything he says. Rae's two features don't tell an impact from an eruption. What follows? Only that Rae hasn't proved her case. It doesn't follow that the impact theory is false. Toma moves from "your evidence is neutral" to "your conclusion is wrong." It's like saying: your alibi witness could be lying, so you were at the crime scene. Prephrase: he treats evidence that fails to support a claim as evidence against it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Toma's premise shows only that the features don't favor impact over eruption. He then rejects the impact hypothesis outright. Neutral evidence is treated as disproof.

Tempting, because a two-option argument often hides a false choice. But Toma never concludes the crater is volcanic. He concludes that no meteorite formed it, and that conclusion doesn't depend on there being only two possible causes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: "The crater isn't from an impact, so it must be volcanic."

choices.note: Toma never says anything about how most raised-rim craters formed. He claims only that volcanic craters can have these features.
His conclusion is about this one crater, not about craters in general.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: "The Vosk crater is volcanic, so most craters in the region are volcanic."

choices.note: This objects to Toma's premise rather than his reasoning. Even if his premise is true and the features look exactly alike, his conclusion still doesn't follow. The flaw is in the step, not the premise.

questions.stimulus:
Dr. Amsel: Researchers may leave an animal out of a study's analysis only if it died or fell ill for reasons unrelated to the treatment being tested. Dropping animals whose results look anomalous lets researchers quietly shape their findings.

Dr. Brack: Choosing which measurements to take shapes findings far more than that. Researchers should be allowed to drop an animal whose results are wildly out of line with the rest, provided the paper reports it.
questions.stem: Dr. Amsel and Dr. Brack disagree over whether
choices: choosing in advance which measurements to take shapes a study's findings more than omitting a single outlier does
readers of a published study should be told about every animal that was left out of its analysis
it can be proper to drop an animal from an analysis just because its results are anomalous
researchers may leave out of an analysis an animal that fell ill for reasons unrelated to the treatment
researchers who drop anomalous results generally do so in order to make their findings look stronger
questions.explanation: Amsel allows excluding an animal only for illness or death unrelated to the treatment, so an animal whose results are merely far out of line may not be excluded. Brack says researchers "should be allowed" to drop exactly such an animal, if the paper reports it. That's (C). (B) is Brack's condition, but Amsel never says what readers must be told; (A) is Brack's premise alone; (D) is Amsel's exception, on which Brack is silent; (E) is a motive Amsel never attributes.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Amsel: Exclude an animal only if it died or fell ill for reasons unrelated to the treatment; dropping anomalies lets researchers quietly shape results.; Brack: Choosing measurements shapes findings more; researchers should be allowed to drop a wildly out-of-line animal if the paper reports it.

breakdown.analysis: Amsel's rule is an "only if": unrelated illness or death is necessary for exclusion. An animal dropped just for being an outlier fails that condition, so Amsel says no. Brack says it outright: researchers "should be allowed" to drop such an animal, with disclosure. Amsel calls such results "anomalous"; that word in the key covers Brack's "wildly out of line" case. Brack's point about choosing measurements is only his reason; Amsel never engages it.

choices.note: Brack's premise. Amsel says nothing about choosing measurements in advance, so she isn't committed either way.

Tempting, because Brack requires reporting and Amsel worries that researchers shape findings "quietly." But Amsel's fix is to forbid the exclusion, not to require reporting it. She takes no position on what readers should be told.

CORRECT. Amsel allows exclusion "only if" an animal died or fell ill for unrelated reasons, so diverging results alone are never enough. Brack: researchers "should be allowed" to drop an animal whose results are "wildly out of line with the rest." Direct clash.
Amsel permits this. Brack never addresses sick animals, so there's no disagreement.
Amsel says dropping anomalies "lets" researchers shape findings. That's about opportunity, not motive. Brack doesn't address motive either.

questions.stimulus:
Pharmacist: Pharmacies should stop selling homeopathic remedies. Their only effect is the placebo effect, and a product that works only as a placebo should not be sold as medicine.

Physician: Granted, they work only as placebos, but placebos do relieve some patients' symptoms. And pharmacies that dropped them would send customers to shops making bolder claims, with no pharmacist on hand to say when real treatment is needed. Pharmacies are right to keep selling them.
questions.stem: The pharmacist and the physician disagree over whether
choices: customers who cannot buy homeopathic remedies at pharmacies would buy them somewhere else
homeopathic remedies can relieve the symptoms of some of the people who take them
it is misleading to sell as medicine a product whose effects come solely from the placebo effect
shops other than pharmacies make more exaggerated claims for homeopathic remedies than pharmacists do
pharmacies ought to go on offering products whose benefits come entirely from users' expectations
questions.explanation: The pharmacist says pharmacies should stop selling homeopathic remedies, which work only as placebos. The physician grants that they work only as placebos and says pharmacies are right to keep selling them. (E) restates that disagreement abstractly: products whose benefits come entirely from users' expectations are placebos. (B) is the trap: the physician asserts it, but the pharmacist never denies that placebos relieve symptoms. (C) is close to the pharmacist's reason, but neither speaker says anything about being misleading.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Pharmacist: Stop selling homeopathic remedies; they work only as placebos, and placebos shouldn't be sold as medicine.; Physician: Granted they're placebos, but placebos relieve some symptoms, and dropping them sends customers to less careful sellers; pharmacies are right to keep selling them.

breakdown.analysis: The physician concedes the pharmacist's factual point ("Granted, they work only as placebos") and then says pharmacies are right to keep selling them. So the clash is the bottom line: keep selling placebo-only remedies or stop. Now find the choice that says "keep selling" without using the word homeopathic. A product whose benefits "come entirely from users' expectations" is a placebo. Hard step: recognizing the description.

choices.note: The physician's prediction. The pharmacist never says where customers would go.

Tempting, because the physician says it. But the pharmacist says the remedies' "only effect is the placebo effect," which admits they have an effect. She never denies that placebos relieve symptoms. No disagreement.

Tempting, because it echoes the pharmacist's "should not be sold as medicine." But the pharmacist never calls such sales misleading; her objection could rest on anything. And the physician argues from consequences: he could think the sales are a little misleading and still prefer them to the alternative. Neither is committed.
The physician implies this. The pharmacist never compares pharmacists' claims with other shops'.

CORRECT. Pharmacist: stop selling remedies that work only as placebos. Physician: granted they're placebos, "pharmacies are right to keep selling them." A product whose benefits come entirely from users' expectations is exactly a placebo remedy.

questions.stimulus:
Curator: The museum should not lend the Hallam tapestry to the touring exhibition. It is more than four hundred years old, and a textile that old cannot travel without being damaged.

Conservator: The Wexley tapestry is older than the Hallam and far more worn, and it has toured three times in the past decade without suffering any damage.
questions.stem: The conservator's response to the curator proceeds by
choices: disputing the curator's claim about how old the Hallam tapestry is
citing a case that conflicts with the general claim on which the curator's conclusion rests
granting the curator's general claim but arguing that the Hallam tapestry is an exception to it
arguing that the value of lending the tapestry outweighs the risk of damaging it
suggesting that the Hallam tapestry is in better condition than the curator assumes
questions.explanation: The curator's conclusion rests on a generalization: a textile that old cannot travel without damage. The conservator cites the Wexley tapestry, older and more worn, which toured three times undamaged. That's a case that conflicts with the generalization, (B). (C) is the near-miss: the conservator doesn't grant the generalization and carve out an exception; his case contradicts the generalization itself. (E) misreads the comparison: he compares the Hallam with the Wexley, not with anything the curator assumed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Curator) Don't lend the Hallam tapestry.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: (Curator) It's over four hundred years old, and a textile that old can't travel without damage. (Conservator) The older, more worn Wexley tapestry toured three times undamaged.

breakdown.analysis: Break the curator down: 1. The Hallam is over 400 years old. 2. Any textile that old can't travel undamaged. 3. So don't lend it. Which part does the conservator hit? Not the age. He gives one tapestry that is older and more worn and that traveled three times without harm. If that's true, premise 2 is false. Prephrase: he cites a case that contradicts the curator's general rule.

choices.note: He never questions the Hallam's age. He says the Wexley is older still, which accepts the curator's figure.
choices.example: Example of this method: "The Hallam is a nineteenth-century copy, not a four-hundred-year-old original."

choices.note: CORRECT. The curator's conclusion depends on "a textile that old cannot travel without being damaged." The Wexley is that old and older, and it traveled three times undamaged. That case conflicts with the general claim.

Tempting, because the conservator is fighting the conclusion about the Hallam. But an exception argument would accept the rule ("old textiles usually can't travel") and then say the Hallam is special. The conservator does the reverse: his case is about the Wexley, and it shows the rule itself is false.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Old textiles usually can't travel, but the Hallam was relined last year and is as sturdy as a new one."

choices.note: No weighing happens. The conservator says nothing about the exhibition's value.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Some risk is worth it: the tour would bring the tapestry to half a million viewers."

choices.note: Tempting, because he says the Wexley is "far more worn" than the Hallam. But that compares the two tapestries; the curator made no claim about the Hallam's condition at all. Her argument rests on age.

questions.stimulus:
Mayor's aide: Making downtown buses free will cut car traffic downtown. When the city of Rellport made its buses free, bus ridership there doubled within a year.

Transit planner: Nearly all of Rellport's new riders had been walking or cycling; the number of people driving downtown there barely changed. And our downtown commuters are, if anything, more attached to their cars than Rellport's were.
questions.stem: The mayor's aide and the transit planner disagree over whether
choices: making downtown buses free would increase the number of people who ride buses downtown
most of the people who began riding Rellport's buses after fares ended had previously walked or cycled
commuters in the aide's city are more reluctant to give up driving than Rellport's commuters were
eliminating bus fares downtown would lead a significant number of people who now drive there to stop
the city should stop charging fares on the buses that serve its downtown area
questions.explanation: The aide predicts that free buses will cut downtown car traffic. The planner argues that free fares didn't pull drivers out of cars in Rellport and that local commuters are even more car-bound, which commits him to rejecting the aide's prediction. (D) states that prediction in other words. (A) is the near-miss: the planner sounds skeptical, but he grants that Rellport's ridership rose and never denies ridership would rise here; his point is about who the riders would be. (E) is the trap for anyone hunting for a recommendation.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Aide: Free buses will cut downtown car traffic; Rellport's ridership doubled when buses went free.; Planner: Rellport's new riders were walkers and cyclists, and driving barely changed; local commuters are even more attached to cars.

breakdown.analysis: This dialogue is about a prediction, not a policy. Aide: free fares → fewer cars downtown. Planner: Rellport shows free fares → more riders but not fewer drivers, and our drivers are even harder to move. The planner never says "it won't work," but both of his points lead there. Careful: he doesn't deny that ridership would rise. He denies that the new riders would be drivers. Look for the prediction about drivers, in new words.

choices.note: Tempting, because the planner is the skeptic. But he never says free buses wouldn't add riders. In Rellport he grants they did; his complaint is that the new riders came from walking and cycling, not from cars. More riders, same drivers: he can accept this choice and still reject the aide's prediction.
The planner's claim. The aide never says where Rellport's new riders came from.
The planner's claim. The aide never compares the two cities' commuters.

CORRECT. The aide: free buses "will cut car traffic downtown." The planner: in Rellport driving "barely changed," and local commuters are even more attached to their cars. One predicts drivers will switch; the other denies it.

Tempting, because most of these items turn on a recommendation. But the aide only predicts an effect, and the planner never says what the city should do. Neither takes a position on the policy itself.

questions.stimulus:
Botanist: A certain mining bee is important to the spread of the marsh orchid. Over the past forty years, the orchid has not colonized a single new wetland in this region where that bee was absent.

Critic: Yet the bee is abundant in dozens of the region's wetlands that the orchid has never colonized. So the bee's presence is evidently not what enables the orchid to spread.
questions.stem: The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that the orchid could survive in any wetland where the bee is abundant
cites evidence that is inconsistent with the botanist's claim about the wetlands that the orchid has colonized
takes for granted that the orchid's spread depended on the bee rather than on some other factor
draws a conclusion about every wetland in the region from observations made in only some of the region's many wetlands
fails to recognize that a condition can be needed for an outcome without being enough to bring it about
questions.explanation: The botanist's evidence shows the bee is necessary: no new colony without it. The critic rebuts this by showing the bee isn't sufficient: plenty of bee wetlands have no orchid. That doesn't touch the botanist's claim, so (E). (B) is the trap: the critic's evidence is fully consistent with the botanist's, since wetlands with the bee but no orchid don't contradict 'no orchid without the bee.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bee's presence isn't what enables the orchid to spread.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The bee is abundant in many wetlands the orchid never colonized.

breakdown.analysis: Botanist: orchid colonizes → bee present. That's the bee as a necessary condition. Critic: bee present, yet no orchid. That shows the bee isn't sufficient. But nobody said it was. Oxygen is needed for a fire, but plenty of oxygen-filled rooms aren't on fire. Prephrase: the critic treats a needed condition as if it were claimed to guarantee the outcome.

choices.note: The critic doesn't need this. His argument isn't about where the orchid could survive. If anything, the botanist's position is the one helped by the orchid's failing to survive in some bee wetlands.
Tempting, because the critic is pushing back. But "no new orchid wetland without the bee" and "many bee wetlands without the orchid" can both be true. No inconsistency.
The critic denies this rather than taking it for granted. It's closer to the botanist's view.
The critic's conclusion is about the bee's role, not a claim about every wetland. And the problem isn't the sample.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: "The bee lives in the ten wetlands we surveyed, so it lives in every wetland in the region."

choices.note: CORRECT. The botanist claims the bee is needed. The critic shows only that it's not enough by itself, then concludes it doesn't matter. Needed and enough are different things.

questions.stimulus:
Ottilie: The 1962 law requiring equal airtime for rival candidates should be applied to streaming services, even though no one in 1962 imagined such a thing. Its authors meant to keep any single outlet from tilting an election, and a large streaming service can do that as easily as a network.

Barnaby: A court that extends a law to things its authors never imagined is not interpreting the law but writing a new one.
questions.stem: Ottilie and Barnaby disagree over whether
choices: the authors of the 1962 law intended it to keep any single broadcaster or other outlet from tilting an election
a law may properly be applied to a kind of case that was unknown when the law was enacted
a large streaming service could influence an election as much as a television network could
a court should not make new law under the guise of interpreting an existing one
the authors of the 1962 law did not foresee the existence of streaming services
questions.explanation: Ottilie wants the law applied to streaming services while granting that no one in 1962 imagined them; Barnaby says extending a law to things its authors never imagined isn't legitimate. That's (B). (E) is the trap: it sounds like the crux, but Ottilie concedes it. (D) is Barnaby's underlying value, but Ottilie never says courts may write new law; she thinks applying the law's purpose is interpretation. (A) and (C) are Ottilie's premises, which Barnaby doesn't address.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ottilie: Apply the 1962 equal-airtime law to streaming, though no one then imagined streaming; the law's purpose covers it.; Barnaby: Extending a law to things its authors never imagined is writing law, not interpreting it.

breakdown.analysis: Barnaby doesn't argue about streaming or elections at all. He states a general rule about interpretation. So the disagreement has to be at that general level: can a law reach cases its authors didn't foresee? Ottilie says yes in this case, after conceding the authors didn't foresee it. Watch for the fact they share: neither thinks 1962 legislators pictured streaming.

choices.note: Ottilie's premise. Barnaby never discusses what the authors wanted.
CORRECT. Ottilie: apply the law to streaming "even though no one in 1962 imagined such a thing." Barnaby: extending a law to things its authors never imagined is "writing a new one." Yes versus no.
Ottilie's premise. Barnaby never discusses streaming services' influence.

Tempting, because it's the value behind Barnaby's remark. But Ottilie never says courts may write new law. She thinks applying the law to streaming fits what its authors "meant," which is interpretation on her view. Both can accept this; they disagree about whether her proposal crosses that line.
Tempting, because it sounds like the heart of the dispute. But Ottilie concedes it ("no one in 1962 imagined such a thing"), and Barnaby's point depends on it. They agree.

questions.stimulus:
Ines: Our district should stop teaching cursive. Hardly any adult writes in cursive anymore, and the hours spent on it could go to keyboarding, a skill every student will need.

Tobias: Students who can't read cursive can't read most of the records in the town archive, which our eighth graders use for local history. So students should at least be taught to read cursive, even if they are no longer taught to write it.
questions.stem: Ines and Tobias disagree over whether
choices: the district should continue to teach its students how to write in cursive
few adults today write in cursive often enough to make teaching students to write it worthwhile
the district should end all of the instruction in cursive that it now gives its students
keyboarding is a skill that every student in the district will need to have
most of the records held in the town archive were written in cursive
questions.explanation: Ines wants all cursive instruction stopped; Tobias wants at least reading cursive taught, so they disagree over whether all cursive instruction should end, (C). (A) is the trap: Ines rejects it, but Tobias explicitly sets writing aside ('even if they are no longer taught to write it'), so he takes no position. (B) and (D) are Ines's claims alone, and (E) is Tobias's.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ines: Stop teaching cursive; hardly anyone writes it, and the time could go to keyboarding.; Tobias: Students need to read cursive to use the town archive; teach at least reading cursive, even if not writing.

breakdown.analysis: Ines wants ALL cursive instruction gone. Tobias wants at least reading cursive kept. So they clash over whether every bit of cursive instruction should end. The trap is about writing cursive. It feels like Tobias is defending cursive, so he must want writing taught. But he says "even if they are not taught to write it." He's neutral on writing. That one clause is the whole question: reading versus writing, and "all" versus "some." Read the scope words in each choice.

choices.note: Tempting, and the most-picked trap. Ines rejects it, but Tobias deliberately sets writing aside: students should learn to read cursive "even if they are no longer taught to write it." He takes no position on writing, so this isn't a disagreement.
Ines's view. Tobias never argues that teaching students to write cursive is worthwhile, so he isn't committed against this.
CORRECT. Ines: "stop teaching cursive," with no exceptions. Tobias: students "should at least be taught to read cursive." One says end all of it; the other says keep some of it.
Ines's claim only. Tobias never mentions keyboarding. He could agree that every student needs it and still want some time kept for reading cursive.
Tobias's claim only (students who can't read cursive "can't read most of the records"). Ines never mentions the archive.

questions.stimulus:
Adaeze: Our district should replace its required summer reading list with a free choice of any book. Students made to read assigned titles mostly skim them, and a student who reads one book eagerly gains more than one who skims three.

Lucian: Free choice would leave many students reading only what they already like. I would keep the list, but let students who read two books from a shelf of approved titles skip it.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Adaeze and Lucian agree that
choices: students should be free to meet the district's summer reading requirement with any books they choose
most students who are required to read assigned titles over the summer do no more than skim them
a student who reads one book eagerly benefits more than a student who skims several books
students should have some way of meeting the summer reading requirement other than reading titles from the list
given a free choice, many students would read only the kinds of books that they already like
questions.explanation: Adaeze wants students to choose any book in place of the list, and Lucian would let students skip the list by reading two books from an approved shelf, so both are committed to some alternative to the list, as (D) says. (A) is the trap: Adaeze holds it, but Lucian limits the alternative to approved titles, so he rejects free choice of 'any' book. (B) and (C) are Adaeze's claims alone, and (E) is Lucian's.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Adaeze: Replace the required list with free choice of any book; students skim assigned titles, and one book read eagerly beats three skimmed.; Lucian: Free choice lets students stick to what they like; keep the list, but let students who read two books from an approved shelf skip it.

breakdown.analysis: Lucian sounds like he's disagreeing; he opens by attacking free choice. But look at his proposal: students can skip the list by reading from an approved shelf. So he also wants a route around the list. Adaeze's route is wide open (any book). Lucian's is limited (approved titles). What do they share? Some alternative to the list exists. What don't they share? The "any book" part. On agreement questions, the right answer is often the lowest common denominator, stated broadly enough that both positions fit inside it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Adaeze's proposal and Lucian also offers an alternative. But Lucian rejects "any books": his alternative is limited to a shelf of approved titles, and he opposes free choice outright. Adaeze yes, Lucian no.
Adaeze's claim only. Lucian never says how students read assigned titles.
Adaeze's claim only. Lucian doesn't weigh eager reading against skimming.

CORRECT. Adaeze: replace the list with free choice, which is one alternative. Lucian: students who read two approved books can "skip" the list, which is another. Both are committed to there being some way around the list.
Lucian's claim only. Adaeze never addresses what students would choose.

questions.stimulus:
Campaign director: Our neighborhood town-hall meetings reach people who have never voted. Last fall, 40 percent of those attending them had never voted before, compared with 15 percent at our rallies.

Strategist: Granted, the town halls drew a larger share of first-time voters. But more first-time voters attended our three largest rallies than attended all of last fall's town halls combined. So the town halls reach few people who have never voted.
questions.stem: The strategist's reasoning is flawed because it
choices: confuses the percentage of an audience made up of first-time voters with the number of first-time voters in that audience
treats the fact that another kind of event reaches more first-time voters as showing that the town halls reach few
relies on attendance figures that are inconsistent with the percentages that the campaign director cites
overlooks the possibility that many of the first-time voters who attended rallies did not go on to vote
presumes, without providing justification, that first-time voters who attend town halls will also attend rallies
questions.explanation: The strategist's evidence is comparative: rallies reached more first-time voters in total. The conclusion is absolute: town halls reach 'few' of them. A smaller number can still be substantial, so (B). (A) is the planted trap: the strategist explicitly separates share from count ('Granted, the town halls drew a larger share') and then argues from counts; he never treats one as the other.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Town halls reach few people who have never voted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Granting that town halls drew a larger share of first-time voters, more first-time voters attended the three largest rallies than all town halls combined.

breakdown.analysis: So what if rallies reached more? That shows town halls reached fewer, not few. If the rallies drew 2,000 first-time voters and the town halls drew 1,500, the town halls still reached a lot of people. It's like saying a sedan carries few passengers because a bus carries more. Watch the switch from a relative claim (fewer) to an absolute one (few). Prephrase: moves from "less than" to "little."

choices.note: Tempting, because the dialogue is full of percentages and counts. But the strategist explicitly keeps them apart: he grants the town halls' larger share, then argues from counts, which do measure reach. The figures don't conflict either: big rallies with a 15 percent share can hold more first-time voters than small town halls with 40 percent.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: "Forty percent of town-hall attendees were first-time voters, so the town halls drew more first-time voters than the rallies did."

choices.note: CORRECT. Comparative evidence (rallies drew more) is turned into an absolute verdict (town halls reach few). Fewer isn't few.
The figures are consistent. Large rallies at 15 percent can easily outnumber small town halls at 40 percent.
Irrelevant. The question is whether the events reach first-time voters, not whether those voters later vote.
The strategist assumes nothing about overlap between the audiences. His argument doesn't turn on it.

questions.stimulus:
Legal scholar: Police should be required to video-record every interrogation of a suspect, whatever the offense. Without a recording, courts must choose between conflicting accounts of what was said, and false confessions go undetected.

Prosecutor: For serious felonies, I agree. But minor-offense suspects are usually questioned briefly at the scene, where recording would be impractical, and the stakes are too low for false confessions to be a real concern.
questions.stem: The legal scholar and the prosecutor disagree over whether
choices: the police should be required to record their interrogations of suspects in serious felony cases
false confessions to minor offenses occur often enough to be a real concern
courts often must choose between conflicting accounts of what was said during an interrogation
an officer who briefly questions a suspected shoplifter in the store should be required to record the questioning
recording every interrogation of suspects in minor cases would cost more than police departments in the state can afford
questions.explanation: The scholar wants every interrogation recorded, 'whatever the offense'; the prosecutor exempts brief on-the-spot questioning about minor offenses. A suspected shoplifter questioned in the store falls exactly in that gap, so they disagree over (D). (A) is common ground. (B) is the trap: the prosecutor rejects it, but the scholar's general worry about false confessions doesn't commit him to any view about minor offenses specifically.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Scholar: Record every interrogation, whatever the offense; otherwise courts face conflicting accounts and false confessions go undetected.; Prosecutor: Yes for serious felonies; for minor offenses, questioning is brief and on the spot, recording is impractical, and false confessions aren't a real concern.

breakdown.analysis: This is a scope dispute. The prosecutor agrees with the rule for one class of cases and rejects it for another. So the disagreement lives in the excluded class: minor offenses, questioned briefly on the scene. No choice will say "minor offenses" in those words. Look for a case that fits that description. A shoplifter questioned in the store is the textbook example.

choices.note: They agree. "For serious felonies, I agree."

Tempting, because the prosecutor clearly rejects it. But the scholar says only that false confessions go undetected without recordings. He never says they're common in minor cases. His rule covers minor cases for both of his reasons, not because of any claim about how often false confessions happen there.
The scholar's premise. The prosecutor never disputes it.

CORRECT. Scholar: record every interrogation, "whatever the offense." Prosecutor: minor-offense suspects are questioned briefly at the scene, where recording would be impractical. A suspected shoplifter questioned in the store is that case. The scholar says record it; the prosecutor says don't require it.
The prosecutor says "impractical," not unaffordable, and the scholar says nothing about cost. Neither is committed.

questions.stimulus:
Gerda: The city should not install facial-recognition cameras downtown. The government should not log the movements of people going about their lawful business.

Lorcan: I'm not sure that's always wrong. In any case, these cameras would flag only faces of people with outstanding warrants and delete every other image within a second. I would oppose them, though, if they often flagged innocent people, and the vendor hasn't released its error rates.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Gerda and Lorcan agree that
choices: the city should reject the cameras if they would frequently mistake people without warrants for people with warrants
the city should not install the facial-recognition cameras that have been proposed for its downtown streets
the government should not keep records of the movements of people going about their lawful business
the city should require the vendor to release its error rates before deciding whether to install the cameras
the proposed cameras would delete every image that did not match a face on the list of people with warrants
questions.explanation: Gerda opposes the cameras unconditionally, so she opposes them in any case, including the case where they often misidentify people. Lorcan says he would oppose them in that case. So both are committed to (A). (B) is the main trap: Lorcan is undecided, not opposed. (C) is Gerda's principle, and Lorcan explicitly declines to endorse it ('I'm not sure that's always wrong').

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Gerda: Don't install the cameras; the government shouldn't log law-abiding people's movements.; Lorcan: Not sure such logging is always wrong; anyway, the cameras would flag only warrant matches and delete everything else in a second; he'd oppose them if they often flagged innocent people, and error rates aren't public.

breakdown.analysis: Gerda: no cameras, period. Lorcan: no cameras IF they often flag innocent people; otherwise undecided. Overlap? An unconditional "no" includes every conditional "no." So both oppose the cameras in the misidentification scenario. Note the paraphrase: "flagged innocent people" becomes "mistake people without warrants for people with warrants." Lesson: an unconditional position agrees with any conditional version of itself.

choices.note: CORRECT. Lorcan: he'd oppose them "if they often flagged innocent people," meaning people with no warrant flagged as matches. Gerda opposes them under any conditions, including that one. Both are committed.
Tempting, because Lorcan sounds skeptical. But he says he'd oppose them only under a condition that hasn't been shown. He's undecided, so he isn't committed to this.

Tempting, because Lorcan's reply then argues the cameras wouldn't log anyone anyway, which can sound like he shares the worry. But he opens by refusing to sign on: "I'm not sure that's always wrong." Gerda yes, Lorcan uncommitted.
Lorcan notes the error rates aren't public but doesn't call for a requirement. Gerda wouldn't care: she opposes the cameras whatever the error rate.
Lorcan's description of the system. Gerda never discusses how the cameras work.

questions.stimulus:
Ilse: The letter signed "J. Marlow" in the county archive was not written by the poet Jane Marlow. Its spelling is careless throughout, while Marlow's published poems are spelled meticulously.

Corin: Marlow's publisher had every manuscript corrected before printing, and her surviving drafts are riddled with misspellings. So the letter's spelling tells us nothing either way about who wrote it.
questions.stem: Ilse and Corin disagree over whether
choices: the careless spelling in the letter is evidence that someone other than Jane Marlow wrote it
the letter signed "J. Marlow" in the county archive was written by the poet Jane Marlow
the poems that Jane Marlow published contain few if any spelling errors
Jane Marlow's publisher corrected the spelling in her manuscripts before printing them
a writer's spelling is usually less careful in private letters than in work meant for publication
questions.explanation: Ilse concludes the letter isn't Marlow's because its spelling is careless. Corin says Marlow's own drafts were full of misspellings, so the spelling 'tells us nothing either way.' They disagree over whether the spelling is evidence against Marlow's authorship, (A). (B) is the trap: Ilse denies it, but Corin explicitly refuses to say who wrote the letter. (C) is common ground, (D) is Corin's alone, and (E) is something neither says.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ilse: The letter isn't Jane Marlow's; its spelling is careless, and her published poems are meticulous.; Corin: Her publisher corrected her manuscripts, and her drafts are full of misspellings; so the spelling tells us nothing either way.

breakdown.analysis: Corin doesn't say Marlow wrote the letter. He attacks Ilse's evidence: the polished poems reflect the publisher's corrections, and Marlow's own drafts were sloppy. Then he states his limit: the spelling "tells us nothing either way." So the dispute is about what the spelling shows, not about who wrote the letter. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. On authorship, Corin says neither.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ilse uses the careless spelling as her reason to deny Marlow wrote the letter. Corin: the spelling "tells us nothing either way about who wrote it." Evidence versus no evidence.

Tempting, because Ilse denies it and Corin is the one defending Marlow. But Corin stops short: the spelling tells us nothing "either way." He never says Marlow wrote the letter, so he isn't committed.
Common ground. Ilse says the poems are "spelled meticulously," and Corin explains why: the publisher corrected them. He doesn't deny the poems are clean.
Corin's claim only. Ilse never mentions the publisher.
Neither says this. Corin's point is about Marlow's drafts, not about writers' letters in general, and Ilse makes no claim about private writing.

questions.stimulus: Business analyst: Small-business owners in Halden who took the city's optional free bookkeeping course were more likely to still be in business three years later than owners who did not. Many credit the course. But owners who signed up and were turned away only because the course was full stayed in business at the same rate as those who took it. So the course did not improve its participants' chances of survival.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the business analyst's argument?
choices: The owners who were turned away were chosen at random from among all the owners who signed up for the course.
Owners who sign up for optional courses are generally more diligent in running their businesses than other owners are.
The owners who took the course went on to use the methods it taught throughout the following three years.
The owners who were turned away did not, for the most part, obtain similar bookkeeping instruction or help elsewhere.
The owners who took the course did not also get bookkeeping help from some other source in those three years.
questions.explanation: The turned-away owners serve as a control group: they wanted the course but didn't get it. They work as a control only if they didn't mostly get equivalent help elsewhere, (D). (E) is its mirror image and the near-miss: if the course-takers also got outside help, the treated group got more help, yet still did no better, which if anything supports the conclusion. (A) would make the control cleaner but is stronger than needed. (B) explains the original correlation but isn't required. (C) would, if false, only fit the conclusion better.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The course didn't improve participants' survival chances.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Owners who signed up but were turned away survived at the same rate as those who took it.

breakdown.analysis: The analyst's comparison is clever: the turned-away owners were just as motivated (they signed up), so self-selection is handled. But the comparison only works if the turned-away group really went without the treatment. What if most of them, frustrated, hired a bookkeeper or took a course elsewhere? Then both groups got the treatment, and equal survival shows nothing. Watch which group the choice is about: help for the control group matters; extra help for the course-takers doesn't.

choices.note: Too strong. Turn-aways could be chosen by sign-up order or any other way unrelated to business skill, and the comparison would still work.
choices.negation: The turned-away owners were not chosen at random. Maybe they were the latest to sign up. That doesn't make them a worse control.

choices.note: Tempting, because it explains why course-takers outlasted non-signers. But the argument already handles that by using the turned-away signers as its comparison. It doesn't need this claim.
choices.negation: Owners who sign up are not more diligent. The argument still rests on the turned-away comparison; nothing breaks.

choices.note: If anything, the opposite fits the conclusion. If participants didn't use the methods, it's even less surprising the course didn't help.
choices.negation: The participants did not keep using the methods. The conclusion that the course didn't improve their chances still stands.

choices.note: CORRECT. If most turned-away owners got similar bookkeeping help elsewhere, they weren't really untreated, and their equal survival rate tells us nothing about whether the help works.
choices.negation: Most turned-away owners did obtain similar instruction or help elsewhere. Then the comparison group got the treatment too, and the argument collapses.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's D turned around. But extra help for the course-takers doesn't hurt the argument. If they got the course plus outside help and still did no better than the turned-away owners, that's even more reason to doubt the course helped.
choices.negation: The course-takers also got bookkeeping help elsewhere. They had more help than the control group and still did no better. The conclusion survives.

questions.stimulus:
Senator Akers: We should not fund the proposed high-speed rail line. Public money ought to go only to projects whose benefits reach a broad share of the public, and only a small fraction of the state's residents will ever ride the line.

Senator Lowe: Then you should not have sponsored last year's rural broadband grants, which reach fewer than one household in twenty. Yet you called that program money well spent.
questions.stem: In responding to Senator Akers, Senator Lowe does which one of the following?
choices: rejects the principle that public money should go only to projects that benefit a broad share of the public
points out that Akers has backed a project that the standard Akers proposes would rule out
grants Akers's standard but contends that Akers has misjudged who would benefit from the line
disputes Akers's estimate of the fraction of the state's residents who will ever ride the line
argues that the rail line would benefit more of the state's residents than the broadband grants do
questions.explanation: Lowe applies Akers's own standard to a program Akers sponsored and praised: the broadband grants reach under one household in twenty, so by Akers's rule they shouldn't have been funded. That's pointing out that Akers backed a project his standard would rule out, (B). (A) overstates: Lowe never says the principle is wrong; he says Akers hasn't followed it. (C) describes a different reply, one that would argue the line's benefits reach beyond its riders. Lowe says nothing about the line at all.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Akers: Don't fund the rail line; public money should go only to broadly beneficial projects, and few residents will ride it.; Lowe: By that rule, Akers shouldn't have sponsored the rural broadband grants, which reach under 5 percent of households, yet he called them money well spent.

breakdown.analysis: Notice what Lowe leaves alone. He doesn't argue about ridership. He doesn't say the line helps drivers too. He doesn't even say the principle is false. He takes Akers's rule, applies it to a program Akers sponsored, and shows the program fails it. Prephrase: he shows Akers's own record conflicts with Akers's standard. Whether that means the rule is wrong or Akers is inconsistent, Lowe leaves unsaid.

choices.note: Tempting, because Lowe's point puts pressure on the principle. But he never says the principle is wrong. He says Akers's past support conflicts with it; Akers could answer by giving up the broadband praise and keeping the rule.
choices.example: Example of this method: "A project can deserve public money even if it helps only a few people, as long as it helps them a great deal."

choices.note: CORRECT. Akers's standard: fund only projects whose benefits reach a broad share of the public. Lowe: the broadband grants reach fewer than one household in twenty, and Akers sponsored and praised them. A project Akers backed fails his own test.
A sensible reply to Akers, but not this one. Lowe never says who would benefit from the rail line.
choices.example: Example of this method: "The line helps far more than its riders: every rider leaves the highways less crowded for drivers."

choices.note: Lowe never mentions ridership. He takes the claim about the line as given and talks only about the broadband grants.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Your ridership figures are years out of date; a third of residents say they'd use the line."

choices.note: Lowe never compares the two projects' reach. He mentions the grants only to show they fail Akers's test.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Governor Eads is often said to have vetoed many bills after 1890, but this is a mistake. Every veto Eads issued was accompanied, as state law required, by a written message to the legislature, and the legislature's archive holds his veto messages from 1883 through 1890 but none from any later year. So Eads issued no vetoes after 1890.
questions.stem: The historian's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Eads did not object to any of the bills that the legislature passed after 1890.
The legislature's archive is complete for the years 1883 through 1890.
Had Eads sent the legislature any veto message after 1890, the archive would now contain it.
Eads remained in the office of governor for at least several years after 1890.
Historians who say Eads vetoed bills after 1890 have not examined the legislature's archive.
questions.explanation: Every veto came with a message, and the archive has no post-1890 messages. To conclude there were no vetoes, the historian must assume that any post-1890 message would have survived in the archive, (C). (B) borrows the stimulus's dates but concerns the wrong period. (D) feels like background the argument needs, but if Eads left office, the conclusion is only more certain. (A) is too strong: he could object to bills without vetoing them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Eads issued no vetoes after 1890.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every veto came with a message to the legislature; the archive has his messages through 1890 and none later.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: veto → message. The archive has no later messages. To get "no later messages were sent," you need: message sent → message in archive. Without that, maybe the later messages were lost, misfiled or destroyed. That's the gap: absence from the archive treated as proof of absence.

choices.note: Too strong and off target. Objecting to a bill isn't vetoing it.
choices.negation: Eads objected to some later bills. He could have objected without vetoing. Harmless.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about the archive's completeness. But it covers the wrong years. The argument depends on the archive keeping later messages, not earlier ones.
choices.negation: The archive is missing some messages from 1883–1890. That doesn't show any later message was lost. Harmless.

choices.note: CORRECT. If later messages could have been lost, their absence proves nothing. The argument needs any post-1890 message to have survived.
choices.negation: Some post-1890 veto message might have been sent and not kept. Then the empty archive doesn't show there were no vetoes; the argument fails.

choices.note: Feels necessary, since a governor who left office couldn't veto. But that would make the conclusion more certain, not less.
choices.negation: Eads left office soon after 1890. Then he certainly issued no later vetoes. The conclusion survives.

choices.note: Not required. Other historians could have seen the archive and still be wrong.
choices.negation: Those historians did examine the archive. Their mistake doesn't affect the historian's reasoning.

questions.stimulus:
Petra: Last year the city began fining households that put recyclables in their trash, and this year the volume of trash it collected fell by 10 percent. The fines evidently caused the drop.

Ewan: The entire drop came from the east side, where the city also began collecting food scraps separately for composting this year. Elsewhere, under the same fines, trash volume didn't budge. The composting, not the fines, produced the drop.
questions.stem: Petra and Ewan disagree over whether
choices: the separate collection of food scraps reduced the volume of trash collected on the east side
the volume of trash that the city collected fell by about 10 percent from last year to this year
the volume of trash collected outside the east side was about the same this year as it was last year
separate collection of food scraps reduces trash volume more than any other program the city has tried
most of this year's decline in collected trash would have occurred even if the city had never begun fining households
questions.explanation: Petra says the fines caused the drop in trash; Ewan says the composting, 'not the fines,' produced it. So they disagree over whether the decline would have happened without the fines, (E). (A) is the trap: it's Ewan's view, but Petra never mentions composting, and nothing she says rules out composting also trimming east-side trash. (B) is common ground, and (C) is Ewan's alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Petra: Fines on recyclables in trash began, and trash volume fell 10%, so the fines caused the drop.; Ewan: The whole drop came from the east side, where composting began; elsewhere, with the same fines, trash didn't budge; composting, not the fines, produced the drop.

breakdown.analysis: Ewan accepts the 10 percent drop and offers a different cause, backed by a comparison: same fines everywhere, drop only where composting started. Petra says the fines caused the drop; Ewan says they didn't. So the dispute is a counterfactual: without the fines, would trash still have fallen? Petra: no. Ewan: yes. Watch the trap: an answer about what composting did is Ewan's alone. Petra never says a word about composting, so she isn't committed against it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the heart of Ewan's reply. But Petra never mentions composting. She credits the fines; she doesn't deny that the food-scrap collection also cut east-side trash. Ewan yes, Petra silent.
Common ground. Ewan accepts the drop and argues about its cause.
Ewan's claim. Petra never breaks the numbers down by district.
Too broad for either speaker. Ewan credits composting with this year's drop but never compares it with every program the city has tried.
CORRECT. Petra: the fines "caused the drop," so without them it wouldn't have happened. Ewan: "the composting, not the fines, produced the drop," so it would have happened anyway. Yes versus no.

questions.stimulus: Science administrator: Every scientist at the Ostrander Institute who has won the national early-career prize spent at least a year at the institute's Arctic field station before winning it. Field work in harsh conditions evidently builds the skills that prize-winning research requires. The institute should therefore keep sending its most promising junior scientists to the station.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the science administrator's argument?
choices: Not every scientist at the institute has spent a year or more at the Arctic field station.
Most of the institute's scientists who spent a year or more at the field station later won the prize.
The field station develops research skills more effectively than any of the institute's other programs.
The prize-winners won the prize for research that they carried out while they were at the field station.
Scientists who win the early-career prize usually go on to do important research later in their careers.
questions.explanation: 'All prize-winners spent time at the station' says nothing if every scientist at the institute did; the prize-winners would just reflect the whole staff. The argument needs at least some scientists not to have gone, (A). (D) is the main trap: the skills could build at the station and pay off in later work. (B) is too strong, and (C) is a comparison the conclusion doesn't need.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keep sending promising junior scientists to the field station.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every prize-winner spent a year there first, so field work builds prize-winning skills.

breakdown.analysis: "Every winner did X" sounds impressive. But what if every scientist did X? Then of course every winner did, the way every winner also drank water. The fact only means something if the station is a filter, if some scientists skipped it. The key is that weak, odd-looking "not every" statement. It looks irrelevant until you negate it.

choices.note: CORRECT. If every scientist at the institute did a year at the station, "every winner did" shows nothing about the station's effect.
choices.negation: Every scientist at the institute spent a year or more at the station. Then the prize-winners' shared background is universal and says nothing about the station. The argument collapses.

choices.note: Too strong. The station could raise the odds without most alumni winning.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the station alumni won. The prize could still require skills the station builds. Survives.

choices.note: A comparison the conclusion doesn't need. The station can be worth keeping even if another program is just as good.
choices.negation: Some other program builds skills as well as the station. Keeping the station is still reasonable.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties the prize to the station directly. But the argument says the station builds skills, which could pay off in research done years later.
choices.negation: The prize-winners won for research done after they left. Consistent with the station's having built their skills. Survives.

choices.note: Irrelevant to whether the station builds prize-winning skills.
choices.negation: Prize-winners don't usually do important later work. The station could still build the skills the prize rewards.

questions.stimulus: Organizer: Last year the county blood drive moved from the high school gym to the new civic center, and donations fell by a quarter. Some blame the move, but the civic center has more parking than the gym and is no farther from town. Moreover, the drive was announced just one week ahead instead of the usual three, too late for many regular donors from outlying villages to arrange time off. So the late announcement, not the move, caused the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the organizer's argument depends?
choices: Most of the people who donated at the drive in earlier years lived in the county's outlying villages.
Parking and distance from town are the only features of a site that affect how many people donate there.
Regular donors from outlying villages usually decide whether to attend a drive at least two weeks in advance.
Other blood drives that were announced late have also seen their donations decline.
Fewer donors from outlying villages gave blood at last year's drive than at earlier drives.
questions.explanation: The organizer's mechanism runs through donors from outlying villages. If just as many of them came last year, the late announcement can't explain the drop, so the argument requires (E). (A) is too strong: village donors needn't be a majority. (B) is too strong too, since the argument needs the move not to have mattered, not that only two features ever could. (C) and (D) would help but aren't required.

setup.label: Conclusion
