setup.text: The late announcement, not the move, caused the decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The new site has more parking and is no farther away; the late notice kept many outlying-village donors from arranging time off.

breakdown.analysis: The late announcement could only cut donations through the people it affected: donors from outlying villages. So it must actually have cut their turnout. If village donors came in the usual numbers, the late notice did nothing, and the cause has to be something else. Prephrase: fewer village donors came.

choices.note: Too strong. Village donors could be a minority and their absence still cause a big part of the drop.
choices.negation: Most past donors did not live in outlying villages. A big drop among a minority could still drive the decline.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument doesn't need a general law about sites. It needs this move not to have hurt donations.
choices.negation: Some other site features also matter. The civic center might score fine on them; the argument survives.

choices.note: Helps explain why one week was too short, but the stimulus already says it was too late for many. Not required.
choices.negation: Village donors usually decide later than two weeks ahead. They still needed time to get off work, which the stimulus says they lacked.

choices.note: Supporting evidence from elsewhere; not required.
choices.negation: Other late-announced drives didn't decline. This drive's own facts can still show the late notice mattered.

choices.note: CORRECT. If village turnout didn't fall, the late announcement didn't cause the decline.
choices.negation: Village donors came in at least the usual numbers. Then the late notice cost nothing, and the argument collapses.

questions.stimulus: Economist: When Corvia cut its tariff on imported steel last year, domestic steel prices fell 8 percent. Some credit increased competition from imports. But the volume of steel imported into Corvia actually declined slightly over the year, while Corvia's construction industry shrank sharply. So the price drop must instead reflect falling demand for steel.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economist's argument depends?
choices: Most of the steel sold in Corvia is bought by companies in the country's construction industry.
The decline in steel imports last year was not itself a result of the shrinking of Corvia's construction industry.
The shrinking of Corvia's construction industry was not itself caused by the cut in the tariff on steel.
Prices of other building materials sold in Corvia also fell during the year after the tariff cut.
Domestic steelmakers did not cut prices to keep buyers from switching to imports that the lower tariff had made cheaper.
questions.explanation: The economist rejects the competition explanation because imports didn't rise. But competition can lower prices without any rise in imports: domestic producers may cut prices precisely to keep buyers from switching. The argument requires that this didn't happen, (E). (B) and (C) sound like defenders but guard against the wrong things; negating either leaves the demand explanation intact. (A) and (D) would help but aren't required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The price drop reflects falling demand, not import competition.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Imports didn't rise (they fell slightly); construction shrank sharply.

breakdown.analysis: Why does "imports didn't rise" rule out competition? Only if competition works by actually selling more imports. But a threat can do the job too. If cheaper imports are now available, domestic mills may cut prices to keep their customers. Then imports stay flat and competition still drives prices down. The argument needs that not to be what happened. That's a defender against an alternative the stimulus never mentions, and that's why the answer is hard to spot. Most students pick (B) or (C): they look like defenders, but each guards the wrong link.

choices.note: Helpful but not required. Construction needn't buy most of the steel for its sharp decline to reduce demand.
choices.negation: Construction companies do not buy most of the steel sold in Corvia. Construction could still be a large enough buyer for its collapse to cut demand. The argument survives.

choices.note: Tempting, because it uses the stimulus's own two facts and sounds like ruling out a link. But if shrinking construction did reduce imports, that fits the demand story perfectly. Nothing breaks.
choices.negation: The decline in imports was a result of the shrinking construction industry. That's consistent with, even supportive of, a falling-demand explanation.

choices.note: Tempting defender. But the conclusion is about the immediate cause of the price drop. Even if the tariff cut somehow caused construction to shrink, the price drop would still "reflect falling demand."
choices.negation: The tariff cut caused construction to shrink. Prices still fell because demand fell. The conclusion holds.

choices.note: This would support the demand explanation, but it isn't required. Steel could have its own price drop from weaker demand regardless of what other materials did.
choices.negation: Prices of other building materials did not fall. A small blow at most; the steel-specific facts still stand.

choices.note: CORRECT. If domestic mills cut prices to head off cheaper imports, import competition caused the drop even though import volumes didn't rise, and the conclusion fails. The argument must assume that didn't happen.
choices.negation: Domestic steelmakers did cut prices to keep buyers from switching to imports. Then competition from imports drove the drop, and the argument's "instead" collapses.

questions.stimulus: Court administrator: This year Ardmore County began sending every defendant awaiting trial text-message reminders of upcoming court dates. This year 84 defendants missed a court date, down from 120 last year. Since the reminders were the only change in how the court handles defendants, they must have reduced the rate at which defendants miss court dates.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption that the court administrator's argument requires?
choices: The number of defendants awaiting trial in Ardmore County was the same this year as it was last year.
Fewer defendants missed court dates in Ardmore County this year than in any other year in the past decade.
The number of defendants awaiting trial in Ardmore County did not fall by 30 percent or more this year.
Text-message reminders have reduced missed court dates in most of the other counties that have adopted them.
This year's defendants were not, as a group, more prone to missing court dates than last year's defendants were.
questions.explanation: The evidence is a count (120 down to 84), but the conclusion is about a rate. 84 is 70 percent of 120, so if the number of defendants fell by 30 percent or more, the rate held steady or rose. The argument requires that the caseload did not fall that much, (C). (A) is the too-strong version: the caseload could fall by 10 percent and the rate would still drop. (E) sounds like a defender but runs the wrong way: more failure-prone defendants would make the reminders look even better.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reminders reduced the rate at which defendants miss court dates.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Missed dates fell from 120 to 84; the reminders were the only change in handling defendants.

breakdown.analysis: Count versus rate. A drop from 120 to 84 is a 30 percent drop in the count. Whether the rate fell depends on the denominator. Work it: 84/120 = 0.7. If the number of defendants fell by exactly 30 percent, the rate is unchanged. If it fell more, the rate went up. So the argument needs the caseload not to have shrunk by 30 percent or more. The key looks oddly specific. That's the sign of a precise necessary assumption.

choices.note: Tempting, the most-picked trap. It would make the argument work, but it's too strong. If the caseload fell 10 percent, the rate still fell (84 of 0.9 × last year's caseload is lower than 120 of last year's).
choices.negation: The caseload changed this year. If it fell only slightly, or rose, the rate still dropped. Survives.

choices.note: A record low count says nothing about the rate, and the argument doesn't need it.
choices.negation: Some earlier year had fewer missed dates. Irrelevant to this year's rate.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the caseload fell 30 percent or more, 84 is at least as large a share as 120 was, and there's no rate reduction to explain.
choices.negation: The caseload fell by 30 percent or more. Then the miss rate stayed the same or rose, and the conclusion fails.

choices.note: Outside support; not required.
choices.negation: Reminders haven't worked in most other counties. Ardmore's own numbers could still show an effect.

choices.note: Tempting because it sounds like ruling out an alternative. But it runs the wrong way. If this year's defendants were more prone to missing dates, the reminders did even better than the numbers show.
choices.negation: This year's defendants were more prone to missing dates. That makes the drop more impressive, not less. Survives.

questions.stimulus:
Defense attorney: Because judges in this state cannot depart from mandatory minimum sentences, some defendants here receive sentences that are plainly unjust. Judges should be allowed to take a defendant's circumstances into account.

Legislator: Not in practice. Whenever a defendant's circumstances call for leniency, prosecutors here drop the charges that carry mandatory minimums. Giving judges discretion would only add a second, less predictable route to the same result.
questions.stem: The defense attorney and the legislator disagree over whether
choices: mandatory minimum sentences should be abolished in the state
the state's prosecutors are better placed than its judges to tell when leniency is warranted
sentencing would become less predictable if judges were allowed to depart from mandatory minimums
the state's sentencing system, as it actually operates, sometimes yields clearly unfair punishments
a sentencing rule that cannot take account of a defendant's circumstances risks producing unjust sentences
questions.explanation: The legislator's 'Not in practice' denies the attorney's factual claim that some defendants here receive plainly unjust sentences: prosecutors already supply the leniency. So they disagree over (D). (E) is the dominant trap: it's the attorney's reasoning in her own terms, but the legislator never denies that a rigid rule creates the risk; he says prosecutors work around it. (A) overstates the attorney, who wants departures allowed, not minimums abolished; (C) is the legislator's alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Attorney: Because judges can't depart from mandatory minimums, some defendants get plainly unjust sentences; judges should be allowed to consider circumstances.; Legislator: Not in practice: prosecutors drop the mandatory-minimum charges whenever leniency is called for; judicial discretion would add a less predictable route to the same result.

breakdown.analysis: Pin down what "Not in practice" is answering. It's the attorney's factual claim: unjust sentences actually happen here. The legislator says they don't, because prosecutors drop the charges. The policy question (should judges get discretion) isn't among the choices, so recommendation-hunters will reach for (E), which uses the attorney's own words. But look at what the legislator concedes: he describes prosecutors working around the rule, which only makes sense if the rule, applied rigidly, would be unfair. Prephrase: they disagree over whether unjust sentences actually result here.

choices.note: Too strong for the attorney. She wants judges allowed to depart, not the minimums abolished. And the legislator never discusses abolition.
Neither says this. The legislator says prosecutors do provide leniency, not that they judge it better than judges would.
The legislator's claim. The attorney never addresses predictability.

CORRECT. Attorney: "some defendants here receive sentences that are plainly unjust." Legislator: "Not in practice," since prosecutors drop the charges whenever leniency is called for. One says the system as it works produces clear injustice; the other denies it.

Tempting, because it echoes the attorney's reasoning. But the legislator doesn't deny it. His point is that prosecutors work around the rigid rule. That assumes the rule, applied rigidly, would sometimes be unfair. Common ground, not a dispute.

questions.stimulus: Economic historian: Prices in the ledgers of 1880s Tarrow shops almost never end in 9, whereas most retail prices there today do. Some say merchants then had not yet learned that a price just below a round figure attracts buyers. But the smallest coin circulating in Tarrow at the time was worth five cents, so a price ending in 9 could not be paid exactly. Merchants probably avoided such prices for that reason.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economic historian's argument depends?
choices: Most retail prices in Tarrow today end in 9 because merchants believe that such prices attract buyers.
The five-cent coin was the coin most widely used in Tarrow's shops during the 1880s.
Merchants in 1880s Tarrow generally rounded the amount owed to the nearest five cents when making change.
Prices ending in 9 were also uncommon in other countries whose smallest coin in the 1880s was worth five cents.
Shops in 1880s Tarrow did not routinely let customers settle small amounts with tokens or store credit instead of coins.
questions.explanation: The argument says that 9-ending prices couldn't be paid exactly because no coin small enough existed. That holds only if shops didn't have another way to settle small amounts. If tokens or store credit were routine, a 9-ending price could be paid exactly after all, and the coin explanation fails. So (E) is required. (C) is the trap: rounding would let merchants charge 9-ending prices, so its truth hurts the argument rather than being assumed by it. (D) would strengthen but isn't required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: 1880s merchants avoided 9-ending prices because the smallest coin was five cents.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A 9-ending price couldn't be paid exactly with coins no smaller than five cents.

breakdown.analysis: The argument jumps from "no small enough coin" to "couldn't be paid exactly." Coins aren't the only way to settle an amount. If shops routinely used tokens or store credit for odd amounts, a price of 49 cents was perfectly payable, and the coin story loses its force. The key defends against an alternative the stimulus never mentions. That's why it's hard to like. The tempting choices are mostly about coins and prices, which the argument already covers.

choices.note: About today's prices, not the 1880s. The argument doesn't need any claim about why prices end in 9 now.
choices.negation: Today's 9-ending prices exist for some other reason. Irrelevant to why 1880s merchants avoided them.

choices.note: Uses the stimulus's coin, but the argument relies on that coin being the smallest, not the most used.
choices.negation: Some other coin was used more often. The five-cent coin was still the smallest. Survives.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's about payment practice. But it runs the wrong way. If merchants routinely rounded, a 9-ending price would cause no trouble, which would weaken the argument. The argument doesn't assume this; it's better off if it's false.
choices.negation: Merchants did not generally round when making change. That helps the argument. Not required.

choices.note: Supporting evidence from elsewhere. Helpful, not required.
choices.negation: 9-ending prices were common in some other five-cent-coin country. That country may have used tokens; Tarrow's case could still hold.

choices.note: CORRECT. If small amounts were routinely settled with tokens or credit, 9-ending prices could be paid exactly, and the coin limit wouldn't explain merchants' avoiding them.
choices.negation: Shops routinely settled small amounts with tokens or store credit. Then a 9-ending price was payable, and the explanation collapses.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Sufficient Assumption & Principle

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The collapse of the late-season moth population in the northern highlands will not harm any of the region’s native wildflower species. Every wildflower species native to the highlands finishes blooming before the first autumn frost, and the late-season moths fly only in the weeks after that frost.
questions.stem: The ecologist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Late-season moths pollinate more of the highlands’ wildflower species than does any other kind of insect active in autumn.
A plant species cannot be harmed by an insect population’s loss unless the plant blooms at some time when those insects are active.
Any wildflower species that is in bloom while the late-season moths are flying would be harmed by a collapse in the moth population.
None of the wildflower species native to the highlands is pollinated by the late-season moths or by any other insect that flies after the frost.
Most wildflower species that finish blooming before the first frost are pollinated chiefly by bees rather than by moths.
questions.explanation: The premises show that native wildflowers and late-season moths never overlap: the flowers are done before the frost, and the moths fly only after it. (B) turns that into the missing rule: harmed by an insect’s loss → in bloom while that insect is active. Contrapositive: never in bloom while the moths fly → not harmed. (D) is the near-miss: it follows from the premises, but ‘not pollinated by moths’ doesn’t rule out every other kind of harm. (C) reverses the needed link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The moth collapse will not harm any native wildflower species.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Native species finish blooming before the first frost; the moths fly only after it. So no native species is ever in bloom while the moths are flying.

breakdown.analysis: So the flowers and the moths never meet. Does that mean nothing bad can happen to the flowers when the moths vanish? Only if overlap in time is the only way a moth collapse could matter to a plant. Chain: native → never in bloom while moths fly → ??? → not harmed. We need: harmed → in bloom while the insects are active. Contrapositive: never in bloom while they’re active → not harmed. Expect the answer in general terms (‘a plant species,’ ‘an insect population’), not the stimulus’s words.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Which insect pollinates the most species doesn’t connect ‘never in bloom while the moths fly’ to ‘not harmed.’

CORRECT. Harmed by the loss → in bloom while the insects are active. Contrapositive: never in bloom while they’re active → not harmed. The native species are never in bloom while the moths fly, so none is harmed.

Tempting, because it uses the stimulus’s own terms. But it reverses the link: it says what happens to species that ARE in bloom while the moths fly. Our species aren’t, so this tells us nothing about them.

Tempting near-miss. It’s true given the premises, but the conclusion is about ANY harm. A plant could suffer from the collapse in some way other than lost pollination, and this answer doesn’t rule that out.
‘Most’ and ‘chiefly’ are too weak, and pollination by bees doesn’t rule out harm from the moth collapse.

questions.stimulus: Musicologist: Of the two surviving manuscripts of the cantata, the Lyon copy is a more reliable guide than the Vienna copy to what the composer actually wrote. Both copies were made after the composer’s death by copyists whose names are unknown. But the Lyon copy was made from the composer’s own draft, whereas the Vienna copy was made from the Lyon copy.
questions.stem: The musicologist’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every error that appears in the Lyon copy of the cantata also appears in the Vienna copy.
A copy made directly from a composer’s own draft is always a reliable guide to what the composer wrote.
Some manuscripts made from a composer’s draft are more faithful to it than are the copies later made from them.
No manuscript copied from another manuscript is as reliable a guide to what a composer wrote as is the manuscript it was copied from.
The copyist who produced the Vienna copy was less familiar with the composer’s style and handwriting than was the copyist who produced the Lyon copy.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is comparative: Lyon is MORE reliable than Vienna. The key fact is that Vienna was copied from Lyon. (D) says any copy of a copy is less reliable than its source, which yields the comparison directly. (A) is the near-miss: if Vienna carries all of Lyon’s errors, Vienna is at best equally reliable, not necessarily less. (B) gives Lyon reliability but no comparison, and (C) is a weak ‘some’ bridge.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Lyon copy is a more reliable guide than the Vienna copy.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lyon was copied from the composer’s draft; Vienna was copied from Lyon.

breakdown.analysis: Why must a copy of Lyon be worse than Lyon? A perfect copyist could reproduce Lyon exactly. The conclusion is a strict comparison, so we need something guaranteeing that copying from Lyon loses reliability. Prephrase: a copy is always less reliable than the manuscript it was copied from. Watch for answers that give only ‘at least as bad’ or that make Lyon reliable without comparing.

choices.note: Tempting. If Vienna carries every Lyon error, Vienna can’t be better. But it could be exactly as good (a flawless copy of Lyon). ‘No better’ isn’t ‘worse,’ and the conclusion needs ‘worse.’
This makes Lyon reliable, but Vienna might be reliable too. An absolute claim doesn’t give you a comparison.
Too weak. ‘Some’ manuscripts beating their copies doesn’t tell us that Lyon beats Vienna.
CORRECT. Vienna was copied from Lyon, so by this principle Vienna is less reliable than Lyon. That’s the conclusion.
Familiarity with style might make errors more likely, but it doesn’t guarantee the Vienna copy is less reliable. Relevant, not sufficient.

questions.stimulus: Photo editor: We were right to print the photograph of the flood rescue exactly as our photographer took it, instead of digitally removing the power line that cuts across the scene. Many readers complain that the line spoils the picture, and removing it would have misrepresented nothing important. But our readers count on the pictures we print to show precisely what our photographers saw.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the photo editor’s reasoning?
choices: What people depend on for a certain kind of accuracy should not be made less accurate, even to remove a flaw they dislike.
An image may be altered before publication only if the alteration misrepresents nothing important about the scene it shows.
A news photograph should be published without alteration whenever most of the publication’s readers would prefer it that way.
Editors should decline to print photographs whose composition is spoiled by objects that the photographer could have avoided.
A photograph should be printed exactly as the photographer took it unless altering it would remove something that many of the publication’s readers complain spoils the picture.
questions.explanation: The editor concedes that readers dislike the power line and that removing it would misrepresent nothing important, then rests the decision on one fact: readers count on the pictures to show precisely what the photographer saw. (A) states that in general terms: what people depend on for a kind of accuracy shouldn’t be made less accurate, even to remove a flaw they dislike. (B) and (E) reuse the stimulus’s wording, but (B) only says when altering is permitted, and (E)’s ‘unless’ clause is met here, so it doesn’t require leaving the photo alone.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Printing the photo unaltered was right.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Readers count on printed photos to show precisely what was seen (despite complaints and the harmlessness of the edit).

breakdown.analysis: The editor concedes two points for editing: readers dislike the line, and removing it hides nothing important. Then the editor pivots to reliance. We need a principle that says: when people rely on an image for exact fidelity, don’t make it less exact, even to please them. The right answer here is abstract, so translate: ‘a particular kind of accuracy’ = showing precisely what was seen; ‘a flaw they dislike’ = the power line. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

choices.note: CORRECT. Readers depend on the photos for one kind of accuracy (precisely what the photographer saw). Removing the line would make the photo less accurate in exactly that way, to remove a flaw readers dislike. The principle says don’t, which is what the editor did.

Tempting. It borrows ‘misrepresents nothing important.’ But it’s an only-if: it says when editing is allowed, and the condition is met here, so if anything it permits the edit. It never says to leave the photo alone.
The condition fails. Most complaining readers wanted the line removed, so this principle doesn’t apply.
This would argue against printing the photo at all, not for printing it unaltered.

Tempting, because it says ‘printed exactly as the photographer took it’ and mentions readers’ complaints. But read the ‘unless’: altering here WOULD remove something readers complain spoils the picture, so the exception kicks in and the principle no longer requires printing it unaltered.

questions.stimulus: Only two things are known to produce a sudden regional cooling as large as the one recorded in the lake sediments of the Ostra Basin: a major volcanic eruption and a sharp drop in the sun’s output. Whenever the sun’s output drops sharply, the carbon-14 in tree rings rises, yet tree rings from the time of the Ostra cooling show no such rise. So the cooling must have been produced by a major volcanic eruption.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: Every major volcanic eruption produces a sudden cooling at least as large as the one recorded in the Ostra Basin sediments.
The Ostra Basin sediments contain a layer of volcanic ash deposited at roughly the time that the cooling began.
Most sudden regional coolings recorded in lake sediments began within a few years of a major volcanic eruption.
The carbon-14 in tree rings rises only when the sun’s output drops sharply.
Every sudden cooling of that size was produced by one of the things known to produce such coolings.
questions.explanation: The premises rule out a solar drop by contrapositive: solar drop → carbon-14 rises; no rise → no solar drop. That leaves the eruption only if the cooling had to come from one of the two known causes. (E) closes exactly that gap. (D) is the trap: it reverses the carbon-14 link, which the argument doesn’t need, and still leaves an unknown cause open. (A) reverses the cause–effect direction, and (B) and (C) are evidence, not guarantees.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Ostra cooling was produced by a major volcanic eruption.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Only eruptions and solar drops are KNOWN to cause such coolings; solar drop → carbon-14 in tree rings rises; tree rings from that time show no rise.

breakdown.analysis: First run the chain: solar drop → carbon-14 rises. Contrapositive: no rise → no solar drop. So the sun is out. Does that leave only the volcano? Only if the two known causes are the only possible ones. ‘Known to produce’ isn’t ‘the only things that can produce.’ We need: every such cooling had one of the known causes.

choices.note: This reverses the direction. It says eruptions always produce such coolings, not that such coolings always come from eruptions. The Ostra cooling could still have an unknown cause.
Ash at about the right time is good evidence, but ‘roughly the time’ doesn’t guarantee the eruption caused the cooling.
‘Most’ is too weak. The Ostra cooling could be among the exceptions.

Tempting, because it reuses the stimulus’s carbon-14 wording. But it reverses the link: rise → solar drop. The argument needs the other direction, which it already has, to rule out the sun. Even with (D), an unknown cause remains open.
CORRECT. With the sun ruled out by the tree rings, this leaves a major volcanic eruption as the only possible cause.

questions.stimulus: A person who damages an item while borrowing it should either have it repaired or pay to replace it. The borrower is released from this obligation, however, if the damage resulted from a defect that the lender knew about but did not mention when lending the item.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Teo dropped a camera he had borrowed from his cousin and cracked its lens, so Teo should pay for a new camera rather than have the lens repaired.
Rafe’s borrowed tent was torn in a storm that no one could have foreseen, so Rafe need not have the tent repaired or replaced.
A ladder rung cracked under Ines along a flaw that her neighbor, the ladder’s owner, had noticed but never mentioned, so Ines need not replace it.
The drill Mae borrowed broke because of a defect its owner had not known about, so Mae need not have the drill repaired.
Jun’s borrowed bicycle broke down because of rusted gears that its owner had pointed out when lending it, so Jun is not obliged to repair the bicycle.
questions.explanation: The release applies only when the damage came from a defect the lender both knew about and failed to mention. Ines’s case meets both conditions, so she is released and need not replace the ladder. Mae’s owner didn’t know of the defect (D), and Jun’s owner did mention it (E), so neither borrower is released. Rafe (B) has no defect at all, and Teo (A) is told to pick one remedy when the principle allows either.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Borrower damages item → repair or replace, UNLESS damage came from a defect the lender knew of AND didn’t mention (then released).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A correct ‘need not’ verdict needs all three: a defect caused the damage, the lender knew of it, the lender didn’t mention it.

breakdown.analysis: This principle has a default rule and a two-part exception. To get a ‘need not repair’ verdict, the exception must be fully met: defect + lender knew + lender kept quiet. Check each ‘need not’ answer against all three. Fault and bad luck aren’t part of the exception.

choices.note: The principle lets the borrower choose: repair OR replace. It never requires replacement over repair.
Tempting, because the storm wasn’t Rafe’s fault. But the only release is a known, unmentioned defect. Bad luck doesn’t count, so Rafe still owes a repair or replacement.
CORRECT. Defect caused the damage; the neighbor knew; the neighbor didn’t say. The exception applies, so Ines is released.
Tempting, since the damage came from a defect. But the owner didn’t know about it, and the release requires a defect the lender knew of. Mae still owes a repair or replacement.
Tempting, since a defect caused the damage and the owner knew. But the owner mentioned it, and the release covers only defects the lender failed to mention.

questions.stimulus: Trellis Hardware’s new rewards program will not increase the chain’s revenue. The program gives rewards only to customers who already shop at Trellis every week, and none of those customers will spend any more at Trellis than they would have spent without the program.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The program cannot increase Trellis’s revenue unless some customers it rewards spend more than they otherwise would.
If the program leads the customers it rewards to spend more than they otherwise would, it will increase Trellis’s revenue.
Customers who shop at a store every week respond less to rewards programs than do customers who shop there only occasionally.
Most rewards programs that benefit only frequent customers fail to increase the revenue of the companies that run them.
Customers who shop at Trellis less than once a week are unlikely to begin shopping there weekly just to earn rewards.
questions.explanation: The only conclusion is the first sentence: the program won’t increase revenue. The premise covers just one route: rewarded customers won’t spend more than they would have. (A) says that route is the only one, so closing it closes them all. (B) reverses the conditional. (E) is the near-miss: it addresses one other route (occasional shoppers turning weekly), but ‘unlikely’ isn’t ‘won’t,’ and revenue could still rise some other way.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rewards program will not increase Trellis’s revenue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Rewards go only to customers who already shop weekly; none of them will spend more than they would have without the program.

breakdown.analysis: So the rewarded customers won’t spend more. Is that the only way the program could bring in money? What about new customers drawn in by the advertising, or occasional shoppers who start coming weekly? We need an answer that makes the rewarded customers’ extra spending the ONLY route: revenue increase → rewarded customers spend more. Contrapositive: they don’t spend more → no revenue increase.

choices.note: CORRECT. Revenue increase → some rewarded customers spend more than they otherwise would. The premise says none will, so by contrapositive the program won’t increase revenue.
This reverses (A). It tells us what happens if rewarded customers do spend more. They won’t, so this says nothing about revenue from any other source.
A comparison between weekly and occasional shoppers. It doesn’t rule out revenue from any source.
‘Most’ programs isn’t this program. Trellis’s could be an exception.

Tempting, because it plugs one hole: occasional shoppers turning into weekly ones. But ‘unlikely’ isn’t ‘won’t,’ and other routes to more revenue (new shoppers who never earn a reward, for instance) stay open.

questions.stimulus: Science editor: The journal was right to retract the study of honeybee navigation. Its authors committed no misconduct, and other laboratories have since reported similar findings. But the authors have learned that their tracking software mislabeled about half of the bees, so the data the article presents do not show what the article claims they show.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the science editor’s reasoning?
choices: A journal should retract a published study only if the study’s authors are found to have acted dishonestly.
A journal should retract any study whose conclusions are later contradicted by the work of other laboratories.
A journal should retract a study if its authors learn that their data were mislabeled but do not promptly inform the journal of the error.
A claim should be withdrawn if the evidence offered for it does not establish it, even if the claim is true and honestly made.
A journal should not retract a study whose findings others have confirmed unless the original data were deliberately falsified.
questions.explanation: The editor concedes two points against retraction (no misconduct; others found similar results) and rests on one: the article’s data don’t show what it claims. (D) says a claim whose presented evidence doesn’t establish it should be withdrawn, even if it’s true (others’ findings) and honestly made (no misconduct). (C) borrows the stimulus’s mislabeling but adds a condition, failing to inform the journal, that we’re never told is met. (A) and (E) would block the retraction, and (B)’s condition fails.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The journal was right to retract the study.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The data don’t show what the article claims (mislabeled bees), even though there was no misconduct and others found similar results.

breakdown.analysis: Why retract a study that might be right and that no one faked? Because the article’s own evidence doesn’t support it. We need a principle that ties retraction to the evidence, not to honesty or to whether the finding is true. The right answer is stated abstractly: ‘a claim,’ ‘the evidence offered for it.’ A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

choices.note: This would forbid the retraction, since no misconduct was found. Opposite.
The condition fails. Other labs confirmed similar findings rather than contradicting them.
Tempting, because it reuses the mislabeling. But it applies only if the authors failed to tell the journal, and we’re never told they did. The condition isn’t shown to be met.

CORRECT. The evidence offered (the mislabeled data) doesn’t establish the article’s claim. That the claim may be true (others found similar results) and was honestly made (no misconduct) doesn’t matter under this principle. Withdraw it.
Others did confirm the findings, and there was no falsification, so this would forbid the retraction.

questions.stimulus: Every beetle species in the cloud forest of Marell Island lays its eggs only in dead wood, and some of those species are found nowhere else in the world. The logging practices that the island’s forestry office adopted this year will remove all dead wood from the cloud forest. It follows that some beetle species found nowhere else in the world are threatened by those practices.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Some beetle species that lay their eggs only in dead wood are threatened by the island’s new logging practices.
A practice threatens a species if it eliminates, from somewhere the species lives, the only kind of material in which that species lays eggs.
The island’s new logging practices will remove more dead wood from the cloud forest than did the practices they replaced.
Beetle species found nowhere else in the world are generally more vulnerable to changes in their habitat than are beetle species found in many places.
Every beetle species that is threatened by the island’s new logging practices lays its eggs only in dead wood.
questions.explanation: Some cloud-forest beetles are endemic, they lay eggs only in dead wood, and the new practices will remove all dead wood from the cloud forest. What’s missing is the link from ‘loses its only egg-laying material in a place where it lives’ to ‘threatened.’ (B) supplies it in general terms. (A) is the near-miss: the threatened dead-wood species might all be the ones found elsewhere too. (E) reverses the needed link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some endemic beetle species are threatened by the new logging practices.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some cloud-forest beetle species are endemic; every cloud-forest beetle species lays eggs only in dead wood; the new practices will remove all dead wood from the cloud forest.

breakdown.analysis: So the endemic beetles will lose the only stuff they lay eggs in, right where they live. Does that mean they’re ‘threatened’? The premises never say so. Chain: endemic species → lives in the cloud forest AND lays eggs only in dead wood → its only egg-laying material is eliminated there → ??? → threatened. We need: losing the only egg-laying material somewhere a species lives → threatened. Expect it in abstract terms.

choices.note: Tempting near-miss. ‘Some’ dead-wood species could be threatened, but they might all be species that also live elsewhere. That doesn’t get us to the endemic ones.
CORRECT. The endemic species live in the cloud forest and lay eggs only in dead wood; the practices eliminate all dead wood there. By this principle, those species are threatened.
A comparison with the old practices. It doesn’t say anything about whether removing dead wood threatens anyone.
Being more vulnerable than other beetles doesn’t mean being threatened by these practices.
This reverses the link: threatened → lays eggs only in dead wood. It doesn’t tell us that any dead-wood species is threatened.

questions.stimulus: A manager who learns that an employee has made a costly mistake should discuss it with that employee privately before reporting it to senior management, unless the mistake endangered anyone’s safety or the employee tried to conceal it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following describes an action that violates the principle stated above?
choices: Lena learned that an analyst had hidden a costly accounting error from the firm’s auditors, and she reported the error to senior management before speaking with him.
Omar learned that a technician’s costly wiring error had left a freight elevator unsafe to ride, and he told senior management before raising it with the technician.
A clerk’s mispricing cost Yuki’s firm thousands, and the clerk promptly admitted it to her; she alerted senior management that afternoon and spoke with him privately the next morning.
Ravi learned of a scheduling error that had cost the firm nothing, and he mentioned it to senior management before discussing it with the employee responsible.
Dina’s assistant made a costly billing error that endangered no one; she discussed it with him privately, and when he then tried to hide it from the client, she reported it to senior management.
questions.explanation: A violation needs a costly mistake, no safety risk, no concealment, and a report to senior management BEFORE the private talk. Yuki’s clerk made a costly, harmless mistake and admitted it, so the rule applied, yet she reported first and talked the next day. Lena (concealment) and Omar (safety) fall under the exceptions; Ravi’s error wasn’t costly; Dina talked first.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Costly mistake AND no safety risk AND no concealment → talk privately with the employee BEFORE reporting to senior management.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A violation needs all three conditions met AND a report to senior management that came before the private talk.

breakdown.analysis: This time you’re hunting for a breach, so every condition has to be checked. Did the mistake cost something? Did it endanger anyone? Did the employee try to hide it? If all three point to the rule applying, did the manager report first? Notice that most answers have the manager reporting first; the question is whether the rule applied.

choices.note: The analyst hid the error, so the concealment exception switches the rule off. Reporting first was allowed.
Tempting, because Omar reported first. But the error left the elevator unsafe, so the safety exception applies.

CORRECT. Costly mistake, no safety risk, and no concealment (the clerk admitted it right away), so the rule applied. Yuki reported to senior management that afternoon and talked with the clerk only the next morning. That’s the wrong order.
The error cost nothing, so the principle never kicks in. Reporting first breaks no rule.
Dina talked with him privately before reporting, which is what the principle asks. His later attempt to hide the error doesn’t make her order of steps wrong.

questions.stimulus: Track coach: Pia will not be picked for the regional team. The selectors consider only times run at meets the athletics federation sanctions, and they pick only runners whose best considered time in the 400 meters is under 61 seconds. Pia has run the 400 meters in under 61 seconds only once, at the Harlow Invitational, where runners were timed only by hand.
questions.stem: The track coach’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: A meet is sanctioned by the federation if it uses electronic timing and is held on a track of regulation length.
Most meets at which runners are timed by hand are not sanctioned by the athletics federation.
Times recorded by hand are generally faster than electronic times recorded for the same race.
The selectors pick every runner whose best time at a sanctioned meet is under 61 seconds.
Only those meets at which runners are timed electronically are sanctioned by the athletics federation.
questions.explanation: Pia’s only sub-61 time came at Harlow, which used only hand timing. If Harlow wasn’t sanctioned, the selectors can’t count that time, so she has no considered time under 61 seconds, and the selectors pick only runners who do. (E) makes electronic timing necessary for sanction, so Harlow wasn’t sanctioned. (A) gives a sufficient condition for sanction, which can’t show Harlow wasn’t sanctioned. (B) is only ‘most.’

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Pia will not be picked.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Selectors consider only sanctioned-meet times; picked → best considered time under 61; Pia’s only sub-61 time was at Harlow (hand timing only).

breakdown.analysis: Picked → has a considered time under 61 seconds. Pia’s only time under 61 came at Harlow, so she can be picked only if Harlow’s time counts, which requires Harlow to be sanctioned. (If she has no other sanctioned times at all, she still has no considered time under 61.) We need Harlow ruled out: hand-timed only → not sanctioned. Equivalently: sanctioned → electronic timing.

choices.note: This tells us what is ENOUGH to be sanctioned. It can’t show Harlow is not sanctioned, since a meet might be sanctioned for other reasons.
Tempting but too weak. Harlow could be one of the hand-timed meets that is sanctioned.
Tempting, because it suggests Pia isn’t really that fast. But if the meet is sanctioned, her recorded time counts regardless of accuracy.
Wrong direction. This gives a sufficient condition for being picked. It says nothing about runners like Pia, whose only sub-61 time may not count.
CORRECT. Sanctioned → electronic timing. Harlow used only hand timing, so it wasn’t sanctioned. Pia then has no considered time under 61 seconds, so she won’t be picked.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: When Dorrin Outfitters learned that one batch of its children’s jackets had zippers that could pinch, it did better to recall every jacket of that model than it would have done by recalling only the faulty batch. Batch numbers appear only on a tag that many parents remove, so a narrower recall would have left many families unable to tell whether their child’s jacket was affected.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist’s reasoning?
choices: Of two responses to a product hazard, the better is the one leaving fewer at-risk people unsure whether they are at risk.
A company should limit a recall to the products it knows to be defective whenever its customers are able to identify those products.
A company should recall a product made for children only if the product’s defect could cause a child physical harm.
Manufacturers should print identifying numbers on their products in places where customers are unlikely to remove them.
When two possible recalls would each remove every defective product from use, a company should choose the less costly of the two.
questions.explanation: The columnist ranks the full recall above the narrow one because the narrow one would leave families unable to tell whether they were affected. (A) states that ranking rule abstractly, so it justifies preferring the full recall. (B) is a trap: its condition isn’t met, and failing it doesn’t make the full recall better. (E)’s condition fails too, since the narrow recall wouldn’t reach every defective jacket.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recalling the whole model was better than recalling only the faulty batch.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many parents remove the batch tag, so a narrow recall would leave many families unable to tell whether they were affected.

breakdown.analysis: This is a comparative conclusion, so we want a comparative principle: a way of choosing between two responses. The deciding fact is uncertainty. Families couldn’t tell whether they were affected. Prephrase: prefer the response that leaves fewer at-risk people in the dark.

choices.note: CORRECT. The full recall leaves no affected family unsure; the narrow one leaves many unsure. By this rule the full recall is better.

Tempting, because it mentions identifying products. But its condition isn’t met, since parents CAN’T identify the batch. And when the condition fails, the principle simply says nothing. It doesn’t say to recall more.
A necessary condition for recalling at all. It doesn’t compare the two recalls.
Good advice for the future, but it doesn’t say which recall was better here.
The condition fails: the narrow recall wouldn’t get every defective jacket out of use. So this doesn’t apply.

questions.stimulus: The blue paint in the recently discovered psalter was not made from indigo. Under ultraviolet light the blue areas glow faintly, and any pigment that glows under ultraviolet light contains a compound that forms only when a pigment has been prepared with alum.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every blue pigment that has been prepared with alum glows faintly when it is viewed under ultraviolet light.
Few of the alum-prepared blue pigments used in medieval manuscripts were derived from indigo.
Indigo-based pigments do not glow under ultraviolet light unless they have been prepared with alum.
Only pigments that contain no indigo can be prepared with alum.
Scribes in the region where the psalter was produced seldom used indigo to make blue paint.
questions.explanation: Chain: the blue glows → it contains the compound → it was prepared with alum. To conclude it isn’t indigo, we need alum → no indigo, which (D) gives in ‘only’ form. (C) is the near-miss: it says glowing indigo must contain alum, which is perfectly consistent with this paint being alum-prepared indigo. (A) reverses the glow link, and (B) and (E) are only probabilistic.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The psalter’s blue was not made from indigo.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The blue glows under UV; glows → contains a compound; compound → prepared with alum.

breakdown.analysis: Follow the chain: glows → compound → alum. So the paint was prepared with alum. Nothing yet links alum to indigo. We need alum → no indigo (equivalently, indigo → no alum). Watch the ‘only’: ‘only X can be Y’ means Y → X.

choices.note: This reverses the first link (alum → glows). We already know the paint was prepared with alum. What we don’t know is whether alum rules out indigo.
Too weak. ‘Few’ isn’t ‘none.’ This paint could be one of the few.

Tempting, because it mentions indigo, glowing and alum together. But it only says glowing indigo has alum. That fits an indigo paint prepared with alum, which is exactly the possibility we need to rule out.
CORRECT. ‘Only pigments with no indigo can be prepared with alum’ means alum → no indigo. The paint was prepared with alum, so it contains no indigo.
‘Seldom’ leaves room for this psalter to be an exception.

questions.stimulus: A teacher may grade a student’s work without consulting a colleague only if either the teacher did not discuss the work with the student while it was in progress or the assignment’s grading criteria leave no room for the grader’s judgment.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Ms. Ruiz never once discussed a student’s project with him while he was working on it, so she was entitled to grade it without consulting any colleague.
Mr. Sall graded Dana’s lab report alone without violating the principle, though he had discussed it with her during the work, so its criteria leave no room for judgment.
Ms. Ortega consulted a colleague before grading an essay she had helped its author draft, which shows that the essay’s grading criteria left room for the grader’s judgment.
Mr. Kahn helped a student revise a short story whose grading criteria call for the grader’s judgment and then graded it himself, so the grade he gave is unfair.
Ms. Tran graded a lab report on her own without violating the principle, so she cannot have discussed the report with its author while he was writing it.
questions.explanation: Grading alone → (no discussion during the work) OR (no room for judgment). Sall graded alone without violating the principle, so one condition must hold; he did discuss the report, so the other must: the criteria leave no room for judgment. (E) is the mirror trap: Tran could have satisfied the ‘no judgment’ condition instead. (A) treats a necessary condition as sufficient. (C) and (D) draw conclusions the principle never licenses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Grade without consulting → (didn’t discuss during the work) OR (criteria leave no room for judgment).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The principle only tells you what must be true when someone grades alone. A conforming judgment must use that: grading alone properly + one condition fails → the other holds.

breakdown.analysis: It’s an ‘only if’ with an OR. Grading alone properly guarantees at least one of the two conditions. So if you know one fails, you can infer the other. What you can’t do: treat a condition as permission (it’s necessary, not sufficient), or pick one side of the OR without ruling out the other. Check each answer for which move it makes.

choices.note: Tempting. Ruiz meets one condition. But the conditions are necessary for grading alone, not sufficient. The principle never says when a teacher IS entitled to grade alone.

CORRECT. Sall graded alone properly (without violating the principle), so at least one condition holds. He discussed the report, so the first fails. That leaves the second: the criteria leave no room for judgment.
Consulting a colleague is always allowed under this principle, so Ortega’s consulting tells us nothing about the criteria.
Kahn did violate the principle (he discussed the story, and the criteria call for judgment). But the principle is about procedure, not whether a grade is fair. ‘Unfair’ doesn’t follow.
Tempting mirror of (B). Tran graded alone properly, so ONE condition holds, but it could be the ‘no room for judgment’ one. Nothing shows she didn’t discuss the report.

questions.stimulus: Finches of the genus Pelora that live on islands have shorter wings than their mainland relatives do, and shorter wings make sustained flight more costly in energy. So island Pelora must fly long distances less often than mainland Pelora do.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the argument’s conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Birds with shorter wings are less able than birds with longer wings to escape from predators by flying.
Island Pelora have less need than mainland Pelora do to fly long distances in order to find food.
Any bird that frequently flies long distances will, over many generations, come to have longer wings.
Some birds for which sustained flight is costly fly long distances only when food is scarce.
Among related birds, those for which sustained flight costs more fly long distances less often.
questions.explanation: The premises give a cost difference (flight costs island finches more); the conclusion is a behavior difference (they fly far less often). (E) links the two for related birds, so it guarantees the conclusion. (B) is the strong trap: less need for long flights to find food doesn’t mean fewer long flights, since there are other reasons to fly. (C) is an evolutionary claim that can’t be run backward to establish current behavior.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Island Pelora fly long distances less often than mainland Pelora.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Island Pelora have shorter wings; shorter wings make sustained flight more costly.

breakdown.analysis: So flying is more expensive for island birds. Does that mean they do it less? Not unless cost governs behavior. It’s like saying gas costs more in town A, so people in town A drive less. Maybe, but you need the link. Prephrase: when flight costs more, related birds fly far less often.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Escaping predators isn’t long-distance flight frequency.
Tempting. It points the right way, but ‘less need to find food’ isn’t ‘fly less often.’ They might fly far for mates, migration or new territory. Need isn’t frequency.

Tempting but it doesn’t work. If frequent long flights lead to longer wings, the island birds’ shorter wings might suggest they fly less. But ‘shorter than the mainland birds’ doesn’t mean they never got longer wings, and the claim is about many generations, not current behavior.
Too weak and off point. ‘Some’ birds flying far only when food is scarce says nothing guaranteed about Pelora.
CORRECT. Island and mainland Pelora are closely related, and flight costs the island birds more, so they fly long distances less often.

questions.stimulus: School counselor: Ms. Abara should let Theo retake the chemistry exam he failed, though she will not offer a retake to the other students who failed it. Theo missed two weeks of class with pneumonia just before the exam, and he lost most of his points on material taught during those weeks. None of the others missed any of that instruction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the school counselor’s argument?
choices: A teacher who offers a retake to any student who failed an exam should offer a retake to every student who failed it.
A student who misses class because of illness should be excused from any exam given within two weeks of the student’s return.
A student deserves another chance at an assessment if the poor result came from being unavoidably kept from learning its material.
A retake should be offered only to students whose absence from class was caused by a documented illness.
Teachers should give students who miss class because of illness notes from each lesson that they missed.
questions.explanation: Theo failed mainly on material taught while illness kept him out of class; the others had no such obstacle. (C) generalizes this: a poor result caused by being unavoidably prevented from learning the material earns another chance. (B) prescribes a different remedy (excusal, not a retake), (D) gives only a necessary condition, and (A) would require retakes for everyone, which contradicts the counselor’s position.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Theo (alone) should get a retake.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Illness kept him from the instruction on which he lost most points; the other failing students missed none of it.

breakdown.analysis: Why Theo and not the others? Because his failure traces to instruction he couldn’t attend. We need a rule that grants a second chance when a bad result comes from being unable, through no choice of one’s own, to learn the tested material.

choices.note: This would require retakes for everyone who failed, which the counselor rejects.
Tempting, because it’s about illness. But it calls for excusal from the exam, not a retake after failing it. Different remedy.
CORRECT. Theo’s failure stems from being unavoidably kept from the material, so he should get another chance. The others weren’t kept from it, so the rule doesn’t extend to them.
An ‘only if’ gives a necessary condition. It permits Theo’s retake at most; it doesn’t say he should get one. We also don’t know his illness was documented.
About notes, not retakes.

questions.stimulus: The sound installation in the library’s atrium is not music, whatever its admirers say. A work is music only if it was composed to be listened to for its own sake, and the installation’s designer composed it chiefly to mask the noise of conversation in the atrium.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Anything that has been composed to be listened to for its own sake is music.
Some works composed to mask unwanted noise are nonetheless listened to for their own sake by many who hear them.
Most works whose composers had a practical purpose in mind are not regarded by critics as music.
No work composed chiefly for a practical purpose was composed to be listened to for its own sake.
No work that its audience listens to chiefly for a practical purpose is music.
questions.explanation: Music → composed to be listened to for its own sake. The installation was composed chiefly to mask noise. The argument needs ‘composed chiefly for a practical purpose → not composed to be listened to for its own sake,’ which is (D). (E) is the near-miss: it shifts from how the work was composed to how the audience listens, and we know nothing about the audience. (A) gives a sufficient condition for music, which can’t show the installation isn’t music.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The installation is not music.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Music → composed to be listened to for its own sake; the installation was composed chiefly to mask conversation noise.

breakdown.analysis: Couldn’t a work be composed chiefly to mask noise and ALSO to be enjoyed for its own sake? The argument assumes not. Chain: masking noise (practical purpose) → ??? → not composed for its own sake → not music. We need: chiefly practical → not composed to be listened to for its own sake.

choices.note: This is the sufficient-condition version (own sake → music). It can’t show that something ISN’T music.
This weakens the argument if anything, and it’s about listeners, not the designer’s purpose.
Shifts to how critics regard works, and ‘most’ is too weak anyway.
CORRECT. The installation was composed chiefly for a practical purpose, so it wasn’t composed to be listened to for its own sake, so it isn’t music.
Tempting, because it sounds like the argument. But it’s about why the AUDIENCE listens, and the stimulus tells us only why the designer composed it. Composer’s purpose isn’t listener’s purpose.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Dr. Ferrante was not wrong to include the nest sites of the falcons, a rare species, in her published survey. Revealing where rare birds nest ordinarily invites egg thieves. But these falcons nest only on offshore sea stacks that no one can reach except by the coast guard’s boats, and the coast guard patrols the stacks throughout the breeding season.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ornithologist’s judgment?
choices: Publishing a fact that could be used to cause harm is not wrong if those who might misuse it are effectively prevented from doing so.
A scientist should publish the locations of rare birds’ nests only if the people who are likely to read the publication have some real need for that information.
The danger that rare birds will be harmed increases whenever information about where they nest is widely published.
Information that ordinarily invites harm to a species may be published whenever that species is protected by law.
A researcher who publishes information that is later misused by others shares responsibility for the harm that results.
questions.explanation: The ornithologist concedes that nest locations usually invite thieves, then argues that here no thief can act on the information: the stacks are reachable only by coast guard boats and are patrolled. (A) says publishing potentially harmful information isn’t wrong when would-be misusers are effectively prevented from misusing it. (D) is tempting but relies on legal protection, which the stimulus never mentions. (B) is only a necessary condition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ferrante was not wrong to publish the nest sites.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nest locations usually invite egg thieves, but these nests can’t be reached except by coast guard boats, and the coast guard patrols them.

breakdown.analysis: The usual worry is misuse. The ornithologist answers it by showing that misuse is practically impossible here. So the principle should say: publishing risky information is acceptable when the people who might misuse it can’t act on it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Egg thieves are the ones positioned to misuse the information, and they can’t get to the nests. By this principle, publishing wasn’t wrong.
An ‘only if’ gives a necessary condition, so it can’t establish that publishing was acceptable. And we aren’t told what the readers need.
This supports the opposite verdict.
Tempting, since the coast guard seems to protect the birds. But the principle turns on LEGAL protection, which the stimulus never mentions. Patrols aren’t a legal status.
If anything this cuts against publishing, and nothing has been misused anyway.

questions.stimulus: More than half of Bellweather Hospital’s nurses work the night shift, and more than half of its nurses have completed the advanced trauma course. So at least one nurse who has completed the advanced trauma course will receive the hospital’s new retention bonus this year.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Most nurses who work the night shift at Bellweather Hospital will receive the new retention bonus this year.
Every Bellweather nurse who has completed the advanced trauma course works the night shift.
Every Bellweather nurse who works the night shift will receive the new retention bonus this year.
Only nurses who work the night shift are eligible to receive the hospital’s new retention bonus.
At least one of Bellweather’s night-shift nurses has completed the advanced trauma course.
questions.explanation: Two groups that each include more than half of the nurses must overlap, so at least one trauma-trained nurse works nights. If every night-shift nurse gets the bonus (C), that nurse gets it. (A) is the trap: ‘most’ night nurses getting the bonus doesn’t guarantee the overlapping nurse is among them. (E) is just the overlap the premises already guarantee, and (D) is the reversed, necessary-condition link.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least one trauma-trained nurse will get the retention bonus.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: More than half the nurses work nights; more than half completed the trauma course.

breakdown.analysis: Two ‘more than half’ groups from the same pool must share at least one member, so some trauma-trained nurse works nights. Now we need night shift → bonus. It has to cover EVERY night nurse, because we don’t know which night nurse is the trauma-trained one.

choices.note: Tempting, but ‘most’ isn’t ‘all.’ The night nurses who get the bonus could all be ones without trauma training.
This links trauma training to night shift, which the overlap already gives us for at least one nurse. It still says nothing about the bonus.
CORRECT. Some trauma-trained nurse works nights (the overlap), and every night nurse gets the bonus, so that nurse gets it.
This reverses the link: bonus → night shift. It limits who can get the bonus but doesn’t say anyone does.
Already guaranteed by the two ‘more than half’ premises. Restating it doesn’t bring in the bonus.

questions.stimulus: A researcher should share her raw data with any scientist who requests it, unless sharing it would break a promise made to the people who supplied the data or the scientist requesting it will not credit the researchers who gathered it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?
choices: Dr. Lund shared her raw data with a scientist who had refused to credit Lund’s team, so Lund acted contrary to the principle.
Dr. Imai made no promises to the agencies whose records supplied her data, and the scientist requesting the data has pledged to credit her team, so she should share it with him.
Because Dr. Sorel’s data were gathered under a promise of confidentiality, he should give those who request the data summaries of it in place of the raw data.
Dr. Osei sent his raw data to a colleague who had not asked for it, so Dr. Osei did what the principle requires.

Dr. Kalla promised her participants only that their names would be withheld, and her data include no names, but the scientist requesting them has not said whether he will credit her team, so she need not share them.
questions.explanation: Request → share, unless (sharing breaks a promise to the data’s suppliers) OR (the requester will not credit the team). Imai has a request, made no promises, and the requester has pledged to credit her team, so neither exception applies and she must share. (E) is the trap: the requester’s silence doesn’t show that he WILL NOT credit Kalla’s team, and her promise isn’t broken, so the principle still says share. (A) treats an exception as a prohibition.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: A scientist requests the raw data AND sharing breaks no promise to the suppliers AND the requester will credit the team → share.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A ‘should share’ verdict needs a request and both exceptions ruled out. A ‘need not share’ verdict needs an exception that actually holds.

breakdown.analysis: The exceptions don’t forbid sharing; they only switch off the duty. And an exception helps only if it is shown to hold. ‘Hasn’t said whether he’ll credit’ isn’t ‘won’t credit.’ For each answer, check: request? promise broken? requester won’t credit?

choices.note: The exception only removes the duty to share. It doesn’t forbid sharing, so Lund didn’t act contrary to the principle.
CORRECT. There’s a request, no promise to break, and a pledge to credit the team. Neither exception applies, so the principle requires Imai to share.
The principle says nothing about summaries. With a broken promise, the duty to share is simply switched off.
No one requested the data, so the principle didn’t require anything of Osei.

Tempting, because the crediting exception is in play. But it applies only if the requester WILL NOT credit the team, and we don’t know that. Kalla’s promise (withhold names) isn’t broken by nameless data either. Neither exception is shown, so the principle says share.

questions.stimulus: Our northern region sold more units this year than our southern region did. Each region sold only two products, the Brio and the Celta, and in each region exactly half of the units sold were Brios. So the northern region brought in more revenue from sales this year than the southern region did.
questions.stem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: In each of the two regions, the Brio sold at a higher average price than the Celta did.
The northern region sold more Celtas this year than the southern region did.
Most of the units sold in the northern region went for prices at least as high as the southern region’s prices for the same product.
The southern region did not charge more for Brios this year, on average, than the northern region did.
For each of the two products, the average price per unit was no higher in the southern region than in the northern region.
questions.explanation: Because each region’s sales were half Brios, the north sold more Brios AND more Celtas than the south. If neither product’s average price was higher in the south (E), the north out-earned the south on each product and so overall. (D) is the near-miss: it covers only the Brio, and southern Celtas could sell for enough more to reverse the result. (B) restates what already follows, and (A) compares the products rather than the regions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: North earned more sales revenue than South.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: North sold more units; each region sold only Brios and Celtas, half of each region’s units Brios.

breakdown.analysis: Revenue = units × price. The half-and-half fact means North sold more of EACH product. What’s missing is price. If South sold at higher prices, it could out-earn North on fewer units. We need: for each product, South’s average price is no higher than North’s. Then North wins product by product.

choices.note: Compares Brio to Celta, not North to South. Since the mix is identical in both regions, this doesn’t decide anything.
Already follows from the premises (half-and-half mix, more units). Restating it doesn’t address price.
‘Most’ units isn’t all, and the rest could be priced far higher in the South. Too weak.
Tempting, since it’s half the answer. But it covers only the Brio. If southern Celtas sold at much higher prices, South could still out-earn North.
CORRECT. North sold more of each product at average prices no lower than South’s, so North’s revenue from each product, and so in total, was higher.

questions.stimulus: Editor: Kemal did the right thing in telling his friend Ana that her novel’s ending does not work, though she had asked him only whether he enjoyed the book. Ana’s publisher will accept revisions until next week, and none of the other people who have read the manuscript had raised the problem with her.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor’s position?
choices: When a friend asks whether one enjoyed her work, one should answer that question honestly, even if the honest answer is unwelcome.
A criticism of someone’s work is worth offering only if it concerns a problem that no one else has pointed out.
Criticism of a work is most useful to its author when it is offered before the work has been published.
It is appropriate to offer an unsolicited judgment if withholding it would probably cost someone an opportunity that will soon be gone.
One should not offer friends criticism of their work unless they have asked for one’s opinion of it.
questions.explanation: Kemal volunteered a criticism Ana hadn’t asked for. The editor’s reasons are that the revision window closes next week and no one else had told her. (D) captures both abstractly: the judgment was unsolicited, and withholding it would likely cost her an opportunity that is about to close. (A) concerns answering the question actually asked, not volunteering more. (B) uses the ‘no one else’ fact but only as a necessary condition, and (C) is a claim about usefulness, not about whether offering the criticism was right.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Kemal was right to tell Ana her ending doesn’t work.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: She asked only whether he enjoyed it; revisions are possible only until next week; nobody else had raised the problem.

breakdown.analysis: Kemal gave criticism nobody asked for. What makes it right? The chance to fix the ending is about to close, and if Kemal stays quiet, nobody else will tell her. We want a principle that permits unsolicited input when keeping quiet would likely cost the person a soon-to-vanish chance. The right answer won’t mention novels, friends or deadlines. It will describe them abstractly.

choices.note: Tempting, because it talks about honesty with a friend. But Ana asked whether he ENJOYED it, and that’s not what Kemal told her. This rule covers answering her question, not volunteering a criticism.
An ‘only if’: it gives a necessary condition, which the case meets, but it never says offering the criticism was right.
This is about when criticism is most useful, not whether giving unrequested criticism is right. Close in topic, wrong claim.
CORRECT. The judgment was unsolicited; withholding it would probably cost Ana her chance to revise (no one else would tell her), and that chance ends next week. So offering it was appropriate.
This would condemn what Kemal did.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The letters long attributed to the abbess Hilde of Ostwald were not written by her. Whoever wrote the letters knew the terms of the royal charter that made Marrow a market town, for the letters describe those terms in detail. Yet records show that Hilde died two years before Marrow’s charter was granted.
questions.stem: The historian’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Anyone who knew the terms of Marrow’s charter lived to see the charter granted.
The detailed references to Marrow’s charter in the letters were not added by a later copyist.
No one knew the terms of Marrow’s charter until the charter had been drafted.
Anyone who knew the terms of Marrow’s charter at that time would have mentioned them in letters.
Hilde’s surviving writings other than the letters make no mention of Marrow or of its market.
questions.explanation: The letter writer knew the charter’s terms; Hilde died before the charter was granted. (A) says anyone who knew the terms was alive when it was granted, so the writer was, and Hilde wasn’t. (C) is the near-miss: the charter could have been drafted before Hilde died, so she could still have known the terms. (B) patches a hole the argument doesn’t have, and (D) is about whether those who knew the terms would write about them.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hilde did not write the letters.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The letters’ writer knew the charter’s terms; Hilde died two years before the charter was granted.

breakdown.analysis: Hilde died before the charter was granted. So what? She could have known the terms before the grant, from drafts or court gossip. We need: knew the terms → alive when it was granted. Contrapositive: dead before the grant → didn’t know the terms → didn’t write the letters. Watch for an answer that pins the knowledge to the wrong event (drafting rather than granting).

choices.note: CORRECT. The writer knew the terms, so by this the writer lived to see the charter granted. Hilde didn’t, so she isn’t the writer.

Tempting. Interpolation is a real worry about old letters. But the premise already says whoever wrote the letters knew the terms, so this patches a hole the argument doesn’t have and leaves open the possibility that the terms were known early.
Tempting near-miss, because it sounds like (A). But it ties the knowledge to the drafting, not the grant. The charter could have been drafted before Hilde died, so she could have known the terms.
This is about whether knowers would write about the terms, not whether Hilde could have known them.
Silence in her other writings is suggestive at most. It can’t show that she didn’t write these letters.

questions.stimulus: A referee should halt play whenever a player appears to have suffered a head injury, unless a team physician has examined the player and judged it safe for play to continue. But no physician’s judgment makes it permissible to continue play if the injured player lost consciousness, however briefly.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: When two players knocked heads but neither showed any sign of being hurt, the referee let play continue, so the referee acted contrary to the principle.
A player who had been knocked unconscious recovered fully within the hour, which shows that the referee’s decision to halt play was unnecessary.
Tomas was knocked out briefly in a collision; the team physician then cleared him, and the referee let play continue, so the referee acted contrary to the principle.
