Because no team physician was present, a referee halted play when a player appeared to hit his head on the goalpost, and in doing so the referee acted wrongly.
After a player seemed dazed by a fall, the team physician examined her and judged it safe for her to continue, so the referee was required to let play go on.
questions.explanation: An apparent head injury requires a halt unless a physician clears the player, but a clearance never counts if the player lost consciousness. Tomas lost consciousness, so the physician’s clearance didn’t matter, and continuing play violated the principle. (E) is the main trap: a clearance only removes the duty to halt; it never requires play to go on. (A) fails because no one appeared injured.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Apparent head injury → halt play, UNLESS a physician clears the player; but lost consciousness → clearance doesn’t count.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: A violation needs an apparent head injury and play continuing with no valid clearance. Any loss of consciousness voids a clearance.

breakdown.analysis: Three layers: the default (halt), the exception (physician clearance), and an exception to the exception (lost consciousness voids clearance). Also note what the exception does: it lets play continue; it doesn’t force play to continue.

choices.note: No one appeared to be injured, so the duty to halt never arose.
The principle governs what a referee should do at the time, not whether a decision turns out to have been necessary. Wrong dimension.
CORRECT. Tomas lost consciousness, so the physician’s clearance doesn’t make continuing permissible. Letting play continue broke the principle.
With no physician there was no clearance, so halting was exactly what the principle calls for.
Tempting, because a valid clearance occurred. But the exception only removes the duty to halt. Nothing in the principle REQUIRES the referee to let play continue.

questions.stimulus: Publisher: None of the novels on this year’s Harwell Prize shortlist will earn back its author’s advance. A novel earns back its advance only if it sells at least 20,000 hardcover copies, and no novel sells that many unless it is reviewed in a national newspaper. And every shortlisted novel is a first novel from a small press.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the publisher’s conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Any novel that is reviewed in a national newspaper goes on to sell at least 20,000 copies in hardcover.
Most first novels from small presses are never reviewed in any national newspaper.
Every novel that earns back its author’s advance has been reviewed in a national newspaper.
At least one novel on this year’s shortlist will not be reviewed in any national newspaper.
Any novel reviewed in a national newspaper is either not a first novel or not from a small press.
questions.explanation: Chain: earns back → 20,000 hardcovers → national review. So a shortlisted novel can’t earn back if it won’t be reviewed nationally. (E), in contrapositive form, says that a first novel from a small press is never reviewed nationally, and every shortlisted novel is one. (D) is the trap for a ‘necessary’ mindset: it covers only one novel, and the conclusion is about all of them. (C) restates a link the premises already supply, and (B) is the weak ‘most’ version.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: No shortlisted novel will earn back its advance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Earns back → 20,000 hardcovers → national review; every shortlisted novel is a small-press first novel.

breakdown.analysis: Contrapositive of the chain: no national review → no 20,000 sales → doesn’t earn back. So we need every shortlisted novel to go unreviewed. Shortlisted = small-press first novel. Prephrase: small-press first novel → not reviewed nationally. The key is hidden in contrapositive form: reviewed → NOT (first AND small press) → not first OR not small press.

choices.note: This reverses a link (review → sales). It tells us when novels sell, not when they fail to.
Too weak. ‘Most’ unreviewed leaves room for a shortlisted novel to be reviewed and sell well.
Already follows from the premises (earn back → 20,000 → review). Saying it again adds nothing about the shortlisted novels.
Tempting, since it looks like something the argument needs. But it covers only ONE novel, and the conclusion is about NONE earning back. The other shortlisted novels could be reviewed and earn back.
CORRECT. Contrapositive: a first novel from a small press is never reviewed nationally. Every shortlisted novel is one, so none is reviewed, none sells 20,000, and none earns back.

questions.stimulus: Conservation biologist: For the Ardel marsh, the agency should choose the plan that quickly restores only the marsh’s northern half, not the plan that restores the whole marsh slowly. The full plan would eventually support more species. But under it, the marsh’s last breeding colony of bitterns would probably die out before any restored habitat was ready, whereas the partial plan would give the colony suitable habitat within two years.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the conservation biologist’s reasoning?
choices: Of two restoration plans, the one that would eventually support the larger number of species should be chosen unless it would cost substantially more to carry out.
Securing a lesser good in time to prevent a probable permanent loss is better than pursuing a greater good that would arrive only after that loss.
No habitat restoration plan should be adopted unless it would increase the number of species that the restored habitat is able to support.
Restoring the full extent of a damaged habitat matters more than restoring part of that habitat quickly.
While part of a habitat is being restored, any colonies of rare birds living there should be moved to suitable habitat elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The biologist grants that the full plan would eventually support more species but prefers the partial plan because, under the full plan, the last bittern colony would probably die out first. (B) states that trade in general terms: the lesser good that comes in time beats a greater good that comes too late to prevent a permanent loss. (A) is the trap: it borrows the ‘more species’ consideration, but its cost exception isn’t triggered, so it favors the full plan. (C) doesn’t choose between two plans that both add species.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Choose the fast, partial plan over the slow, full plan.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The full plan eventually supports more species, but the bittern colony would probably die out first; the partial plan would likely save it.

breakdown.analysis: The biologist concedes the full plan’s bigger long-run payoff and still rejects it, because by the time that payoff comes, something permanent will probably be lost. Prephrase: prevent the irreversible loss now rather than take a bigger benefit that arrives too late. A comparative conclusion needs a comparative principle.

choices.note: This favors the FULL plan: it supports more species, and nothing says it costs much more. It runs against the conclusion.

CORRECT. Translate: the ‘lesser good’ is restoring only the northern half; the ‘greater good’ is the full plan’s extra species; the ‘permanent loss’ is the last breeding colony dying out. The principle says take the partial plan, which is the biologist’s conclusion.
Both plans presumably add species, so this doesn’t pick between them.
This favors the full plan, the opposite of the conclusion.
This introduces a remedy (moving the colony) that neither plan includes. It doesn’t say which plan to choose.

questions.stimulus: The portrait of the cloth merchant Joos Verlaet in the Hanne Museum cannot have been painted from life, whatever the museum’s catalog says. Verlaet died in 1618, and the portrait’s canvas has a herringbone weave that no workshop produced before 1621.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: No painter of that period is known to have portrayed a dead sitter except by working from an earlier likeness.
The portrait’s canvas has not been relined or replaced at any time since the Hanne Museum acquired the portrait.
Verlaet did not sit for any portrait painter during the last several years of his life.
The portrait was painted on the canvas it is on now rather than transferred to it from some earlier support.
Most portraits of merchants painted in the 1620s were painted on canvas with a herringbone weave.
questions.explanation: The canvas dates from 1621 or later, after Verlaet’s death, but that dates the painting only if the paint was applied to this canvas. Old paintings are sometimes transferred from a damaged support onto a new one. (D) rules that out, so the painting was made in 1621 or later and couldn’t have been painted from life. (B) is the near-miss: it excludes changes only since the museum acquired the work, so a transfer before then remains possible. (C) still allows an earlier sitting with a later transfer.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The portrait wasn’t painted from life.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Verlaet died in 1618; the canvas is a type first made in 1621.

breakdown.analysis: The canvas is too late, but is the painting? Paintings can be moved from a decaying panel or canvas onto a new one. If that happened, the paint could be older than the canvas, and a portrait from life before 1618 is still possible. We need: the painting was made on this canvas, i.e., no transfer from an earlier support. Hard to prephrase. The key defends against an alternative the stimulus never mentions.

choices.note: This is about how posthumous portraits get made, not about whether this one was painted after 1618.
Tempting: it seems to say the canvas is original. But it only covers the period since the museum acquired the work. A transfer before then would leave the painting older than the canvas.
Even if he didn’t sit late in life, he could have sat earlier, and that painting could later have been transferred to this canvas.
CORRECT. No transfer means the paint went onto this canvas, which didn’t exist before 1621, three years after Verlaet died. So the portrait couldn’t have been painted from life.
Popularity of the weave in the 1620s doesn’t date this painting or rule out a transfer.

questions.stimulus: A museum should return an object to the community from which it was taken whenever that community asks for it, unless returning it would put the object at serious risk of destruction or some other community has a claim to it every bit as strong.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: A village has asked for the carved mask that the Weld Museum holds; a second village also claims the mask, though on far weaker grounds, so the museum need not return it.
An island community has asked for a canoe taken from it, which it plans to keep in an open shed where salt spray would almost certainly ruin it, so the museum should return the canoe.
A town that has never asked for the return of a tapestry taken from it could keep it safe, and no one else claims it, so the museum should return the tapestry.
A museum returned a ceremonial drum to the community it came from, which later sold the drum to a private collector, so the museum should not have returned it.
A harbor town asked for a figurehead taken from it, but the town where the ship was built has as good a claim, so the museum is not obliged to return it.
questions.explanation: The duty to return requires a request and is cancelled by either a serious risk of destruction or a rival claim of equal strength. The harbor town asked, but the shipbuilding town’s claim is just as good, so the exception applies and the museum isn’t obliged to return the figurehead. (A) is the main trap: the rival claim is far weaker, so it doesn’t cancel the duty. (B)’s community asked, but the serious risk cancels the duty. (C) involves no request.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Community asks → return, UNLESS (serious risk of destruction) OR (another community has an equally strong claim).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: ‘Should return’ needs a request and no exception. ‘Not obliged’ needs a request and either exception (or no request).

breakdown.analysis: Check three things in each answer: Was there a request? Is there a serious risk of destruction? Is there a rival claim that is EQUALLY strong? Watch for degree words: ‘far weaker’ isn’t ‘every bit as strong.’

choices.note: Tempting, because there’s a rival claim. But it’s on far weaker grounds, and the exception requires a claim every bit as strong. The museum should return the mask.
The canoe would almost certainly be ruined, which is a serious risk of destruction. The exception applies, so the principle doesn’t call for returning it.
The principle applies only when the community asks. The town never asked.
The principle doesn’t judge returns by what happens afterward. And the drum wasn’t destroyed; it was sold.
CORRECT. There was a request, but the shipbuilding town’s claim is as strong as the harbor town’s, so the exception applies and the museum isn’t obliged to return the figurehead to the harbor town.

questions.stimulus: Licensing official: A home inspector’s license lapses unless the inspector completed forty hours of approved courses during the preceding calendar year. Hours count as approved only if the course’s provider was registered with the board when the course was taken. All forty of Gil Varga’s course hours last year came from the Harrowgate Institute, which registered with the board in June of last year. So Varga’s license has lapsed.
questions.stem: The licensing official’s conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Varga completed no approved course hours last year from any provider other than the Harrowgate Institute.
Not all of Varga’s Harrowgate course hours last year were taken after the institute registered with the board.
The Harrowgate Institute offered at least some of its courses last year before it registered with the board.
Hours from a course count as approved if the course’s provider was registered with the board when it was taken.
Most of the hours Varga took at the Harrowgate Institute last year came from courses held in the first half of that year.
questions.explanation: Varga had exactly forty hours, all from Harrowgate. If even one hour was taken before Harrowgate registered, that hour doesn’t count, he has fewer than forty approved hours, and his license lapses. (B), ‘not all were taken after registration,’ guarantees at least one unapproved hour. (E) is the hardest trap: courses ‘in the first half of the year’ include June, and Harrowgate registered in June, so all of them could have come after registration. (C) concerns Harrowgate’s schedule, not the hours Varga took.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varga’s license has lapsed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lapse unless 40 approved hours last year; approved → provider registered when taken; all 40 of Varga’s hours were from Harrowgate, which registered in June of last year.

breakdown.analysis: Varga has exactly forty hours, so losing even ONE hour sinks him. An hour is lost if it was taken before Harrowgate registered. Did he take any before June? The stimulus doesn’t say. Prephrase: at least one of his Harrowgate hours came before registration. The key says it with a ‘not all,’ which hides it.

choices.note: Already given: all forty of his hours came from Harrowgate. This adds nothing about when he took them.
CORRECT. ‘Not all after registration’ = at least one hour before registration. That hour isn’t approved, so he has fewer than forty approved hours, and the license lapses.
Tempting, because it uses the stimulus’s words. But Harrowgate offering early courses doesn’t mean VARGA took any of them.
This turns the necessary condition into a sufficient one. It tells us which hours DO count, which can’t show his license lapsed.

Very tempting. But ‘the first half of the year’ runs through June, and Harrowgate registered in June. All of those hours could have come in late June, after registration. No unapproved hour is guaranteed.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Of this year’s two finalists for the Aldous Prize, Brandt’s study of the 1848 uprising is the more deserving. Corr’s study draws on three times as many archival sources and is, line for line, the more careful work. But each of its findings confirms what historians already believed, whereas Brandt’s shows that the uprising’s leaders were not, as long assumed, urban artisans.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian’s reasoning?
choices: A study that draws on more archival sources should be preferred to one that draws on fewer, unless its findings are less original.
Historians should give greater weight to evidence found in archives than to the assumptions of earlier historians.
Prize committees should judge each study by the standards that the study’s own author set out to meet.
In judging scholarly work, the extent to which it changes its field’s understanding should outweigh its thoroughness.
No study should win a prize for scholarship if a competing study is more carefully argued from one line to the next.
questions.explanation: The historian concedes Corr’s superior thoroughness but ranks Brandt higher because Brandt overturns an accepted view while Corr only confirms accepted views. (D) makes impact on the field outweigh thoroughness, which yields the ranking. (A) is the dominant trap: its exception cancels Corr’s advantage from sources, but cancelling a reason to prefer Corr doesn’t establish that Brandt is MORE deserving. (B) is about method, not ranking studies, and (E) favors Corr.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Brandt’s study is more deserving than Corr’s.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Corr’s study is more thorough (more sources, more careful), but it only confirms existing beliefs; Brandt’s overturns a long-held assumption.

breakdown.analysis: Corr wins on thoroughness; Brandt wins on changing what historians think. To call Brandt ‘more deserving,’ the principle must make the second factor beat the first. Watch for principles whose exception merely removes Corr’s advantage. That gives a tie at best, not a win for Brandt.

choices.note: Very tempting, because it fits the facts: Corr has more sources, and its findings are less original. But the ‘unless’ only cancels the preference for Corr. It never says Brandt should be preferred. Removing a reason for one side isn’t a reason for the other.
This is a rule for doing history, not for ranking two studies. Brandt’s study may well rest on archives too.
We aren’t told what standards either author set, so this can’t decide anything.
CORRECT. Brandt changes the field’s understanding; Corr is more thorough but changes nothing. If the first outweighs the second, Brandt’s study is more deserving.
This favors Corr, the opposite of the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Charities in a certain country report that the total number of hours people volunteer for them each year has fallen steadily over the past decade. At the same time, national surveys over the same period show that the percentage of adults who do at least some volunteer work during the year has risen.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The surveys count as a volunteer anyone who has done any unpaid work for a charity at any time in the past year.
Retired people, who volunteer more hours on average than working people do, make up a growing share of the country's adults.
More and more volunteers give their time through one-day events rather than through regular weekly commitments.
The country's adult population has grown by several percent over the past decade.
Many charities now find their volunteers through online listings instead of through churches and clubs.
questions.explanation: The two figures measure different things: how many people volunteer and how much they give in total. (C) reconciles them: more people volunteer, but in one-off events, so each contributes fewer hours. (A) is the near-miss: it describes how a one-off volunteer is counted, but without a shift toward light volunteering it explains nothing.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: A larger share of adults volunteer, yet total volunteer hours have fallen.

breakdown.analysis: Counting volunteers isn't the same as counting hours. Ten people giving one hour each is less than two people giving ten each. We need an answer that says the typical volunteer now gives less time. Watch for answers that push hours up (more retirees, more adults); they make the puzzle worse.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shows how a light volunteer gets counted. But the surveys counted people this way throughout the decade, so it doesn't explain a change by itself.
This should push total hours up, so it deepens the puzzle.
CORRECT. More people volunteer, but each gives far fewer hours. A rising share of volunteers and a falling total of hours fit together.
More adults and a higher share volunteering should mean more hours, not fewer. This deepens the puzzle.
How volunteers are recruited says nothing about how many hours each gives.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, half of the bean fields on a research farm were sprayed with an insecticide that kills over 95 percent of the aphids it contacts. A week later, aphids were far scarcer in the sprayed fields than in the unsprayed ones. Six weeks after spraying, however, the sprayed fields held considerably more aphids than the unsprayed fields did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the change in the aphid populations of the sprayed fields relative to the unsprayed fields?
choices: The aphids that survived the spraying had mostly been sheltered on the undersides of leaves rather than being resistant to the insecticide.
Aphid numbers in the unsprayed fields rose steadily throughout the six weeks after the spraying.
Aphids harm bean plants mainly by spreading plant viruses as they feed.
Aphids reproduce so quickly that a population cut by 95 percent can regain its former size within a few weeks.
The spray also kills the beetles and lacewings that eat aphids, and those insects multiply far more slowly.
questions.explanation: Recovery is easy to explain; overshooting the unsprayed fields is not. (E) gives a difference between the fields that lasts: the spray killed the slow-breeding predators, so the rebounding aphids had no check. (D) is the trap: fast breeding explains recovery, not overshoot, since aphids breed fast everywhere.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Spraying killed most aphids, yet six weeks later sprayed fields had more aphids than unsprayed ones.

breakdown.analysis: Read the last fact closely: not just 'aphids came back' but 'more than in fields never sprayed.' So something must make sprayed fields better for aphids afterward. What else could the spray kill? We need an answer that changes the sprayed fields in a lasting way.

choices.note: How the survivors escaped doesn't explain why the sprayed fields ended up with more aphids than fields that were never sprayed.
If anything this makes it harder to see how the sprayed fields pulled ahead.
How aphids do damage is irrelevant to how many there are.
Tempting. It explains recovery to the old level, but the puzzle is that the sprayed fields overshot the unsprayed ones. Fast breeding happens in both sets of fields.
CORRECT. Spraying wiped out the aphids' predators too. Aphids rebounded quickly with nothing to eat them, while in unsprayed fields the predators kept them in check.

questions.stimulus: Over the past fifteen years, farms around a certain lake have cut the phosphorus washing off their fields into the lake by nearly half. Because phosphorus feeds the algae that cloud the lake each summer, scientists expected the summer algae blooms to shrink. Yet in recent summers the blooms have been as large and as frequent as they were fifteen years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Some of the phosphorus that reaches the lake comes from sources other than farms, such as the sewage systems of nearby towns.
The farms have cut their runoff chiefly by planting strips of grass along streams, which trap soil before it reaches the lake.
Phosphorus from earlier decades remains in the lake's bottom mud, from which warm water releases it.
Large algae blooms harm many of the lake's fish.
Algae blooms on the lake are largest in summers that follow unusually wet springs.
questions.explanation: Cutting new phosphorus helps only if the lake depends on new phosphorus. (C) says it doesn't: decades of old phosphorus in the mud keep the supply up. (A) is the trap: other sources matter only if they grew, and nothing says they did.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Farm phosphorus runoff was halved, yet the algae blooms it feeds are as big as ever.

breakdown.analysis: What else could be feeding the algae? Something that didn't drop when the farms cleaned up. An old store in the lake itself works. Be careful with 'other sources': an unchanged source explains why blooms didn't vanish, not why they didn't shrink at all.

choices.note: Tempting. But these other sources were there fifteen years ago too, and nothing says they grew. Unchanged sources can't offset a halving of farm runoff.
This explains how the farms cut runoff, not why the algae didn't respond.
CORRECT. The lake has a store of old phosphorus that keeps feeding the algae every summer, so cutting new inputs doesn't shrink the blooms for years.
An effect of the blooms, not a reason they persist.
Without any sign that recent springs were wetter, this doesn't explain the trend.

questions.stimulus: Product manager: Customers who complete the optional online tutorial for our accounting software renew their subscriptions at nearly twice the rate of customers who skip it. Evidently the tutorial teaches people to get real value from the software. So if we require every new customer to complete the tutorial before using the software, renewals will rise substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the product manager's argument?
choices: Customers usually complete the optional tutorial only after they have already decided that the software suits their needs.
The tutorial was redesigned last year to cover the features that customers use most often.
Customers who renew their subscriptions rate the software's ease of use more highly, on average, than customers who let their subscriptions lapse.
Several competing accounting programs offer tutorials, though none requires customers to complete one.
Some customers who completed the tutorial nevertheless failed to renew their subscriptions.
questions.explanation: The argument reads a correlation as cause: tutorial, then renewal. (A) shows the arrow could run the other way: people take the tutorial because they've already decided the software is worth keeping. (E) fails because a few exceptions don't undercut a difference in rates.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Requiring the tutorial will raise renewals substantially.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Customers who complete the optional tutorial renew at about twice the rate of those who skip it.

breakdown.analysis: Who chooses to do an optional tutorial? Probably the people already sold on the product. If so, the tutorial isn't creating loyal customers; loyal customers are taking the tutorial. It's like noticing that people who buy the extended warranty keep their cars longer and concluding warranties make cars last. We want an answer showing the completers differ from the skippers before the tutorial.

choices.note: CORRECT. Then completing the tutorial is a sign of a decision already made, not its cause. Customers who were going to renew anyway are the ones who take it, and forcing doubters through it needn't change their minds.
This makes the tutorial sound more useful, which if anything helps the argument.
Expected, and beside the point. It doesn't show whether the tutorial causes renewals.
What competitors do tells us nothing about whether requiring the tutorial would work here.
A few exceptions don't touch a claim about rates. The completers still renew at twice the rate.

questions.stimulus: During last summer's severe drought in a certain lowland region, the number of mosquitoes there fell to less than half its usual level. Nonetheless, cases of Varo fever, a disease that mosquitoes transmit from infected birds to people, were more numerous in the region last summer than in any previous year on record.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, contributes most to an explanation of the rise in Varo fever cases despite the drop in mosquito numbers?
choices: Several bird species that carry Varo fever left the region early last summer to search for water in other, wetter areas.
Varo fever tends to cause more severe illness in elderly people than it does in the younger adults who catch it.
The mosquitoes that carry Varo fever breed in standing water, much of which the drought eliminated.
With water scarce, birds and mosquitoes crowded around the same few pools, so a far larger proportion of mosquitoes became infected.
Cases of Varo fever are generally recorded only when patients become ill enough to seek care at a hospital.
questions.explanation: Cases depend on how many mosquitoes carry the virus, not just how many mosquitoes there are. (D) raises the infected share: drought pushed birds and mosquitoes together. (C) is the trap: it explains the drop in mosquitoes, one side only.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Mosquitoes fell by half, yet the mosquito-borne fever hit a record.

breakdown.analysis: Half as many mosquitoes doesn't mean half as many infected mosquitoes. If the share infected went way up, the infected number could rise. We need something that makes each mosquito more likely to carry the virus, or more likely to bite people. Answers that only explain the mosquito decline are one-sided.

choices.note: Fewer infected birds means fewer infected mosquitoes, so this deepens the puzzle.
Severity isn't the issue; the number of cases is.
This explains why mosquitoes were scarce, which we already knew. It does nothing for the rise in cases.
CORRECT. Fewer mosquitoes can spread more disease if many more of them carry it. Crowding at shared pools raises the infected share enough to outweigh the smaller number.
Tempting as a recording issue, but nothing says the recording rule changed last summer.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago a supermarket chain moved sugary soft drinks away from its checkout counters to discourage impulse purchases. Since then, the chain's sales of sugary soft drinks have fallen by 10 percent. Even so, sugary soft drinks now make up a larger percentage of all the beverages the chain sells, by volume, than they did two years ago.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent conflict described above?
choices: Moving the soft drinks away from the checkout counters mainly reduced purchases of single cans and small bottles.
The chain has since stopped selling bottled water, until then its best-selling beverage by volume.
Sales of sugar-free soft drinks at the chain have risen substantially over the past two years.
The total number of customers shopping at the chain's stores has risen slightly over the past two years.
Most of the sugary soft drinks the chain now sells are bought in multi-bottle packs by customers stocking up.
questions.explanation: A share can rise while sales fall if the total falls faster. (B) removes the chain's top-selling beverage, shrinking the total. (C) is the trap: it reuses 'soft drinks' but growing other sales would lower the sugary drinks' share.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Sugary soft-drink sales fell 10 percent, yet their share of beverage sales rose.

breakdown.analysis: Percent versus amount, a classic. A share is a part over a whole. The part fell 10 percent; for the share to rise, the whole must have fallen by more. So we want something that shrank the rest of the chain's beverage sales. Watch for answers that grow the other beverages; they push the share down.

choices.note: This explains how sales fell, not why the share rose.
CORRECT. If the biggest beverage category vanished, total beverage volume shrank far more than 10 percent. Soft drinks fell, but the whole fell faster, so their share grew.
Tempting, because it's about beverage sales. But more sugar-free sales grow the total, which shrinks the sugary drinks' share. This deepens the puzzle.
More customers would raise sales of all beverages; it says nothing about the share.
How the drinks are bought doesn't explain a rising share.

questions.stimulus: Court records from a certain medieval market town list far more prosecutions for theft in years of good harvests than in famine years. Letters and chronicles written in the town at the time, by contrast, agree that theft was much more common in famine years than in years of plenty.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, contributes most to an explanation of the difference between the court records and the letters and chronicles?
choices: Anyone who wished to bring a theft case before the town court first had to pay the court a fee.
Punishments for theft imposed by the town court were harsher in famine years than in years of good harvests.
In famine years, many of the town's poorest residents left to look for food in the surrounding countryside.
The town's court records survive for nearly every year of the period, with very few gaps.
Most thefts prosecuted in the town court were of livestock or grain rather than of money or goods.
questions.explanation: Prosecutions measure thefts that reached the court, not thefts. (A) gives a reason many famine-year thefts never got there: bringing a case cost money that hungry victims lacked. (B) is the trap: harsher punishment says nothing about why fewer cases were brought.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: More theft prosecutions in good years, but contemporaries say more theft in famine years.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of prosecutions really the number of thefts? Only if every theft gets prosecuted. We need something that keeps famine-year thefts out of court. A fee does it: in a famine, few victims can pay. Watch for answers that talk about punishment or record-keeping without touching the gap between crimes and cases.

choices.note: CORRECT. In famine years, victims of theft were short of money too, so fewer could afford to bring a case. Theft could be common while prosecutions were rare.
Tempting, because it ties the court to famine years. But harsher punishment would, if anything, discourage theft, and it gives no reason why fewer of the thefts that did occur reached the court.
This would mean fewer people in town to steal in famine years, which makes the chroniclers' claim harder to believe, not easier.
This rules out missing records as an explanation, which makes the puzzle stand firmer.
What was stolen doesn't explain why the number of prosecutions moved opposite to the number of thefts.

questions.stimulus: For a year, a kitchenware store displayed a single espresso machine, priced at $300, and sold few of them. The store then placed a deluxe model priced at $650 on the shelf beside it. Few customers bought the deluxe model. Even so, monthly sales of the $300 machine nearly doubled, though its price, its features, and the store's overall traffic were unchanged.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why sales of the $300 machine rose?
choices: The deluxe model has several features, such as a built-in grinder, that the $300 machine lacks.
The store makes a larger profit on each deluxe model it sells than it does on each $300 machine.
Most people who bought the $300 machine had already decided to buy an espresso machine before they entered the store.
Shoppers unsure what an appliance should cost often judge a price by comparing it with nearby prices.
Machines priced above $500 account for only a small share of the espresso machines sold nationwide.
questions.explanation: Nothing about the $300 machine changed except what stood next to it. (D) explains how a neighbor can matter: shoppers who judge prices by comparison see $300 as moderate beside $650. (A) is the trap: a feature gap would push buyers toward the deluxe model, not the cheaper one.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Hardly anyone bought the new $650 model, yet adding it nearly doubled sales of the unchanged $300 model.

breakdown.analysis: The deluxe model barely sold, so how could it matter? Only if its mere presence changed how shoppers saw the $300 machine. We need an answer connecting the two prices. Answers about store motives or about the deluxe model's features miss the point: the question is why shoppers' choices changed.

choices.note: Tempting, because it points to a difference between the two machines. But extra features in the deluxe model would draw buyers toward it, not toward the $300 machine.
This explains why the store might want to display the deluxe model. It says nothing about why shoppers started buying the cheaper one.
So? This could have been just as true before the deluxe model appeared. It doesn't explain a change.
CORRECT. Next to a $650 model, $300 looks moderate. If shoppers judge price by comparison, the same machine at the same price now seems like a reasonable deal, so more of them buy it.
National sales patterns don't explain what changed in this store.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: Winters around a large northern lake have warmed over the past forty years. Since warmer winters bring a larger share of precipitation as rain rather than snow, one would expect snowfall in the towns just downwind of the lake to have declined. Instead, those towns now receive more snow each winter, on average, than they did forty years ago. Most of their snow falls when frigid winds cross open stretches of the lake and pick up moisture there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the climatologist's statements?
choices: Ice now covers the lake for a much smaller part of each winter than it did forty years ago.
The downwind towns receive more snow than do towns at the same distance upwind of the lake.
Snow now stays on the ground in the downwind towns for fewer days each winter than it did forty years ago.
Rain falls in the downwind towns more often in early and late winter than it does in midwinter.
In the downwind towns, the coldest days of each winter now tend to come later in the season.
questions.explanation: Warming cuts the share of precipitation falling as snow, so the towns must be getting more moisture. The stimulus says their snow comes from winds crossing open lake water, and (A) says there is now much more open water each winter. (B) only describes how the towns compare with others, which says nothing about a change over time.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Winters warmed (more rain, less snow expected), yet downwind towns get more snow.

breakdown.analysis: If a smaller share falls as snow, how can there be more snow? Only if there's more moisture to begin with. The last sentence tells you where the towns' snow comes from: winds picking up moisture over open lake water. So we need a change that gives those winds more open water to cross. An answer that describes the towns without any change over forty years explains nothing about a trend.

choices.note: CORRECT. The towns' snow depends on winds crossing open water, and ice shuts that supply off. With the lake open for much more of the winter, the winds pick up far more moisture, enough to outweigh the shift toward rain.
So? This compares the towns with upwind towns at one time. It fits the lake's role, but nothing in it changed over forty years, so it can't explain why snowfall rose.
This is about snow cover, not snowfall. Melting faster fits warmer winters but says nothing about more snow falling.
When rain falls within the winter doesn't explain more snow overall.
Shifting the timing of cold days doesn't add moisture or snow.

questions.stimulus: The oaks of a certain forest produce enormous acorn crops every few years and small crops in the years between. Mice and squirrels eat far more acorns in the bumper-crop years than in other years. Even so, it is mainly in the bumper-crop years that large numbers of new oak seedlings take root in the forest.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: In years between bumper crops, the forest's mice and squirrels eat more seeds of other plants than they do in bumper-crop years.
How many mice and squirrels the forest holds in a given autumn depends mainly on the previous year's food supply.
Acorns that escape being eaten often fail to sprout if they land on a thick layer of fallen leaves.
In bumper-crop years, the forest's mice and squirrels eat acorns almost to the exclusion of any other food.
Seedlings that sprout in bumper-crop years are no likelier to survive to maturity than other seedlings.
questions.explanation: Eating more acorns is compatible with leaving more behind: what matters is how many escape. (B) shows why the animals can't keep up with a bumper crop: their numbers were set by the lean year before, so they eat only a small share of the huge crop. (D) is the trap: it explains why more acorns are eaten, which we already knew.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Animals eat more acorns in bumper years, yet that's when most new seedlings appear.

breakdown.analysis: So what if more acorns get eaten? The question is how many are left. Eating more of a much bigger pile can still leave far more behind, like a bakery that gives away more samples on its biggest baking day and still has more bread to sell. We need a reason the animals can eat only a small share of a bumper crop. Watch for answers that explain only why more acorns are eaten; that side isn't puzzling.

choices.note: Interesting, but it only tells us what the animals eat instead of acorns in lean years. It says nothing about how many acorns are left over in bumper years.

CORRECT. Since bumper crops come only every few years, the animal population in a bumper autumn was built on the previous, lean year's food. So there are too few animals to eat more than a small share of the huge crop. They eat more acorns in total, but far more acorns survive to sprout.
This happens every year, big crop or small. A constant can't explain a difference between years.
Tempting, because it explains why so many acorns get eaten in bumper years. But that side of the puzzle needed no explaining, and it makes the seedling boom harder to understand, not easier.
This is about what happens after seedlings take root. The puzzle is why so many take root in the first place.

questions.stimulus: To attract new listeners, a city's orchestra cut ticket prices for its weekday concerts in half last season. Weekday attendance roughly doubled. Nevertheless, the number of different people who attended at least one of the orchestra's concerts during the season was no greater than in the season before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the number of different people attending the orchestra's concerts did not rise?
choices: Many young residents of the city say that ticket prices are the main reason they seldom attend orchestral concerts.
Attendance at the orchestra's weekend concerts, where prices did not change, was about the same as in the previous season.
Before the price cut, the orchestra's weekday concerts usually played to a hall that was less than half full.
Only people already on the orchestra's list of past ticket buyers were told about the reduced weekday prices.
Weekday concerts feature shorter programs than weekend concerts and end early enough for listeners to catch the last trains home.
questions.explanation: Attendance counts visits; the other figure counts people. Both can hold if the same people came more often. (D) says why: the price cut was advertised only to past buyers. (C) is the trap: spare capacity explains how attendance could double, not why the crowd was made up of the same people.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Weekday attendance doubled, yet no more different people attended than the year before.

breakdown.analysis: Tickets sold aren't the same as people. One subscriber going to five concerts counts five times in attendance and once in 'different people.' So the extra attendance must have come from existing listeners. We want a reason the cheaper tickets reached only them. Answers about capacity or schedules don't touch who came.

choices.note: This makes the cheap tickets look like a strong draw for new listeners, which deepens the puzzle.
Background only. Steady weekend attendance doesn't explain who filled the extra weekday seats.
Tempting: it explains how attendance could double without selling out. But room for more people doesn't tell us why no new people came.

CORRECT. Only existing patrons heard about the cheaper tickets, so the extra weekday seats were filled by people who already came, now coming more often. Attendance doubled while the number of different people stayed flat.
This describes weekday concerts but was presumably true before the price cut, so it can't explain the change.

questions.stimulus: Literary historian: The national library holds about 4,000 novels first published in this country during the 1890s. Throughout that decade, the law required publishers to deposit a copy of every new book they issued with the national library. So roughly 4,000 novels must have been published here in the 1890s.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the literary historian's argument?
choices: Many of the novels published in the 1890s have long been out of print and are now almost entirely forgotten.
The deposit law remained in force, essentially unchanged, well into the twentieth century.
A fire in 1921 destroyed much of the national library's collection of nineteenth-century newspapers and magazines.
More novels were published in the country during the 1890s than during any earlier decade.
Officials rarely enforced the deposit law against small provincial printers, who issued many cheap novels.
questions.explanation: The historian treats what the law required as what actually happened. (E) shows a large gap between the two: many cheap provincial novels were never deposited. (C) is the trap: a fire could shrink the holdings, but it burned periodicals, not novels.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: About 4,000 novels were published in the 1890s.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The library holds about 4,000 such novels; the law required a copy of every new book to be deposited.

breakdown.analysis: Does a law requiring deposit mean every publisher deposited? Only if it was obeyed. The argument quietly assumes the library's shelves are a complete sample. We want an answer showing a lot of novels slipped past the library. Watch the scope: losses of other kinds of material don't count.

choices.note: Being out of print now doesn't mean a novel was never deposited. The library's holdings are what matter.
How long the law lasted afterward says nothing about whether it was obeyed in the 1890s.
Tempting: a fire could explain missing books. But it destroyed newspapers and magazines, not novels, so the novel count is untouched.
This compares the 1890s with earlier decades; it doesn't bear on whether 4,000 is the right count.

CORRECT. The argument needs the library's holdings to capture virtually every novel published. If a whole class of publishers often ignored the law, many novels never reached the library, and the true number was well above 4,000.

questions.stimulus: Education consultant: Smaller classes do not improve children's reading. In our district, students who spent all three of the early grades in classes of fewer than 18 scored lower on third-grade reading tests, on average, than students who spent those grades in larger classes. Nor can a delay explain this, since the gains attributed to small classes are said to appear within a single year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the education consultant's argument?
choices: Teachers of the district's smaller classes report spending more time with each student than teachers of larger classes do.
Gains in reading attributed to small classes are often reported to fade within a few years after students move to larger classes.
Small classes cost the district considerably more per student than larger classes do.
Reading scores in the district have risen over the past five years in classes of every size.
District policy limits to 17 students any class in which more than a third of the students are still learning English.
questions.explanation: The consultant compares two groups without asking whether they started out alike. (E) shows they didn't: small classes are reserved for classes full of English learners, who would score lower regardless. (B) is the trap: it echoes the timing concession but these students were tested while still in small classes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Smaller classes don't improve reading.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Students in small classes scored lower than students in larger ones; a delay can't explain it since gains are said to show within a year.

breakdown.analysis: Were the two groups the same to begin with? If the district fills small classes with students who struggle in English, of course they score lower. That's like noting that hospital patients die more than people at home and concluding hospitals are deadly. We need a reason small-class students differ. Note the consultant already handled timing, so answers about delay or fading won't land.

choices.note: This makes small classes sound helpful, but the argument is about test results; more teacher time doesn't explain the lower scores.
Tempting, since it echoes the consultant's point about timing. But these students were tested at the end of their small-class years, before any fading could occur.
Cost is a different issue from whether small classes help reading.
Rising scores everywhere don't explain why small classes score lower.

CORRECT. Small classes are where the district puts many children still learning English, who would be expected to score lower on a reading test in English. The lower scores may reflect who is in small classes, not what small classes do.

questions.stimulus: Over the past forty years, the average summer temperature in a certain farming valley has risen by about one degree Celsius. Over the same period, however, the number of summer days on which the temperature in the valley climbs above 32 degrees Celsius has fallen by nearly a third.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the two findings described above?
choices: Summer nights in the valley have warmed considerably more over the forty years than summer afternoons have.
The valley's hottest days usually come during droughts, which have become less frequent there in recent decades.
Expanded irrigation has left the valley's air more humid, which cools summer afternoons slightly but keeps summer nights much warmer.
Many of the valley's farmers have switched to crop varieties that suffer heat damage only on days above 32 degrees Celsius.
Days above 32 degrees now come mostly in late summer rather than in midsummer, as they did forty years ago.
questions.explanation: An average covers the whole day and night; the hot-day count depends on afternoon peaks. (C) moves them in opposite directions: cooler afternoons, much warmer nights. (A) and (B) each explain only one half, and (B) actually works against the rising average.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Average summer temperature rose, yet there are a third fewer days above 32°C.

breakdown.analysis: An average can rise while the peaks fall if the low end rises more. So we want something that raises nights and trims afternoons. Watch for one-sided answers: one that explains fewer hot days but would lower the average, or one that raises the average without touching the peaks.

choices.note: Tempting: warmer nights could raise the average. But if afternoons also warmed, even a little, we'd expect more hot days, not fewer. It explains one half only.
Tempting: fewer droughts means fewer scorching days. But droughts are hot, so fewer of them should pull the average down, which leaves the rising average unexplained.
CORRECT. One cause does both jobs: cooler afternoons mean fewer days above 32, and much warmer nights pull the average up.
This is about crop damage, not about the temperatures themselves.
When the hot days come doesn't explain why there are fewer of them.

questions.stimulus: Meteorologist: The number of tornadoes recorded each year in a certain plains region has tripled since the 1960s. Some take this as evidence that tornadoes there have become more frequent. But in the 1990s the region installed Doppler radars, which can detect brief, weak tornadoes that once touched down unnoticed in empty farmland. So the rise reflects improved detection, not a real increase in tornadoes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the meteorologist's argument?
choices: The yearly count of strong or violent tornadoes in the region has also roughly tripled.
Doppler radar can detect the rotation that precedes a tornado but cannot by itself confirm that one has touched down.
Tornado damage in the region, adjusted for inflation, has risen sharply since the 1960s.
Tornadoes in the region occur most often in late spring and early summer.
Most of the tornadoes that the radars have added to the record lasted less than five minutes.
questions.explanation: The detection story can only account for tornadoes the old methods missed: the brief, weak ones. (A) shows a tripling among strong tornadoes too, which radar didn't help anyone notice. (C) is the trap: damage depends on what's in the path, not just how many tornadoes there are.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tripled tornado count reflects better detection, not more tornadoes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Radars installed in the 1990s detect brief, weak tornadoes that used to go unnoticed.

breakdown.analysis: If radar explains the rise, the extra tornadoes should all be the kind radar newly catches. Find a category radar didn't affect and see if it rose too. Strong tornadoes were never missed, so a rise there is real. Watch for damage figures: they rise with population, not just with tornadoes.

choices.note: CORRECT. Radar's gain is in spotting brief, weak tornadoes. Strong ones were never missed. If strong tornadoes tripled too, better detection can't explain the rise; tornadoes really have become more common.
This suggests radar may even overcount, which supports the detection explanation. Wrong direction.
Tempting, since more damage sounds like more tornadoes. But damage also rises when more buildings stand in a tornado's path, so this doesn't show more tornadoes.
Seasonal timing is irrelevant to the trend.
This supports the meteorologist: the added tornadoes are the brief, weak kind that used to go unnoticed.

questions.stimulus: After a medical clinic began phoning patients the day before each scheduled appointment to remind them of it, the number of appointments that patients simply failed to show up for fell sharply. Surprisingly, over the same period the number of patients the clinic's doctors actually saw each week also fell.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the two trends described above?
choices: Before the calls began, most patients who missed appointments said afterward that they had simply forgotten them.
Reminded patients sometimes cancel appointments they no longer need, and the clinic can rarely fill a slot freed only a day ahead.
The calls are made by the clinic's nurses, during hours they once spent preparing patients for examination by the doctors.
The clinic began the reminder calls at the start of the season in which demand for appointments is usually highest.
The clinic's doctors spend more time with each patient than doctors at most other clinics do.
questions.explanation: Fewer no-shows should mean more patients seen, so something else must be slowing the doctors. (C) supplies it: the calls eat the nurse time that kept patients moving. (B) is the trap: a late cancellation wastes the slot, but a no-show wasted it before, so nothing changes.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Fewer patients miss appointments, yet the doctors see fewer patients each week.

breakdown.analysis: Compare before and after for the same patient. A patient who no longer needs the visit used to just not come; now she cancels a day ahead. Either way the slot is empty. So cancellations can't be the answer. We need something that cuts the doctors' capacity. Who makes the calls, and what were they doing before?

choices.note: This explains why reminders cut no-shows, the side that needed no explaining.

Tempting, because it describes a slot that goes unused. But before the calls, that same patient would have simply not shown up, and the slot would have been wasted then too. Swapping a no-show for an unfilled cancellation doesn't reduce the number of patients seen.
CORRECT. The calls take nurse time away from getting patients ready, so the doctors move through patients more slowly and see fewer each week, even though more patients show up.
Higher demand should mean more patients seen, so this deepens the puzzle.
If this was true before and after, it can't explain a change.

questions.stimulus: Over the past thirty years, the land area of a large river delta has shrunk steadily as the sea has claimed land along its coastal edge. Measurements show that the river delivers as much sediment to its mouth each year as it did thirty years ago, and in earlier centuries that much sediment was enough to keep the delta growing.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Heavy pumping of groundwater from beneath the delta over the past thirty years has caused its land surface to sink.
Silt from farms that have spread along the upper river has offset the sediment now held back by a dam built upstream thirty years ago.
The sediment now reaching the river's mouth is mostly fine clay that drifts offshore, whereas it was once mostly sand that settled along the coast.
Sea level along the delta's coast has risen faster over the past thirty years than in any earlier century.
Mangrove forests that once broke the force of storm waves along the coastal edge were mostly cleared about thirty years ago.
questions.explanation: Four answers give a way the same sediment no longer keeps up: the land sinks, the sediment is a kind that drifts away, the sea rises faster, or waves erode more. (B) only explains why the sediment amount didn't change, which is already given. (C) looks like (B) because it's about sediment, but it changes what the sediment does.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The same amount of sediment that once grew the delta now arrives, yet the delta shrinks.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers resolve, one doesn't. Prephrase the resolvers: something changed on the delta side (sinking, sea level, erosion) or the sediment changed in kind even if not in amount. The odd one out will explain something we already know or nothing at all. Don't eliminate an answer just because it's about sediment.

choices.note: Helps. Sinking land is lost to the sea even if sediment arrives as before.
CORRECT. This only explains why the amount of sediment stayed the same, which the stimulus already tells us. Same amount, same kind of contribution: it gives no reason the delta now loses ground.
Helps. The amount is the same, but sediment that drifts offshore doesn't build the coast. This is the tricky one, since it's also about sediment.
Helps. Faster sea-level rise needs more sediment to keep pace.
Helps. Without the mangroves, waves erode the coast faster than the sediment can rebuild it.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the average hourly wage of a certain country's workers, adjusted for inflation, has risen by 8 percent. Yet within every level of education, from workers who never finished secondary school to those with graduate degrees, the average inflation-adjusted wage has fallen over the same decade.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent conflict described above?
choices: Workers with graduate degrees earn, on average, more than twice as much per hour as workers who never finished secondary school.
Workers with university degrees have gone from a small minority of the workforce to nearly half.
Wages have fallen most steeply among workers who never finished secondary school, and least among those with graduate degrees.
Inflation in the country was lower over the past decade than over the decade before it.
The government's wage figures leave out people who work for themselves rather than for an employer.
questions.explanation: An overall average depends on each group's average and on how many people are in each group. (B) supplies the shift in mix: many more workers in the better-paid degree groups. (A) is the near-miss: a pay gap between groups is needed, but on its own it changes nothing.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The overall average wage rose, yet the average wage fell within every education group.

breakdown.analysis: How can every part go down while the whole goes up? Only if the parts' sizes changed. Picture two groups, one paid 10 and one paid 30. If both drop by 1 but most workers move into the second group, the overall average climbs. We need a shift toward the higher-paid groups. Answers about the gap alone, or about inflation, don't do it.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's part of the picture: better-educated workers earn more. But that was true ten years ago too. Without a shift in how many workers are in each group, it resolves nothing.
CORRECT. Each group's pay fell, but far more workers are now in the higher-paid groups. The overall average rises because of the change in mix.
This would pull the overall average down, if anything.
The figures are already adjusted for inflation, so its rate is irrelevant.
If the figures leave out the self-employed every year, this explains no change.

questions.stimulus: Forest researcher: Gray buckthorn, an invasive shrub, suppresses native tree seedlings mainly by shading them, not through the compounds its roots release. Granted, those compounds slow the germination of some native seeds in laboratory dishes. But buckthorn leafs out weeks before native plants each spring, deeply shading the forest floor, and in plots where we removed it, native seedlings became three times as numerous as in plots where it remained.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the forest researcher's argument?
choices: Where buckthorn was cut to the ground every spring but its roots were left alive, native seedlings did not increase.
The laboratory tests used the root compounds at concentrations far higher than any found in forest soil.
Some native shrubs also leaf out early in spring, though none shades the forest floor as deeply as buckthorn does.
The root compounds remain in the soil for several years after buckthorn shrubs have been dug out.
Native seedlings in the plots cleared of buckthorn grew taller during their first year, on average, than seedlings in the plots where it remained.
questions.explanation: The removal experiment took away both shade and roots, so it can't tell them apart. (A) separates them: shade gone, roots kept, and seedlings still suppressed. (D) is the trap: it mentions the compounds, but it cuts in the researcher's favor.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Buckthorn suppresses native seedlings mainly by shade, not root compounds.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It leafs out early and shades the floor; removing it tripled seedlings (the compounds only slowed germination in lab dishes).

breakdown.analysis: Removing buckthorn removes its shade and its roots at once, so the tripling fits either cause. To weaken the shade claim, we want a test that removes the shade but keeps the roots, with no recovery. Read the direction carefully: two answers talk about the compounds but make them look weaker, which helps the researcher.

choices.note: CORRECT. Cutting the shrubs each spring removes the shade but leaves living roots, and their compounds, in place. If seedlings still didn't recover, shade can't be the main cause; the roots look responsible.
Wrong direction: it makes the laboratory evidence for the compounds weaker.
Other shrubs' shade is irrelevant to which feature of buckthorn suppresses seedlings.
Wrong direction. If the compounds lingered in the cleared plots and seedlings still tripled, the compounds look unimportant. This supports the researcher.
This is about growth, not numbers, and taller seedlings in the open fits the shade story anyway.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from plants buried by a lava flow that runs into a certain lake shows that the flow cooled about 3,000 years ago. The shells of freshwater snails that lived on the flow's submerged surface, found lying where they lived, give radiocarbon ages of about 5,000 years. The snails built their shells from carbon dissolved in the lake water.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the geologist's statements?
choices: Snails of the kind found on the lava flow live for only two or three years.
Charcoal can give radiocarbon ages that are too old when the burned wood came from trees that were already centuries old.
The snails also take in a small amount of carbon from algae, which draw their carbon from the air.
The charcoal was taken from several different spots along the lava flow, and all of the samples gave similar ages.
Much of the carbon dissolved in the lake comes from limestone bedrock that formed many millions of years ago.
questions.explanation: The snails can't be older than the rock they grew on, so their shells must read too old. (E) explains why: their carbon comes partly from ancient limestone with no radiocarbon left. (B) is the trap: it questions a date, but in the direction that widens the gap.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: The lava flow is about 3,000 years old, yet snails that grew on it date to about 5,000 years.

breakdown.analysis: The snails grew on the flow, so they can't really be older than it. One of the dates must be off, and to close the gap either the shells read too old or the charcoal reads too young. Radiocarbon dating assumes an object's carbon started with the normal amount of radiocarbon. What if the snails' carbon came from somewhere that had already lost it? Check the direction of every answer about dating errors.

choices.note: A short life span means the shells' ages should match when the snails lived. It doesn't explain why they read too old.
Wrong direction. If the charcoal reads too old, the flow is even younger than 3,000 years, which widens the gap.
Carbon from the air would make the shells read younger, not older. Wrong direction.
This supports the charcoal date. It doesn't explain the shells.

CORRECT. Carbon from rock millions of years old has lost all its radiocarbon. Shells built partly from that carbon contain less radiocarbon than their true age warrants, so they read thousands of years too old.

questions.stimulus: Botanist: Thrushes eat the berries of the bitterberry shrub and later excrete the seeds. In our trials, bitterberry seeds collected from thrush droppings germinated at twice the rate of seeds sown inside whole berries picked from the same shrubs. We conclude that passing through a thrush's digestive tract alters bitterberry seeds in a way that promotes their germination.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the botanist's argument?
choices: Thrushes often excrete bitterberry seeds far from the parent shrub, in places where the young seedlings face much less competition for light.
Bitterberry seeds recovered from thrush droppings have noticeably thinner seed coats than seeds taken from whole berries.
Many bitterberry seeds swallowed by thrushes are crushed and destroyed in the birds' digestive tracts.
Bitterberry pulp contains a substance that keeps the seed inside dormant until the pulp has rotted away.
Seeds of several other shrubs germinate at higher rates after passing through the digestive tracts of birds.
questions.explanation: The trial compares seeds from droppings with seeds still inside pulp, so it changes two things at once: digestion and the presence of pulp. (D) shows the pulp alone could account for the result. (A) is the trap: a real advantage of thrushes, but not one the trials measured.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Digestion alters the seeds in a way that promotes germination.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Seeds from droppings germinated at twice the rate of seeds sown inside whole berries.

breakdown.analysis: What's the control group? Seeds sown inside berries. So the dropping seeds differ in two ways: they went through a gut, and they lost their pulp. If the pulp itself holds seeds back, the gut may do nothing. We want an answer that gives the difference to the pulp. Watch for answers that praise thrushes for other reasons.

choices.note: Tempting, since it's a real benefit of passing through a thrush. But it's about where seedlings grow, not about germination rates in the trials, where all seeds were sown the same way.
This suggests digestion does change the seed, which supports the botanist.
Crushed seeds never reach the droppings, so this doesn't affect the germination rate of the seeds that were tested.
CORRECT. Seeds in whole berries were held back by the pulp, while the thrush strips the pulp off. That alone could explain the difference, with no change to the seed itself.
This supports the botanist by analogy.

questions.stimulus: In the cliffs of a certain basin, each sediment layer laid down before about 100 million years ago contains, on average, fossils of more clam species than does each layer laid down since then. Paleontologists studying the basin are nonetheless confident that more clam species lived there at any one time after 100 million years ago than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Each of the younger layers is thicker, on average, than each of the basin's older layers.
Each of the older layers took far longer to accumulate than did each of the basin's younger layers.
Many clam species that had lived in the basin for millions of years became extinct about 100 million years ago.
Clams were the most common shellfish in the basin both before and after 100 million years ago.
Clams that lived in the basin after 100 million years ago were, on average, larger than earlier clams, and their shells were thicker.
questions.explanation: A layer is a sample of a span of time, not a snapshot. (B) says the older layers each sample a much longer span, so they pile up species that lived one after another. (A) is the trap: it swaps time for thickness, and thickness doesn't settle how much time a layer covers.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Older layers hold more clam species per layer, yet more species lived at any one time later on.

breakdown.analysis: Per layer versus at any one time. If a layer covers a million years, it collects every species that came and went during that million years. So a 'richer' layer might just be a longer one. We need an answer about time span. Watch out for an answer about thickness: it sounds like the same thing but isn't.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the key. But thickness isn't time: a thick layer can build up quickly. And a bigger layer would, if anything, hold more species, which deepens the puzzle.

CORRECT. A layer that took longer to form collects fossils from a longer stretch of time, including species that lived one after another. So older layers can hold more species even if fewer lived at any one moment.
Extinctions at the boundary explain nothing about how many species lived at one time on either side of it.
Irrelevant: this compares clams with other shellfish, not clam species across time.
Larger, thicker shells fossilize better, which should make the younger layers hold more species, not fewer. Deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago, hospitals in a certain region began using a far more sensitive scan to look for a type of thyroid cancer. Since then, the percentage of patients diagnosed with that cancer who survive at least five years after diagnosis has risen sharply. Nonetheless, the number of people in the region who die of that cancer each year is no lower than it was before the new scan came into use.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why deaths from the cancer have not fallen even though survival after diagnosis has risen?
choices: The new scan allows the cancer to be found at an earlier stage, when treatment is far more likely to succeed.
No treatment for this type of thyroid cancer has become more effective over the past ten years.
Many tumors the new scan detects grow too slowly ever to cause illness.
The new scan costs considerably more than the older method, so some hospitals use it only for patients at high risk.
Most people who die of this cancer are diagnosed only after it has spread beyond the thyroid.
questions.explanation: A survival percentage depends on who gets counted as a patient. (C) shows the scan inflates the pool with tumors that were never dangerous: they all 'survive,' raising the rate, while the deadly cases and the deaths are unchanged. (A) is the trap: real early-treatment gains would cut deaths.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Since the sensitive scan arrived, a far larger share of diagnosed patients survive, yet deaths from the cancer haven't fallen.

breakdown.analysis: A rate is survivors over diagnosed patients. It can rise because fewer people die, or because more people who were never going to die get added to the bottom of the fraction. Deaths didn't fall, so it must be the second. Picture 100 patients, 20 of whom die; add 100 harmless cases and survival goes from 80 to 90 percent with the same 20 deaths. The dominant trap is the answer that makes treatment sound better: it can't be right if deaths stayed flat.

choices.note: Tempting, and most students pick it: it explains the better survival rate. But if treatment really worked better, fewer people would die, and deaths haven't fallen. It explains one side and deepens the other.
This fits the unchanged deaths, but then why did the survival rate jump? One side only.

CORRECT. The scan adds many harmless cases to the pool of diagnosed patients. They all survive, which lifts the survival percentage, but the people who would die of the cancer are the same as before, so deaths don't fall.
Limiting the scan to some patients doesn't explain either fact.
This could have been true before the new scan as well. It doesn't explain how survival rose while deaths held steady.

questions.stimulus: In a certain country, rises in the price of gasoline have reliably led people to drive fewer total kilometers. Last year, gasoline prices there rose to the highest level ever recorded, and the total distance driven in the country was greater than in any previous year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, contributes most to an explanation of why the total distance driven rose last year?
choices: Most of last year's increase in distance driven came from long trips of several hundred kilometers each.
Sales of large, fuel-hungry vehicles in the country fell sharply last year.
Gasoline prices rose most steeply during the summer months, when people in the country do the most driving.
The rise in gasoline prices was caused mainly by the shutdown of a large refinery rather than by any rise in the price of crude oil.
Last year, for the first time, domestic airfares in the country rose even more steeply than gasoline prices did.
questions.explanation: Higher gas prices make driving dearer, but if an alternative gets dearer still, people may drive more. (E) says that last year, unlike before, airfares outpaced gasoline, so travelers switched from flying to driving. (A) fits this story but explains nothing alone, and (B) describes the normal response to high prices.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Gasoline price rises have always cut driving, but last year record prices came with record driving.

breakdown.analysis: Driving got more expensive. What could make people drive more anyway? Something else got even more expensive. And it has to be something new last year, because price rises reliably cut driving before. The correct answer doesn't mention driving at all; you have to see that people substitute driving for flying when flying gets relatively dearer. The long-trips answer is a stepping stone, not a resolution. This one is hard because the key looks off-topic at first.

choices.note: Tempting: long trips are where driving and flying compete, so this fits the right story. But by itself it doesn't say why people took more long drives when driving got more expensive.
This is the normal response to high prices, and it happens in every year of rising prices. It doesn't explain why last year broke the pattern.
This makes the rise in driving harder to understand: the price hit hardest when people drive most.
Why gasoline cost more doesn't matter; drivers pay the same at the pump either way.

CORRECT. Last year, and only last year, flying got more expensive relative to driving. Travelers who would have flown drove instead, and those long trips can push total distance up even while gasoline costs a record amount. Because it's new, it explains why last year differed from the reliable pattern.

questions.stimulus: Ornithologist: Over the past thirty years, springs in a large coastal marsh have warmed considerably, and many birds that breed there now arrive weeks earlier than they once did. The tawny reed warbler, however, which winters in central Africa, still arrives in the marsh on almost the same dates as thirty years ago. So this warbler must time its spring migration by day length, which has not changed, rather than by temperature.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ornithologist's argument?
choices: Birds that time their migrations by day length generally arrive at their breeding grounds on nearly the same dates every year.
