Tawny reed warblers in the marsh now raise fewer chicks than before, because the insects their chicks eat peak earlier in spring.
Many bird species that are known to time their migrations by day length spend the winter in central Africa.
Spring has not warmed over the past thirty years where the tawny reed warbler spends the winter.
Most of the birds that now reach the marsh earlier spend the winter only a short distance to the south.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes that a temperature-timed warbler would have felt the marsh's warming. (D) undercuts that: the warbler decides when to leave in Africa, where spring hasn't warmed, so temperature timing predicts the same unchanged dates. (A) is the trap: it restates the conclusion's prediction in reverse.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The warbler times its migration by day length, not temperature.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Marsh springs warmed and other birds arrive earlier; the warbler, wintering in Africa, arrives on the same dates.

breakdown.analysis: Which temperature would the warbler respond to? It starts its trip in central Africa, so it can only feel the temperature there. If African springs haven't warmed, a temperature-timed warbler would behave exactly as observed. We need an answer that makes 'temperature' predict the same unchanged arrival. Watch for answers that sound like day-length evidence but only restate what day-length birds do.

choices.note: This is the reverse of what's needed: day-length birds arrive on fixed dates, but a fixed arrival date doesn't show a bird uses day length. It fits the argument rather than weakening it.
A consequence of arriving at the same time, not evidence about what cue the bird uses.
This supports the argument by making a day-length cue sound common among such birds.

CORRECT. A bird leaving Africa can respond only to conditions where it is, not to the marsh's temperature. If temperatures there haven't changed, a temperature-timed warbler would also leave and arrive on the same dates. Its unchanged arrival no longer points to day length.
Tempting, because it hints that early arrivers sense warmth near the marsh. But on its own it doesn't show anything about the warbler's cue.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars blame the nineteenth-century decline of a certain river port on the railway that reached the region in 1858, which carried goods more cheaply than river barges did. But the port's trade fell most steeply between 1848 and 1858, before a single train ran there. So the railway is unlikely to have caused the port's decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the historian's argument?
choices: Trade through the port continued to decline for several decades after the railway reached the region.
Shipping goods by rail in the region cost considerably less than shipping them by river barge.
Several river ports in neighboring regions that no railway reached declined during the same years.
During the 1850s, the river ran unusually low for several summers, stranding loaded barges for weeks at a time.
The railway's route was announced in 1847, and merchants soon began moving their warehouses to towns along it.
questions.explanation: The historian assumes a cause can't act before it physically exists. (E) shows how the railway could: once its route was announced, merchants relocated in anticipation. (A) is the trap: later decline fits both sides, and the scholars' premise in (B) was never in dispute.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The railway probably didn't cause the port's decline.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The port's trade fell most steeply in the decade before any train ran.

breakdown.analysis: Does a railway have to be running to affect trade? Not if people act on what they know is coming. It's like a shop losing customers the day a big store announces it will open next door. We need an answer that lets the railway work before 1858. Several answers cut the wrong way; check direction before choosing.

choices.note: Tempting, because it ties continued decline to the railway years. But the historian doesn't deny later decline; the point is that the steepest fall came first. This fits both views.
This just repeats the scholars' premise, which the historian already grants. It doesn't answer the timing point.
Wrong direction: decline without any railway supports the historian.
Wrong direction: this offers another cause for the 1850s decline, which helps the historian.

CORRECT. The railway could cause decline before it ran: once the route was known, merchants moved their business toward it. The steep pre-1858 fall is then the railway's doing, and the timing argument collapses.

questions.stimulus: City official: Our rule requiring fast-food restaurants within 500 meters of a school to close during school lunch hours has done what it was meant to do: reduce the amount of fast food schoolchildren eat. Those restaurants' midday sales have fallen by 40 percent. Critics point out that their total daily sales have fallen only 5 percent. That figure misleads, since most of their customers are adults who eat there in the evening.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the city official's argument?
choices: Adults account for well over half of the evening sales at the fast-food restaurants located near schools.
Midday sales have fallen more at restaurants near schools than at fast-food restaurants elsewhere in the city.
Children who regularly ate fast food at lunch had poorer diets overall than children who did not.
Most restaurants near schools now open early and sell breakfast to students on their way to class.
The rule was adopted after a survey found that many parents did not know what their children ate at lunch.
questions.explanation: The official measures children's fast-food eating by midday sales. (D) shows the eating moved to another time of day, so falling lunch sales no longer show children eat less. (A) is tempting only because it echoes the official's reply to the critics, which the argument already takes as given.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lunch-hour closing rule has reduced how much fast food schoolchildren eat.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Midday sales at nearby restaurants fell 40 percent; the small fall in total sales is because most customers are adults eating in the evening.

breakdown.analysis: Is the midday sales figure really the measure of what children eat? Only if they didn't just eat fast food at some other time. The official deals with the critics, but never asks where the children's purchases went. We want an answer showing the children substituted. Don't be distracted by answers that defend the official's reply about adults; that point isn't in question.

choices.note: This restates the official's answer to the critics. Confirming a premise doesn't weaken the argument.
Wrong direction: it ties the midday drop to the rule, which supports the official.
This explains why the rule was wanted, not whether it worked.

CORRECT. The children's fast food has moved from lunch to breakfast at the same restaurants. Midday sales fall, but the amount schoolchildren eat need not, which is exactly what the official claims the rule achieved.
Background on why the rule was adopted; irrelevant to its effect.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: In a recent study, forty adults kept a gratitude journal, writing down each evening three things for which they were thankful. After eight weeks, the group’s average score on a standard life-satisfaction questionnaire was markedly higher than it had been when the study began. Clearly, keeping a gratitude journal increases a person’s satisfaction with life.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether people who already report high life satisfaction tend to describe themselves as more grateful than other people do.
Whether the participants’ scores would have continued to rise had the study run for longer than eight weeks.
Whether comparable adults who kept no journal showed any change in their life-satisfaction scores over the same eight weeks.
Whether a different standard questionnaire would have rated the participants’ life satisfaction at the start of the study as higher.
Whether people who have kept gratitude journals for many years report greater life satisfaction than people who have kept them only briefly.
questions.explanation: The study has no comparison group: scores rose over eight weeks, but they might have risen anyway, say because the study began in a gloomy season. (C) supplies the missing group: if similar adults without journals rose just as much, the journal did nothing; if their scores stayed flat, the journal looks responsible. (A) is the trap because it sounds like reversed causation, but the study tracked the same people before and after, and a stable link between gratitude and satisfaction can’t explain why these scores went up.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keeping a gratitude journal increases a person’s satisfaction with life.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Forty adults kept gratitude journals; after eight weeks their average life-satisfaction score was markedly higher than at the start.

breakdown.analysis: Higher than what? Higher than their own starting point. But moods drift. The study might have started in February and ended in April, when almost everyone feels better. Without a group that kept no journal, we can’t tell whether the journal did anything. It’s like taking a vitamin while you have a cold, feeling better in a week, and crediting the vitamin. We want the missing comparison: did people who kept no journal also improve? Most students who miss this pick (A), because it sounds like a causation problem. But the evidence is a change within the same forty people, and a fixed trait can’t produce a rise.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like reversed causation. But the evidence is a rise within the same forty people. Whether satisfied people tend to be grateful doesn’t explain why these people’s scores went up, so either answer leaves the argument where it was.
So? Whether the gains would keep growing tells us nothing about whether the journal caused the gains we already have.

CORRECT. This is the missing comparison group. If similar adults who kept no journal improved just as much, something else (the season, the attention of being studied) explains the rise, and the argument collapses. If their scores stayed flat, the journal looks like the cause.
Irrelevant. The argument is about the change in scores on one questionnaire. How another questionnaire would have rated the starting level says nothing about why the scores rose.

Tempting, because it looks like more evidence about journals. But long-term keepers chose to keep going, so a yes could just mean contented people stick with the habit, and a no could mean benefits level off. Either way it doesn’t tell us what caused this group’s rise.

questions.stimulus: To learn how residents of Wenlow feel about extending the city’s commuter rail line, the transit authority surveyed 1,500 people waiting on the line’s station platforms during the morning rush hour. Of those surveyed, 72 percent favored the extension. The authority concluded that most Wenlow residents favor extending the line.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the survey was conducted at every station on the line rather than only at the line’s busiest stations.
Whether the extension would shorten the daily commutes of most of the people who now ride the line each weekday.
Whether more than 1,500 people board the line on a typical weekday morning.
Whether residents who favor the extension are more likely than those who oppose it to vote in local elections.
Whether Wenlow residents who ride the line differ in their views on the extension from residents who do not.
questions.explanation: Everyone surveyed was a rail rider, but the conclusion is about all residents. (E) tests whether that matters: if riders and non-riders feel differently, the sample misleads; if they feel the same, riders stand in fine for everyone. (A) is the trap: surveying every station would give a better picture of riders, but it would still survey only riders.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Wenlow residents favor extending the commuter rail line.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 72 percent of 1,500 people waiting on the line’s platforms at morning rush hour favored the extension.

breakdown.analysis: Who was asked? People standing on the train platform. Of course rail riders like more rail. The conclusion is about every resident, including people who never ride. It’s like polling people in a gym about whether the city should build another gym. We need to know whether riders’ views match everyone else’s. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it sounds like a sampling fix. But it only spreads the survey across more riders; it never reaches the people who don’t ride.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like a sampling problem. But every station is still full of riders. A yes or a no leaves the gap between riders and non-riders untouched.
So? Benefits to riders might explain why riders like the plan, but the question is whether residents as a whole do.
Irrelevant. A sample of 1,500 is plenty large. The problem is who is in the sample, not how many, and how many people board each morning doesn’t change that.
Wrong dimension. Who votes matters for whether the extension gets approved, not for what most residents think.
CORRECT. If riders and non-riders feel differently, a platform survey overstates support and the conclusion fails. If they feel the same, the riders are a fair stand-in and the conclusion holds up.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: Our policy is to print a correction whenever a figure we have reported is shown to be false, not merely disputed. Last week we reported that the city’s new bridge came in 40 percent over budget. Yesterday the city released its final audited accounts for the project, which show an overrun of only 15 percent. So our figure has been shown to be false, and our policy requires a correction.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the mayor publicly disputed last week’s figure in the days before the city released its audited accounts.
Whether the audited accounts count the same kinds of costs, such as land purchases, as last week’s figure did.
Whether the reporter obtained the 40 percent figure from an employee of the city’s public works department.
Whether other newspapers in the city also reported an overrun much closer to 40 percent than to 15 percent last week.
Whether a 15 percent overrun would be unusually large for a bridge project of this size and type.
questions.explanation: The policy requires a correction only if the figure is shown false. The audit shows a different number, but two figures can both be accurate if they measure different things. (B) asks whether they do: if the audit leaves out costs the newspaper’s figure included, the 40 percent may be right and nothing has been shown false; if the audit counts the same costs, the figure is refuted. (D) is the trap: other papers repeating 40 percent sounds like support, but they could all be counting the same way or copying one another, and it doesn’t touch whether the audit refutes the figure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reported 40 percent figure has been shown false, so the policy requires a correction.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Policy: correct a figure shown false, not one merely disputed; the newspaper reported a 40 percent overrun; the city’s audited accounts show 15 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Does 15 percent refute 40 percent? Only if both numbers measure the same thing. Over budget compared with which budget, counting which costs? If the newspaper counted land and design fees and the audit counts only construction, both numbers can be true. It’s like one friend saying dinner cost $40 and another saying $25 because she didn’t count the tip. We need to know whether the audit and the story count the same costs. Most students who miss this pick (D), because other papers backing the 40 percent figure feels relevant. But corroboration from papers that may have used the same source or method doesn’t tell us whether the audit shows the figure false.

choices.note: Tempting, because the policy mentions disputes. But the editor doesn’t rely on any dispute; the argument rests on the audit. Whether the mayor complained earlier changes nothing.

CORRECT. If the audit leaves out costs the newspaper counted, the two numbers measure different things, and the 40 percent figure hasn’t been shown false. If the audit counts the same costs, the figure is refuted and the policy calls for a correction.
So? Where the reporter got the number doesn’t tell us whether the audit has shown it false.

Tempting. It sounds like evidence for the 40 percent figure. But other papers may have used the same source or method, and their figures don’t show whether the audit refutes the newspaper’s. This is corroboration, not an answer to the question the policy asks.
Irrelevant. The policy is about whether the reported figure is false, not about whether the real overrun is large.

questions.stimulus: Researchers gave the same set of logic puzzles to sixty volunteers. Thirty of the volunteers worked at standing desks and thirty worked seated, and on average those who stood solved more of the puzzles in the time allowed. The researchers concluded that standing while working improves a person’s ability to solve problems.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether any of the volunteers had attempted puzzles from the same set at some time before the study.
Whether the volunteers decided for themselves whether they would stand or sit while working on the puzzles.
Whether the volunteers who stood reported feeling more tired at the end of the session than those who sat.
Whether most of the volunteers had ever worked at a standing desk before taking part in the study.
Whether the volunteers who stood would have solved even more of the puzzles if they had been given additional time.
questions.explanation: The two groups are compared as if they differed only in posture. (B) asks how they were formed: if the volunteers chose, the energetic or confident ones may have picked standing, and the difference could reflect who they were rather than how they worked; if they were assigned, posture is the likelier cause. (A) is the trap: prior exposure to the puzzles would help whoever had it, but nothing suggests those people were concentrated among the standers, so the answer doesn’t bear on the comparison by itself.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Standing while working improves a person’s ability to solve problems.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Of sixty volunteers given the same puzzles, the thirty who stood solved more on average than the thirty who sat.

breakdown.analysis: Who ended up standing? If volunteers picked, the restless, alert or puzzle-loving ones might have chosen the standing desks. Then the gap could come from the people, not the posture. It’s like letting students pick the front row and then crediting the front row for their grades. We need to know how volunteers were sorted into groups. Most students who miss this pick (A), because familiarity with the puzzles would raise scores. But that would matter only if the familiar volunteers ended up mostly in one group, and (A) says nothing about that.

choices.note: Tempting, because familiarity would raise scores. But both groups got the same puzzles, and nothing here says the familiar volunteers clustered on one side. Without that, a yes or a no doesn’t change the comparison.

CORRECT. If volunteers chose their posture, the standers may have differed from the sitters from the start, and the result tells us little about posture. If they were assigned (say, at random), the difference is much more likely due to standing.
So? Standing might be tiring, but the argument is about puzzle-solving, and the standers solved more either way.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Inexperience with standing desks would apply to both groups’ members alike, and the standers still did better. It doesn’t tell us whether posture caused the gap.
Irrelevant. What more time would have done doesn’t tell us why the standers did better in the time they had.

questions.stimulus: Planner: Four years ago the town of Ashby closed its main shopping street to cars, and sales at the street’s shops have since risen by a fifth. Our main street is about the same length as Ashby’s and has a similar number and mix of shops. So if we close our main street to cars, its shops can expect a comparable rise in sales.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether sales at Ashby’s shops rose more in the first year after the closure than in the years that followed.
Whether our main street’s shops now have lower total sales than Ashby’s shops had before the closure.
Whether most of Ashby’s shop owners supported keeping the street closed once the closure had taken effect.
Whether shoppers on our main street are about as likely as Ashby’s shoppers were to arrive there by car.
Whether residents of our town who shop on the main street say they would prefer it to be closed to cars.
questions.explanation: The prediction rests on the two streets being alike, but the planner compares only length and shops, not how shoppers get there, which is exactly what closing a street to cars affects. (D) checks that: if far more of our shoppers drive in, closing the street could cost us customers Ashby never lost; if the proportions match, the analogy holds up better. (B) is the trap: lower sales here might seem to matter, but the prediction is a proportional rise, and a smaller starting figure can still rise by a fifth.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If our main street is closed to cars, its shops can expect a rise in sales comparable to Ashby’s.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ashby closed its main street to cars and sales rose by a fifth; our street is similar in length and in the number and mix of shops.

breakdown.analysis: Similar in the ways that matter? Length and shop mix are the planner’s evidence, but closing a street to cars matters most to people who come by car. If Ashby’s shoppers mostly walked or took the bus while ours mostly drive, the same move could cut our traffic. It’s like concluding a diet that worked for your marathon-running friend will work the same for you because you’re the same height. We need the relevant similarity: how shoppers arrive. Most students who miss this pick (B), because a difference between the towns sounds like an analogy problem. But the prediction is a percentage rise, and starting lower doesn’t stop a rise of a fifth.

choices.note: So? The planner predicts the overall rise. When within those four years Ashby’s gains came doesn’t affect whether our street would get a comparable one.

Tempting, because it’s a real difference between the towns. But the prediction is a rise of a fifth, a proportion. Starting from lower sales doesn’t stop a proportional rise, so the answer doesn’t bear on the prediction.
Irrelevant. Shop owners’ opinions about the closure don’t show what it would do to our sales.

CORRECT. Closing a street to cars matters most to shoppers who drive there. If ours drive in much more often than Ashby’s did, the closure could cost our shops customers, and the analogy breaks down. If the share is about the same, the comparison is fairer.
Tempting, but preferences aren’t sales. People can like a car-free street and still shop less there if they can’t park nearby. And it doesn’t compare our town with Ashby.

questions.stimulus: Last March, Dunmore County installed signs along County Road 12 that flash each approaching driver’s speed. In the twelve months since, crashes on that road have fallen by 35 percent compared with the previous twelve months, while crashes on other county roads have not declined. So the signs have reduced crashes on County Road 12 by getting drivers to slow down.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the average speed of vehicles on County Road 12 has fallen since the signs were installed.
Whether drivers on County Road 12 have reported finding the flashing signs distracting.
Whether most of the crashes on County Road 12 before last March took place after dark.
Whether other counties that installed such signs saw crashes fall by more than 35 percent.
Whether the county plans to install similar signs on its other roads during the coming year.
questions.explanation: The argument already has a comparison (other roads didn’t improve), but its conclusion names a mechanism: the signs worked by slowing drivers down. (A) tests that link directly: if speeds fell, the mechanism is confirmed; if speeds stayed the same, the crash drop must have some other cause, and the argument fails. (D) is the trap: it compares the size of the drop with other counties, but bigger or smaller drops elsewhere don’t show why crashes fell here.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The signs reduced crashes on County Road 12 by getting drivers to slow down.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: After speed-display signs went up, crashes on County Road 12 fell 35 percent, while crashes on other county roads didn’t decline.

breakdown.analysis: Did drivers actually slow down? The argument has a control, so the usual ’what about other roads?’ worry is covered. But it claims a specific mechanism. If speeds on the road didn’t change, the signs can’t have worked by slowing people, and something else (new pavement, a closed bar, a rerouted truck route) did the work. It’s like crediting a new alarm clock for your getting to work on time, without checking whether you’re actually waking up earlier. We need to know whether speeds fell. Most students who miss this pick (D), because comparing with other counties feels like testing the result. But how much crashes fell elsewhere can’t tell us why they fell here.

choices.note: CORRECT. The conclusion says the signs worked by slowing drivers. If average speeds dropped, that’s just what the argument predicts. If they didn’t, the crash decline has another cause, and the argument falls apart.
So? Even if drivers found the signs distracting, crashes fell. A complaint about distraction doesn’t tell us whether slower driving is what cut crashes.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. When crashes used to happen doesn’t tell us whether drivers slowed down or why crashes fell.
Tempting, because it measures the result against other places. But a larger or smaller drop elsewhere doesn’t show whether drivers here slowed down. Different roads, different drivers.
Irrelevant. Future plans don’t bear on what caused last year’s drop.

questions.stimulus: Researchers have concluded that playing action video games improves a person’s visual attention. Their evidence is that teenagers who play such games for at least five hours a week score markedly higher on standard tests of visual attention than do teenagers of the same age who rarely play them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the frequent players already scored higher on such tests before they began playing action games regularly.
Whether the frequent players’ advantage is as large on tests of auditory attention as on tests of visual attention.
Whether the frequent players’ advantage is large enough to make a difference in everyday tasks such as driving.
Whether the teenagers who rarely play action games spend as many hours as the frequent players do watching videos.
Whether adults who play action video games also score higher on these tests than adults who rarely play them.
questions.explanation: A correlation between playing and attention doesn’t show which came first. (A) checks: if the frequent players already had sharper attention before they started, they may have been drawn to games they’re good at, and the games did nothing; if they started out even, the games look responsible. (E) is the trap: finding the same gap in adults repeats the correlation in a new group, but it doesn’t show the games caused it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Playing action video games improves a person’s visual attention.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Teenagers who play action games at least five hours a week score markedly higher on visual-attention tests than those who rarely play.

breakdown.analysis: Which came first? Kids with sharp eyes may love fast games because they’re good at them. Then the games are a symptom, not a cause. It’s like noticing that basketball players are tall and concluding that basketball makes you grow. We need to know whether the players were already ahead before they played much. Most students who miss this pick (E), because finding the same gap in adults feels like confirmation. But it’s the same correlation in a different group, with the same question about which came first.

choices.note: CORRECT. If frequent players were already ahead before they started playing much, the gap reflects who chooses these games, not what the games do. If they started out even and pulled ahead, the games look like the cause.
Irrelevant. The conclusion is about visual attention only. Whether the gap extends to hearing doesn’t bear on what caused it.
So? The argument is about whether games improve attention, not whether the improvement is big enough to matter on the road.
Tempting, because it looks for a hidden difference between the groups. But there’s no reason to think video-watching affects these test scores, so a yes or a no doesn’t change the picture.

Tempting, because it looks like confirming evidence. But it’s the same correlation in another group, and adults who are good at attention tasks may also gravitate toward these games. It can’t settle which way the cause runs.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Among users of the Mailvane e-mail service, those who have turned on two-step verification are more likely than other users to report that their accounts have been broken into at some point. Two-step verification, then, does nothing to protect accounts from intruders and may even make them easier to break into.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Do most Mailvane users who have turned on two-step verification also use it for their other online accounts?
Do intruders who break into accounts protected by two-step verification usually do so by stealing the user’s phone?
Were some of the break-ins reported by Mailvane users carried out by people whom the users knew personally?
Is the number of Mailvane users who report break-ins larger this year than it was last year?
Did most users who reported a break-in turn on two-step verification only after that break-in occurred?
questions.explanation: The columnist treats two-step verification as coming before the break-ins, but the users report break-ins that happened “at some point.” (E) asks about time order: if most of them turned the feature on after being broken into, the break-ins explain the verification, not the reverse, and the argument fails; if they had it on beforehand, the columnist’s worry gains force. (B) is the trap: it describes how protected accounts get broken into, but a way of beating the feature doesn’t show it does nothing, and a no wouldn’t help the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Two-step verification does nothing to protect accounts and may make them easier to break into.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Mailvane users with two-step verification turned on are more likely than other users to report having been broken into at some point.

breakdown.analysis: Which came first, the lock or the burglary? People often add security right after something goes wrong. If most of these users turned on two-step verification after an intruder got in, the break-ins explain the feature, not the other way around. It’s like noticing that houses with alarm systems are more likely to have been burgled and concluding that alarms attract burglars. We need to know when the feature was switched on. Most students who miss this pick (B), because it’s about how two-step accounts get broken into. But knowing one way around a protection can’t show it never helps.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What users do with their other accounts doesn’t tell us whether the feature protects their Mailvane accounts.

Tempting, because it seems to explain how two-step accounts get broken into. But a way around a protection doesn’t show the protection does nothing, and a no doesn’t make the argument any stronger or weaker.
So? Some intruders being acquaintances doesn’t bear on whether two-step verification protects accounts.
Irrelevant. A year-to-year change in total break-ins says nothing about whether users with the feature are more or less protected.

CORRECT. This is the time-order question. If most victims turned on two-step verification after being broken into, the break-ins caused the feature, and the correlation says nothing about protection. If they had it on before, the columnist’s worry looks more serious.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: Employers in Dresk have been required since 2010 to record every complaint of workplace bullying. In 2019 a new law gave bullying its first precise legal definition, and since then the number of complaints recorded per thousand employees has risen by 60 percent. Clearly, bullying has become far more common in Dresk’s workplaces since 2019.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Does the 2019 definition count as bullying some conduct that employees would not previously have reported as bullying?
Are complaints of workplace bullying in Dresk more often made by younger employees than by older employees?
Has the total number of people employed in Dresk grown since the new law took effect in 2019?
Had the number of complaints recorded per thousand employees also been rising in the years between 2010 and 2019?
Will the rise in recorded complaints lead Dresk’s employers to adopt stricter workplace policies?
questions.explanation: The sociologist reads a rise in complaints as a rise in bullying, but the rise began when the definition changed. (A) tests whether the measure itself shifted: if the new definition covers conduct people didn’t report before, complaints could rise with no more bullying than before; if it covers the same conduct, the rise more likely reflects real change. (D) is the trap: an earlier upward trend would matter if the argument credited the law, but the conclusion only says bullying grew since 2019, and an earlier rise neither shows nor rules out that complaints now overstate it. (C) is answered by the per-thousand figure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bullying has become far more common in Dresk’s workplaces since 2019.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Employers have recorded bullying complaints since 2010; since a 2019 law precisely defined bullying, recorded complaints per thousand employees rose 60 percent.

breakdown.analysis: More bullying, or more things counted as bullying? When a law draws a new line around a term, conduct that used to be shrugged off can suddenly count. Then the records rise even if workplaces behave exactly as before. It’s like a school redefining “late” as one minute instead of ten and announcing that lateness has soared. We want to know whether the definition widened what gets reported. Most students who miss this pick (D), because a pre-existing trend is a familiar thing to check. But the conclusion doesn’t say the law caused anything; it says bullying became more common. An earlier trend doesn’t tell us whether today’s complaints measure bullying the same way as before.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the 2019 definition sweeps in conduct people didn’t report before, the rise could come from the new definition rather than from more bullying, and the argument collapses. If it covers the same conduct people already reported, the rise is more likely real.
Irrelevant. Who complains more doesn’t tell us whether the rise reflects more bullying or a broader definition.
Tempting, because more workers would mean more complaints. But the figure is per thousand employees, so workforce growth is already accounted for.

Tempting, because checking an earlier trend is a standard move. But the argument doesn’t credit the law; it says bullying itself grew. Whether complaints were climbing before 2019 doesn’t show whether the post-2019 count measures the same thing.
So? What employers do next is a consequence. It doesn’t tell us whether bullying actually became more common.

questions.stimulus: When interviewers asked a random sample of Brindmoor residents in person whether they had driven after drinking alcohol in the past year, 18 percent said yes. In an anonymous online survey of a different random sample of residents, 31 percent said yes. Since people are reluctant to admit such behavior to an interviewer, the online survey evidently gives the more accurate estimate.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the interviewers who questioned the first sample were themselves residents of Brindmoor.
Whether driving after drinking is more common in Brindmoor than in the towns that surround it.
Whether residents of other towns also report driving after drinking more often in anonymous online surveys than they do in person.
Whether people answering anonymous surveys are inclined to claim risky behavior in which they have not actually engaged.
Whether the online survey’s estimate would have been higher still if it had asked about the past two years rather than one.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes the gap between the surveys comes only from underreporting in person. (D) raises the other possibility: if anonymous respondents sometimes claim risky behavior they never engaged in, the 31 percent may be inflated and the truth could lie anywhere between the two figures; if they don’t, the higher online figure is the more believable one. (C) is the trap: the same gap in other towns makes the pattern look real, but a gap could come from underreporting or overreporting, so its recurrence can’t tell us which figure is accurate. (A) only bears on the reluctance the argument already grants.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The anonymous online survey gives the more accurate estimate of how many Brindmoor residents drove after drinking.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 18 percent said yes in person; 31 percent said yes in an anonymous online survey of a different random sample; people are reluctant to admit such behavior to an interviewer.

breakdown.analysis: Is the error all on one side? The argument explains the gap by people hiding things from interviewers. But anonymity cuts both ways: with no one watching, some people exaggerate or joke. If so, the online figure is too high, and the truth could be anywhere in between. It’s like deciding that the higher of two bathroom scales must be right because the lower one is known to read light. We need to know whether anonymous respondents overreport. Most students who miss this pick (C), because finding the same gap elsewhere feels like confirmation. But a gap produced by online overreporting would show up in every town too.

choices.note: Tempting, because neighbors as interviewers would make people even more reluctant. But the argument already grants that people underreport in person. This could only support that premise; it doesn’t tell us whether the online figure is accurate.
Irrelevant. How Brindmoor compares with nearby towns doesn’t tell us which survey measured Brindmoor correctly.

Tempting, and the main trap. A gap that shows up in other towns looks like a real effect of the survey method. But it would show up either way: from people hiding things in person or from people exaggerating online. So it can’t pick between the two figures.

CORRECT. If anonymous respondents sometimes claim behavior they never engaged in, the 31 percent overstates the truth, and the online survey may be no more accurate than the interviews. If they don’t, the online figure is the better estimate.
So? A two-year question would count more people, but that says nothing about which one-year estimate is accurate.

questions.stimulus: Of the forty pumps at the Ressel water treatment plant, the twelve fitted with a new seal design have needed seal repairs only twice in the past five years, while the twenty-eight with the older design have needed thirty seal repairs. So the new design makes pump seals far more reliable.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether seal repairs on the older-design pumps have taken the plant’s crews longer to complete than repairs on the new-design pumps.
Whether seal repairs account for most of the repairs that the plant’s pumps have needed over the past five years.
Whether the pumps with the new seal design were put into service only within the past year.
Whether some of the seal repairs on the older-design pumps were needed because of mistakes made during installation.
Whether replacing the older seals with the new design would require shutting down the plant for several days.
questions.explanation: The comparison counts repairs over five years, which is fair only if both groups of pumps were running for all five years. (C) checks this: if the new-design pumps have been in service for only a year or so, they’ve had far less time to fail, and new parts rarely fail early anyway; if they’ve run the whole period, the new design looks much better. (D) is the trap: it offers another reason for the older pumps’ repairs, but only “some” of thirty, which can’t erase a gap of 2 repairs for 12 pumps against 30 for 28.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new seal design makes pump seals far more reliable.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Over the past five years, the twelve new-design pumps needed two seal repairs; the twenty-eight older-design pumps needed thirty.

breakdown.analysis: Were the new pumps even running for five years? If they were installed last year, two repairs in one year is no better than the old pumps’ record, and fresh parts fail least. It’s like comparing the dents on a car you bought last month with the dents on a car you’ve driven for five years. We need to know how long the new-design pumps have been in service. Notice that the per-pump numbers are already given: 2 for 12 versus 30 for 28, so count-versus-rate isn’t the issue. Most students who miss this pick (D), because it offers an alternative cause. But a few installation mistakes can’t account for a gap that large.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. How long a repair takes has nothing to do with how often seals fail.
Irrelevant. The argument compares seal repairs only. What share of all repairs they make up doesn’t affect the comparison.

CORRECT. This is about time in service. If the new-design pumps started running only a year or so ago, they’ve had a fraction of the time to fail, and the comparison is lopsided. If they’ve been running all five years, the comparison is fair and the new design looks much better.
Tempting, because it’s an alternative cause for some old-design repairs. But “some” of thirty can’t close a gap like this one, and a no wouldn’t strengthen the argument much either.
So? Disruption from switching is a reason for or against adopting the design, not evidence about whether it’s more reliable.

questions.stimulus: A six-month study tested a phone app meant to help people drink fewer sugary beverages. Of the 200 people who enrolled, 80 were still using the app at the end of the study, and those 80 were drinking, on average, 60 percent fewer sugary beverages than when they enrolled. The app’s developers concluded that the app is highly effective at helping people cut back on such beverages.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the people who enrolled had been drinking more sugary beverages than the average adult does.
Whether some of the 80 people who kept using the app cut back by much more than 60 percent.
Whether the 80 people who kept using the app also ate fewer sweetened foods during the six months.
Whether most of the 80 people who kept using the app said they would recommend it to a friend.
Whether people who stopped using the app tended to stop because they were not managing to cut back.
questions.explanation: The results come only from the 80 people who stayed, and those who stayed may be the ones who were succeeding. (E) tests that selection effect: if people quit because they weren’t cutting back, the 60 percent figure reflects only the success stories and overstates the app’s effectiveness; if they quit for unrelated reasons, the 80 are a fairer sample. (C) is the trap: cutting back on sweets too might look like a sign of a general diet change rather than the app’s effect, but the conclusion is only about beverages, and either answer leaves the dropout problem untouched.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The app is highly effective at helping people cut back on sugary beverages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Of 200 enrollees, the 80 still using the app after six months were drinking 60 percent fewer sugary beverages than at enrollment.

breakdown.analysis: What about the other 120? Only the people who stuck with the app were counted. If people quit because it wasn’t working for them, the 80 who stayed are the success stories, and of course they did well. It’s like a diet company bragging about the weight lost by customers who renewed their memberships. We need to know why the dropouts dropped out. Most students who miss this pick (C), because a broad change in eating habits sounds like an alternative explanation. But people who resolve to cut sugar may do both with the app’s help, and either answer still leaves the 120 dropouts unexplained.

choices.note: Interesting fact, but not relevant. Heavy drinkers may be the people who want such an app, but how much they drank before doesn’t tell us whether the 60 percent figure represents everyone who tried it.
So? 60 percent is an average, so some people cutting back by more is built in. A yes or a no leaves the argument unchanged.

Tempting, because it suggests a general diet change. But the app could have prompted both changes, and a yes or a no tells us nothing about the 120 people who quit, which is where the argument is weakest.
So? Willingness to recommend is opinion, not evidence that the app caused the drop, and it still comes only from the people who stayed.

CORRECT. This targets who was left in the sample. If the dropouts quit because they were failing, the 80 are the app’s success stories and the 60 percent figure flatters it. If they quit for unrelated reasons (lost phones, busy schedules), the 80 are a fairer picture.

questions.stimulus: Clinic director: Nearly a fifth of our appointment slots go unused because patients fail to show up. Starting next month, we will charge a $25 fee for any appointment that is missed without being canceled. Since the fee will sharply cut the number of no-shows, our doctors will be able to see substantially more patients each week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether most of the patients who missed appointments last year missed more than one.
Whether $25 is more than the clinic loses, on average, each time an appointment slot goes unused.
Whether slots freed when patients cancel shortly before their appointments can usually be filled by other patients.
Whether other clinics that have begun charging such fees have seen their rates of no-shows fall.
Whether patients who miss appointments are disproportionately ones with minor complaints rather than serious conditions.
questions.explanation: The fee applies only to appointments missed without a cancellation, so a patient who would have skipped can avoid it by canceling, perhaps at the last minute. Fewer no-shows means more doctor time only if those freed slots get used. (C) tests that: if late cancellations can usually be refilled, the plan delivers; if not, slots go empty under a different name and no more patients are seen. (D) is the trap: it supports the claim that the fee cuts no-shows, which the director already treats as given; the weak link is what happens to the slots.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Charging a $25 no-show fee will let the clinic’s doctors see substantially more patients each week.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly a fifth of slots go unused because of no-shows; the fee applies to appointments missed without cancellation; the fee will sharply cut no-shows.

breakdown.analysis: So the no-shows drop. Does the empty slot go away? A patient who would have skipped can dodge the fee by calling to cancel an hour before. That’s no longer a no-show, but the slot is just as empty unless someone else can take it. It’s like a restaurant fining diners who don’t show up: if they cancel at 6:55 for a 7:00 table, the table still sits empty. We need to know whether last-minute openings get filled. Most students who miss this pick (D), because evidence that such fees work elsewhere sounds like a direct test of the plan. But the argument already takes for granted that no-shows will fall; the gap is between fewer no-shows and more patients seen.

choices.note: Tempting, because repeat offenders might shrug off a fee. But the argument already asserts that no-shows will fall; the open question is whether that means more patients are seen.
Wrong dimension. Whether the fee covers the clinic’s losses is about money, not about how many patients the doctors see.

CORRECT. Patients can avoid the fee by canceling late. If those last-minute openings usually get filled, cutting no-shows means more patients are seen. If they usually can’t be filled, the slots go unused anyway and the plan gains nothing.

Tempting, and the main trap. It looks like a test of the plan, but it only supports a claim the director already makes: that no-shows will fall. Even if they do, the doctors see more patients only if the freed time gets used.
Irrelevant. The argument is about how many patients are seen, not which kinds of patients miss appointments.

questions.stimulus: Hiring manager: Over the past year, applicants who learned programming at a twelve-week coding school scored higher, on average, on our technical interview than applicants with four-year degrees in computer science. Our interview consists entirely of short, timed coding exercises. So the coding school’s graduates are, on the whole, better programmers than the degree holders who apply to us.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether graduates of the coding school have also outscored degree holders in the technical interviews of other companies.
Whether the coding school trains its students on timed exercises much like those in technical interviews.
Whether the exercises in the company’s interview were written by the company’s own senior programmers or by an outside firm.
Whether the coding school admits only applicants who first pass a demanding entrance test.
Whether the degree holders who apply to the company are typical of computer science graduates in general.
questions.explanation: The manager treats interview scores as a measure of programming skill. (B) asks whether the scores could reflect something else: if the coding school drills its students on exactly this kind of timed exercise, its graduates may score higher because they’ve practiced the format, not because they program better; if it doesn’t, the scores are a fairer measure. (D) is the trap: a selective entrance test would explain why the graduates are good, but the conclusion only says they are better, not that the school made them so. (E) fails because the conclusion is limited to degree holders who apply to this company.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The coding school’s graduates are, on the whole, better programmers than the degree holders who apply to the company.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Coding-school applicants scored higher on average than degree holders on the company’s technical interview, which consists entirely of short, timed coding exercises.

breakdown.analysis: Does the interview measure programming, or practice at interviews? If the coding school spends its twelve weeks drilling exactly these timed puzzles, its graduates walk in knowing the format cold. Their higher scores might show interview prep, not better programming. It’s like concluding that students from a test-prep course are smarter because they scored higher on the test the course taught. We need to know whether the school trains for this format. Most students who miss this pick (D), because it offers another explanation. But it explains why the graduates might be better, not whether they are; the conclusion makes no claim about the school causing anything.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like confirming evidence. But if the graduates have practiced interview-style exercises, they’d outscore degree holders at every company’s interview. More of the same measurement can’t show the measurement is valid.

CORRECT. If the school trains students on this very format, the scores may measure practice with the format, not programming ability, and the conclusion is in trouble. If it doesn’t, the scores are a better guide to who programs better.
So? Who wrote the exercises doesn’t tell us whether they favor one group or measure programming fairly.

Tempting, because it raises a selection effect. But the conclusion isn’t that the school makes people better programmers; it’s that its graduates are better. Selective admission would explain that, not undercut it.
Tempting, but the conclusion is limited to degree holders who apply to this company. Whether they are typical of all computer science graduates doesn’t matter.

questions.stimulus: Automaker: Most car buyers who decide against an electric car say that worry about running out of charge on the road is their main reason. Yet in a survey of people who own our electric cars, 90 percent said they rarely or never worry about running out of charge. So most buyers who now reject electric cars for this reason would stop worrying about it once they owned one.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether most of the owners surveyed already worried little about running out of charge before they bought their cars.
Whether buyers who reject electric cars because of this worry also mention the cars’ purchase prices as a reason.
Whether more buyers would choose the automaker’s electric cars if their worry about running out of charge were eliminated.
Whether some of the owners surveyed actually ran out of charge on the road at least once during the past year.
Whether owners of other automakers’ electric cars say they worry about running out of charge as rarely as these owners do.
questions.explanation: The owners surveyed are people who chose electric cars, so they may never have shared the worry that keeps other buyers away. (A) tests that selection effect: if the owners worried little even before buying, their calm says nothing about what ownership would do for anxious buyers; if many of them worried beforehand, ownership looks like it cured the worry. (E) is the trap: the same calm among other brands’ owners repeats the survey with the same kind of self-selected people, so it can’t show that ownership changes anyone’s mind.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most buyers who reject electric cars because of range worry would stop worrying once they owned one.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most buyers who reject electric cars cite range worry; 90 percent of the automaker’s electric-car owners rarely or never worry about it.

breakdown.analysis: Who buys an electric car? Probably the people who weren’t worried about running out of charge in the first place. If so, the owners’ calm is a filter, not a transformation. It’s like surveying people at a roller coaster’s exit and concluding that riding cures fear of heights. We need to know whether the owners worried before they bought. Most students who miss this pick (E), because a bigger survey sounds like stronger evidence. But other brands’ owners also chose their cars, so the same filter applies.

choices.note: CORRECT. This targets who ended up in the sample. If the owners were unworried even before buying, their answers tell us nothing about what ownership would do for worried buyers, and the argument collapses. If many of them worried before, owning the car seems to have removed the worry.
Irrelevant. Price is a separate reason to reject a car. The argument is only about whether the worry would fade with ownership.
Tempting, because it’s about the same worry. But it asks what would happen if the worry vanished, not whether owning a car would make it vanish, which is what the conclusion claims.
So? Owners who ran out of charge and still don’t worry might seem to support the argument, but either way it says nothing about whether the surveyed owners were ever worried to begin with.

Tempting, and the main trap. More owners saying the same thing looks like confirmation. But they too chose electric cars, so the same filter applies, and the answer can’t tell us whether ownership changes anyone’s mind.

questions.stimulus: Museum director: Our mission is to bring art to as many of the city’s residents as possible. City residents enter free by showing a resident pass, and last year the number of resident-pass admissions was 40 percent higher than in any previous year. Clearly, then, last year we fulfilled our mission more fully than ever before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the museum’s total attendance, including visitors from outside the city, also rose by 40 percent last year.
Whether last year’s rise in resident-pass admissions was due mainly to a single popular special exhibition.
Whether the city’s population grew substantially between the year before last and last year.
Whether residents who visited last year came more times each, on average, than resident visitors in earlier years.
Whether residents who visited last year spent more time in the galleries on each visit than resident visitors in earlier years did.
questions.explanation: The mission is about how many residents the museum reaches, but the evidence counts admissions, and one resident can be admitted many times. (D) tests whether those come apart: if the same people simply came back more often, more admissions need not mean more residents reached; if visits per person held steady, more admissions mean more people. (B) is the trap: a blockbuster exhibition would explain the rise, but the conclusion is about whether the mission was fulfilled, not why, and a show that draws more residents still draws more residents.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Last year the museum fulfilled its mission (reaching as many residents as possible) more fully than ever.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Resident-pass admissions last year were 40 percent higher than in any previous year.

breakdown.analysis: Admissions or people? The mission counts residents reached, but the premise counts trips through the door. If a few hundred enthusiasts came back every weekend, admissions soar while the number of people reached stays flat. It’s like a gym counting check-ins and claiming more members than ever. We need to know whether visits per person changed. Most students who miss this pick (B), because a one-time blockbuster sounds like a reason to discount the rise. But the director isn’t predicting next year or crediting a policy; residents drawn by a special show are still residents reached.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The mission is about the city’s residents. Visitors from elsewhere don’t count either way.

Tempting, and the main trap. It explains the rise, but the conclusion is about whether the mission was fulfilled, not about what caused it. If a special show brought in more residents, the museum still reached more residents.

Tempting, because a bigger city might seem to make the rise less impressive. But the mission is to reach as many residents as possible, a number, not a share. Population growth doesn’t change how many were reached.

CORRECT. Admissions count visits, not people. If residents came more times each, the 40 percent rise could reflect the same people returning, and the museum may have reached no more residents than before. If visits per person held steady, more admissions do mean more residents reached.
So? Longer visits might mean residents got more out of the museum, but the mission as stated is about how many residents are reached, not how deeply.

questions.stimulus: Phosphorus from lawn fertilizer is the main source of the phosphorus that feeds the summer algae blooms in Lake Orrin. Two years ago the county banned phosphorus fertilizers on lawns near the lake, and last summer’s blooms were the smallest in a decade. Some credit last summer’s cool weather instead, but blooms were large in several other cool summers. So the ban is what shrank the blooms.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the blooms in those other cool summers were as large as the blooms in the decade’s warmest summers.
Whether phosphorus from lawn fertilizer typically takes a decade or more of slow movement through the soil to reach the lake.
Whether most residents who live near the lake supported the ban when it was first proposed.
Whether farms upstream of the lake contribute at least some of the phosphorus that reaches it.
Whether the lake’s blooms are expected to keep shrinking for as long as the ban remains in force.
questions.explanation: The argument answers the weather explanation, but crediting the ban also requires that the ban could have had an effect by last summer. (B) tests the timing: if fertilizer phosphorus takes many years to reach the lake, the phosphorus feeding last summer’s blooms was applied before the ban, so the ban can’t be what shrank them; if it arrives quickly, the ban could well be responsible. (D) is the dominant trap: an extra phosphorus source sounds like a rival cause, but the stimulus already makes lawns the main source, and farm runoff that didn’t change can’t explain a drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ban on lawn phosphorus fertilizer is what shrank last summer’s algae blooms.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lawn fertilizer is the lake’s main phosphorus source; the ban took effect two years ago; last summer’s blooms were the smallest in a decade; cool weather isn’t the explanation, since other cool summers had large blooms.

breakdown.analysis: Could the ban have worked yet? The argument handles the weather rival nicely. But a cause has to arrive before its effect. If phosphorus spread on lawns seeps through soil for years before reaching the lake, then last summer’s lake was still being fed by fertilizer applied long before the ban. The ban would be too recent to get the credit. It’s like crediting this morning’s diet for the weight you lost last week. We need to know how long fertilizer takes to reach the water. Most students who miss this pick (D), because another phosphorus source feels like a rival explanation. But the stimulus already says lawns are the main source, and an unchanged farm contribution can’t explain why the blooms shrank.

choices.note: Tempting, because it digs into the argument’s rebuttal. But the rebuttal only needs those cool-summer blooms to be large. Whether they matched the very biggest ones doesn’t matter.

CORRECT. Timing. If fertilizer phosphorus reaches the lake only after years in the soil, what fed last summer’s blooms was applied before the ban, and the ban can’t explain the drop. If it reaches the lake quickly, the ban’s timing fits.
So? Supporting a ban isn’t obeying it, and opinions at the time of the proposal don’t tell us what shrank the blooms.

Tempting, and the main trap. It sounds like a rival source of phosphorus. But the stimulus already makes lawn fertilizer the main source, and a farm contribution that hasn’t changed can’t explain why blooms shrank.
Irrelevant. Predictions about future summers don’t tell us what caused last summer’s small blooms.

questions.stimulus: Last spring, new control software was installed in eight of the twenty elevators in the Tolvane Tower. Each of those eight has broken down less often since then than it did in the year before, while the other twelve have broken down about as often as they did before. So the new software reduces elevator breakdowns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the twelve elevators without the software are used about as heavily as the eight that received it.
Whether the eight elevators with the software have broken down less often since last spring than the twelve without it have.
Whether any of the breakdowns in the eight elevators before last spring were caused by mechanical faults rather than by software faults.
Whether the eight elevators were chosen for the software because they had broken down unusually often the year before.
Whether the building’s maintenance staff were trained to service the new software before it was installed.
questions.explanation: The argument even has a comparison group, which makes it look airtight. But if the eight elevators were picked because they’d just had an unusually bad year, they would likely break down less the next year anyway, the way an unusually bad stretch tends to be followed by a more ordinary one. (D) tests this: a yes means the improvement may be a return to normal; a no (say, the eight were picked at random) makes the software the best explanation. (B) is the trap: it compares the two groups’ current breakdown levels, but the argument rests on each elevator’s change from its own past, which a level comparison can’t test.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new software reduces elevator breakdowns.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The eight elevators that got the software each broke down less often than in the year before; the twelve without it broke down about as often as before.

breakdown.analysis: Why those eight? If someone picked the elevators that had the worst year, some of that bad year was probably bad luck, and bad luck rarely repeats. Next year they’d look better with or without new software. It’s like a coach sending his coldest shooters to a week of special drills, then crediting the drills when their shooting returns to normal. This is called regression to the mean; it’s worth knowing. We need to know how the eight were chosen. Most students who miss this pick (B), because comparing the two groups head to head feels rigorous. But the evidence is each elevator’s change; the eight could still break down more than the twelve and have improved.

choices.note: Tempting, because heavier use means more breakdowns. But each elevator is compared with its own past. A difference in use between the groups matters only if use changed, and this doesn’t ask that.

Tempting, and the main trap. It looks like a better comparison. But the argument rests on change over time, not on which group breaks down less now. The eight could still break down more than the twelve and have improved because of the software, or could break down less without the software deserving credit.

Only matters one way. Some breakdowns being mechanical just means the software couldn’t fix everything. It doesn’t show the software didn’t cut the rest, and a no wouldn’t tell us how the eight were picked.

CORRECT. If the eight were chosen for their bad year, they were likely to improve anyway as their luck evened out, and the software may deserve no credit. If they were chosen at random, the improvement is much more likely due to the software.
Irrelevant. Staff training affects how the software is maintained, not whether the drop in breakdowns came from the software.

questions.stimulus: Dean: In a trial, a new software tool correctly flagged 95 percent of a set of essays known to have been produced by text-generating programs. So if we use the tool to screen the essays our students submit, nearly every essay it flags will be one that was produced by such a program.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the tool flagged 95 percent of the program-produced essays no matter which text-generating program had produced them.
Whether some students at the school have admitted to submitting essays produced by text-generating programs.
Whether the program-produced essays that the tool failed to flag had been edited by hand after they were generated.
Whether essays produced by text-generating programs tend to receive lower grades than essays students write themselves.
Whether the tool often flags essays that were written entirely by students without the help of such programs.
questions.explanation: The trial shows the tool catches most program-produced essays, but the conclusion is about the essays it flags, and that depends on how often it flags honest work too. (E) asks exactly that: if the tool often flags student-written essays, then among the school’s many honest essays it will flag plenty, and many flagged essays will be innocent; if it rarely does, flagged essays will mostly be program-produced. (A) is the trap: it sounds like a rigorous check of the 95 percent figure, but that figure only concerns essays the tool should catch, so either answer says nothing about false alarms.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Nearly every essay the tool flags will be one produced by a text-generating program.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a trial, the tool flagged 95 percent of essays known to be produced by such programs.

breakdown.analysis: Catching most of the guilty isn’t the same as accusing only the guilty. Suppose 1,000 essays come in and 50 are program-made. Even if the tool catches 95 percent of those (about 48), it could also flag 10 percent of the 950 honest essays, about 95. Then most flagged essays are honest. It’s like a smoke alarm that never misses a fire but also goes off whenever someone makes toast: most of its alarms are toast. We need to know how often the tool flags honest work. Most students who miss this pick (A), because it digs into the 95 percent figure. But that figure is about catching program essays; it can’t tell us how many honest essays get flagged.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It probes the trial result. But that result is about how many program essays the tool catches. Whether it catches all kinds equally says nothing about how often it flags honest work, which is what the conclusion depends on.
Tempting, because how common cheating is matters here. But “some” admitting it gives no rate at all, and it says nothing about how often the tool flags honest essays.
So? Why the tool missed 5 percent is about the essays it didn’t flag. The conclusion is about the ones it does flag.
Irrelevant. Grades don’t tell us how often the tool flags honest essays.

CORRECT. This is the false-alarm rate. If the tool often flags student-written work, then with many honest essays in the pile, a large share of flagged essays will be innocent, and the conclusion fails. If it rarely does, flagged essays will mostly be program-made.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: Some researchers blame a fungal infection for the collapse of toad populations in the Merrow Valley’s lowland ponds. Admittedly, this fungus has wiped out toad populations in other regions. But toads in the valley’s upland ponds, where populations have held steady, carry the fungus just as often as lowland toads do. So the fungus is probably not what is killing the lowland toads.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether the fungus was first detected in the valley’s upland ponds or in its lowland ponds.
Whether the fungus also infects the frogs and salamanders that live in the valley’s ponds.
Whether conditions that differ between the lowland and upland ponds affect how likely an infected toad is to die.
Whether the researchers who blame the fungus have themselves collected and tested toads from the upland ponds.
Whether the fungus has been shown in controlled laboratory experiments to kill toads that were previously healthy.
questions.explanation: The biologist reasons that because infection is equally common where toads thrive and where they die, infection can’t be what kills them. That holds only if an infection is equally dangerous in both places. (C) tests that: if something about the lowland ponds (warmer water, say, or pollution that weakens toads) makes infected toads far likelier to die, the fungus could be killing lowland toads while upland carriers survive; if conditions make no difference, equal infection with unequal outcomes points away from the fungus. (E) is the dominant trap: proof that the fungus can kill toads seems to answer the biologist, but the biologist already concedes it is deadly elsewhere; the question is why it would be harmless in the uplands.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The fungus is probably not what is killing the lowland toads.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The fungus has wiped out toads in other regions (conceded); upland toads, whose populations are stable, carry the fungus as often as lowland toads do.

breakdown.analysis: Same infection, same danger? The biologist’s inference works only if carrying the fungus means the same thing in every pond. But a disease can be mild in one setting and deadly in another: heat, pollution or crowding can tip an infected animal over. If lowland conditions make infection lethal, the fungus could be the killer there even though upland carriers shrug it off. It’s like noting that as many people carry a cold virus in a healthy town as in a nursing home and concluding the virus isn’t what’s sickening the residents. We need to know whether local conditions change how deadly infection is. The answer is hard to like because it never mentions the fungus’s deadliness directly. Most students who miss this pick (E), because lab proof of lethality sounds like a direct reply to the biologist. But the biologist already grants the fungus kills toads; the argument is about why it isn’t killing the upland ones.

choices.note: Tempting, because timing questions often matter. But either answer leaves the key fact in place: both groups now carry the fungus equally, yet only one is dying. Where it showed up first doesn’t explain that.
Irrelevant. Other species aren’t part of the argument, which is about toads in two kinds of ponds.

CORRECT. The argument needs infection to be equally dangerous everywhere. If lowland conditions make infected toads much likelier to die, equal infection rates are just what we’d expect even if the fungus is the killer, and the argument fails. If conditions make no difference, the biologist’s point stands.
So? Whether the researchers checked the uplands is about them, not about whether the fungus is killing lowland toads. The biologist has already reported the upland data.

Tempting, and the main trap. Proof that the fungus kills toads sounds like a direct answer. But the biologist already concedes the fungus is deadly in other regions. The argument doesn’t deny it can kill; it argues that it isn’t what’s killing these toads, and lab results don’t touch that.

questions.stimulus: In the Orsley housing estate, buildings in which each entrance and stairwell serves only four apartments suffer far less vandalism than buildings in which each entrance serves twenty or more apartments. Evidently, residents who share an entrance with only a few households come to recognize one another, and so they readily notice and challenge strangers who enter their building.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Repair records confirm that the housing authority spends much less money fixing vandalism damage in the small-entrance buildings than in the others.
Vandalism in Orsley's large-entrance buildings is concentrated in the stairwells, which in those buildings are long, windowless, and poorly lit.
Orsley's small-entrance buildings are scattered among its large-entrance buildings rather than grouped together in one part of the estate.
Several housing estates in other cities have recently been redesigned so that each entrance serves fewer apartments than before.
Residents of Orsley's large-entrance buildings are more likely than other residents to say that they would move elsewhere if they could.
questions.explanation: The argument credits entrance size, through neighbors recognizing each other, for the vandalism gap. One rival is location: if the small-entrance buildings sat together in a quieter or better-patrolled corner, place rather than design could explain the gap. (C) rules that out, since the two building types are mixed together across the estate. (A) is the main trap: lower repair costs just restate that the small-entrance buildings suffer less vandalism, which is the premise, not the explanation. (B) offers a rival cause (dark stairwells) and so weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Small-entrance buildings have less vandalism because residents recognize one another and challenge strangers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In Orsley, buildings with four apartments per entrance have far less vandalism than buildings with twenty or more per entrance.

breakdown.analysis: The correlation is given. The question is why. Could something other than entrance size be doing the work? Lighting, tenants, or plain location: maybe the small buildings all sit in a quiet corner by the police station. We need an answer that knocks out a rival or backs the recognize-the-neighbors story. Think of two cafés with different seating where one gets fewer thefts; before you credit the seating, check they aren't on different streets. Most students pick (A) because it mentions vandalism in the small-entrance buildings. It fails because cheaper repairs just repeat the premise in money terms. It says nothing about why.
