choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Lower repair bills are what you'd expect if there's less vandalism, which we already know. Confirming a premise doesn't touch the gap between the correlation and the explanation.
This points to a rival cause: dark, windowless stairwells invite vandalism. If anything it weakens the recognition story.

CORRECT. If the small-entrance buildings are mixed in among the large ones, they share the same streets, patrols and surroundings. That rules out location as the explanation and leaves design, and the recognition mechanism, standing.
So? Other estates copying the design doesn't show the design works, let alone why it works.
Interesting fact, but not relevant. Wanting to move out could reflect noise, size or anything else. It doesn't link entrance size to vandalism.

questions.stimulus: Architect: The proposal to replace the Halsey Building's original steel-framed windows with sealed modern units should be rejected. Because occupants could no longer open their windows on mild days, sealed units would make the building more dependent on mechanical ventilation. And that added dependence would cancel most of the energy savings the units' better insulation is supposed to provide, which is the proposal's chief justification.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the architect's argument by the claim that sealed units would make the building more dependent on mechanical ventilation?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, which is supported by the claim that occupants could no longer open their windows on mild days.
It is a premise offered in direct support of the main conclusion, and no other claim in the argument is offered in support of it.
It is a claim that the proposal's supporters use to justify replacing the windows, and the architect seeks to refute it.
It is an objection to the proposal that the architect concedes is outweighed by the energy savings that better insulation would bring.
It is a conclusion drawn from one claim and offered in support of another claim that bears on the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The claim is supported by the 'because' clause (occupants could no longer open the windows) and in turn supports the next claim, that the added dependence would cancel most of the savings, which undercuts the proposal's chief justification and so supports rejecting it. That makes it an intermediate conclusion, as (E) says. (B) is the trap: it treats the claim as a bare premise, but the 'because' clause supports it. (A) mistakes it for the main conclusion, which is the first sentence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The proposal to replace the Halsey Building's windows with sealed units should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Occupants couldn't open sealed windows on mild days; so the building would depend more on mechanical ventilation; that would cancel most of the insulation savings, the proposal's main justification.

breakdown.analysis: Map the chain: 1. occupants can't open windows → 2. more dependence on mechanical ventilation → 3. most savings cancelled → conclusion: reject the proposal. Our claim is step 2. It gets support ("Because ...") and gives support ("that added dependence would cancel..."). Something that's both supported and supporting is a subsidiary, or intermediate, conclusion. Most students pick (B) because the claim sits early and reads like a reason. It fails because B says nothing supports the claim, and the "Because" clause does.

choices.note: Wrong role. The main conclusion is the first sentence: reject the proposal. This claim is one step on the way there.

Tempting, and the main trap. It's right that the claim helps support the conclusion. But B adds that nothing supports it, and the "Because occupants could no longer open their windows" clause is offered precisely to support it.
The proposal's supporters rely on insulation savings, not on ventilation. And the architect asserts this claim; she doesn't refute it.
Backward. The architect doesn't concede that the savings outweigh anything. She argues the ventilation problem cancels most of the savings.
CORRECT. It's drawn from the claim about opening windows and supports the claim that the savings would be cancelled, which in turn bears on rejecting the proposal.

questions.stimulus: Transit official: To ease crowding on morning trains between 7:30 and 9:00, the agency will cut fares by 30 percent for trips that begin before 7:00. Many riders on the crowded trains could start work earlier if they chose to, and the discount gives them a reason to do so. So the plan should noticeably reduce crowding on the peak-hour trains.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the transit official's argument?
choices: Most riders on the peak-hour trains pay for each trip separately rather than buying monthly passes, whose price does not depend on when a trip is taken.
Crowding on the agency's peak-hour trains has grown steadily worse over the past five years, and complaints about it have risen accordingly.
Riders who already travel before 7:00 will also receive the discount, which will reduce the agency's fare revenue from those trips.
When the city's bus system offered a similar early-morning discount, it was used mostly by riders who had already been traveling at that hour.
Some riders take the peak-hour trains because the trains connect with buses that do not begin running until after 7:00.
questions.explanation: The plan works only if the discount actually changes what peak riders pay. Riders on monthly passes pay the same whenever they travel, so a per-trip discount gives them no reason to shift. (A) says most peak riders pay per trip, so the incentive reaches the people it targets. (D) is the main trap: it is about a similar plan, but it suggests the discount mostly rewards people who already travel early, which weakens. (C) is about revenue, not crowding.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The early-morning discount should noticeably reduce peak-hour crowding.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many peak riders could start work earlier; the discount gives them a reason to do so.

breakdown.analysis: A discount is only a reason to switch if you'd actually save money. Who on the crowded trains wouldn't save anything? Anyone whose fare doesn't depend on the time they ride. We want an answer that shows the incentive actually reaches the peak riders. It's like a store offering a discount on weekday mornings: that only moves shoppers who pay at the register, not members who already paid a flat annual fee. Most students reach for (D) because it's about a similar discount, but it points the wrong way.

choices.note: CORRECT. If most peak riders paid a flat monthly price, the discount would change nothing for them. Since most pay per trip, the discount really does lower their cost of shifting earlier, which is the plan's precondition.
So? This explains why the agency wants a plan. It says nothing about whether this plan will work.
Wrong dimension. Lost revenue is a cost of the plan, not evidence about crowding.
Tempting, because it's the closest analogy. But it says the similar discount went mostly to people already traveling early. That suggests few riders shifted, so it weakens.
This weakens: some peak riders can't shift earlier because their connecting buses aren't running yet.

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: Researchers studying the Kaleru, a forest people, conclude that the Kaleru have no concept of private property, since Kaleru hunters share every kill with the whole village. Admittedly, the sharing of game is nearly universal among the Kaleru. But each hunter's arrows bear his personal mark, and no one else may use them without his consent. So the researchers' conclusion is mistaken.
questions.stem: The claim that the sharing of game is nearly universal among the Kaleru plays which one of the following roles in the anthropologist's argument?
choices: It is a premise that, together with the claim about the hunters' arrows, supports the argument's main conclusion.
It is the conclusion that the researchers draw from their observations of how Kaleru hunters behave.
It is a claim that the anthropologist attempts to refute by describing how the Kaleru treat hunters' arrows.
It grants the accuracy of an observation on which the researchers base a conclusion that the argument goes on to reject.
It is evidence the anthropologist offers to show that the Kaleru treat game differently from other kinds of possessions.
questions.explanation: The researchers infer 'no private property' from universal sharing of game. The anthropologist grants the sharing ('Admittedly') but rejects the inference, citing the marked arrows. So the claim concedes the researchers' observation while the rest of the argument rejects their conclusion, as (D) says. (A) is the main trap: the claim does not support the conclusion that the researchers are mistaken; it cuts the other way and is conceded. (E) reads a contrast into the claim that the argument never draws from it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The researchers' conclusion that the Kaleru have no concept of private property is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each hunter's arrows bear his mark and no one may use them without his consent.

breakdown.analysis: "Admittedly" is your signal. The anthropologist is granting something the other side relies on. Does the sharing of game help show the researchers are wrong? No. If anything it's their best fact. The anthropologist accepts the fact and fights the inference: sharing game doesn't mean nobody owns anything, because arrows are clearly owned. Note that the claim itself doesn't deny anything; the denial comes in the later sentences. Most students pick (A) because the claim sits in the argument next to the arrows evidence. It fails because it points the opposite way from the conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting. The claim appears alongside the arrow evidence, but it doesn't support the conclusion that the researchers are mistaken. It's the researchers' own observation, conceded.
The researchers' conclusion is that the Kaleru have no concept of private property. Universal sharing is the observation they reason from, not their conclusion.
The anthropologist doesn't try to refute it; "Admittedly" means it's accepted. The arrows are used against the researchers' conclusion, not against this fact.
CORRECT. The anthropologist accepts that game is shared almost universally, the observation the researchers rely on, and then the rest of the argument rejects the conclusion they drew from it.

Tempting if you read ahead: game vs. arrows sounds like a contrast. But the claim isn't offered to show anything; it's conceded. And the argument's point is that arrows are owned, not that game is treated specially.

questions.stimulus: Dozens of intact clay jars have been recovered from the bottoms of wells in the ancient town of Hesk. Some researchers think the jars were simply dropped by people drawing water. But a jar dropped down a deep shaft would almost always shatter against the stones lining it or at the bottom, so the jars must have been lowered deliberately, most likely as offerings.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Families in Hesk sometimes kept perishable food cool by lowering it in jars to just above the water in their wells.
None of the jars from Hesk's wells has the lugs or narrow neck that Hesk's potters gave to the vessels they made for drawing water.
Jars of the same types as those found in the wells have also been recovered in large numbers from the ruins of houses throughout Hesk.
Inscriptions indicate that offerings at Hesk's temples consisted mostly of small metal figurines rather than of pottery.
Several of the wells in Hesk were abandoned and filled with debris within a few decades of being dug.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects the view that the jars were dropped while drawing water. (B) strengthens it by showing the jars lack the features of Hesk's water-drawing vessels, so they likely weren't water vessels at all. (A) is the trap: it shows jars were sometimes lowered into wells deliberately, but for keeping food cool, an everyday purpose that competes with the offering explanation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The jars were lowered into the wells deliberately, most likely as offerings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The jars are intact; a jar dropped down a deep shaft would almost always shatter.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the two steps. Step 1, not dropped, so lowered on purpose: the premise handles that. Step 2, lowered on purpose, so offerings: nothing handles that, and the researchers' rival story is that these were ordinary water jars lost in the well. We want an answer that shows the jars weren't water jars. (B) does: they lack the features Hesk's potters gave to water-drawing vessels. Most students pick (A) because it shows people really did lower jars into wells on purpose. It fails because it gives a non-offering reason for doing so, which competes with the conclusion instead of supporting it.

choices.note: Tempting, because it shows people did deliberately lower jars into wells, which fits 'lowered deliberately.' But it supplies an everyday reason for doing so, which competes with the offering explanation instead of supporting it.

CORRECT. The rival view is that the jars were water vessels dropped while drawing water. These jars lack the features Hesk's potters gave to vessels made for drawing water, so they probably weren't water vessels at all. That removes the leading rival and leaves deliberate placement, most likely as offerings, as the best explanation.
If anything this suggests the jars were ordinary household ware, which fits the water-drawing story better than the offering story.
This cuts against the argument: if offerings were usually metal figurines, pottery offerings look less likely.
Irrelevant. When the wells were abandoned says nothing about how the jars got to the bottom.

questions.stimulus: Editorial: The city should not renew its waste-collection contract with Pemberly Disposal. Pemberly's monthly reports to the council described collection as complete, yet the company's own logs show that it missed nearly a quarter of its scheduled pickups last year. A contractor that misrepresents its performance to the public body that hired it should not be retained, however low its price, and Pemberly's bid is the lowest the city received.
questions.stem: The claim that a contractor that misrepresents its performance to the public body that hired it should not be retained figures in the editorial's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the editorial, and it is supported by the evidence from Pemberly's own logs.
It is a consideration that the editorial concedes counts in favor of renewing Pemberly's contract.
It is a general principle that, applied to the facts about Pemberly, is used to support the editorial's conclusion.
It is offered to explain why Pemberly was able to submit a lower bid than the other companies did.
It is a claim that the editorial attempts to show is consistent with Pemberly's having submitted the lowest bid.
questions.explanation: The conclusion is the first sentence: don't renew. The logs versus the reports show Pemberly misrepresented its work, and the general rule says such contractors should not be kept, whatever their price. The rule plus the facts yields the conclusion, so (C). (A) is the main trap: the rule is normative and sounds like a conclusion, but it is general, while the conclusion is about Pemberly; nothing in the editorial supports the rule. (B) confuses the rule with the low bid, which is the point that counts in Pemberly's favor.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city should not renew its contract with Pemberly.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pemberly reported complete collection though its logs show many missed pickups; a contractor that misrepresents its performance should not be retained, however low its price.

breakdown.analysis: Two "should" statements, so which is the conclusion? Ask which supports which. The rule about contractors in general supports the claim about Pemberly, not the reverse. It works like a syllogism: contractors who mislead the city shouldn't be kept; Pemberly misled the city; so Pemberly shouldn't be kept. The claim in question is the general rule. Most students pick (A) because it's the most opinionated sentence. It fails because nothing is offered to support it; it's applied, not argued for.

choices.note: Tempting. It's a "should" claim, but it's general and nothing in the editorial supports it. The logs support the factual claim that Pemberly misrepresented its work, which the rule then turns into a verdict about Pemberly.
That's the low bid, not this rule. The editorial acknowledges the low bid; the rule says it doesn't matter.
CORRECT. A general rule (misrepresenting contractors shouldn't be kept) plus the facts about Pemberly (its reports didn't match its logs) produces the conclusion (don't renew Pemberly).
Nothing explains the bid. The rule says what to do with a misrepresenting contractor; it isn't a cause of anything.
Borrows "however low its price," but the editorial isn't trying to show consistency. The rule simply says price can't save a contractor that misrepresents its work.

questions.stimulus: Engineer: The suspension bridge planned for the Strand estuary should be designed with dampers to control swaying in high winds. The Elsby bridge, two hundred kilometers up the coast, had to be fitted with dampers after it swayed alarmingly during its first winter, and the Strand bridge will have nearly the same span and the same deck design as the Elsby bridge.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the engineer's argument?
choices: The winds that set the Elsby bridge swaying blow across the Strand estuary from the same direction and at similar speeds.
The Elsby bridge has not swayed alarmingly at any time since its dampers were fitted, even during severe winter storms.
Fitting dampers to a bridge during construction costs considerably less than adding them once the bridge is in use.
Several bridges of other designs along the same coast have stood for decades without needing dampers.
The deck of the Strand bridge will be made of a newer steel that is lighter than the steel used in the Elsby bridge.
questions.explanation: The argument reasons from Elsby to Strand on the basis of shared span and deck design. Swaying depends on the wind as well as the structure, so the analogy is incomplete until the two sites face similar winds. (A) supplies that. (B) is the main trap: it shows dampers work, but the question is whether the Strand bridge needs them. (C) supports a different conclusion, about when to install dampers if needed. (E) points to a difference, so it weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Strand bridge should be designed with dampers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Elsby bridge, with nearly the same span and deck, needed dampers after swaying in high winds.

breakdown.analysis: An argument by analogy is only as good as the match on the features that matter. Same span, same deck: but what made Elsby sway? Wind. If the Strand estuary is sheltered, the comparison breaks down. We want an answer that matches the two cases on the condition that caused the problem. It's like saying my coat was too thin for Minneapolis, so it'll be too thin in Miami: same coat, different weather. Most students pick (B) because it praises dampers. It fails because it shows dampers solve the problem, not that Strand will have the problem.

choices.note: CORRECT. The analogy already matches structure. This matches the cause of the swaying too: same wind direction, similar speeds. Now Elsby's experience is a much better guide to Strand's.
Tempting. It shows dampers work. But the argument is that Strand needs them, and Elsby's success with them says nothing about whether Strand would sway without them.
Wrong conclusion. This is a reason to install dampers early if they're needed. It doesn't show they're needed.
Other designs aren't the comparison. The argument rests on Strand's similarity to Elsby; bridges unlike either don't bear on it.
This weakens: it's a difference between the two bridges that could change how each responds to wind.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: A new state standard requires at least one nurse for every five patients on overnight shifts, and our hospital currently falls short of that ratio on most nights. But we need not hire more night nurses to comply. Many of our overnight patients stay only because their discharge paperwork could not be completed before evening, and a faster discharge process would let them go home during the day.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the administrator's argument?
choices: Most other hospitals in the state also fall short of the new staffing standard on their overnight shifts.
Patients who stay overnight only because of delayed paperwork need much less nursing care than other overnight patients do.
On most nights, the number of patients staying only because of delayed paperwork exceeds the number the hospital would need to shed to meet the standard.
Speeding up the discharge process would also reduce the hospital's costs for meals and laundry on overnight shifts.
The hospital has had difficulty recruiting night nurses for several years because of competition from other hospitals.
questions.explanation: The standard is a head count: patients per nurse. The administrator says sending the paperwork-only patients home would bring the hospital into compliance without new nurses. That works only if there are enough such patients to close the gap. (C) says there are. (B) is the main trap: it sounds like these patients don't really burden the nurses, but the standard counts patients, not the care they need, so it doesn't bear on compliance.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The hospital need not hire more night nurses to meet the new standard.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many overnight patients stay only because of delayed discharge paperwork; faster discharge would send them home during the day.

breakdown.analysis: "Many" is the soft spot. How many is many, compared with how far short the hospital is? If it's short by twenty patients and only five are paperwork cases, faster discharge won't get it there. We want an answer that says the paperwork patients are enough to close the gap. Most students pick (B) because it seems to say these patients don't really count. But the standard counts heads, not hours of care.

choices.note: So? Other hospitals' shortfalls don't tell us whether this hospital can comply without hiring.
Tempting. It makes these patients seem like a light load, but the rule is one nurse per five patients, whatever care they need. Their light needs don't change the count.
CORRECT. If the paperwork-only patients outnumber the hospital's shortfall, sending them home during the day brings the overnight ratio within the standard without a single new hire.
Wrong dimension. Savings on meals and laundry are a bonus, not evidence about meeting the staffing ratio.
This explains why the administrator wants to avoid hiring. It doesn't show that hiring is unnecessary.

questions.stimulus: Commentator: Lower-compression tennis balls do strike the racket with less force than standard balls, so each stroke strains a player's wrist less. Even so, the Torvale tennis federation's new rule requiring them in junior matches, whatever its other merits, will do little to reduce wrist injuries among juniors. These balls bounce lower and travel more slowly, so rallies will last longer, and juniors will therefore hit far more strokes in each match.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the commentator's argument?
choices: Junior players using lower-compression balls will hit far more strokes in each match than they would with standard balls.
Because lower-compression balls strike the racket with less force, each stroke a junior hits will strain the wrist less.
The Torvale tennis federation's rule requiring lower-compression balls in junior matches has merits other than its effect on juniors' wrists.
Requiring juniors to play with lower-compression balls is unlikely to bring about a substantial reduction in their wrist injuries.
The Torvale tennis federation should withdraw its rule requiring juniors to use lower-compression balls in their matches.
questions.explanation: The first sentence is a concession ('do ... even so'). The last sentence, with 'therefore', is a subsidiary conclusion: more strokes per match. That supports the unflagged claim in the middle: the rule will do little to reduce wrist injuries, which (D) restates. (A) is the main trap: it is flagged with 'therefore' but serves the main claim. (C) turns 'whatever its other merits' into an assertion the commentator never makes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rule requiring lower-compression balls will do little to reduce juniors' wrist injuries.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The balls bounce lower and travel more slowly, so rallies last longer, so juniors hit far more strokes per match (despite less strain per stroke).

breakdown.analysis: Don't follow the indicator words blindly. "Therefore" sits in the last sentence, but ask: why does it matter that juniors hit more strokes? Because more strokes cancel the gain from less strain per stroke. So "more strokes" supports something else: the rule won't do much for wrists. The first sentence is a concession ("do ... Even so"). Test: the conclusion is the claim everything else supports. Most students pick (A) because of "therefore." It fails because it's a step on the way, not the destination.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It's flagged with "therefore," but it's a subsidiary conclusion: more strokes per match is the reason the rule won't help wrists much.
That's the concession. The commentator grants it and then argues it doesn't add up to fewer injuries.
"Whatever its other merits" leaves open whether the rule has other merits. The commentator doesn't assert that it does, let alone argue for it.
CORRECT. This restates the middle sentence, which the rest of the argument supports: less strain per stroke but far more strokes, so little reduction in injuries.
Too far. The commentator says the rule won't do much for wrists, not that it should be withdrawn, and even allows it may have other merits.

questions.stimulus: At the Bronze Age site of Kettu, a row of stone storerooms stands beside the settlement's largest house. The storerooms are identical in size and construction, which indicates that they were built as a single project rather than one at a time as individual households needed them. So the storerooms were most likely controlled by whoever lived in the large house.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Analysis of the stone shows that all of the storerooms were built of blocks cut from a single quarry at about the same time.
Storerooms of similar size have been found standing beside ordinary houses at several other Bronze Age sites in the region.
Sealings from every storeroom door bear the impression of one seal, which also appears on sealings found in the large house.
The large house at Kettu was built several generations after the row of storerooms had been completed.
Some of the storerooms at Kettu held pottery that had been made in regions far from the settlement.
questions.explanation: The argument has two steps: identical design shows a single building project, and a single project shows control by the large house. The second step is the gap, since a community could build storerooms together and still give one to each household. (C) bridges it: the storerooms were all closed under one seal, also used in the large house, which points to one controller and to that house. (A) is the dominant trap: it supports the first step (one project), which the argument already reached; it leaves the household-ownership view standing. (D) weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Kettu storerooms were most likely controlled by whoever lived in the large house.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The storerooms are identical in size and construction, so they were built as one project; they stand beside the largest house.

breakdown.analysis: Spot the chain: identical → one project → controlled by the big house. The first arrow is fine. The second is shaky. A village can pool labor to build ten identical sheds and still hand one to each family, the way a housing developer builds identical homes for different owners. So we need evidence of a single controller, ideally the big house. Most students pick (A) because one quarry at one time sounds like strong archaeological proof. It fails because it proves the step we already had: one project. One project doesn't mean one owner.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Same quarry, same time: more proof of a single building project. But that's the intermediate conclusion the argument already reached. It doesn't show who controlled the rooms once built.
If anything this weakens: similar storerooms beside ordinary houses elsewhere suggest households could have their own.
CORRECT. One seal on every door means one authority controlled access, and the same seal turns up in the large house. That links the storerooms to that household and undercuts separate ownership.
This weakens. If the large house came generations later, its occupants didn't plan or originally control the storerooms.
Irrelevant. Imported pottery tells us about trade, not about who controlled the rooms.

questions.stimulus: Mayor Duvall says the proposed downtown stadium will pay for itself, because most of the crowds it draws on game days will come from outside the city and spend money here. She also says the stadium will not add to downtown traffic, because most fans will be city residents who walk or take transit to games. Whatever the merits of the stadium, then, at least one of the mayor's reasons for supporting it must be mistaken.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: showing that two predictions the mayor makes about the stadium cannot both turn out to be true
arguing that the stadium will not pay for itself because the crowds it draws will add to downtown traffic
questioning the mayor's motives for supporting a stadium in the downtown area rather than elsewhere
disputing the evidence on which the mayor bases her estimate of how many fans the stadium will draw
pointing out that the grounds offered for one of the mayor's claims conflict with the grounds offered for another
questions.explanation: The mayor's two claims are that the stadium will pay for itself and that it won't add to traffic. Those could both be true. What can't both be true are her reasons: most crowds come from outside the city, and most fans are city residents. The argument concludes only that one of her reasons is mistaken, which (E) describes. (A) is the trap: it moves the inconsistency from the reasons to the predictions, and the argument explicitly sets the stadium's merits aside. (B) draws a conclusion the argument never draws.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least one of the mayor's reasons for supporting the stadium is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Her case for revenue says most crowds will come from outside the city; her case on traffic says most fans will be residents.

breakdown.analysis: Read the conclusion closely: "at least one of the mayor's reasons ... must be mistaken," and "whatever the merits of the stadium." So the author isn't attacking the stadium or even the mayor's predictions. The target is the support. Could the stadium pay for itself AND leave traffic alone? Sure, for some other reason. What can't be true is that most fans come from outside AND most fans are residents. We want an answer about the reasons clashing. Most students pick (A) because "cannot both be true" sounds exactly right. It fails because it attaches that to the predictions, not the reasons.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The clash is real, but it's between the mayor's reasons, not her predictions. Paying for itself and not adding traffic could both happen. The author even sets aside "the merits of the stadium."
choices.example: Method example: "The mayor predicts the stadium will both be full every game and leave every downtown parking garage empty. Both can't happen."

choices.note: Too far. The author never concludes the stadium won't pay for itself, and never says the crowds will add traffic.
choices.example: Method example: "The stadium won't pay for itself, since the traffic it brings will drive shoppers away from downtown."

choices.note: No motives are discussed. The author examines what the mayor said, not why she said it.
choices.example: Method example: "The mayor owns land near the site, so her support for the stadium is suspect."

choices.note: No estimate of total attendance is questioned. The issue is where the fans come from, and the author uses the mayor's own statements against each other.
choices.example: Method example: "The mayor's attendance figure comes from the team's own promotional survey."

choices.note: CORRECT. The ground for "pays for itself" (most crowds from outside) conflicts with the ground for "no added traffic" (most fans are residents). Since both can't hold, at least one reason is mistaken, which is exactly the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Analyst: Thornfield Foods could sell its new line of frozen meals under its own label or sell the meals to supermarkets to be marketed as the supermarkets' store brands. Store-brand versions would sell more meals, since they would be priced lower. But Thornfield's profit on each meal sold under its own label would be about three times its profit on each meal sold as a store brand. So Thornfield will probably earn more by using its own label.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst's argument?
choices: Thornfield's accountants have confirmed that its profit per meal would be roughly three times higher under its own label than as a store brand.
Store-brand frozen meals have steadily gained market share over the past decade at the expense of meals sold under manufacturers' labels.
Total sales of frozen meals in the region have risen in each of the past five years and are expected to keep rising.
Among frozen meals of comparable quality, store-brand versions rarely sell even twice as many units as versions sold under the maker's own label.
Several of Thornfield's competitors sell some of their meals under their own labels and others as supermarket store brands.
questions.explanation: Total profit is profit per meal times meals sold. The own label wins on profit per meal by about three to one; the store brand wins on volume by an unstated amount. If store brands sold more than three times as many meals, they'd earn more. (D) caps the volume gap at under two to one, so three times the margin more than makes up for it. (A) is the main trap: it confirms the margin, which is already a premise, and says nothing about volume. (B) points toward a larger store-brand advantage, so if anything it weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Thornfield will probably earn more under its own label than through store brands.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Store brands would sell more meals; own-label profit per meal is about three times store-brand profit per meal.

breakdown.analysis: How many more meals would the store brands sell? "More" could mean 10 percent more or five times more. Profit is margin times volume. Own label: 3 units of profit per meal. Store brand: 1 unit per meal. If store brands sell fewer than three times as many meals, the own label wins. We want an answer that keeps the volume gap below three to one. Quick check with (D): sell 100 own-label meals at 3 = 300; store brands sell under 200 at 1 = under 200. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like hard evidence. It fails because it backs up a premise we already accept and ignores volume, the real unknown.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It confirms the three-to-one margin, which the argument already states. Proving a premise again doesn't fill the gap, which is about how many more meals store brands would sell.
If anything this weakens: store brands gaining share suggests their volume advantage may be large.
Irrelevant. A growing market lifts both options; it doesn't tell us which earns more.
CORRECT. If store brands rarely sell even twice as many units, a threefold profit per meal for the own label more than offsets the volume gap. That's exactly the missing comparison.
So? That competitors use both routes doesn't tell us which route earns Thornfield more.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: Removing the Askel River dam, as the state now plans, is the right decision. But anyone who expects the river's salmon run to recover within a decade will be disappointed. Salmon spawn only in gravel beds free of fine silt. Once the dam comes down, the sediment trapped behind it for eighty years will wash downstream, so the spawning beds below the dam will be choked with silt for well over a decade.
questions.stem: The claim that anyone who expects the river's salmon run to recover within a decade will be disappointed plays which one of the following roles in the ecologist's argument?
choices: It is a claim that the ecologist concedes to opponents of the state's plan before arguing that removing the dam is the right decision.
It is the conclusion that the argument as a whole is structured to support.
It is an intermediate conclusion that is offered in support of the claim that removing the dam is the right decision.
It is a prediction that the ecologist attributes to supporters of the state's plan and then argues is unlikely to be borne out.
It is a premise that, together with the claim that salmon spawn only in silt-free gravel, supports the claim that the spawning beds will be choked with silt.
questions.explanation: Everything after the second sentence supports it: salmon need silt-free gravel; the released sediment will choke the beds for over a decade; so no recovery within a decade. The first sentence is an aside nothing supports. So the claim is the main conclusion, (B). (D) is the main trap: the claim mentions people's expectations, but it is the ecologist's own prediction that they will be disappointed, not a view attributed to others. (E) reverses the support: the silt claim supports this claim, not the other way around. (C) links it to the wrong claim.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The salmon run will not recover within a decade (anyone expecting that will be disappointed).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Salmon spawn only in silt-free gravel; sediment released by removing the dam will choke the spawning beds for over a decade.

breakdown.analysis: Don't be fooled by "so" near the end. That flags a subsidiary conclusion (the beds will be choked), which in turn supports the bigger point: no recovery within a decade. And the opening sentence, that removal is right, gets no support at all; it's the ecologist's position on the plan, set aside. Test: which statement does everything else support? Only the claim in the stem. Most students pick (D) because the claim talks about what other people expect. It fails because the ecologist asserts the claim herself; the expectation is theirs, but the prediction that they'll be disappointed is hers.

choices.note: The ecologist doesn't concede this to anyone; she argues for it. And nothing in the argument supports "removing the dam is the right decision."
CORRECT. The silt-free requirement and the decade of silt support it; nothing it supports comes after. That's the main conclusion, even though it isn't flagged and a "so" appears later.
Wrong target. This claim isn't offered for the first sentence. Long-delayed recovery would hardly support removing the dam.
Tempting. The claim mentions others' expectations, but the claim itself, that they will be disappointed, is the ecologist's own view, and she argues for it rather than against it.
Backward. The silt claim supports this one: choked beds for over a decade, so no recovery within a decade. This claim isn't evidence that the beds will be choked.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Last year in Tarvia, prices of used pickup trucks rose sharply even as prices of new pickups fell. This is less puzzling than it may seem. Nearly all new pickups sold there last year were electric, and rural buyers, who make most pickup purchases, have largely avoided electric models because charging stations remain scarce outside the cities. Those buyers have therefore been competing for a limited supply of used gasoline trucks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the economist's argument by the statement that prices of used pickup trucks rose sharply even as prices of new pickups fell?
choices: It is the main conclusion of the argument, and the remaining statements are offered in support of it.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that rural buyers have largely avoided electric models.
It is a claim that the economist argues is less accurate than it may at first seem.
It is a hypothesis that the economist considers and then rejects in favor of an account based on rural buyers' preferences.
It reports a state of affairs that the argument as a whole seeks to show is not anomalous.
questions.explanation: The economist's conclusion is 'This is less puzzling than it may seem'; the rest explains why used prices could rise while new prices fell. The statement in the stem is the 'this': a fact that the argument sets out to make unsurprising, as (E) says. (C) is the main trap: it borrows 'less ... than it may seem' but changes 'puzzling' to 'accurate'; the economist never doubts the price facts. (A) mistakes the phenomenon for the conclusion about it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The rise in used-pickup prices while new-pickup prices fell is less puzzling than it may seem.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly all new pickups were electric; rural buyers, most of the market, avoid electric models; so they compete for limited used gasoline trucks.

breakdown.analysis: What does the economist argue for? Not that prices moved this way; that's reported as fact. The point is that the movement makes sense. So the statement in the stem is the thing being explained, and "This is less puzzling" is the conclusion about it. Most students pick (C) because it echoes "less ... than it may seem." But the economist says the facts are less puzzling, not less accurate. One word, and the answer is wrong.

choices.note: Close but wrong. The conclusion is that the price pattern is less puzzling than it seems, not the price pattern itself. The other statements explain the pattern; they don't establish it.
Backward. Rural buyers' avoidance of electric models is part of the explanation; the price pattern isn't offered as evidence for it.
Tempting, and the main trap. It reuses the stimulus's wording but swaps "puzzling" for "accurate." The economist accepts the price facts and argues only that they're explainable.
The economist never rejects the price pattern. It's a reported fact, and the rural-buyer account is offered to explain it, not to replace it.
CORRECT. The statement describes what happened, and the rest of the argument shows why it isn't really an anomaly. That's a phenomenon the argument seeks to explain.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: Males of a certain species of tree frog have two calls, a low call and a high call. In experiments, females move toward speakers playing the low call but ignore speakers playing the high call. Since the high call evidently plays no role in attracting mates, it most likely serves to warn rival males away from the caller's territory.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologist's argument?
choices: Males of the species seldom give the high call except when another calling male is within a few meters of them.
Females ignore the high call even in experiments in which no low calls are being played anywhere nearby.
Females that approach a male giving the low call almost always mate with that male.
Rival males often approach a male that is giving the high call and fight him for his calling site.
The high call carries much farther through the dense vegetation where the frogs live than the low call does.
questions.explanation: The argument rules out mate attraction and jumps to warning off rivals. Support should tie the high call to rivals. (A) does it indirectly: males give the call almost only when a rival is near, which is when a warning would be useful. (B) is the main trap: it shores up the premise that the high call doesn't attract females, which the argument already accepts, and says nothing about rivals. (D) reuses 'rival males' but shows the call failing to keep them away, so it weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The high call most likely serves to warn rival males away.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Females move toward the low call but ignore the high call, so the high call doesn't attract mates.

breakdown.analysis: Ruling out one function doesn't establish another. The high call could mark location, signal alarm to predators, or do nothing in particular. What would make "warning rivals" more likely? Evidence that the call shows up when rivals do. Think of a dog that barks only when someone approaches the gate: that pattern is what tells you the bark is a warning. Most students pick (B) because it's more evidence that the high call doesn't attract females. It fails because that half of the argument is already settled.

choices.note: CORRECT. If males give the high call almost only when a rival male is nearby, the call is tied to the presence of rivals, which is exactly what a warning signal would look like.
Tempting. It strengthens the premise that the high call doesn't attract females. But that step isn't in doubt; the gap is whether the call is aimed at rivals.
This is about the low call. It confirms the low call's role in mating and says nothing about what the high call does.
Tempting because it mentions rival males. But rivals approaching and fighting suggests the call doesn't warn them off. If anything it weakens.
This hints at a long-range function but doesn't say which. Carrying farther fits signaling to anyone, including distant females or predators, so it doesn't favor warning rivals.

questions.stimulus: Average speeds on Fenn Avenue fell by eight kilometers per hour in the month its lanes were repainted to be a meter narrower, the same month speed cameras were installed there. The cameras photograph only cars exceeding the limit by a wide margin, and few drivers on the avenue ever came close to that margin. So the city's plan to install the same cameras on Kinnear Road, without narrowing its lanes, will probably do little to slow traffic there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Since they were installed, the cameras on Fenn Avenue have photographed only a small fraction of the cars that use the avenue each day.
On Mabry Street, where identical cameras were installed that same month but the lanes were left unchanged, average speeds hardly changed.
Signs warning drivers about the new speed cameras were posted at both ends of Fenn Avenue when the cameras were installed.
Drivers on Kinnear Road exceed the speed limit by a wide margin far more often than drivers on Fenn Avenue ever did.
Before its lanes were repainted, average speeds on Fenn Avenue had been rising slowly for several years.
questions.explanation: The argument credits Fenn's slowdown to the narrower lanes, not the cameras, and predicts that cameras alone will do little on Kinnear. Its weak spot is deterrence: cameras could slow drivers who are never photographed. (B) supplies a test case: cameras alone, on Mabry Street, did almost nothing. (A) is the main trap: it echoes the premise that cameras photograph few cars, which ignores deterrence. (C) suggests deterrence did work, and (D) suggests Kinnear differs in a way that would make cameras more effective, so both weaken.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Cameras on Kinnear Road without narrower lanes will probably do little to slow traffic.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Fenn's speeds fell when lanes narrowed and cameras went in; cameras photograph only flagrant speeders, which few Fenn drivers were.

breakdown.analysis: So what if the cameras rarely snap anyone? A camera can slow drivers who never get photographed, simply because they know it's there. That's the hole. We need evidence that cameras on their own don't slow traffic. The cleanest is a place that got cameras but no lane change. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like the premise in hard numbers. It fails because counting photos ignores drivers who slowed down to avoid them.

choices.note: Tempting. It restates the premise: few cars photographed. But that's what you'd expect if the cameras deterred speeding, too. It doesn't separate the two causes.

CORRECT. Same cameras, same month, no lane change, and speeds barely moved. That's a near-perfect control: cameras alone didn't slow traffic, which supports both the credit to narrow lanes and the prediction for Kinnear.
This weakens. Warning signs give the cameras a way to deter drivers who are never photographed.
Tempting because it's about Kinnear. But more flagrant speeders there means the cameras would catch, and deter, more drivers. That weakens the prediction.
This makes the drop more impressive but doesn't say which change caused it.

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: Some jurists hold that a law means only what its words would have meant to an ordinary reader when it was enacted. On that view, a 1920s ordinance forbidding "noise-making devices" in city parks after dark would not apply to battery-powered speakers, which no reader in the 1920s could have imagined. Yet no one seriously thinks the ordinance permits blasting music from a speaker in a park at midnight. So the jurists' view, at least in its strict form, must be rejected.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the legal scholar's argument by the claim that the 1920s ordinance would not apply to battery-powered speakers?
choices: It is a premise that the scholar accepts and uses to show that the ordinance should be revised to cover modern devices.
It is the conclusion that the jurists draw from their view about how laws ought to be read.
It is evidence that ordinary readers in the 1920s understood the ordinance more narrowly than readers do today.
It is a concession that the jurists' view yields acceptable results when it is applied to laws enacted recently.
It is presented as a consequence of a position the scholar opposes, a consequence the scholar takes to be unacceptable.
questions.explanation: The scholar derives the claim from the jurists' view ('On that view') and then says no one accepts it, so the view must be rejected. The claim is an implication the scholar regards as absurd, as (E) says. (B) is the main trap: the claim follows from the jurists' view, but nothing says the jurists draw it, and the argument depends on their not accepting it. (A) has the scholar asserting the claim, but she rejects it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The jurists' view, at least in its strict form, must be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: On their view, a 1920s noise ordinance would not cover battery-powered speakers; no one thinks the ordinance permits such noise.

breakdown.analysis: Does the scholar believe the ordinance doesn't cover speakers? No. She says that's what the jurists' view would imply, and then points out that nobody accepts that result. It's the absurd outcome used to sink the rule. It's like arguing: if "vehicle" meant only what it meant in 1850, a law against vehicles in the park would allow motorcycles, and no one believes that. Most students pick (B) because the claim does come from the jurists' view. It fails because the jurists never draw it; the scholar draws it for them, as a problem.

choices.note: The scholar doesn't accept the claim. Her point is that it's unacceptable, and she proposes no revision to the ordinance.
Tempting. The claim follows from the jurists' view, but the scholar is the one who draws it, as an objection. Nothing suggests the jurists conclude the ordinance permits speakers.
The claim is about what the ordinance would cover under the jurists' view, not evidence about how 1920s readers actually understood it.
No concession about recent laws appears. The argument targets the view's results for old laws.
CORRECT. "On that view" marks the claim as an implication of the jurists' position, and "no one seriously thinks" marks it as unacceptable. Rejecting the view because of it is the whole argument.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Dr. Szabo dates the burial of the Lisk coin hoard to the reign of Aldric, because the latest coins in it were minted under Aldric. But a hoard's latest coin shows only the earliest date at which the hoard could have been buried. And since Aldric's successor minted far fewer coins, a hoard buried during the successor's reign could easily contain none of them. So Szabo's dating, though possible, is not established.
questions.stem: The archaeologist's argument proceeds by
choices: rejecting Szabo's conclusion as false on the grounds that the evidence offered in support of it is insufficient
arguing that the evidence Szabo relies on is compatible with an alternative to the conclusion he draws from it
questioning the reliability of the methods by which Szabo determined when the coins in the hoard were minted
offering a date for the burial of the hoard that the available evidence supports better than Szabo's date
conceding that Szabo's dating may be correct while arguing that his evidence fits a burial before Aldric's reign just as well
questions.explanation: The archaeologist shows that Szabo's evidence (the latest coins are Aldric's) fits equally well with burial under the successor, whose scarce coins could easily be missing, and so concludes the dating is possible but not established. (B) describes that. (A) is the dominant trap: it names a familiar flaw, rejecting a conclusion as false because its support is weak, but the archaeologist explicitly says Szabo's dating is 'possible.' (D) is wrong because no better date is offered; the successor's reign is raised only as a possibility. (E) has the right shape but the wrong direction: the latest coin rules out a burial before Aldric's reign.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Szabo's dating of the hoard, though possible, is not established.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A hoard's latest coin gives only the earliest possible burial date; the next ruler minted few coins, so a hoard buried under him could easily lack them.

breakdown.analysis: The archaeologist never says Szabo is wrong. Read the last line: "though possible, is not established." The move is: your evidence fits your conclusion, but it fits this other scenario just as well. It's like a detective saying the suspect's footprints prove he was at the scene, and his partner replying that the prints only show he was there at some point after the mud formed. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like what critics usually do. It fails because the archaeologist is careful not to call the dating false.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. This describes a real flaw, but the archaeologist doesn't commit it. "Though possible" means she isn't calling Szabo's date false, only unproven. Example of this method: "There's little evidence the hoard dates from Aldric's reign, so it must date from some other time."
CORRECT. Latest coins from Aldric fit both burial under Aldric and burial under his successor. Showing the evidence fits an alternative is exactly how she gets to "not established."

She accepts that the coins were minted under Aldric. Her point is about what that implies, not about how it was determined. Example of this method: "Szabo dated the coins by their style alone, which often misleads."

She proposes no better date. The successor's reign is raised as a possibility, not defended as the answer. Example of this method: "The hoard was most likely buried under Aldric's successor, since its pot is of a later type."

Tempting, because it has the right shape: concede possible, show an alternative. But the alternative is in the wrong direction. A hoard can't be buried before its latest coin was minted; the archaeologist's alternative is a later burial, under the successor.
choices.example: Method example: "Szabo's date is possible, but the evidence fits a burial a generation earlier just as well."

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: It is widely believed that Lindmark's high rate of home ownership is a result of the generous tax deduction the country allows for mortgage interest. But the deduction was enacted in 1962, when most Lindmark households already owned their homes, and it passed largely because so many voters were homeowners who stood to gain from it. Widespread ownership, then, did more to produce the deduction than the deduction did to produce widespread ownership, though the deduction may since have helped to sustain it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the sociologist's argument?
choices: The mortgage-interest deduction may have helped to keep the rate of home ownership in Lindmark high since 1962.
Most households in Lindmark already owned their homes by the time the mortgage-interest deduction was enacted.
Lindmark's high rate of home ownership is not the result of any of the country's tax policies.
The mortgage-interest deduction is better explained as an effect of Lindmark's high rate of home ownership than as its cause.
Lindmark's mortgage-interest deduction passed largely because so many voters were homeowners who stood to gain from it.
questions.explanation: The conclusion, flagged by 'then', is a comparison: ownership did more to produce the deduction than the reverse. (D) restates that as 'better explained as an effect than as a cause'. (E) is the main trap: it is the premise closest to the conclusion, a claim about why the deduction passed, but it supports the comparison rather than being it. (A) is the hedge the sociologist tacks on, which is allowed rather than argued for. (C) overstates: the sociologist allows that the deduction may help sustain ownership.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Widespread home ownership did more to produce the mortgage-interest deduction than the deduction did to produce widespread ownership.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The deduction came in 1962, after most households already owned homes; it passed largely because homeowner-voters stood to gain.

breakdown.analysis: The popular view: deduction → ownership. The sociologist's answer: mostly the other way round. The two premises do different jobs: the date shows ownership came first; the politics shows ownership helped cause the deduction. Together they support a comparison: ownership did more to produce the deduction than vice versa. The final "though" clause is a hedge, not something argued for. Most students pick (E) because it already sounds like "ownership caused the deduction." It fails because it's one of the two reasons, and it doesn't address the popular view, that the deduction produced ownership.

choices.note: That's the hedge. The sociologist allows this ("may"), but nothing is offered to support it.
A premise. The timing is evidence for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.
Too strong. The sociologist claims the deduction did less to produce ownership than the reverse, and even grants it may help sustain ownership. That's far from "not the result of any tax policy."

CORRECT. Rephrased, "ownership did more to produce the deduction than the deduction did to produce ownership" says the deduction is better seen as an effect of ownership than as its cause. Both premises support exactly that.

Tempting, and the main trap. This is the premise closest to the conclusion, but it's one of the reasons. It explains why the deduction passed; the conclusion weighs that against the popular claim that the deduction drove ownership.

questions.stimulus: Zoologist: Ravens at a municipal landfill often drop bottle caps beside sleeping foxes and then hop away when the foxes wake. Some observers suppose the ravens are trying to drive the foxes off so they can take the foxes' food. But in hundreds of recorded episodes, no raven was seen to approach a fox's food afterward, so the behavior gains the ravens nothing to eat. And since young ravens do this far more often than adults do, it is most likely a form of play.
questions.stem: The statement that no raven was seen to approach a fox's food afterward figures in the zoologist's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It supports a claim that is used to undermine an alternative to the explanation the zoologist favors.
It is offered in direct support of the conclusion that the ravens' behavior is most likely a form of play.
It is evidence that the observers cite in support of their view that the ravens are after the foxes' food.
It is the zoologist's main conclusion, which is supported by the claim that young ravens do this far more often than adults do.
It describes the behavior that the zoologist's argument as a whole seeks to explain.
questions.explanation: The statement supports the subsidiary conclusion flagged by 'so': the behavior gains the ravens nothing to eat. That claim knocks out the observers' food-stealing explanation, which leaves room for play. So the statement supports a claim used against a rival explanation, as (A) says. (B) is the main trap: the statement does ultimately help the play conclusion, but only through the 'gains nothing to eat' step, and it is not what positively supports play (that is the age pattern). (E) picks the wrong behavior: the cap-dropping is what is explained.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The ravens' behavior is most likely a form of play.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: No raven approached a fox's food afterward, so the behavior gains them no food (ruling out the observers' theory); young ravens do it far more than adults.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: 1. no raven approaches the food → 2. so the behavior gains them nothing to eat → this defeats the observers' food theory. Separately: 3. young ravens do it more → play. The statement in the stem is step 1. It doesn't touch play directly; it supports step 2, which eliminates a rival. Most students pick (B) because the statement is clearly on the zoologist's side. It fails on one word: "direct." The statement's work runs through the "so" claim and is aimed at the food theory, not at play itself.

choices.note: CORRECT. The statement supports "gains the ravens nothing to eat," and that claim is what undermines the observers' food-stealing explanation, the alternative to play.
Tempting, and the main trap. The statement helps the zoologist, but not directly. It supports the "so" claim, which rules out the food theory. The positive evidence for play is the age pattern.
Backward. The observers would hardly cite the fact that ravens never go for the food; the zoologist uses it against them.
The main conclusion is that the behavior is play. This statement is an observation, not something argued for.
Tempting if you skim: it's about the behavior. But the behavior to be explained is dropping caps beside sleeping foxes. This statement is evidence about what happens afterward.

questions.stimulus: Recorded shipwrecks near the port of Calvadi fell sharply after 1840, the year a lighthouse was built at the harbor mouth. The decline coincided with the region's shift from sailing ships to steamships. But steamships were wrecked on open coasts about as often as sailing ships were, so the lighthouse, not the change in ships, was most likely responsible for the decline.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Insurance records from the period show that, throughout the region, steamships and sailing ships were lost on open coasts at similar rates.
Calvadi's lighthouse was paid for by a tax on the cargoes of ships entering the harbor during its first decade of operation.
After 1840, many ships entering Calvadi's harbor took on local pilots who knew the channels and hazards near the harbor mouth.
Among sailing ships entering Calvadi's harbor, the proportion wrecked near its mouth was far lower in the 1840s than in the 1830s.
Shipwrecks also fell sharply after 1840 near several other ports in the region that had no lighthouse at the time.
questions.explanation: The rival cause is the shift to steamships. The argument answers it with open-coast data, but Calvadi's wrecks happen at a harbor mouth, where steamships, which don't depend on the wind, might well be safer. (D) sidesteps that: even among sailing ships alone, the wreck rate near the mouth fell sharply, so the decline can't be just a change in which ships came in. That leaves the lighthouse. (A) is the main trap: it repeats the open-coast premise, which is exactly the evidence that doesn't fit a harbor. (C) and (E) point to other causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lighthouse, not the shift to steamships, most likely caused the decline in wrecks near Calvadi.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wrecks fell after the 1840 lighthouse; steamships were wrecked on open coasts about as often as sailing ships.

breakdown.analysis: Open coasts aren't harbor mouths. A steamship can hold its course into a tricky harbor entrance against the wind; a sailing ship can't. So the premise doesn't really rule out the steamship explanation where it matters. What would? Look within one kind of ship. If sailing ships themselves were wrecked far less after 1840, the drop isn't a shift in the mix of ships. Think of a school whose test scores rise just as it enrolls stronger students: if the scores of the students who were already there also rose, enrollment can't explain it. Most students pick (A) because it sounds like hard evidence for the premise. It fails because it restates the open-coast point, the weak link.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. It confirms the premise about open coasts, but the problem is that open coasts may not tell us about a harbor mouth. More of the same evidence doesn't fix that.
Irrelevant. How the lighthouse was paid for says nothing about whether it prevented wrecks.
This introduces another cause, local pilots, so it weakens the case for the lighthouse.

CORRECT. Holding the type of ship fixed, the wreck rate near the mouth still fell sharply after 1840. So the decline isn't explained by steamships replacing sailing ships, which leaves the lighthouse as the likeliest cause.
This weakens: ports with no lighthouse saw the same drop, which points to something region-wide, like the change in ships.

questions.stimulus: Cycling club secretary: Last year, members of the Renfield Cycling Club who did most of their riding in groups reported fewer crashes, on average, than members who rode mostly alone. So riding in a group makes cycling safer, presumably because drivers more readily notice, and give room to, a group of cyclists than a lone rider.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the secretary's argument?
choices: Members of the club who rode mostly in groups were also less likely than members who rode mostly alone to report being injured in a crash.
Members who rode mostly alone were more likely than those who rode mostly in groups to do much of their riding after dark.
Most of the club's members say that they feel safer when riding with others than when riding by themselves.
Most of the crashes reported by members who rode mostly alone did not involve any motor vehicle.
On average, members who rode mostly in groups covered more kilometers last year than members who rode mostly alone.
questions.explanation: Fewer crashes per member could just mean group riders rode less. (E) says they rode more, so their crash rate per kilometer is even lower, which removes the exposure explanation. (A) is the main trap: fewer injuries follow from fewer crashes and add nothing. (D) says lone riders' crashes mostly didn't involve motor vehicles, which undercuts the driver-noticing mechanism, so it weakens. (B) offers a rival cause (riding after dark).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Riding in a group makes cycling safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, club members who rode mostly in groups reported fewer crashes on average than members who rode mostly alone.

breakdown.analysis: Fewer crashes per member isn't the same as safer. What if the group riders just rode less? Someone who rides 100 km a year will have fewer crashes than someone who rides 5,000, even on the same roads. Safety is a rate: crashes per kilometer. We need the group riders' exposure to be at least as high. Watch for count-versus-rate traps; this is the classic one. Most students pick (A) because fewer injuries sounds like more proof of safety. It fails because it has the very same problem: group riders who ride less will also get hurt less.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. Fewer injuries is what you'd expect from fewer crashes, so it adds nothing new. And it has the same hole: if group riders ride less, they'd get hurt less no matter how safe groups are.
This weakens. Night riding is a rival explanation for the solo riders' extra crashes.
Feeling safe isn't being safe. This supports what members believe, not the claim that groups reduce crashes.

Tempting because it's about lone riders' crashes. But if most of those crashes didn't involve cars, drivers' noticing groups can't explain why lone riders crash more. It undercuts the "presumably because" mechanism, so it weakens.
CORRECT. Group riders logged more kilometers and still had fewer crashes, so their crash rate per kilometer is clearly lower. That rules out "they just rode less" as the explanation.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Supporters of the proposed toll on the Mercer Street bridge predict that it will substantially ease rush-hour congestion downtown. The toll may well reduce traffic on the bridge itself; tolls on single bridges in other cities have done so. But studies of those tolls found that most drivers simply detoured to nearby untolled bridges leading to the same districts. So whatever its effect on the bridge, the toll is unlikely to do much for congestion downtown.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the columnist's argument by the claim that the toll will substantially ease rush-hour congestion downtown?
choices: It is a prediction that the columnist grants may be borne out but argues has not been adequately supported by the toll's supporters.
It is a premise from which the toll's supporters infer that the toll will reduce traffic on the Mercer Street bridge.
It is the claim that the argument as a whole seeks to cast doubt on, while allowing that a more limited claim may be true.
It is the columnist's main conclusion, which is supported by evidence from studies of tolls in other cities.
It is a concession the columnist makes before arguing that the toll will not reduce traffic on the bridge itself.
questions.explanation: The columnist's conclusion, that the toll is unlikely to do much for downtown congestion, denies the supporters' prediction. Along the way the columnist allows a narrower claim, that traffic on the bridge itself may fall. (C) captures both. (A) is the main trap: it blends the concession into the prediction; what the columnist grants is the narrower claim about the bridge, and the argument offers evidence against the prediction rather than faulting the supporters' support. (E) reverses the concession. (D) mistakes the opposed claim for the conclusion that denies it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The toll is unlikely to do much to ease congestion downtown.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Single-bridge tolls elsewhere reduced traffic on the tolled bridge, but most drivers detoured to nearby untolled bridges into the same districts.

breakdown.analysis: Two claims about the toll float around here, and the answer depends on keeping them apart. 1. The toll will cut traffic on the bridge: the columnist allows this ("may well"). 2. The toll will substantially ease downtown congestion: the supporters' prediction, which the conclusion denies. The stem asks about claim 2. So it's the target of the argument, with claim 1 as the narrower point the columnist lets stand. Most students pick (A) because it mixes a concession with a rejection, which sounds like the structure. It fails because the concession is about claim 1, not claim 2, and the columnist argues claim 2 is unlikely, not merely unsupported.

choices.note: Tempting, and the main trap. The columnist does grant something, but it's the narrower claim about traffic on the bridge. And the argument doesn't say the supporters' case is thin; it offers counterevidence that makes the prediction unlikely.
Backward. Easing downtown congestion would be the payoff the supporters expect from less bridge traffic, not their reason for expecting less bridge traffic.

CORRECT. The conclusion ("unlikely to do much for congestion downtown") is aimed squarely at this prediction, and "may well reduce traffic on the bridge itself" is the more limited claim the columnist allows.
The columnist's conclusion is the denial of this claim, not the claim itself. Watch the direction.
Reversed. The columnist allows that the toll may reduce traffic on the bridge; the concession isn't this claim, and the columnist never argues bridge traffic won't fall.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Dialogue, Assumption & Structure

questions.stimulus:
Reyes: The city should take the full-size buses off Route 9 and run smaller vans instead. Ridership on the route has fallen by half in five years; the fare receipts show it.

Abiola: The receipts show nothing of the kind. Since rides became free for students and seniors, most Route 9 riders pay no fare, and the door sensors count more boardings every year. Still, vans do make sense there: full-size buses cannot turn onto Hill Street without blocking traffic.
questions.stem: Reyes and Abiola disagree over whether
choices: the city should replace the full-size buses that now run on Route 9 with smaller vans
full-size buses on Route 9 block traffic whenever they turn onto Hill Street
most of the people who ride Route 9 are students or seniors who pay no fare
fewer people make use of Route 9 now than made use of it five years ago
fare receipts would give an accurate count of Route 9's riders if every rider paid a fare
questions.explanation: Reyes says ridership has fallen by half; Abiola says the receipts miss the riders who pay nothing and that boardings rise every year, so she denies that use of the route has fallen. That is (D). (A) is the trap: the two end up agreeing that vans make sense, for different reasons. (B) and (C) are Abiola's points alone, and (E) is something neither disputes.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Reyes: Switch Route 9 to vans; ridership has fallen by half, as fare receipts show.; Abiola: The receipts miss the many riders who ride free, and door sensors show boardings rising; but vans make sense because big buses block traffic on Hill Street.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Don't stop at the bottom lines. Here they actually match: Reyes wants vans, and Abiola says "vans do make sense there." So the disagreement has to be lower down, in the reasons. Reyes's reason is that ridership has fallen by half. Abiola attacks that reason: the receipts undercount because most riders pay nothing, and the sensors show boardings going up. So the live issue is whether fewer people use the route than before.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Reyes's recommendation. But Abiola agrees with it ("vans do make sense there"), just for a different reason. Agreement is not disagreement.
Abiola's point only. Reyes says nothing about Hill Street or traffic.
Abiola's remarks suggest this, but Reyes never addresses who the riders are or whether they pay. One speaker's view isn't a disagreement.
CORRECT. Reyes: ridership "has fallen by half in five years." Abiola: the sensors "count more boardings every year." One says use has dropped; the other says it hasn't.
Neither speaker denies this. Abiola's complaint is that many riders don't pay, which implies she'd accept receipts as a fair count if everyone did. Reyes relies on receipts, so he'd accept it too.

questions.stimulus: Last year a clinic moved all of its asthma patients from their old inhalers to a new one that delivers its medication in much finer particles. In the twelve months after the switch, these patients made only half as many emergency visits for asthma attacks as they had made in the twelve months before it. So the new inhaler controls asthma better than the old inhalers did.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The twelve months after the switch did not bring conditions, such as unusually low pollen counts, that made asthma attacks much rarer for asthma sufferers in general.
The finer particles that the new inhaler delivers reach deeper into the lungs than the particles delivered by the old inhalers did.
Every patient who switched to the new inhaler made fewer emergency visits for asthma in the year after the switch than in the year before it.
The asthma attacks that the clinic's patients suffered after the switch were, on average, no less severe than those they suffered before it.
Most of the clinic's asthma patients had made at least one emergency visit for an asthma attack during the year before the switch.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the inhaler with a before/after drop, so it needs the drop not to come from something else that changed between the two years. (A) rules out one such rival: a year in which attacks became rarer for everyone. Negated, the halving could be the weather, not the inhaler. (B) is the trap: it explains how the inhaler might work, but the conclusion doesn't depend on any mechanism. (D)'s negation (attacks got milder) fits the conclusion, and (C) is far too strong.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new inhaler controls asthma better than the old inhalers did.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All patients switched; in the year after, emergency visits for asthma were half what they had been the year before.

breakdown.analysis: So what else changed between those two years? Before/after evidence is only as good as the assumption that nothing else changed. The argument never mentions the weather, pollen, flu season or anything else that drives asthma attacks for everyone.
