If the year after the switch happened to be an easy year for all asthma sufferers, the drop proves nothing about the inhaler. We need an answer that rules that out. It's like crediting a new umbrella for keeping you dry in a month when it barely rained.

choices.note: CORRECT. It rules out a rival cause the argument never mentions: a year that was easier on every asthma sufferer. Negate it and the halving could just as well come from the low pollen as from the inhaler.
choices.negation: The year after the switch did bring conditions that made asthma attacks much rarer for everyone. The drop could then have nothing to do with the inhaler, and the argument collapses.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the reason the new inhaler would work. But the conclusion is only that it works better, not why. The argument stands even if the particles help in some other way.
choices.negation: The finer particles don't reach deeper. The inhaler could still work better for another reason, so the argument isn't hurt.

choices.note: Too strong. A halving of visits overall is consistent with a few patients doing worse.
choices.negation: At least one patient made more visits (or the same number) after the switch. The overall drop still stands, so the argument is fine.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a check on the result. But negate it: attacks after the switch were milder. That fits the claim that the inhaler controls asthma better. A required assumption can't be one whose denial helps the argument.
choices.negation: Attacks after the switch were on average less severe. That's consistent with better control, so the argument isn't hurt.

choices.note: Irrelevant detail. The total number of visits halved; it doesn't matter whether most patients, or only a few, had made a visit before.
choices.negation: Fewer than half of the patients had made an emergency visit the year before. The total still fell by half, so the argument isn't affected.

questions.stimulus: Historian of science: The astronomer Lisette Varo is often credited with the first sighting of the comet of 1781 because of a letter, dated March 3 of that year, in which she describes it. But the letter says the comet's tail pointed toward the star Vega, and the tail could not have pointed that way until the comet rounded the Sun in late April. The letter, then, must have been misdated, and Varo's claim to the first sighting rests on no reliable evidence.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the historian's argument by the claim that the letter must have been misdated?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim about the direction in which the comet's tail pointed is offered in support of it.
It is a hypothesis that the historian attributes to those who credit Varo with the first sighting and then goes on to reject.
It is a premise offered in support of the claim that the comet's tail could not have pointed toward Vega until late April.
It is a claim the historian concedes to Varo's defenders before arguing that her priority is nevertheless unproven.
It is a conclusion drawn from claims about the comet's appearance, and it is used in turn to support a further conclusion.
questions.explanation: The tail evidence supports 'the letter must have been misdated,' and the misdating is what leaves Varo's claim without reliable evidence, so the claim is an intermediate conclusion (E). (A) is the trap: the claim is a conclusion, but not the last stop. The main conclusion is that Varo's priority rests on no reliable evidence. (C) reverses the support, and (B) and (D) misassign the claim to Varo's defenders.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varo's claim to the first sighting rests on no reliable evidence.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Varo's credit rests on a letter dated March 3; the letter describes the tail pointing toward Vega, which couldn't happen until late April; so the letter was misdated.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The comet facts (tail toward Vega, impossible before late April) lead to "the letter must have been misdated." Then the misdating leads to the final point: since Varo's credit rested on that letter's date, her claim has no reliable support. So the claim in the stem is both supported and supporting. That is a subsidiary (intermediate) conclusion. Watch for the "then" in the last sentence: it marks the claim as a conclusion, which makes (A) attractive.

choices.note: Tempting, because the claim is introduced with "then" and is supported by the tail evidence. But the argument doesn't stop there. The misdating is offered to show Varo's claim rests on no reliable evidence, and that's the main point.
Varo's defenders rely on the date being right. The misdating is the historian's own conclusion, not something attributed to defenders and rejected.
This reverses the support. The tail claim supports the misdating, not the other way around.
Varo's defenders would never concede that the letter was misdated; that's the historian's attack on their evidence.
CORRECT. It is drawn from the facts about the tail's direction and is then used to support the main conclusion that Varo's claim rests on no reliable evidence.

questions.stimulus:
Moreau: The orchestra was wrong to switch from gut to steel strings for its Baroque series. People attend that series to hear the music as its composers heard it, and steel strings make that impossible.

Achebe: People attend that series for the program. In our survey, almost no one in the audience had noticed the switch, and ticket sales are unchanged. Even so, the orchestra should go back to gut strings: the players were never consulted, and most say steel strains their hands.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Moreau and Achebe disagree over whether
choices: the orchestra should return to using gut strings rather than steel strings for its Baroque series
people attend the Baroque series chiefly to hear the music as its composers heard it
the use of steel strings makes it impossible to hear Baroque music as its composers heard it
most of the orchestra's players find steel strings harder on their hands than gut strings
the orchestra ought to have consulted its players before changing the strings used in the series
questions.explanation: Moreau says people attend the series to hear the music as its composers heard it; Achebe says they attend for the program and backs this with a survey showing almost no one noticed the strings. They disagree over (B). (A) is the trap: both want gut strings back, for different reasons. (C) is Moreau's claim alone, and (D) and (E) are Achebe's alone.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Moreau: The switch to steel was wrong; audiences come to hear the music as the composers heard it, and steel prevents that.; Achebe: Audiences come for the program (almost no one noticed the switch, and sales are unchanged); still, go back to gut because the players weren't consulted and steel strains their hands.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Check the bottom lines first: Moreau thinks the switch was wrong, and Achebe wants to switch back. That's agreement, so the answer is not the policy. Look for where Achebe pushes back. Her first sentence answers Moreau's second: Moreau says people come to hear the music as the composers heard it; Achebe says they come for the program, and almost nobody noticed the change. That's the point at issue.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like the subject of the argument. But both speakers want gut strings back. Moreau thinks the switch was wrong; Achebe says "the orchestra should go back to gut strings."

CORRECT. Moreau: people attend "to hear the music as its composers heard it." Achebe: they attend "for the program," and almost nobody noticed the switch. One says this is the draw; the other says it isn't.
Moreau's claim only. Achebe never says whether steel strings change the sound; her survey shows the audience didn't notice, which is a different point.
Achebe's point only. Moreau doesn't mention the players at all.
Achebe's complaint. Moreau doesn't say anything about consulting the players.

questions.stimulus: When Norvland abolished its tariff on imported shoes, critics predicted that the country's shoe industry would shed jobs. Yet in the three years since, the number of shoe factories operating in Norvland has not fallen. So abolishing the tariff has not cost Norvland's shoe industry any jobs.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Had the tariff remained in place, more shoe factories would now be operating in Norvland than are operating there today.
Imports of shoes into Norvland have not increased by much since the country abolished its tariff on them.
If abolishing the tariff had cost the shoe industry jobs, at least some of those jobs would have been lost through factories' closing.
The critics who predicted job losses did not base their prediction on what happened in other countries that had abolished similar tariffs on shoes.
Not a single shoe factory in Norvland has closed in the three years since the tariff on imported shoes was abolished.
questions.explanation: The evidence is about factories; the conclusion is about jobs. The argument needs a link: if jobs had been lost, the losses would have shown up at least partly as closings (C). Negate it and jobs could vanish through layoffs at factories that stay open, so the factory count proves nothing. (E) is the trap: the count can hold steady even if some factories closed and others opened, so it isn't required. (A) actually describes a way the tariff's removal could have cost jobs.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Abolishing the tariff has not cost Norvland's shoe industry any jobs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the tariff was abolished, the number of shoe factories has not fallen.

breakdown.analysis: Factories aren't jobs. Can an industry lose jobs without losing factories? Easily: every factory can stay open and lay off half its workers. The evidence only counts if job losses would have shown up in the factory count at all. We need an answer that ties the two together: losses, if any, would have come at least partly through closings.

choices.note: This is closer to a weakener. If more factories would have opened with the tariff, removing it may have cost jobs that would otherwise exist.
choices.negation: Had the tariff stayed, no more factories would be operating than now. That's no problem for the argument.

choices.note: Tempting, because rising imports are what the critics feared. But the argument rests on the factory count, not on imports. Imports could rise a lot while domestic jobs hold steady (say, if the market grew).
choices.negation: Imports have risen a lot. The argument can still say no jobs were lost, so the argument isn't hurt.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the bridge from factories to jobs. Negate it and job losses could come entirely from layoffs at factories that stay open, so a steady factory count says nothing about jobs.
choices.negation: Any jobs lost would have been lost without a single closing. Then the factory count is useless as evidence, and the argument falls apart.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Where the critics got their prediction doesn't affect whether the factory count shows that no jobs were lost.
choices.negation: The critics did rely on other countries' experience. The evidence is unchanged.

choices.note: Tempting, because a steady factory count sounds like "no closings." But the number can hold even if some factories closed and others opened. The argument doesn't need zero closings.
choices.negation: At least one factory closed (while others opened). The count still didn't fall, so the argument isn't destroyed.

questions.stimulus: Critic: Readers who dismiss Hal Vesey's late novels as sentimental are mistaking a happy ending for sentimentality. A novel is sentimental when it asks for more feeling than its events have earned, and an ending can be happy without doing that. Vesey's late novels reach their reconciliations only after hundreds of pages of hard-won grief, so by that standard they are among the least sentimental books he wrote.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the critic's argument?
choices: Those who call Vesey's late novels sentimental mistake a feature of their endings for a fault it need not involve.
No novel that ends happily can properly be called sentimental, no matter how much feeling it asks of readers before reaching that ending.
Vesey's late novels are among the least sentimental of all the books that he wrote.
A novel is sentimental when it asks readers for more feeling than the events in it have earned.
Vesey's early novels are more sentimental than the late novels that many readers dismiss as sentimental.
questions.explanation: The critic's main point is the first sentence: readers who dismiss the late novels as sentimental are mistaking happy endings for sentimentality. The definition shows that a happy ending need not be sentimental, and the 'so' sentence shows that these particular novels are not. Both support the first claim. (A) restates it abstractly. (C) is the trap: it carries 'so,' but it is a subsidiary conclusion offered to show the dismissal is mistaken. (B) overstates the definition.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Readers who dismiss Vesey's late novels as sentimental are mistaking a happy ending for sentimentality.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sentimentality = asking for more feeling than events have earned; a happy ending needn't do that; the late novels earn their endings, so by that standard they're among his least sentimental.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The definition explains why a happy ending isn't automatically sentimental. The last sentence shows these novels in particular aren't sentimental. What do those two points prove? That the readers in sentence one have made a mistake, specifically, they've taken a happy ending for sentimentality. The "so" in the last sentence marks a subsidiary conclusion, not the main one. This is the classic main-conclusion trap: the indicator word sits on the wrong sentence.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the first sentence in abstract dress: the "feature of the endings" is their happiness, and the "fault" is sentimentality. The definition and the claim about the late novels both support it.
Too strong. The critic says an ending "can be" happy without being sentimental, not that a happy ending makes sentimentality impossible.
Tempting, because it follows "so." But ask what it's for: it shows that the readers' charge is wrong in these novels' case. It supports the first sentence, so it's a subsidiary conclusion.
This is the critic's definition, a premise. It's used to show that happy endings and sentimentality can come apart.
The critic says the late novels are among Vesey's least sentimental, but never compares them with his early novels in particular. This adds a claim.

questions.stimulus:
Grady: Among the species of one family of fruit bats, those that migrate long distances have, on average, larger brains relative to their body size than those that do not migrate. Navigating over thousands of kilometers must therefore be what drives the evolution of larger brains in these bats.

Sato: Brains are costly to fuel, and a bat that migrates can follow abundant food through every season. Migration may matter, then, not because navigating is demanding but because migrating lets a species afford a large brain.
questions.stem: Sato responds to Grady by
choices: denying that migratory species have larger brains, relative to body size, than nonmigratory species do
arguing that navigating over long distances places few demands on the brains of the bats that do it
proposing that having a large brain is what enables a species to migrate over long distances
conceding that migration may promote larger brains while proposing a different explanation of how it does so
suggesting that some third factor accounts both for a species' migrating and for its having a large brain
questions.explanation: Grady says migration leads to big brains because navigation is demanding. Sato keeps the direction (migration may well 'matter') but swaps the mechanism: migrating gives a bat year-round food, which pays for an expensive brain. That is (D). (C) is the trap for students who expect the stock 'reversed causation' reply, and (E) is the stock 'common cause' reply. Sato offers neither. (B) overstates: Sato says navigation may not be the reason, not that it is easy.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grady: navigating long distances drives the evolution of larger brains in these bats.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Grady: migratory species have larger brains relative to body size. Sato: brains are costly; migrants can follow food all year; so migration may matter because it lets a species afford a big brain.

breakdown.analysis: Read Sato's last sentence slowly: "Migration may matter, then, not because navigating is demanding but because..." Sato doesn't deny that migration leads to bigger brains. She accepts the link and even the direction. What she disputes is why: Grady says navigation, Sato says food. So she accepts the connection and offers a different mechanism for it. Students who reach for the textbook replies (reversed cause, third factor) will miss it. Neither fits: in Sato's story migration still comes first.

choices.note: Sato never questions the brain-size data; her account takes it for granted.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Actually, when you control for body mass properly, migrants' brains are no bigger at all."

choices.note: Too strong. Sato says navigation may not be why migration matters. She doesn't say navigating is undemanding.
choices.example: Example: "Bats navigate by simple cues like the sun's angle, which take almost no brainpower."

choices.note: Tempting, because "reversed causation" is the most familiar reply to a causal claim. But in Sato's account migration still comes first: migrating gets the food, and the food pays for the brain. She doesn't say big brains make migration possible.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Perhaps only bats with large brains are able to migrate in the first place."

choices.note: CORRECT. Sato grants that migration "may matter" for brain size but says it matters through food supply, not through the demands of navigation.
Tempting, because abundant food sounds like an outside factor. But in Sato's account the food comes from migrating; it isn't a separate cause of both migration and big brains.
choices.example: Example of this method: "A long breeding season might cause both migration and larger brains."

questions.stimulus: Since lynx were reintroduced to the Brenn Forest twelve years ago, oak saplings have become far more common in the forest's clearings. Roe deer, which eat oak saplings, now spend little time in the clearings, where lynx can easily spot and stalk them. Thus it is the return of the lynx that has allowed the oaks to regenerate in the clearings.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Lynx kill more roe deer in the clearings of the Brenn Forest than they kill in all of the other parts of the forest combined.
It is not the case that oak saplings would have become just as common in the clearings had there been no lynx.
The number of roe deer living in the Brenn Forest has not declined since the lynx were reintroduced.
Oak saplings cannot survive in any clearing where roe deer feed regularly.
Roe deer that now avoid the clearings eat fewer oak saplings in total than the deer in the forest ate before the lynx returned.
questions.explanation: To credit the lynx, the argument must assume the saplings would not have come back anyway. (B) says exactly that, in negated form. Negate it (they would have come back just as much without lynx) and the lynx did nothing. (C) is the trap: if lynx thinned the deer by killing them, the lynx would still deserve the credit, so a decline in deer doesn't hurt this conclusion. (E)'s negation is harmless, since deer could eat saplings elsewhere while the clearings recover.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The return of the lynx is what allowed the oaks to regenerate in the clearings.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the lynx returned, saplings have increased in clearings; deer, which eat saplings, now avoid clearings, where lynx can stalk them.

breakdown.analysis: Notice what the conclusion actually claims. It doesn't say the lynx worked by scaring deer rather than killing them. It says the lynx's return is what allowed the recovery. So the one thing the argument can't survive is the saplings coming back anyway, lynx or no lynx. Any rival story (a wetter decade, a change in grazing law) works by making that true. We need the defender: without the lynx, the recovery wouldn't have been as great.

choices.note: Not needed. Where lynx do their killing doesn't matter; the conclusion only needs the lynx's return to be what made the difference.
choices.negation: Lynx kill more deer somewhere other than the clearings. The deer still avoid the clearings, so the argument stands.

choices.note: CORRECT. The "not the case" phrasing hides a plain defender: without the lynx, the saplings would not have done as well. Negate it and the recovery would have happened anyway, so the lynx can't be what allowed it.
choices.negation: The saplings would have become just as common without the lynx. Then the lynx's return didn't allow anything, and the conclusion is false.

choices.note: Tempting, because the argument talks about deer behavior, and a drop in deer numbers looks like a rival explanation. But the conclusion is about the lynx, not about behavior. If lynx cut the deer population by eating deer, the lynx still caused the recovery.
choices.negation: The deer population has declined. If lynx did that, the conclusion is even better supported. No damage.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs deer to hurt saplings, not to wipe out every one wherever they feed.
choices.negation: Some saplings can survive in clearings where deer feed. Deer could still hold saplings back, so the argument is fine.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the deer must be eating less. But the conclusion is about the clearings. Deer could eat just as many saplings in the forest interior while the clearings recover.
choices.negation: Deer eat as many saplings in total, just elsewhere. The clearings can still recover because of the lynx. No damage.

questions.stimulus:
Arden: Judges should stop instructing jurors to disregard testimony that has been struck from the record. Research shows that jurors cannot simply forget what they have heard, so the instruction has no effect on verdicts.

Mbeki: Of course jurors cannot forget it; the instruction was never meant to make them. It tells them that a conviction resting on struck testimony could be overturned, and jurors who know that look harder for other grounds before they vote to convict.
questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Arden and Mbeki disagree over whether
choices: jurors are able to put out of mind testimony that has been struck from the record
a conviction that rests on struck testimony is likely to be overturned on appeal
research on jurors' memory has been carried out under realistic courtroom conditions
jurors who have heard struck testimony are more likely than others to vote to convict
telling jurors to disregard struck testimony makes any difference to how they reach their verdicts
questions.explanation: Arden says the instruction 'has no effect on verdicts'; Mbeki says it makes jurors look harder for other grounds before convicting. They disagree over (E). (A) is the trap: both say jurors can't forget struck testimony. (B) is Mbeki's alone, and she says only that such a conviction 'could' be overturned. (C) and (D) are raised by neither.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Arden: Stop the instruction; jurors can't forget what they hear, so it has no effect on verdicts.; Mbeki: Jurors can't forget, but the instruction warns that such a conviction could be overturned, so jurors look harder for other grounds before convicting.

breakdown.analysis: Mbeki opens by agreeing ("Of course jurors cannot forget it"), so the memory point isn't the issue. The fight is over Arden's inference from that fact: since jurors can't forget, the instruction "has no effect on verdicts." Mbeki gives a different route by which it does affect verdicts: jurors who've been warned look harder before convicting. So they split on whether the instruction changes how jurors decide. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's the factual core of Arden's argument. But Mbeki agrees: "Of course jurors cannot forget it."
Mbeki says such a conviction "could" be overturned, not that it's likely to be. Arden says nothing about appeals.
Neither speaker questions the research. Mbeki accepts its finding.
Neither speaker compares jurors who heard struck testimony with jurors who didn't.

CORRECT. Arden: the instruction "has no effect on verdicts." Mbeki: it makes jurors "look harder for other grounds before they vote to convict." One says no difference; the other says it changes how jurors decide.

questions.stimulus: The outermost growth ring of an oak beam in the old Haddon granary formed in 1412, so the tree it came from was felled no earlier than that year. Builders in the region at that time used timber within a year or two of felling it, and the beam shows none of the extra joint cuts typical of timbers reused from older buildings. The granary was therefore most likely built around 1413.
questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choices: Oak was the timber that builders in the region used most often for granaries during the early 1400s.
Every beam in the Haddon granary came from a tree that was felled in either 1412 or 1413.
Little, if any, of the beam's outer wood was cut away when the beam was shaped.
Tree-ring dating has also been used to date other buildings in the region that were built in that era.
No beam in the granary came from a tree felled after the granary was first built.
questions.explanation: The outermost surviving ring dates the felling only if that ring was the last one the tree grew. If the builders trimmed off the outer wood, the tree could have been felled years or decades after 1412, and the date of 1413 falls apart. (C) protects that step. (E) is the trap: it sounds like a guard against later replacement, but its negation (some other beam is a later replacement) leaves this beam's date untouched. (B) is far stronger than needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The granary was most likely built around 1413.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The beam's outermost ring formed in 1412, so the tree was felled no earlier than 1412; timber was used within a year or two; the beam wasn't reused.

breakdown.analysis: The argument checks two ways the date could be off: slow use of timber (ruled out) and reused timber (ruled out). But it skips a step in its own method. The outermost ring on the beam tells you when the tree was felled only if nothing outside it was removed. Carpenters square off beams. If they cut away twenty years of outer wood, the tree was felled around 1432, not 1412. The premise even hints at this: "no earlier than." We need an answer that says the outer wood wasn't trimmed away.

choices.note: Irrelevant. What other granaries were made of doesn't affect when this beam's tree was felled.
choices.negation: Some other timber was more common. This beam is still oak, dated to 1412. No effect.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument rests on one beam; other beams could be from other years.
choices.negation: Some beam came from a tree felled in another year. This beam still dates the building. No damage.

choices.note: CORRECT. It protects the hidden step: the beam's last surviving ring is the tree's last ring. Negate it and much outer wood was cut away, so the tree could have been felled long after 1412, and so could the granary have been built.
choices.negation: A lot of the beam's outer wood was cut away. Then 1412 is just a lower limit, and the building could be decades younger. The argument fails.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the method was used elsewhere doesn't affect this beam.
choices.negation: No other building in the region has been dated this way. The beam's evidence is unchanged.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like it guards against a beam being a later replacement. But it's about all the beams. Negate it: some beam is a later replacement. That beam needn't be this one, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: At least one beam came from a later tree, perhaps from a repair. This beam can still be original, so the argument isn't destroyed.

questions.stimulus: Historian: The town records of Merrow from the 1600s are badly flawed: whole decades are missing, and many entries were written years after the events they describe. Even so, they are the best guide we have to the town's grain prices in that century. The only other sources, travelers' accounts, mention prices only when prices were startlingly high or low, and so give a distorted picture of ordinary years.
questions.stem: The claim that the town records of Merrow from the 1600s are badly flawed plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?
choices: It concedes weaknesses in a source that the argument nonetheless holds to be better than the only alternative.
It describes weaknesses that the argument goes on to show are less damaging than they might at first appear.
It is offered as evidence that the travelers' accounts give a distorted picture of grain prices in ordinary years.
It is a premise that, together with the claim about travelers' accounts, directly supports the main conclusion.
It is the main conclusion of the argument, which the claims about the travelers' accounts are offered to support.
questions.explanation: The historian grants that the records are flawed and then argues that they are still the best guide, because the alternative is worse. So the claim is a concession, and the argument holds the source superior anyway (A). (B) is the trap: the historian never says the flaws are less serious than they look, only that the alternative is worse. (D) gets the role wrong: the flaws work against the conclusion, not for it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Merrow town records are the best guide we have to the town's grain prices in the 1600s.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The only other source, travelers' accounts, mentions only extreme prices and so distorts ordinary years. (Conceded: the records are badly flawed.)

breakdown.analysis: "Even so" is the hinge. Everything before it is a concession: the historian admits the records have serious problems. Everything after supports the conclusion that they're still the best guide, because the competitor is worse. A concession doesn't support the conclusion. It's a point against it that the author grants and then outweighs. Don't confuse "outweighed" with "minimized": the historian never says the gaps and late entries are less serious than they look.

choices.note: CORRECT. The historian concedes the flaws, then argues that the records still beat the only alternative, travelers' accounts.
Tempting, but the historian never shrinks the flaws. There's no claim that the missing decades or late entries matter less than they seem. The argument wins by comparison, not by minimizing.
The records' flaws have nothing to do with why the travelers' accounts are distorted. That's explained by the accounts' focus on extreme prices.
The flaws count against the records. They can't directly support the claim that the records are the best guide.
The main conclusion is that the records are the best guide, which comes after "Even so." The flaws are what the conclusion overcomes.

questions.stimulus:
Vargas: The county's free glaucoma screenings at pharmacies have not been worth what they cost. Most of the people who came for a screening had already been diagnosed with glaucoma and were being treated for it, so for them the screening accomplished nothing.

Lindahl: Several of those people learned from the screening that their eye pressure was still high and went back to their doctors to change their treatment. I grant, though, that too few undiagnosed people came.
questions.stem: Vargas and Lindahl disagree over whether
choices: the screenings reached too few people who had not already been diagnosed with glaucoma
the county's free glaucoma screenings at pharmacies have been worth what they have cost
most of the people who came for a screening had already been diagnosed with glaucoma
the screenings did anything of value for people who were already being treated for glaucoma
people whose eye pressure stays high despite treatment usually find this out from their own doctors
questions.explanation: Vargas says the screening 'accomplished nothing' for people already under treatment; Lindahl says several of them learned their treatment wasn't working and went back to their doctors. That is (D). (B) is the trap: it is Vargas's conclusion, but Lindahl never says the program was worth its cost. She only rebuts one premise and concedes another weakness. (A) and (C) are points Lindahl accepts.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Vargas: The screenings weren't worth the cost; most people screened were already diagnosed and treated, so it did nothing for them.; Lindahl: Several of those people learned their pressure was still high and got their treatment changed; but too few undiagnosed people came.

breakdown.analysis: Students go straight for the bottom line, but Lindahl never gives one. She attacks a premise and then concedes a weakness. Does she think the program was worth the money? We can't tell. What we can tell is that she flatly contradicts "for them the screening accomplished nothing": some of them changed their treatment because of it. The disagreement is over that sub-claim. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Here only the sub-claim gets a yes and a no.

choices.note: Lindahl explicitly grants this, and Vargas's point that most people screened were already diagnosed points the same way. That's agreement, not disagreement.

Tempting, because it's Vargas's conclusion and Lindahl argues with her. But Lindahl never says the program was worth its cost. She disputes one reason and concedes another problem. We don't know her overall verdict.
Lindahl doesn't dispute this. She talks about "those people," accepting Vargas's description of who came.

CORRECT. Vargas: for people already treated, "the screening accomplished nothing." Lindahl: several of them found their pressure was still high and changed their treatment. That is a yes and a no on the same point.
Neither speaker says how such people usually find out. Lindahl's point is that some found out at the screening.

questions.stimulus: Human resources director: Many managers treat exit interviews as their most reliable guide to why employees quit. They are wrong to do so. Departing employees usually still want good references, so they tend to cite inoffensive reasons for leaving, such as a better offer elsewhere, rather than complaints about their managers. Exit interviews thus systematically understate the role that poor management plays in employees' departures.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the director's argument?
choices: Exit interviews systematically understate how often poor management leads employees to quit their jobs.
Managers should not regard exit interviews as their most reliable source of information about why employees quit.
Poor management is a more common reason for employees to quit than are better offers from other employers.
Managers who want to learn why their employees quit should rely on sources of information other than exit interviews.
Managers who rely on exit interviews are more likely than other managers to overlook their own shortcomings.
questions.explanation: The director rejects a view ('They are wrong to do so') and then supports that rejection: departing employees want references, so they give inoffensive reasons, so exit interviews understate poor management, so they aren't a reliable guide. (B) restates the rejection. (A) is the trap: it is the last sentence and carries 'thus,' but it is an intermediate conclusion offered as the reason managers are wrong to rely on exit interviews. (D) overshoots: denying that exit interviews are the most reliable guide doesn't mean managers should stop relying on them, and (C) compares two reasons the argument never ranks.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Managers are wrong to treat exit interviews as their most reliable guide to why employees quit.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Departing employees want good references; so they cite inoffensive reasons instead of complaints about managers; thus exit interviews understate the role of poor management.

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. "They are wrong to do so" is a flat rejection of what many managers do. Everything after it is the case for that rejection. Why are they wrong? Because exit interviews understate poor management. Why do they understate it? Because people want references. So the "thus" sentence at the end is a middle step: it's supported by the references point and it supports the rejection. Classic setup: the main conclusion comes early, right after the opposing view, and the last sentence is an intermediate conclusion with an indicator word.

choices.note: Tempting, because it comes last and carries "thus." But it answers the question "why are the managers wrong?" That makes it support for the main conclusion, not the main conclusion itself.
CORRECT. This is "They are wrong to do so" spelled out: managers shouldn't treat exit interviews as their most reliable guide to why people quit. Every other claim backs this up.
Too strong. The director says exit interviews understate poor management's role. That doesn't mean poor management is a more common reason than better offers.

Tempting, because it sounds like the practical upshot of "They are wrong to do so." But it's stronger than what the director says. Exit interviews aren't the most reliable guide; that doesn't mean managers should stop using them. They could still be one useful source among several.
The director never compares managers who rely on exit interviews with other managers. This adds a claim the argument doesn't make.

questions.stimulus: The Delvin Charter of 1290 survives only in a copy made in 1340, and some historians treat that copy as a faithful record of the original. But the copy uses three legal terms that appear in no surviving document written before 1320. So the surviving text of the charter is not exactly as its drafters wrote it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The scribe who made the 1340 copy intended to change the meaning of the charter.
No document written before 1320, whether or not it survives, used any of the three legal terms in question.
The three legal terms alter the legal effect of the provisions of the charter in which they appear.
The 1340 copy was made directly from the original charter rather than from some earlier copy of it.
At least one of the three terms was not yet in use at the time that the charter was drafted.
questions.explanation: The premise is about surviving documents; the conclusion is about what the drafters wrote. The argument needs absence from the record to reflect absence from the language, at least for one of the terms (E). Negate it (all three terms were already in use in 1290, just unrecorded) and the copy could be faithful. (B) is the trap: it looks like the premise made airtight, but a lost document from, say, 1305 using one term wouldn't show the term existed in 1290, so (B) isn't required.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The surviving text of the charter is not exactly as its drafters wrote it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 1340 copy uses three terms that appear in no surviving document from before 1320.

breakdown.analysis: Not being on record isn't the same as not existing. Plenty of words were spoken and written for decades before the first surviving document happens to use them. The argument treats "appears in no surviving document before 1320" as if it meant "didn't exist in 1290." For the conclusion to follow, at least one of those terms must really have been unavailable to the drafters. One is enough: a single anachronism shows the copy was altered.

choices.note: Not required. A scribe could alter the text without meaning to change its sense, for instance by modernizing the wording. The conclusion is only that the text differs.
choices.negation: The scribe didn't intend to change the meaning. The text can still differ from the original, so the argument stands.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like the premise made airtight. But it's about every document before 1320, including lost ones. Negate it: some lost document from 1305 used one of the terms. That doesn't put the term in use in 1290, so the argument survives.
choices.negation: Some document written before 1320 used one of the terms. It might date from after 1290, so the copy could still be altered. No damage.

choices.note: Not required. The conclusion is about the wording, not the legal effect. New words that mean the same thing still make the text inexact.
choices.negation: The terms don't change the legal effect. The wording still differs, so the conclusion still follows.

choices.note: Not required. Whether there was an intermediate copy affects when the change entered, not whether the text differs from the original.
choices.negation: The 1340 copy was made from an earlier copy. The surviving text can still differ from what the drafters wrote.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the link from "not on record" to "not written in 1290." Negate it and all three terms existed when the charter was drafted. Then the copy could reproduce the original exactly, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: All three terms were already in use in 1290. The drafters could have used them, so the copy may be faithful. The argument fails.

questions.stimulus: Philosopher: Some researchers define a tool as any object that an animal uses to achieve a goal. But by that definition, a log that a squirrel climbs onto in order to reach a bird feeder would be a tool, and no one would describe the squirrel as using a tool. So whatever makes an object a tool, it cannot be merely that an animal uses the object to achieve a goal.
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument proceeds by
choices: offering a counterexample to show that a proposed definition fails to cover some objects that are clearly tools
rejecting a definition on the grounds that the researchers who propose it disagree about how it should be applied
appealing to a judgment about a particular case to deny that a certain condition suffices for membership in a category
proposing a new definition of a category and showing that it handles a troublesome case better than a rival definition does
rejecting a proposed condition for membership in a category on the grounds that some members of the category fail to meet it
questions.explanation: The squirrel's log meets the researchers' condition (used to achieve a goal), yet we judge it not a tool. So the condition isn't sufficient. That is (C): an intuitive verdict about one case is used to show a condition doesn't suffice. (E) is the trap: it describes showing a condition is not necessary (a tool that fails the test), the reverse of what happens. (A) makes the same mistake, calling the definition too narrow when the problem is that it's too broad.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Being used by an animal to achieve a goal can't be all that makes an object a tool.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: By the researchers' definition, a squirrel's log would be a tool; no one would call it one.

breakdown.analysis: Is the definition too broad or too narrow? The log is let in by the definition but shouldn't be. That's too broad: the condition "used to achieve a goal" lets in a non-tool, so it isn't sufficient for being a tool. The philosopher doesn't claim the condition isn't necessary. Tools may well all be used for goals. Watch the traps that flip this: one says the definition misses real tools, and another says some tools fail the condition. Both describe the opposite move.

choices.note: Tempting, because there is a counterexample. But it's the wrong kind: the log is a non-tool that the definition lets in, not a real tool the definition leaves out. That makes the definition too broad, not too narrow.
choices.example: Example of this method: "If tools must be held in the hand, then a beaver's dam-building stick held in its mouth wouldn't count, yet it's clearly a tool."

choices.note: No disagreement among the researchers is mentioned. The objection is to the definition itself.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Those who define tools this way can't even agree whether a nest counts, so the definition is useless."

choices.note: CORRECT. The "judgment about a particular case" is that the squirrel isn't using a tool. The "condition" is being used to achieve a goal. The philosopher uses the case to show that condition isn't enough by itself.
The philosopher proposes no definition. The conclusion only says that something more is needed.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Let's define a tool as an object modified for a purpose. Unlike the rival definition, this rules out the squirrel's log."

choices.note: Tempting, because the words sound like a counterexample argument. But this describes showing that a condition is not necessary (a real tool that fails the test). The philosopher shows the condition is not sufficient (a non-tool that passes it).
choices.example: Example of this method: "Tools can't require hands, since an otter's stone is a tool and otters hold it with their paws."

questions.stimulus:
Halvorsen: The finches on Corra Island evidently prefer to nest in the junipers on the island's cliffs rather than in its pines. Of the nests we found last spring, nine of every ten were in junipers.

Ruiz: We searched for nests only along the coastal paths, and the island's pines grow almost entirely in its interior.
questions.stem: Ruiz responds to Halvorsen by
choices: pointing out that Halvorsen's evidence was gathered in a way that could produce it even if his conclusion is false
presenting evidence that the finches on Corra Island in fact prefer to nest in pines rather than in junipers
questioning whether the nests found last spring were in fact built by finches rather than by other birds
suggesting that junipers greatly outnumber pines on Corra Island taken as a whole
arguing that the finches avoid the island's interior because few junipers grow there
questions.explanation: Ruiz's point is that the search covered the coast, where the junipers are, and missed the interior, where the pines are. So a nine-in-ten juniper count is what you'd expect even if finches liked pines just as well. That is (A). (D) is the trap: it offers a different rival explanation (more junipers overall) that Ruiz never states. (B) overstates: Ruiz shows the evidence is weak, not that the opposite is true.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halvorsen: finches on Corra prefer junipers to pines for nesting.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Halvorsen: 90% of nests found were in junipers. Ruiz: the search covered only the coastal paths, and pines grow almost only in the interior.

breakdown.analysis: Where did they look? Only along the coast. Where are the pines? Inland. So of course nearly every nest they found was in a juniper; they barely saw a pine. Ruiz doesn't say finches prefer pines or that Halvorsen is wrong. She says his evidence can't tell, because the search itself built in the result. It's like surveying a beach and concluding people prefer sand to grass.

choices.note: CORRECT. A coast-only search would turn up mostly juniper nests whether or not finches prefer junipers. Ruiz shows the way the data were collected could produce the result by itself.
Too strong. Ruiz doesn't claim finches prefer pines. She only says the search couldn't detect it if they did.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Our interior survey found twice as many nests per pine as per juniper."

choices.note: Ruiz never questions who built the nests.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Many of those nests look like they were built by wrens."

choices.note: Tempting, because "more junipers overall" is a familiar rival explanation. But Ruiz says nothing about how many trees of each kind there are on the island. Her point is about where the search took place.
choices.example: Example of this method: "Junipers make up nine of every ten trees on the island, so of course most nests are in them."

choices.note: Ruiz offers no theory of why finches nest where they do. She mentions the interior only to show it went unsearched.

questions.stimulus:
Kessler: A newspaper should name the sources behind a story unless naming them would put them in danger. Readers can judge how reliable a story is only if they know who supplied its information.

Tamura: Most sources who ask not to be named fear for their jobs, not their safety. Name every source who is not in danger, and such people will stop talking; the stories readers most need will go unwritten. Fear of being fired is reason enough to withhold a source's name.
questions.stem: Kessler and Tamura disagree over whether
choices: readers can judge how reliable a story is only if they know who supplied its information
a newspaper should print the name of a source whose only risk in being named is the loss of a job
most sources who ask not to be named are concerned mainly about their own physical safety
a newspaper should withhold the name of a source who would be put in danger by being named
the stories that readers most need depend on information from sources who are not named
questions.explanation: Kessler's rule says to name a source unless naming would endanger the source. A source who risks only a job isn't endangered, so Kessler would name that source; Tamura says fear of being fired is reason enough to withhold the name. They disagree over (B). (D) is the trap: both would withhold the name of an endangered source. (A), (C) and (E) are each raised by only one speaker.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Kessler: Name sources unless naming them would endanger them; readers need to know sources to judge reliability.; Tamura: Most anonymous sources fear for their jobs; naming them would dry up important stories; fear of firing is reason enough to withhold a name.

breakdown.analysis: Apply Kessler's rule to Tamura's case. Kessler: name the source unless naming would put the source in danger. A source who would merely lose a job isn't in danger, so under Kessler's rule that source gets named. Tamura says that very source should not be named. That's the clash. To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no, and here each is committed through their own words.

choices.note: Kessler's reason. Tamura doesn't deny it; she argues that naming sources would cost more than it gains.
CORRECT. Under Kessler's rule, a source facing only job loss isn't in danger, so the paper should name the source. Tamura: "Fear of being fired is reason enough to withhold a source's name."
Tamura denies this, but Kessler never says what most sources fear.

Tempting, because it's about naming sources. But there's no clash here: Kessler's rule makes an exception for endangered sources, and Tamura, who would withhold even the names of sources who fear only for their jobs, certainly wouldn't name them.
Tamura's claim. Kessler doesn't address which stories depend on anonymous sources.

questions.stimulus: Court watcher: Last year Judge Morrow's rulings made up 10 percent of the trial rulings that the district's appeals court reviewed but 25 percent of the rulings it reversed. The appeals court reverses a ruling only when it finds a legal error. So Judge Morrow is evidently less careful in applying the law than the district's other trial judges are.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the court watcher's argument depends?
choices: Each of Judge Morrow's rulings that the appeals court reversed last year contained the same kind of legal error.
Judge Morrow's rulings were appealed more often last year than were the rulings of any other trial judge in the district.
The appeals court reversed at least a quarter of the rulings by Judge Morrow that it reviewed last year.
The cases assigned to Judge Morrow are not disproportionately of kinds in which even careful judges' rulings are frequently reversed.
Every reversal that the appeals court issued last year was based on an error that a careful trial judge would have avoided.
questions.explanation: The numbers do show that Morrow's reviewed rulings were reversed about three times as often as the other judges' rulings were. The leap is from more reversals to less care. If Morrow's docket is heavy with case types where everyone gets reversed often (novel or unsettled areas of law), the gap could reflect her assignments, not her care. (D) rules that out. (E) is the trap: it sounds like the premise made airtight, but the argument survives if a few reversals involved errors a careful judge might make. (C) is a calculation trap: the shares tell us the relative rate, not the absolute one.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Judge Morrow is less careful in applying the law than the district's other trial judges.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Morrow's rulings were 10% of those reviewed but 25% of those reversed; reversal happens only on finding a legal error.

breakdown.analysis: Run the numbers first: 10% of the reviewed rulings, 25% of the reversals. Work it out and her reviewed rulings were reversed at about three times the rate of the other judges' rulings (25/10 versus 75/90). Fine. But why? The court watcher picks one explanation: she's careless. What if she's the judge who gets the hard cases, like new statutes or complex commercial disputes, where even the best judges get reversed a lot? Then her record could reflect her docket, not her care. The argument needs that not to be so. It's like calling a surgeon careless because more of her patients die, when she takes all the riskiest operations.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the errors were all of one kind or many kinds says nothing about carefulness compared with other judges.
choices.negation: Her reversed rulings contained different kinds of errors. She can still be less careful. No damage.

choices.note: Not required, and the data don't depend on it. The argument compares reversal rates among reviewed rulings; how often each judge was appealed doesn't matter.
choices.negation: Some other judge was appealed more often. Morrow's reversal share is still out of line, so the argument stands.

choices.note: Tempting if you start calculating. But the shares give only a relative rate (about three times the others'), not an absolute one. Morrow's reversal rate could be 12% while the others' is 4%, and the argument would be just as strong.
choices.negation: Fewer than a quarter of her reviewed rulings were reversed. Her rate can still be far above the others', so the argument is fine.

choices.note: CORRECT. It rules out the rival explanation that her caseload, not her care, drives the reversals. Negate it: her cases are disproportionately the kind that get reversed a lot even for careful judges. Then the gap tells us nothing about her care.
choices.negation: Her cases are disproportionately of kinds in which careful judges are often reversed. Her reversal rate could then come from her docket, and the argument fails.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like what is needed to connect reversal with carelessness. But "every" is too strong. If a few reversals involved errors that careful judges also make, Morrow's much higher rate still points to less care.
choices.negation: At least one reversal involved an error a careful judge might have made. That barely touches the comparison, so the argument survives.

questions.stimulus: Nutrition scientist: Advocates of requiring warning labels on sugary drinks point out that in trials, shoppers who saw such labels bought fewer of the drinks. But in each of those trials, purchases returned to their former level within a few months, as shoppers grew used to the labels. So even if a label requirement imposed only a modest burden on manufacturers, it would do little to reduce the amount of sugar people consume over the long term.
questions.stem: The claim that in trials, shoppers who saw warning labels bought fewer sugary drinks figures in the scientist's argument in which one of the following ways?
choices: It is a claim that the scientist disputes by citing evidence that the effect of the labels did not last.
It is a premise that, together with the claim about shoppers' growing used to the labels, supports the main conclusion.
It is cited in support of a position that the scientist's conclusion is meant to undercut.
It is the main conclusion of an argument that the scientist goes on to reject as unsupported by the trials.
It is offered as support for the view that a label requirement would impose only a modest burden on manufacturers.
questions.explanation: Advocates cite the drop in purchases to support requiring labels; the scientist's conclusion, that labels would do little over the long term, works against that position. That is (C). (A) is the main trap: the scientist doesn't dispute the drop. She grants it and shows it was temporary. (D) gets the role half right: the claim belongs to the advocates, but it is their premise, not their conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A label requirement would do little to reduce long-term sugar consumption.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In the trials advocates cite, purchases returned to their former level within months as shoppers got used to the labels.

breakdown.analysis: Whose claim is it, and what is it for? The advocates cite the trials' drop in purchases as a reason to require labels. Does the scientist deny that purchases fell? No. "Returned to their former level" means they did fall. She accepts the fact and argues it doesn't show what the advocates need, a lasting effect. So the claim supports the other side's position, and her conclusion undercuts that position. Don't confuse "shows the effect didn't last" with "disputes the claim."

choices.note: Tempting, because the scientist does bring in evidence that the effect didn't last. But that's not disputing the claim. Purchases did fall at first, and "returned to their former level" grants exactly that.
The scientist's conclusion rests on the effect fading, not on the initial drop. The drop is the advocates' evidence.
CORRECT. Advocates offer it in support of requiring labels. The scientist's conclusion, that labels would do little long term, is aimed at that position.
Half right: it does come from the advocates. But it's their premise, not their conclusion. Their conclusion is that labels should be required.
The modest burden is only granted for the sake of argument ("even if"). The trial results aren't offered as support for it.

questions.stimulus:
Brandt: The government should not fund the proposed dam on the Selk River. It would flood farmland in the Selk valley, and wind turbines could generate the same electricity more cheaply.

Osei: Wind is cheaper only where the grid can store power for calm days, and ours cannot. I would oppose the dam myself if it flooded farmland, but its reservoir would fill only the gorge above the valley. Whether the dam is worth its price, I have not yet decided.
questions.stem: Brandt and Osei disagree over whether
choices: the government should provide funding for the proposed dam on the Selk River
a dam that would flood farmland in the Selk valley ought not to be built
the country's electricity grid is able to store power for days when there is little wind
the reservoir created by the dam would fill the gorge above the Selk valley
building the dam would cause farmland in the Selk valley to be lost
questions.explanation: Brandt says the dam would flood valley farmland; Osei says the reservoir would fill only the gorge above the valley, so it would not. That is (E). (A) is the trap: Osei explicitly withholds judgment on whether the dam is worth funding. (B) is common ground: Osei says he too would oppose a dam that flooded farmland. (C) and (D) are claims only Osei makes; Brandt never mentions storage or the gorge.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Brandt: Don't fund the dam; it would flood valley farmland, and wind would be cheaper.; Osei: Wind is cheaper only with storage, which the grid lacks; I'd oppose the dam if it flooded farmland, but the reservoir would fill only the gorge; undecided on funding.

breakdown.analysis: Osei's conditional is the key: "I would oppose the dam if it flooded farmland." So Osei agrees with Brandt's principle that flooding farmland is a reason to oppose. What he denies is the fact: "its reservoir would fill only the gorge above the valley," so no valley farmland is lost. And watch his last sentence. He has not decided on funding, so the bottom line isn't a disagreement. (They also clash over whether wind is cheaper, but that isn't among the choices.)

choices.note: Tempting, because it's Brandt's conclusion and Osei argues against Brandt's reasons. But Osei says outright that he hasn't decided whether the dam is worth its price.
Common ground. Osei: "I would oppose the dam myself if it flooded farmland." Brandt's argument assumes the same.
Osei's claim. Brandt says wind is cheaper but never mentions storage, so we don't know his view on it.
Osei says this, but Brandt doesn't deny it. The reservoir could fill the gorge and the valley too, for all Brandt says.
CORRECT. Brandt: the dam "would flood farmland in the Selk valley." Osei: the reservoir "would fill only the gorge above the valley," so no valley farmland is lost.

questions.stimulus: In a study, museum visitors were asked either to sketch or to photograph a set of exhibits. A week later, the sketchers recalled far more details of the exhibits than the photographers did, even though the photographers had recorded far more of those details. Because sketching is slow, sketchers must choose which features to record. Thus, choosing what to record does more to fix things in memory than recording everything does.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: None of the visitors who sketched the exhibits attempted to record every feature of the exhibits that they sketched.
Choosing what to record improves memory for every kind of material, not merely for museum exhibits.
The visitors who sketched and the visitors who photographed were equally familiar with the exhibits beforehand.
The visitors who photographed the exhibits were less selective about what they recorded than the sketchers were.
The visitors who photographed the exhibits did not look at their photographs during the week before they were tested.
questions.explanation: The argument credits the sketchers' better memory to selecting, so it needs the photographers to have selected less (D). If the photographers chose just as carefully, selecting can't explain the difference. (C) is the trap: it sounds like a needed control, but its negation ('not equally familiar') includes the case where the photographers knew the exhibits better, which only strengthens the result. (A) is too strong, and (E)'s negation would make the photographers' poor recall even more striking.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Choosing what to record does more to fix things in memory than recording everything does.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sketchers recalled far more details a week later, though photographers recorded more; sketching is slow, so sketchers must choose what to record.

breakdown.analysis: The argument explains a difference between two groups by a feature it says one group had: selecting. That only works if the other group lacked it, or had less of it. The stimulus tells us sketchers had to choose. It never says photographers didn't. "Recorded more" isn't the same as "chose less": a photographer could frame every shot deliberately. We need an answer that says the photographers really were less selective. Watch the "equally" trap: its negation can cut either way, so it's not required.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs sketchers to have been more selective than photographers, not perfectly selective. A sketcher who tried to record everything and failed is no problem.
choices.negation: At least one sketcher tried to record everything. The group as a whole was still more selective. No damage.

choices.note: Too broad. The conclusion is about memory for what one records, drawn from exhibits. It doesn't need to hold for every kind of material.
choices.negation: Selecting doesn't help for some other kind of material. The museum result stands.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like the control a good study needs. But negate it: the groups were not equally familiar. That includes the case where the photographers knew the exhibits better, which makes the sketchers' win more impressive. A choice whose negation can help the argument isn't required.
choices.negation: The groups weren't equally familiar. If the photographers knew the exhibits better, the argument gets stronger. So the negation doesn't destroy it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The difference in memory is pinned on selecting, so the photographers must have selected less. Negate it and both groups selected equally, so selecting can't explain the gap.
choices.negation: The photographers were at least as selective as the sketchers. Then selecting can't explain the sketchers' better memory, and the argument fails.

choices.note: Not required. If photographers reviewed their photos and still recalled less, the sketchers' advantage looks even stronger.
choices.negation: Photographers did look at their photos. They still recalled less, which if anything helps the argument.

questions.stimulus: Economist: Over the past decade, house prices in the town of Ebbing have risen far faster than rents there. The likeliest explanation is that buyers expect the planned rail line to the capital to turn Ebbing into a commuter town. If that is right, cancelling the line would cause Ebbing's house prices to fall sharply. So the regional authority should not cancel the line without first warning the banks that hold mortgages on Ebbing houses.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the economist's argument by the claim that buyers expect the planned rail line to turn Ebbing into a commuter town?
choices: It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim that house prices have outpaced rents is offered in support of it.
It is put forward to explain a trend the argument describes, and a prediction based on it supports the argument's recommendation.
It is a prediction that the economist derives from a trend and then uses to argue that the rail line should not be cancelled.
It is a hypothesis that the economist considers and then rejects in favor of an explanation based on the gap between prices and rents.
It is offered as evidence for the claim that cancelling the line would cause prices to fall sharply, which is the main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The claim explains the price-rent gap. From it the economist predicts a sharp price fall if the line is cancelled, and that prediction supports the recommendation to warn the banks first. (B) traces this chain. (E) is the trap: it gets the first link right but calls the predicted price fall the main conclusion, when the main conclusion is the recommendation. (C) calls the claim a prediction and misstates the recommendation; the economist never says the line shouldn't be cancelled.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The regional authority should not cancel the line without first warning the banks that hold Ebbing mortgages.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: House prices have outpaced rents; best explanation: buyers expect the rail line to make Ebbing a commuter town; if so, cancelling the line would make prices fall sharply.

breakdown.analysis: Map the chain: trend (prices outpace rents) → explanation (buyers expect a commuter town) → prediction ("if that is right," cancelling crashes prices) → recommendation (warn the banks first). The claim in the stem is the explanation. It isn't the conclusion and it isn't the prediction. It's the hypothesis the prediction depends on. Also note what the recommendation actually says: not "don't cancel," but "don't cancel without warning the banks."

choices.note: The main conclusion is the recommendation in the last sentence. The claim about buyers is an explanation offered along the way.
CORRECT. It explains the trend (prices outpacing rents), and the prediction drawn from it ("if that is right") supports the recommendation to warn the banks first.
Two errors. The claim is an explanation, not a prediction, and the economist never argues that the line shouldn't be cancelled, only that the banks should be warned first.
The economist calls it "the likeliest explanation" and builds on it. Nothing is rejected.
Tempting, because the first half is right: the claim does support the predicted price fall. But that prediction isn't the main conclusion. It supports the recommendation in the last sentence.

questions.stimulus:
Imani: The university's rule barring students who miss more than a fifth of the lectures from the final exam is unfair to students who master the material on their own. They are kept out of the exam despite knowing the subject.

Grant: The rule is fair. A university may impose any requirement that helps its students learn, and studies of this very rule show that it makes students learn more, on average, than they would if attendance were optional.
questions.stem: Grant's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: infers that requiring attendance improves learning merely from the fact that students who attend lectures tend to learn more
takes for granted that students who miss lectures generally do so in order to study the material on their own
presumes, without providing justification, that a rule cannot be unfair if most of the students subject to it support it
attacks Imani's motives for objecting to the rule rather than addressing the reasons she gives for her objection
overlooks the possibility that a requirement can help students on average without helping the particular students on whose behalf Imani objects
questions.explanation: Imani objects on behalf of one group: students who learn the material on their own. Grant answers with an average: the rule makes students in general learn more. An average gain is compatible with no gain, or a loss, for the group Imani describes, so Grant never meets her objection (E). (A) is the trap: correlation-to-causation is the familiar flaw, but Grant's premise is already causal ('studies of this very rule show that it makes students learn more'), so he doesn't commit it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Grant: the attendance rule is fair.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Grant: a university may impose any requirement that helps students learn; studies show the rule makes students learn more on average. (Imani's objection: it's unfair to students who master the material on their own.)

breakdown.analysis: Who is Imani talking about? Not students in general, but the ones who learn on their own and get barred anyway. Who is Grant talking about? Students "on average." An average can go up while one group gets nothing or loses out. If 90% of students learn more because of the rule, the average rises even if the self-taught 10% gain nothing. Grant answers a claim about everyone when the objection was about a subgroup. Before picking the correlation/causation answer, check the premise: Grant cites studies of "this very rule" showing it "makes" students learn more. That's a causal claim.

choices.note: Tempting, because correlation-versus-causation is the flaw everyone looks for. But Grant doesn't reason from a correlation. His premise is that studies show the rule itself makes students learn more.
choices.example: Example of the flaw: "Students who attend lectures get better grades, so requiring attendance will raise grades."

choices.note: Grant assumes nothing about why students miss lectures. If anyone makes an assumption here, it's Imani's description, and Grant doesn't build on it.
choices.example: Example of the flaw: "Absent students are just studying on their own, so absences don't matter."

choices.note: Grant never mentions what students think of the rule. His argument rests on learning, not approval.
choices.example: Example of the flaw: "Most students voted for the rule, so it can't be unfair."

choices.note: Grant never mentions Imani's motives. He addresses the rule's effects, just not on the right students.
choices.example: Example of the flaw: "Imani only objects because she skips lectures herself."

choices.note: CORRECT. Imani's objection concerns self-taught students; Grant's evidence is about students on average. A rule can raise the average without helping the very students Imani has in mind, so Grant's reply misses her point.

questions.stimulus: Ten years ago Harlan University began assigning every entering student a personal academic adviser. Of the students who entered after the program began, 62 percent graduated within six years, compared with 50 percent of those who entered in the years just before it. Hence the advising program has made entering students less likely to leave the university during their first year.
questions.stem: The argument requires the assumption that
choices: part of the rise in the six-year graduation rate reflects a drop in the share of students who leave the university during their first year
most students who would have left in their first year without an adviser went on to graduate within six years because of their advisers
no change at Harlan other than the advising program has had any effect on how likely entering students are to leave the university
the share of students who leave after their first year but before graduating has not risen since the advising program began
students who were assigned an adviser rate their first year at the university more favorably than earlier students did
questions.explanation: The evidence is a rise in the six-year graduation rate; the conclusion is about first-year departures. Graduation rates can rise in other ways: fewer students leaving in later years, or more students finishing within six years instead of seven or eight. The argument needs at least part of the rise to come from fewer first-year departures (A). (D) is the trap: if later departures rose, then with graduation up, first-year departures or slow finishers must have fallen even more, so its negation doesn't sink the argument. (B) and (C) are far stronger than needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The advising program has made entering students less likely to leave during their first year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Six-year graduation rate: 50% for entrants just before the program, 62% for entrants after.

breakdown.analysis: Six-year graduation and first-year departures aren't the same thing. Break the 38% who didn't graduate in six years into pieces: students who left in year one, students who left later, and students still enrolled after six years. The graduation rate can rise by shrinking any of those pieces. The argument quietly assumes the year-one piece shrank. If the whole 12-point gain came from fewer late dropouts or fewer slow finishers, the evidence says nothing about the first year. We need: at least some of the gain came from fewer first-year departures.

choices.note: CORRECT. It ties the evidence to the conclusion. Negate it: none of the rise came from fewer first-year departures. Then the graduation data say nothing about the first year, and the conclusion has no support.
choices.negation: None of the rise reflects fewer first-year departures; it all came from later years or faster finishing. The argument collapses.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs some reduction in first-year departures, not that most would-be leavers went on to graduate thanks to advising.
choices.negation: Fewer than most such students graduated because of their advisers. The program could still have reduced first-year departures. No damage.

choices.note: Far too strong. Other changes could have some effect as long as the program had its own.
choices.negation: Some other change also had an effect. The program can still have reduced first-year departures.

choices.note: Tempting, because it looks like ruling out a rival. But negate it: later departures rose. With graduation up 12 points, something else must have fallen even more, quite possibly first-year departures. The negation doesn't sink the argument, so this isn't required.
choices.negation: Later departures rose. Then first-year departures (or slow finishing) must have dropped even more for graduation to rise. That can fit the conclusion, so the argument survives.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How students rate their first year doesn't tell us whether fewer of them left.
choices.negation: Advised students rate their first year no better. They could still have left less often. No effect.

questions.stimulus: Arts council member: Our rule lets a theater receive a grant only if it has balanced its budget in each of the past three years. Supporters say the rule rewards prudence. Yet a theater that balanced its books by dropping every risky production would qualify, while one that ran a deficit to stage the season's most acclaimed new play would not. Such a rule rewards timidity as much as prudence. It should be loosened, not scrapped, since some evidence of financial care is still worth requiring.
questions.stem: The claim that a theater that balanced its books by dropping every risky production would qualify plays which one of the following roles in the council member's argument?
choices: It is offered to show that the rule does not reward prudence at all, which is the main conclusion of the argument.
It describes a consequence of the rule that the argument cites as direct support for its recommendation that the rule be loosened.
It is a consideration that the rule's supporters cite as evidence that the rule rewards prudence in the theaters that receive grants.
It describes an implication of the rule that supports a subsidiary conclusion, which in turn helps to support the main conclusion.
