It is the argument's main conclusion, and the claim that some evidence of financial care is worth requiring is offered in support of it.
questions.explanation: The example of the timid theater that qualifies (paired with the bold one that doesn't) supports 'such a rule rewards timidity as much as prudence.' That claim, together with the point that some evidence of financial care is worth requiring, supports the main conclusion: loosen the rule, don't scrap it. So the claim supports a subsidiary conclusion (D). (B) is the trap: the claim bears on the recommendation only through the timidity claim, not directly. (A) overstates 'as much as prudence' as 'not at all.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The grant rule should be loosened, not scrapped.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A timid theater would qualify while a bold one wouldn't; so the rule rewards timidity as much as prudence; some evidence of financial care is still worth requiring.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: implication (the timid theater qualifies, the bold one doesn't) → subsidiary conclusion ("rewards timidity as much as prudence") → main conclusion ("loosened, not scrapped"), with a second premise ("some evidence of financial care is worth requiring") supporting the "not scrapped" half. The claim in the stem is the first link. Two traps hide in near-identical wording. One skips the middle step ("direct support"). The other inflates "as much as prudence" into "not at all." Read each role answer for the relation, not just the label.

choices.note: Two errors. The council member says the rule rewards timidity "as much as" prudence, not that it rewards no prudence. And that claim isn't the main conclusion; the recommendation is.
Tempting, because the claim does end up supporting the recommendation. But it does so through the subsidiary claim that the rule rewards timidity as much as prudence. It's not direct support.
Supporters say the rule rewards prudence, but this example is the council member's objection to them, not their evidence.
CORRECT. The implication supports "such a rule rewards timidity as much as prudence," and that subsidiary conclusion helps support the recommendation to loosen, not scrap, the rule.
The main conclusion is the recommendation in the last sentence, and the claim in the stem is a premise, not the conclusion.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Sufficient Assumption, Principle & Parallel

questions.stimulus: Conservator: Tree-ring analysis shows that the oak boards of our unsigned Annunciation panel came from a tree felled no earlier than 1441. Painters of that era sometimes kept boards for years before using them, but no unseasoned board would hold the gesso ground on which every such panel was painted. So the Annunciation cannot have been painted before 1443.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Most painters of that era waited at least two years after a tree was felled before they would paint on boards cut from it.
Any oak board that had been seasoned for two years or more would hold a gesso ground well enough to be painted on.
No oak board of that era could be seasoned enough to hold gesso in less than two years from the felling of its tree.
The tree from which the Annunciation's boards were cut was felled in 1441 and not in any later year.
Panels as costly as the Annunciation were never painted on boards cut from trees that had been felled only recently.
questions.explanation: Felled in 1441 at the earliest, plus a seasoned board, has to get us to 1443 at the earliest; the missing piece is that seasoning takes at least two years. (C) supplies it. (B) reverses the link: two years is enough, not required. (A) is a weak 'most' about habit, (D) pins the felling date but still gives no seasoning time, and (E) rests on the vague 'recently'.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Annunciation was not painted before 1443.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tree felled 1441 or later; painted panel → gesso held → board seasoned.

breakdown.analysis: So the board had to be seasoned. How long does seasoning take? The argument never says, yet the conclusion needs a two-year gap: 1441 + 2 = 1443. Chain: painted → seasoned → (at least two years after felling) → 1443 or later. We need an answer that says seasoning can't be done in under two years. It's like saying "the bread was baked from flour milled in May, so it wasn't eaten before June". That works only if milling-to-loaf takes at least a month.

choices.note: Tempting, but 'most' painters isn't all, so this painter could have been one of the quick ones. And it's about what painters chose to do, not about how long seasoning takes.
This reverses the needed link. It says two years is enough to season a board. We need two years to be required, so that an earlier date is ruled out.
CORRECT. If seasoning takes at least two years, a board from a tree felled in 1441 or later couldn't hold gesso before 1443, so the panel couldn't have been painted earlier.
So? Knowing the tree came down in 1441 still tells us nothing about how soon the board could be used. Without a minimum seasoning time, 1442 stays possible.
"Recently" is vague. A board cut a year earlier may not count as recent, so 1442 isn't ruled out. Plus, we don't even know this panel counted as costly.

questions.stimulus: Most of the comets detected by a recent survey have orbital periods longer than 200 years, and every comet with so long a period originates in the Oort cloud. Thus, most of the comets the survey detected originate in the Oort cloud.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the letters in the Pruett family archive must have been written before 1900, since most of those letters are written in iron-gall ink, and any letter in that archive that is written in iron-gall ink predates 1900.

Most of the actors in the touring company trained in London, and most of the actors who trained in London have performed in Shakespeare's plays. Thus, most of the actors in the touring company have performed in Shakespeare's plays at some point.

Every patient in the clinic's asthma study is under twelve years old, and most patients under twelve respond well to the new inhaler. Thus, most of the patients in the clinic's asthma study respond well to the new inhaler.

Most of the sculptures in the museum's east gallery are bronze, and every sculpture that the museum acquired from the Lenz estate is bronze. Thus, most of the sculptures in the east gallery came from the Lenz estate.

Most of the volunteers in the clinic's sleep study went to bed after midnight, and every volunteer in the study who did so reported daytime fatigue. Thus, most of the clinic's patients reported daytime fatigue.
questions.explanation: Pattern: most X are Y; all Y are Z; so most X are Z. (A) has it with the conclusion moved to the front. (E) copies the order and wording pattern but shifts its conclusion to a different group (the clinic's patients rather than the study volunteers). (B) and (C) link 'most' with 'most' or 'all' with 'most', and (D) reverses the 'all' statement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most detected comets originate in the Oort cloud.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most detected comets have periods over 200 years; every comet with such a period originates in the Oort cloud.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most X are Y; all Y are Z; so most X are Z (valid).

breakdown.analysis: Strip out the comets: most X are Y, all Y are Z, so most X are Z. It's valid: the majority that is Y carries Z along with it. Now match the skeleton, not the order. Parallel answers can put the conclusion first. Check three things: the quantifiers (most, all, most), which way the 'all' runs, and that the conclusion is about the same group the argument began with.

choices.note: CORRECT. Most letters are in iron-gall ink (most X are Y); every archive letter in that ink predates 1900 (all Y are Z); so most letters predate 1900 (most X are Z). The conclusion comes first, but the skeleton is identical.
Most + most. Most X are Y and most Y are Z doesn't give most X are Z: the London-trained actors in the company might be the ones who never did Shakespeare. Different (and invalid) structure.
All + most: every X is Y, and most Y are Z. The quantifiers are in the wrong slots. The patients in the study could be the minority of under-twelves who don't respond well.
This reverses the 'all' statement. All Lenz pieces are bronze doesn't mean all bronzes are Lenz pieces, so the conclusion doesn't follow.

Tempting: it runs in the same order with the same quantifiers. But the conclusion jumps from the study's volunteers to all of the clinic's patients. The original stays with the group it started with (the survey's comets).

questions.stimulus: Principle: A physician should not discuss a patient's diagnosis with members of the patient's family without the patient's consent, unless the patient is unable at the time to make medical decisions and the family is making those decisions on the patient's behalf.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Because Mr. Lim had consented to having his family told about his diagnosis, Dr. Okafor was obligated to tell them about it.
Ms. Reyes was unconscious and her daughter was making her medical decisions, but since Ms. Reyes never consented, Dr. Sato should not have discussed the diagnosis with the daughter.
Mr. Teague was fully able to make his own decisions, but because his brother handled his insurance claims, Dr. Fenn did nothing wrong in discussing the diagnosis with the brother without consent.
Ms. Ito, who is in a coma, named her attorney rather than a relative to make her medical decisions, so Dr. Grant was right to discuss her diagnosis with her sister without her consent.
After a stroke left Mr. Dube unable to make medical decisions, his wife began making them for him; Dr. Abara did nothing wrong in discussing his diagnosis with her, though he never consented.
questions.explanation: The rule bars discussing a diagnosis with family without consent, except when the patient can't decide AND the family is deciding for the patient. (E) meets both parts of the exception, so the bar doesn't apply and the doctor did nothing wrong. (B) ignores the exception, (C) and (D) each meet only one half of it, and (A) turns permission into a duty.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Discuss diagnosis with family → patient consented, UNLESS (patient can't decide AND family is deciding for the patient).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: To approve a disclosure without consent, both parts of the exception must hold. Consent only permits disclosure; it never requires it.

breakdown.analysis: What does 'unless' do here? It switches the consent rule off, but only when BOTH conditions hold: the patient can't decide, and the family is deciding. When the rule is off, disclosure without consent isn't wrong. And notice the principle never makes anyone disclose anything. It's like a sign that says "No entry without a badge, unless you're an escorted visitor". An escorted visitor may go in; a visitor without an escort may not; and having a badge doesn't oblige you to enter.

choices.note: The principle only limits disclosure. Consent removes the limit; it doesn't create a duty to tell.

Tempting if you read only the first clause. But Ms. Reyes is the textbook exception: she can't decide, and her daughter is deciding. So the consent rule doesn't apply, and the verdict gets it backward.
Half the exception. Mr. Teague can make his own decisions, so the exception is off and consent was required. Handling insurance claims isn't making medical decisions anyway.
Close, but the family isn't the one deciding. Ms. Ito's attorney is. With only one half of the exception met, the consent rule still applies to her sister.
CORRECT. Mr. Dube can't decide, and his wife is deciding for him: both halves of the exception hold, so the consent requirement is lifted and the disclosure was not wrong.

questions.stimulus: Ecologist: The disease that devastated eelgrass beds in neighboring bays was not what killed the eelgrass in Harrow Bay this August. The organism that causes that disease becomes active only in water warmer than 18°C, and the temperature buoys in Harrow Bay recorded no reading above 16°C at any time this year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: In the neighboring bays, eelgrass died this year only in places where the water was warmer than 18°C.
Nowhere that eelgrass grows in Harrow Bay was the water warmer this year than the highest temperature its buoys recorded.
If the water in Harrow Bay had risen above 18°C this year, the disease would have killed the bay's eelgrass.
The eelgrass in Harrow Bay began dying several weeks later than the eelgrass in the neighboring bays did, according to monitoring crews.
Most of Harrow Bay's eelgrass grows close to the buoys that record the bay's water temperature.
questions.explanation: The argument goes from the buoys' readings to the water where the eelgrass grows. (B) closes that gap: wherever eelgrass grows, the water was never warmer than the buoys' maximum of 16°C, so the organism was never active there. (E) is the near-miss, since 'most' leaves some beds unaccounted for. (C) reverses the condition, (A) only confirms the pattern in other bays, and (D) is a timing detail that proves nothing.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The neighboring bays' disease didn't kill Harrow Bay's eelgrass.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Disease kills → organism active → water above 18°C; buoys never read above 16°C.

breakdown.analysis: So the buoys stayed cool. Were the eelgrass beds at the buoys? A buoy in deep, cool water says little about a warm, shallow bed. Chain: disease killed the eelgrass → organism active where the eelgrass grows → water there over 18°C. We know only the buoys' readings. We need an answer that ties the eelgrass beds' water to those readings. It's like proving a room never got hot using a thermometer in the hallway; that works only if the room never ran warmer than the hallway.

choices.note: Interesting, but it only confirms the temperature link in other bays. It tells us nothing about the water where Harrow Bay's eelgrass grows.
CORRECT. If the eelgrass beds were never warmer than the buoys' highest reading (16°C), they were never above 18°C, so the organism was never active there and couldn't have killed the eelgrass.
This reverses the condition. Warm water is necessary for the disease, not a guarantee of it. And we need to know the beds stayed cool, not what would happen if they hadn't.
So? A later die-off might hint at a different cause, but it can't rule out the disease. Outbreaks can start at different times in different places.
Tempting, because it's the right idea. But 'most' isn't enough: the beds far from the buoys might have been warmer, and the disease could have struck there.

questions.stimulus: No manuscript in the abbey's library was copied after 1300 unless it bears the scriptorium's later seal. Yet some of the library's manuscripts lack that seal. Therefore, some of the manuscripts in the abbey's library were copied in 1300 or earlier.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Every fossil in the cabinet that came from the Dorsey quarry is labeled in red ink, and some of the fossils in the cabinet are labeled in red ink. Therefore, some of the fossils in the cabinet came from the Dorsey quarry.

No juror on the panel was dismissed unless she missed a session of the trial. Yet some of the jurors on the panel were not dismissed. Therefore, some of the jurors on the panel never missed a session of the trial.
Most of the excavated pots that predate the fire bear soot marks. Yet some of the excavated pots bear no soot marks. Therefore, some of the excavated pots do not predate the fire.

Some of the orchestra's violinists must not have studied at the conservatory, for only those who passed its entrance audition studied there, and some of the orchestra's violinists did not pass that audition.

No poem in the collection was written after the poet's illness unless it was dictated. Yet some of the poems in the collection were not dictated. Therefore, the editors should label those poems as early work.
questions.explanation: Pattern: X → Y; some lack Y; so some lack X (a valid contrapositive). (D) has it in different words ('only those who passed... studied there') with the conclusion first. (B) copies the 'No... unless' wording but negates the wrong term: from 'not dismissed' nothing follows. (A) affirms the necessary condition, (C) weakens 'all' to 'most', and (E) ends in a recommendation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some manuscripts were copied in 1300 or earlier.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Copied after 1300 → has the seal; some manuscripts lack the seal.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X → Y; some lack Y; so some lack X.

breakdown.analysis: Translate 'No A unless B' as A → B: copied after 1300 → seal. Some lack the seal, so by the contrapositive some weren't copied after 1300. Now ignore the wording and find the same moves. The trap is the answer that sounds the most like the stimulus ('No... unless... Yet some...') but runs the logic the other way. The right answer may say 'only those who' instead of 'unless' and put the conclusion first.

choices.note: This affirms the necessary condition: quarry → red ink, and some have red ink, so some came from the quarry. That's invalid; red ink could come from anywhere.

Tempting, since its wording matches almost word for word. But here the premise is 'some were NOT dismissed', which negates the sufficient condition (dismissed → missed). Nothing follows from that; the original negated the necessary condition.
'Most' instead of 'every'. With only most pre-fire pots sooty, an unsooted pot could still be an old one. The certainty the original has is gone.
CORRECT. Studied there → passed audition; some violinists didn't pass; so some didn't study there. Same valid contrapositive, just reworded and with the conclusion first.
The premises match, but the conclusion is a recommendation ('should label'), not the factual 'some were written before the illness'.

questions.stimulus: Festival director: We should not invite the Velde Quartet back next summer. Their concerts this year sold out and drew glowing reviews. But they skipped two of their scheduled rehearsals with our student orchestra without notice, and training young musicians is the main reason our festival exists.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the festival director's argument?
choices: A festival should invite back only those performers whose concerts have sold out in a previous season.
An organization should not renew ties with a party that broke commitments bearing on its chief purpose, however well that party served its other aims.
Performers who miss commitments without giving notice should be allowed to explain themselves before a festival decides whether to invite them back.
In deciding which performers to invite back, a festival should give more weight to how they serve its central mission than to the ticket sales they bring in.
A festival should invite back every performer who drew excellent reviews unless that performer canceled a public concert.
questions.explanation: The director drops a successful act because it broke commitments tied to the festival's core purpose of training. (B) states exactly that, in general terms: broken commitments on the chief purpose outweigh success elsewhere. (D) is close but says nothing about what to do with performers who skipped rehearsals. (E) would support inviting the quartet back, since rehearsals aren't public concerts. (A) gives only a necessary condition, which the quartet meets.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Don't invite the Velde Quartet back.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: They sold out and got great reviews; but they skipped rehearsals with the student orchestra without notice; training students is the festival's main purpose.

breakdown.analysis: Why drop a sold-out act? Because it let down the festival's main mission. We need a principle that says breaking commitments on the core mission beats success at the side goals. Expect it to be worded abstractly ('an organization', 'a party', 'chief purpose'), not in festival terms. A justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says: not invite them back.

choices.note: This is a necessary condition, and the quartet meets it (they sold out). Meeting a necessary condition can't tell you NOT to invite them.

CORRECT. The festival is the organization, training is its chief purpose, the skipped rehearsals are broken commitments, and the sold-out concerts are 'its other aims'. Verdict: don't renew. Exactly the conclusion.
This only adds a step (a chance to explain). It doesn't tell the festival what to decide afterward.

Tempting, since it favors the mission over ticket sales. But it doesn't say that skipping rehearsals disqualifies a performer. The festival could weigh its mission heavily and still invite the quartet back with a warning.
Wrong direction. The quartet drew excellent reviews and canceled no public concert (they skipped rehearsals), so this principle would require inviting them back.

questions.stimulus: Under the rules of a state appeals court, a brief may run longer than thirty pages only if the court has granted leave for it to do so, and the court grants such leave only in cases that raise a constitutional question. Last week the court accepted a forty-page brief in a contract dispute. So that dispute must raise a constitutional question.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The court does not accept any brief that fails to comply with its rules on length.
The court grants leave to file a longer brief in every case that raises a constitutional question.
Most briefs longer than thirty pages that the court has accepted were filed in cases that raise constitutional questions.
Contract disputes rarely raise constitutional questions unless one of the parties to the dispute is a government body.
Every brief for which the court grants leave to exceed thirty pages concerns a case that raises a constitutional question.
questions.explanation: The rules say what a long brief MAY do; the premise says only that the court accepted one. The gap is that acceptance means the rules were followed. (A) supplies it: accepted → complies → leave granted → constitutional question. (E) merely restates the premises, (B) reverses the leave rule, and (C) is a weak 'most'.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The contract dispute raises a constitutional question.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brief over 30 pages (properly) → leave granted → constitutional question; the court accepted a 40-page brief.

breakdown.analysis: So the court accepted it. Does that mean the brief was allowed under the rules? Courts make mistakes, and the rule only says what a brief may do. Chain: 40 pages, permitted → leave → constitutional question. We need: accepted → permitted. It's like proving a guest was invited because the doorman let her in; that works only if the doorman never admits anyone without an invitation.

choices.note: CORRECT. If the court accepts only briefs that meet the length rules, the 40-page brief had leave, and leave is granted only in constitutional cases. The chain is complete.
This reverses the leave rule (constitutional → leave). We need to go from leave to a constitutional question, and that we already have; what's missing is whether there was leave at all.
'Most' can't support 'must'. This brief could be one of the exceptions.
Irrelevant, and if anything it points the other way. It doesn't connect accepting the brief to the rules.
Tempting, because it sounds like the key rule. But it just restates the premises (leave → constitutional question). It still doesn't show this brief had leave.

questions.stimulus: Unless a kidney transplant patient's kidney function improves within a week of surgery, the patient is put back on dialysis. Every patient who is put back on dialysis is reassessed by the hospital's transplant board. Mr. Haldane's kidney function did not improve within a week of his surgery. So he will be reassessed by the transplant board.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choices: Unless the Wickham Museum receives the grant, it will close its east wing. If it receives the grant, it will extend its weekend hours. The museum will receive the grant. So it will extend its weekend hours and keep its east wing open.

If the choir adds a second concert, it will hire a pianist. If it hires a pianist, it will rent a larger hall. The choir rented a larger hall this year. So it must have added a second concert this year.

A debate team member not chosen for the traveling squad joins the practice squad, and no one is on the practice squad without attending the summer workshop. Odile was not chosen for the traveling squad, so she will attend the workshop.

Unless the county hires another inspector, restaurant inspections will be delayed. If inspections are delayed, some restaurants will go uninspected for a year. Some restaurants will go uninspected for a year. So the county will not hire another inspector.

The observatory will close for repairs unless its grant is renewed, and if it closes, the summer interns will be sent to the field station. The grant probably will not be renewed. So the interns will probably be sent to the field station.
questions.explanation: Pattern: not A → B; B → C; not A; so C. (C) has it, with the first link phrased as 'who is not chosen... joins' and the second as 'no one... without', so it looks different on the surface. (E) has the same chain but downgrades the premise and conclusion to 'probably'. (D) copies the 'Unless... If...' wording but affirms the consequent, and (B) reasons backward through a chain.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mr. Haldane will be reassessed.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Function doesn't improve → dialysis; dialysis → reassessed; his function didn't improve.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Not A → B; B → C; not A; therefore C.

breakdown.analysis: Translate first. 'Unless A, B' = not A → B. Then B → C. Then not A, so C. A valid chain. Now beware the answers that copy the stimulus's words ('Unless... If...'). Real parallel answers often restate the same links in other forms, like 'no one is X without Y' for X → Y. Also check the certainty level: the original says 'will', not 'probably'.

choices.note: Different chain. It uses A → (extend hours) instead of not A → B → C, and its conclusion adds a second claim (keeping the wing open) that isn't drawn the same way.
This reasons backward through a chain (C, so A). That's affirming the consequent. The original moves forward from the first condition.
CORRECT. Not chosen → practice squad; practice squad → workshop ('no one... without' = needs); Odile wasn't chosen; so workshop. Same valid chain, reworded.
Tempting, since it starts with 'Unless... If...' just like the stimulus. But it affirms the end of the chain and concludes the start. That's invalid.
Tempting, since it's the same chain. But the premise and conclusion are only 'probably', while the original is certain. Parallel answers have to match the strength of the claims too.

questions.stimulus: Historian: No one who was away from the capital on the day the treaty was signed could have witnessed the signing. Admittedly, the diary entry describing the ceremony gets its details right. But the entry appears in Corwin's diary in his own hand, and Corwin's account book records a payment made that same day in a market town two days' ride from the capital. So the entry was not written by an eyewitness.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Accurate details about the treaty ceremony could have been learned from printed reports that circulated soon after the signing.
Anyone who was in the market town on the day of the signing could not also have been in the capital that day.
Anyone who was in the capital on the day the treaty was signed witnessed the signing.
Corwin was not in the capital at any time during the week before the treaty was signed.
Every payment recorded in Corwin's account book was made by Corwin in person.
questions.explanation: The account book shows a payment in the market town that day, but not that Corwin was the one who made it; an agent could have paid for him. (E) closes that gap: Corwin paid in person, so he was two days away and couldn't have witnessed the signing. (B) only repeats what 'two days' ride' already implies, (C) reverses the witnessing condition, (D) covers the wrong days, and (A) addresses the concession without proving anything.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The diary entry wasn't written by an eyewitness.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Witnessed → in the capital that day; Corwin wrote the entry; his account book records a payment that day in a town two days away; (concession: the details are accurate).

breakdown.analysis: So a payment was made in the market town. Who says Corwin made it himself? A merchant's clerk or servant could carry the money. Chain: Corwin an eyewitness → in the capital that day. To deny that, we need Corwin in the market town, and the account book places only the payment there. We need an answer that puts Corwin with the payment. The concession about accurate details is a distraction. It's like proving someone skipped a meeting because their credit card was used across town; that works only if nobody else uses their card.

choices.note: This explains away the concession, but it doesn't prove anything. 'Could have learned' leaves open that Corwin was there.
Tempting, because it sounds like the missing link. But 'two days' ride' already tells us that. The real gap is whether Corwin was in the town at all.
This reverses the conditional. The stimulus says being in the capital is necessary for witnessing; this makes it sufficient. And it would help show Corwin was a witness, not that he wasn't.
Wrong days. Being away the week before says nothing about the day of the signing itself.
CORRECT. If Corwin made every recorded payment in person, he was in the market town on the day of the signing, two days from the capital, so he couldn't have witnessed it.

questions.stimulus: Botanist: Our team should not publish the exact location of the orchid colony we found, even though publishing it would let other botanists confirm the discovery. Every site of this species that has been made public has been stripped by collectors, and we can arrange for confirmation by privately showing the colony to a few qualified botanists.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the botanist's reasoning?
choices: Researchers should publish the location of a discovery whenever doing so is the only way for other researchers to confirm it.
Protecting a rare species matters more than the credit that researchers receive for being the first to discover a new population of it.
Botanists who confirm a discovery privately should be bound not to reveal the location of what they have been shown.
Information that would endanger the subject of a study should be withheld if the purposes of releasing it can be met some other way.
A discovery should not be announced until qualified researchers other than its discoverers have confirmed it independently.
questions.explanation: Publishing the site would expose the orchids to collectors, and the one benefit of publishing, confirmation, can be had privately. (D) states that trade-off abstractly. (A) is the trap: its condition (publishing is the only way to confirm) isn't met, so it says nothing about withholding. (E) concerns announcing the discovery, not revealing the location; (B) brings in credit, which no one mentioned; (C) governs the confirming botanists.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Don't publish the colony's exact location.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Published sites get stripped by collectors; confirmation, the benefit of publishing, can be done privately.

breakdown.analysis: Two facts do the work: publishing puts the colony at risk, and publishing's purpose can be met another way. We need a principle that says: when disclosure endangers what you study and you can get its benefit some other way, keep it back. It's like not posting your house key's hiding spot online when you can just tell your neighbor.

choices.note: Tempting, since it uses the stimulus's own words (location, confirm). But its trigger is 'the only way to confirm', and here private showings also work. So it's silent, and it never says to withhold anything.
Credit isn't in the argument. The botanist's reason is the risk to the colony, not who gets credit.
This is about what the confirming botanists should do later. It doesn't tell the team whether to publish.
CORRECT. The location is information that endangers the colony, and its purpose (confirmation) can be met privately. So it should be withheld, which is the conclusion.
This is about when to announce a discovery, not whether to reveal the location. The team could wait for confirmation and still publish the site.

questions.stimulus: Paleontologist: The dinosaur trackways at the Ridley site are better preserved than those at the Tumble Creek site. Every trackway at Ridley was pressed into mud that later hardened into stone, and no trackway formed in such mud has eroded more than slightly.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Any trackway that has eroded no more than slightly is better preserved than every trackway at the Tumble Creek site.
None of the trackways at the Tumble Creek site was pressed into mud that later hardened into stone.
Any trackway that is better preserved than all of those at Tumble Creek has eroded no more than slightly.
Most of the trackways at the Tumble Creek site have eroded considerably since they were first uncovered.
Trackways pressed into mud that later hardened into stone are found at more sites than trackways formed in any other way.
questions.explanation: The premises establish only that every Ridley trackway has eroded no more than slightly; they say nothing about Tumble Creek. (A) links that property to the comparison: anything eroded that little beats every Tumble Creek trackway. (B) is the trap: it denies Tumble Creek the hardened mud, but the premises never say what happens to trackways in other mud, so they might be just as well preserved. (C) reverses the bridge, and (D)'s 'most' leaves the comparison open.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ridley's trackways are better preserved than Tumble Creek's.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ridley trackway → hardened mud → eroded no more than slightly.

breakdown.analysis: Read the premises again. Do they mention Tumble Creek at all? They don't. Chain: Ridley → hardened mud → little erosion. The conclusion compares with Tumble Creek, so we need a bridge from 'little erosion' to 'better preserved than Tumble Creek'. Watch for the answer that tells you Tumble Creek lacks hardened mud: that's negating the sufficient condition. Mud that never hardened might also protect a trackway.

choices.note: CORRECT. Every Ridley trackway has eroded no more than slightly, and this makes any such trackway better preserved than every Tumble Creek trackway. The conclusion follows.

Tempting, and it's the answer most people pick. But hardened mud is sufficient for little erosion, not necessary. Tumble Creek trackways in other mud might have eroded just as little. We'd also still need a link between erosion and 'better preserved'.
This reverses the bridge. It tells us what is true of trackways that are already known to beat Tumble Creek, so it can't show that Ridley's do.
'Most' leaves some Tumble Creek trackways that might be better preserved than Ridley's, and it still doesn't say Ridley's are better than the rest.
How common hardened-mud trackways are has nothing to do with how these two sites compare.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A composer employed in a salaried post should not claim personal ownership of music written as part of the duties of that post. Music that such a composer writes outside those duties and on his or her own time, however, belongs to the composer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Mr. Moreau scored his film studio's latest release at home over several weekends. Because he did that work on his own time, the score is his to claim, even though scoring the studio's films is his job.
Because Ms. Quist was paid a single fee by a music festival to write a string quartet for it, she should not claim personal ownership of the quartet.
Ms. Ferreira holds a salaried post as a cathedral's organist, which requires her to play at services but not to compose. The anthem she wrote at home one summer belongs to her.
Mr. Sandoval, a salaried arranger for a theater, wrote a song during his paid hours on a day with no arranging to do. Since writing songs is not among his duties, the song belongs to him.
Ms. Liang, a salaried staff composer for a radio network, wrote jingles as part of her job, so the network should credit her by name whenever one of them is broadcast.
questions.explanation: The ownership rule needs a salaried composer AND music written outside the post's duties AND on the composer's own time. (C) meets all three: the organist's post doesn't require composing, and she wrote the anthem at home. (A) meets 'own time' but the score was part of his job. (D) meets 'outside duties' but was written on paid hours. (B) involves no salaried post, and (E) answers a question (credit) the principle never addresses.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Salaried composer + music written as part of the post's duties → shouldn't claim it. Salaried composer + outside duties AND on own time → it belongs to the composer.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: To award ownership, all three must hold: salaried post, outside the duties, own time. To deny ownership, the music must be part of a salaried post's duties.

breakdown.analysis: This one is about the scope of the terms. What counts as 'part of the duties'? What counts as 'own time'? Those are two separate tests, and the second sentence needs both. Where you wrote it doesn't change what it is: a score written at home is still part of the job if scoring is the job. And the principle covers only salaried composers; a one-time commission falls outside it entirely.

choices.note: Tempting: he worked at home on weekends. But scoring the studio's films is his job, so the score is part of his duties. The first sentence says he shouldn't claim it.
A single fee isn't a salaried post, so the principle doesn't reach her at all. It can't support 'should not claim'.
CORRECT. Salaried post: yes. Composing outside her duties: yes (the post requires playing, not composing). Own time: yes (at home, in summer). All three conditions hold, so the anthem is hers.
Close. It's outside his duties, but he wrote it during paid hours, so 'own time' fails. The principle then doesn't say who owns it.
Credit by name is a different question. The principle settles only who may claim ownership, not how anyone should be credited.

questions.stimulus: A Tamberly pet insurance policy covers a condition only if the condition was not present before the policy began, and a condition counts as present before then if a veterinarian recorded any symptom of it before that date. Mira's dog was diagnosed with hip dysplasia two months after her policy began, but a veterinarian's notes made a year before the policy began record that the dog limped after long walks. So Tamberly will not cover the dog's hip dysplasia.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: Limping after long walks is among the most common early symptoms of hip dysplasia in dogs.
Any limping by a dog that is eventually diagnosed with hip dysplasia is a symptom of that condition.
Every condition that was present before a Tamberly policy began had a symptom that a veterinarian recorded before that date.
Limping after long walks is a symptom of hip dysplasia in any dog that already has the condition at the time it limps.
Tamberly does not cover any condition that a veterinarian diagnosed before the date on which the pet's policy began.
questions.explanation: The notes predate the policy, but they record limping, not dysplasia; the argument needs that limp to count as a symptom of the dysplasia. (B) makes it one. (D) is the near-miss: it works only if the dog already had dysplasia a year earlier, which is not established. (A) is a 'most common' link, (C) reverses the definition, and (E) concerns earlier diagnoses, which didn't happen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Tamberly won't cover the dysplasia.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Covered → not present before the policy; symptom recorded before the policy → present before; notes from before the policy record limping.

breakdown.analysis: Timing is settled: the notes came a year before the policy. So what's missing? The notes say 'limped', not 'dysplasia'. Was that limp a symptom of the dysplasia, or of a sore paw? Chain: recorded symptom of the condition before the policy → present before → not covered. We need: this dog's limping was a symptom of its dysplasia.

choices.note: Tempting, but 'most common symptom' doesn't make every limp a symptom. This dog's limp could have had another cause.
CORRECT. The dog was eventually diagnosed with dysplasia, so its recorded limping counts as a symptom. A symptom recorded before the policy means the condition was present, so it isn't covered.
This reverses the definition (present → recorded symptom). We need the direction from a recorded symptom to 'present', and we already have that. The question is whether the limp was a symptom.
Close, but it applies only to a dog that already has dysplasia when it limps. We don't know this dog had it a year before the policy, which is the very thing in question.
Irrelevant. The diagnosis came two months after the policy began, so a rule about diagnoses made before then doesn't apply.

questions.stimulus: Editor: We should publish Dr. Brisco's study of the new blood-pressure drug, even though the drug's manufacturer paid for the research. The study passed our peer review, and the funding agreement gave the manufacturer no access to the raw data and no say over whether or where the results would appear.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's reasoning?
choices: A journal should publish a study funded by a company whose product it tests only if the company had no say over the study's data or over the decision to publish it.
Studies paid for by the makers of the products they test should be held to stricter standards of peer review than other studies are.
A journal should tell its readers who paid for each study it publishes, including studies that have passed its peer review.
A journal should not publish a study whose sponsor stands to profit from its findings unless the study has passed the journal's peer review.
A journal should publish any study that passes its peer review unless the study's sponsor had a say over the study's data or over the decision to publish it.
questions.explanation: To justify 'should publish', the principle must make passing review plus an independent sponsor enough to publish. (E) does: passing peer review triggers publication, and its 'unless' clause isn't met. (A) lists only a necessary condition, so it can block publication but never require it. (D) is the negated version, which can only say when not to publish. (B) and (C) don't yield a verdict.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Publish the study.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It passed peer review; the manufacturer had no data access and no say over publication.

breakdown.analysis: The conclusion is a positive 'should publish', so we need a principle whose sufficient condition is met here and whose result is 'publish'. Two traps live nearby. 'Only if' gives a requirement, not a green light. And 'should not... unless' tells you when to refuse, never when to publish. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says.

choices.note: Tempting, since its condition matches the facts perfectly. But 'only if' makes independence a requirement, not a reason to publish. A study could meet it and still be rejected.
Stricter review standards don't settle whether this study should run. It passed the review the journal has.
Disclosure is a separate issue. This principle says nothing about whether to publish.
Tempting, since it uses every key term. But it's built to forbid. It says unreviewed studies with profit-seeking sponsors shouldn't run; for a reviewed study it says nothing at all.
CORRECT. The study passed peer review, and the manufacturer had no say over the data or the publication, so the exception doesn't apply. Verdict: publish.

questions.stimulus: Under a certain nation's heritage law, an antiquity may be taken out of the country only with an export permit, and no permit is issued for any object that lacks a documented chain of ownership. A dealer in that nation is offering a bronze figurine to foreign buyers, but the figurine has no documented chain of ownership. So the dealer may not legally export the figurine.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every antiquity that is offered for sale in that nation lacks a documented chain of ownership.
Most bronze figurines offered for sale in that nation without a documented chain of ownership are antiquities.
No document establishing the figurine's chain of ownership could be produced before the dealer's sale to a foreign buyer is completed.
Any object offered for sale in that nation that is not an antiquity has a documented chain of ownership.
If the figurine were an antiquity, the dealer would be unable to obtain an export permit for it.
questions.explanation: The export rule covers only antiquities, and nothing says the figurine is one. (D) supplies that in contrapositive form: a non-antiquity offered for sale has documented ownership, so the undocumented figurine must be an antiquity. (A) is the reversal. (E) only repeats what the premises already yield, (C) is a timing decoy, and (B)'s 'most' leaves room for an exception.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The figurine can't legally be exported.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Antiquity exported → permit → documented chain of ownership; the figurine (for sale) lacks a documented chain.

breakdown.analysis: The figurine certainly can't get a permit. But does it need one? The law only restricts antiquities. Chain: antiquity → needs permit → needs documentation. We need: this figurine is an antiquity. Expect it to show up in disguise. 'Undocumented → antiquity' can be written as its contrapositive, 'not an antiquity → documented'. It's like a rule that only members need ID: you can't conclude a guest without ID is barred until you know the guest is a member.

choices.note: This reverses the bridge (antiquity → undocumented). We need undocumented → antiquity. The figurine could be a modern piece that just has no paperwork.
'Most' isn't enough for a must-conclusion. The figurine could be one of the non-antiquities.
We already know it can't get a permit. Timing isn't the problem. Whether the law applies to it is.
CORRECT. Contrapositive: an undocumented object offered for sale is an antiquity. The figurine is such an object, so it's an antiquity, needs a permit, and can't get one.
Tempting, but it's already in the premises (antiquity → permit → documentation, and the figurine has none). It never says the figurine IS an antiquity.

questions.stimulus: Principle: A museum should return an object to the community from which it was taken if that community requests its return and the object was taken without its owners' consent. If, however, returning the object would expose it to a serious risk of destruction, the museum should postpone the return until that risk has passed.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: A village has asked the Halvorsen Museum for a mask taken from it without its owners' consent, but a flood just destroyed the village's only storehouse. The museum should agree to return the mask but not send it yet.

The Ferris Museum bought a drum from a community's leaders, with its owners' full consent, a century ago. Since the community now has a secure place to keep the drum and has formally asked for it, the museum should return it.
The Morland Museum holds a textile taken without consent from a town that has never asked for it back but has excellent facilities for its care. The museum should return the textile.

Because fighting in the region makes it likely that a statue would be destroyed if returned, the Tresham Museum should refuse the request of the community from which the statue was taken without consent.

A city government has asked the Ashby Museum for a headdress that was taken without consent from a family that once lived in that city. The museum should therefore return the headdress to the city government.
questions.explanation: The duty to return needs a request from the source community and a taking without consent; a serious risk of destruction postpones the return but doesn't cancel it. (A) meets both conditions and applies the postponement. (D) turns 'postpone' into 'refuse'. (B) lacks the taking without consent, (C) lacks a request, and in (E) the requester isn't the community the object was taken from.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Request from the source community AND taken without consent → return. Exception: serious risk of destruction → postpone (not cancel) the return.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: The answer must meet both conditions; if there's a serious risk, the verdict must be 'return, but later'.

breakdown.analysis: Read the exception closely. Does it cancel the duty? No, it delays it ('until that risk has passed'). So a correct answer with a serious risk has to say both things: the object goes back, and not yet. Also watch who's asking. The principle says 'the community from which it was taken', so a different body asking doesn't count.

choices.note: CORRECT. Request: yes. Taken without consent: yes. Serious risk: the only storehouse is gone. So the museum owes the return but should postpone it, exactly what the judgment says.
The drum was bought with the owners' consent, so the duty never arises. A secure home doesn't fill that gap.
No request. The principle's duty needs one, however good the town's facilities are.
Tempting, since the risk is real. But the principle says postpone, not refuse. Refusing outright goes beyond what the exception allows.
Wrong requester. The headdress was taken from a family; the city government isn't 'the community from which it was taken', so the principle doesn't require returning it to the city.

questions.stimulus: Most of the frescoes in the chapel were painted by the master's assistants, and most of the frescoes in the chapel have been restored at least once. It follows that at least one fresco painted by the master's assistants has been restored.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the orchestra's violinists trained in Vienna, and most musicians who trained in Vienna began playing before age six. It follows that at least one of the orchestra's violinists began playing before age six.
Most of the volcanoes in the chain are dormant, and every dormant volcano in the chain is monitored by satellite. It follows that at least one of the volcanoes in the chain is monitored by satellite.
Most of the plays the company staged last season were comedies, and most of the plays it staged last season sold out. It follows that most of the comedies the company staged last season sold out.

Some of the patients in the trial took the new drug, and some of the patients in the trial reported headaches. It follows that at least one patient in the trial who took the new drug reported headaches.
At least one of the senators who voted for the bill must also have voted for the amendment, since most of the senators voted for the bill and most of them voted for the amendment.
questions.explanation: Pattern: most of one group are X and most of the same group are Y, so at least one is both X and Y (two majorities of one group must overlap). (E) has it with the conclusion first. (A) changes the second group (musicians who trained in Vienna, not the orchestra), which breaks the overlap. (C) overreaches to 'most', (D) uses 'some' and 'some', which needn't overlap, and (B) uses 'most' and 'all', a different though valid structure.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least one assistant-painted fresco has been restored.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most of the chapel's frescoes are assistant-painted; most of the chapel's frescoes are restored.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most G are X; most G are Y; so at least one G is both X and Y.

breakdown.analysis: Is this valid? Yes. Two majorities of the same group must share at least one member: more than half plus more than half is more than the whole. The key is that both 'most' statements are about the SAME group. Imagine 10 frescoes: 6 by assistants and 6 restored means at least 2 are both. Now look for an answer with two 'most' statements about one group and a modest 'at least one' conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, since it has two 'most's and the same conclusion. But the second 'most' is about musicians trained in Vienna, a different group. The violinists could be the Vienna-trained minority who started late.
Valid, but a different structure: 'most' plus 'all', not two overlapping majorities.
Right premises, wrong conclusion. Two majorities guarantee overlap, not that most of one falls inside the other. With 10 plays, 6 comedies and 6 sell-outs could share only 2.
'Some' and 'some' needn't overlap. The drug-takers and the headache-reporters could be entirely different patients.
CORRECT. Most senators voted for the bill and most (of the same senators) voted for the amendment, so at least one did both. Same skeleton, conclusion first.

questions.stimulus: Musicologist: At least one of the songs in the newly discovered songbook must have been composed before 1600. The Hartwell catalog, after all, lists no song composed after 1599. Admittedly, some of the songbook's songs appear in no published catalog at all, but that is typical of collections of this kind.
questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Not every song in the songbook is missing from all published catalogs.
Every song composed before 1600 that has survived in a songbook is listed in the Hartwell catalog.
Not all of the songs in the songbook are missing from the Hartwell catalog.
Most songs in collections of this kind that appear in no published catalog were composed before 1600.
Every song listed in the Hartwell catalog was copied into at least one songbook of the kind just discovered.
questions.explanation: The only dating premise is that the Hartwell catalog lists nothing composed after 1599, so the argument needs at least one songbook song in that catalog. (C) says exactly that, in double-negative form. (A) is the trap: the same form, but 'all published catalogs' only puts a song in some catalog, not necessarily Hartwell's. (B) runs from age to listing, the wrong direction; (D) is about the uncatalogued songs and only 'most'; (E) never ties the catalog to this songbook.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least one songbook song was composed before 1600.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Listed in the Hartwell catalog → composed before 1600; (concession: some songbook songs are in no published catalog).

breakdown.analysis: What do we actually know about dates? Only this: in the Hartwell catalog → before 1600. So the conclusion follows if at least one songbook song is in that catalog. That's the whole gap. The hard part is the wording. 'Not all are missing from X' means 'at least one is in X'. And the concession about uncatalogued songs is bait: an answer about 'published catalogs' in general sounds right but misses the one catalog that matters.

choices.note: This is the trap. It means some songbook song is in some published catalog, but that catalog needn't be Hartwell's, and only Hartwell's guarantees a date before 1600.
This runs from 'before 1600' to 'listed'. We need a songbook song in the catalog; this doesn't put any there, since none of the songbook's songs is known to be from before 1600.
CORRECT. 'Not all missing from the Hartwell catalog' = at least one songbook song is in it. Everything in the catalog dates from before 1600, so that song does too.
This is about the uncatalogued songs, and 'most' can't support 'must'. Even a pre-1600 majority among such songs doesn't guarantee that any of this songbook's songs is old.
Every catalog song turns up in some songbook of this kind, but not necessarily in this one. The link to the newly found songbook is missing.

questions.stimulus: Editor: The new edition of Ada Lindqvist's novel should not include the unfinished chapter found among her papers. Admittedly, readers would value the chapter, and Lindqvist never asked that it be destroyed. But in a letter to her publisher, she called the chapter unfit to print.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's reasoning?
choices: A writer's unfinished work should be published only if the writer left no instruction, in a will or elsewhere, that it be destroyed.
A writer's own stated judgment that a work should not appear in print should outweigh whatever value the work would have for readers.
An editor should publish a writer's unfinished work if readers would value it and the writer did not ask that it be destroyed.
Material that a writer considered unfit to print may be published only after the writer's death.
The more widely read a novelist is, the more weight an editor should give to readers' interest in the novelist's unpublished work.
questions.explanation: The editor concedes two reasons to include the chapter and overrides them with Lindqvist's own verdict that it was unfit to print. (B) states that ranking: the author's stated judgment against printing beats readers' interest. (A) is the trap: its necessary condition is met here, so it can't forbid inclusion. (C) points the other way, (D) only allows publication after death, and (E) favors readers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Leave the unfinished chapter out.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Readers would value it and she never asked that it be destroyed (conceded); but she called it unfit to print.

breakdown.analysis: The editor admits two points for including the chapter. Why do they lose? Because the author herself said it shouldn't be printed. So we need a principle that ranks the author's stated wish above readers' interest. Note that the concession about destruction is meant to tempt you: 'never asked that it be destroyed' meets a condition. It doesn't trigger a ban.

choices.note: Tempting, since it uses the stimulus's own fact. But 'only if' sets a requirement, and Lindqvist meets it (no destruction order). Meeting a requirement can't tell you to exclude the chapter.
CORRECT. Lindqvist stated that the chapter was unfit to print, and this principle says that judgment outweighs its value to readers. So the chapter stays out.
This points the opposite way. Both conditions are met (readers would value it; no destruction order), so it would require including the chapter.
This only permits publication after death and is silent on whether the edition should include the chapter. If Lindqvist has died, it even allows publication.
This boosts readers' interest, which works against the editor's conclusion.

questions.stimulus: At the county archive, a person other than the donor of a sealed collection may view it only if that person is listed on the collection's access register or presents a court order, and the archive never lists a member of the press on any access register. Last week a reporter viewed the sealed Ambler collection. So the reporter must have presented a court order.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Anyone who views a sealed collection at the archive by presenting a court order is someone other than that collection's donor.
Reporters who donate collections to the archive rarely ask that those collections be sealed.
No one who is listed on an access register at the archive has ever needed to present a court order to view a sealed collection.
No one who is absent from a sealed collection's access register is that collection's donor.
The reporter who viewed the Ambler collection last week was not listed on that collection's access register.
questions.explanation: The rule binds only non-donors, so the argument needs the reporter not to be the Ambler collection's donor. (D) secures that indirectly: donors are always on their collection's register, reporters never are, so the reporter isn't the donor and must have used a court order. (E) just restates what the premises already give, (A) reverses the court-order relation, and (B) is a weak 'rarely' version of the missing point.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reporter presented a court order.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Non-donor views → on register OR court order; press never on a register; a reporter viewed the Ambler collection.

breakdown.analysis: The reporter wasn't on the register, so... court order? Only if the rule applies to the reporter at all. It covers people 'other than the donor'. What if the reporter donated the collection? Chain: non-donor viewer → register or court order; not on register → court order. We need: the reporter isn't the donor. You'll look for an answer that says that directly; there isn't one. Instead the key gives a general rule in contrapositive form: off the register → not the donor.

choices.note: This reverses the link: court order → non-donor. We need non-donor established first so the rule applies; this doesn't do that.
'Rarely' is the weak version of what we need. Some reporters do donate sealed collections, and the reporter could have donated this one.
Irrelevant. The reporter wasn't on any register, so what registered people need tells us nothing.
CORRECT. Donors are always on their own collection's register. The reporter, as press, is on no register, so isn't the donor. A non-donor who isn't listed needs a court order.
Tempting, but we already know it: the archive never lists press. It doesn't touch the real gap, whether the reporter is the donor.

questions.stimulus: Principle: Evidence found in a search conducted without a warrant should be excluded from trial, unless the officers who searched reasonably believed that waiting for a warrant would allow the evidence to be destroyed. No evidence that would inevitably have been discovered by lawful means, however, should be excluded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: Officers searched a car without a warrant, unreasonably fearing that its driver would destroy evidence. A lawful inventory of the car that afternoon would certainly have turned up the evidence, but it should be excluded.

Officers who searched an office without a warrant had good reason to think its occupant would destroy the documents there. Since it turned out that he had no means of doing so, the documents should be excluded.
Officers searched a warehouse under a valid warrant. Because the evidence they found there would not otherwise have been discovered by any lawful means, that evidence should be excluded from trial.

Officers searched a shed without a warrant and with no reason to fear that evidence would be destroyed, and the evidence would not otherwise have been found. Since it is reliable, it should not be excluded.

Officers searched a storage unit without a warrant or any reason to fear the loss of evidence. Since a court-ordered inventory the next day would inevitably have found it, the evidence should not be excluded.
questions.explanation: Two rules: a warrantless search's evidence is excluded unless the officers reasonably feared its destruction, and evidence that would inevitably have been found lawfully is never excluded, which overrides the first. (E) is the override applied correctly. (A) applies only the first rule and ignores the override. (B) treats a reasonable but mistaken belief as if it didn't count, though the principle asks only whether the belief was reasonable. (C) applies the rule to a search that had a warrant, and (D) adds a reliability exception the principle doesn't contain.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Warrantless search AND no reasonable fear of destruction → exclude. Override: would inevitably have been found lawfully → do not exclude.

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment whose verdict the principle actually delivers; when the two rules collide, the 'inevitably discovered' rule wins.

breakdown.analysis: Two principles, and they can conflict. Which wins? The second one, flagged by 'however' and 'no evidence': inevitable discovery means never exclude. Then check the scope words. 'Reasonably believed' asks whether the fear was sensible at the time, not whether it turned out to be true. And the whole first rule is about searches WITHOUT a warrant. It's like a rule that says "late homework loses points unless you were sick, but no work submitted before grades close loses points". The second clause trumps the first.

choices.note: Tempting, since the first rule is satisfied (no warrant, unreasonable fear). But the evidence would certainly have been found anyway, and the override says such evidence is never excluded.

Tempting, if you read 'reasonably believed' as 'correctly believed'. The officers had good reason, so the exclusion rule is switched off; it doesn't matter that the fear turned out to be wrong. Nothing in the principle supports excluding it.
This search had a warrant, so the exclusion rule doesn't apply. Whether the evidence would otherwise have been found matters only for the override.
The first rule says exclude (no warrant, no reasonable fear), and the override doesn't apply (it wouldn't have been found otherwise). Reliability is no exception in this principle.
CORRECT. The first rule alone would exclude it (no warrant, no reasonable fear). But the evidence would inevitably have been found lawfully, so the override applies: it should not be excluded.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Explain & Weaken II

questions.stimulus: When a grocery chain installed self-checkout machines in half of its stores, its managers expected shoplifting losses at those stores to rise, since self-checkout makes it easy to leave items unscanned. Over the following year, however, shoplifting losses fell at the stores with the machines while holding steady at the chain’s other stores.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Most customers at the stores with self-checkout machines continued to use the staffed checkout lanes for the bulk of their purchases.
Self-checkout machines cost the chain less to operate each year than the staffed checkout lanes that they replaced did.
To make room for the machines, the chain moved its cashiers to stations beside the exits, which every shopper passes.
Shoplifting losses at grocery stores throughout the region fell somewhat that year as police patrols were increased.
Employees at the stores with machines now spend much of each shift helping customers use them rather than walking the aisles.
questions.explanation: Something else changed at the self-checkout stores: the cashiers now stand at the exits, where every shopper must pass them, which deters theft more than the machines invite it. That is (C). (A) is the trap: it shows why the machines might not raise losses, but not why losses fell. (D) applies to every store, and (E) deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Self-checkout should make shoplifting easier, but losses fell at the stores that got the machines while staying flat at the others.

breakdown.analysis: Why would a store that makes stealing easier lose less to theft? Only if something else about those stores changed for the better. We need a difference between the two groups of stores that pushes theft down at the self-checkout stores. Watch the trap that just cancels the expected harm: “the machines didn’t hurt” isn’t the same as “losses fell.”

choices.note: Tempting. If customers mostly avoided the machines, the machines wouldn’t raise losses much. But that only gets the two groups of stores to equal. It gives no reason losses actually fell at the self-checkout stores.
Operating cost is a different dimension from theft. Irrelevant.

CORRECT. The installation came with a second change: cashiers now sit by the exits, and every shopper walks past them. That’s a deterrent the other stores don’t have, so losses can fall even though the machines themselves are easier to cheat.
A regional decline would hit the chain’s other stores too, yet their losses held steady. It can’t explain a difference between the groups.
Fewer employees walking the aisles should make theft easier. This deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: When the water off the Sennick coast is warm, the plankton that the coast’s anchovies feed on grows poorly, and the total number of anchovies in Sennick waters falls. The Sennick fishing fleet, which has the same number of boats every year, nevertheless lands more anchovies in warm years than in cool ones.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many of the larger fish that prey on anchovies leave Sennick waters when the water there is warm, returning once it cools.
Anchovies landed in warm years are, on average, smaller and bring a lower price than those landed in cool years.
The anchovies that die off in warm years are mostly young fish too small to be kept by the mesh of the fleet’s nets.
Fleets from neighboring coasts, which fish with similar boats and gear, also land more anchovies in warm years than in cool ones.
In warm years, the anchovies that remain are packed into a far smaller area of water than they occupy in cool years.
questions.explanation: Fewer fish can mean a bigger catch if the fish become easier to catch. (E) says warm years pack the remaining anchovies into a much smaller area, so the same boats find dense schools and land more. (C) is the near-miss: it explains why the catch need not fall, not why it rises. (D) just repeats the puzzle on another coast.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Warm years mean fewer anchovies in Sennick waters, but the same-sized fleet lands more anchovies in warm years.

breakdown.analysis: How do the same boats catch more of a smaller population? The catch depends on how many fish there are AND on how easy they are to find. We need something about warm years that makes anchovies easier to catch. The right answer won’t say “easier to catch” outright; it gives you a fact you have to turn into that.

choices.note: Fewer predators doesn’t change the fact that the total number of anchovies falls in warm years. It says nothing about why the fleet catches more.
Size and price don’t bear on how many anchovies are landed. Irrelevant.
Tempting. If the die-off is mostly fish the nets can’t keep anyway, the catch needn’t drop. But the puzzle is that the catch goes UP. This explains only half.
So the pattern holds elsewhere too. That restates the puzzle; it doesn’t resolve it.
CORRECT. Packed into a small area, the anchovies form dense schools that the boats can find and fill their nets from quickly. Fewer fish overall, but far more per boat-hour.

questions.stimulus: Pharmacist: Last year, 140 of our customers told us they had developed a rash after starting a new medication. More of them had started Drug Q than had started any other single medication. So among the medications we dispense, Drug Q is the one most likely to cause a rash in the people who take it.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the pharmacist’s argument?
choices: Drug Q is newly prescribed to far more of the pharmacy’s customers each year than any other medication the pharmacy dispenses.
Most of the rashes reported by customers who had started Drug Q were mild and cleared up within a few days.
A few of the customers who reported a rash after starting Drug Q had started a second medication at about the same time.
Rash is listed as a possible side effect on the labels of many of the medications that the pharmacy dispenses.
Customers who develop a mild rash after starting a medication often do not mention it to their pharmacist at all.
questions.explanation: The pharmacist moves from the largest NUMBER of rash reports to the highest LIKELIHOOD of a rash. If far more customers start Drug Q than any other drug, it would top the count even with an ordinary or low rash rate. That is (A). (C) is tempting but covers only a few cases, and (E) affects every medication alike.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Drug Q is the medication most likely to cause a rash in people who take it.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Of 140 customers reporting a rash after starting a medication, more had started Drug Q than any other single drug.

breakdown.analysis: Most reports isn’t the same as most likely. If half the town takes Drug Q, it will lead the rash count even if it’s gentler than everything else. It’s like saying Toyotas are the most dangerous cars because more Toyotas crash than any other make. We need an answer that says Drug Q is taken by far more people. That’s a base-rate attack, and it’s worth knowing.

choices.note: CORRECT. If Drug Q is started by far more customers than any other drug, it would produce the most rash reports even with a low per-person rate. The count tells you nothing about likelihood.
Severity is a different question from likelihood. Irrelevant.
Tempting, since it hints at another cause. But it’s only a few customers, and Drug Q could still lead the count without them. It barely dents the argument.
Many drugs can cause rashes. So what? That doesn’t tell us which is MOST likely to.
Underreporting would shrink every drug’s count, not just Drug Q’s. Unless it hits Drug Q differently, it doesn’t change the comparison.

questions.stimulus: Glassmakers at the Halbeck works add a small amount of a certain metal compound to their molten glass. Glass that contains this compound and nothing else that colors glass has a faint purple tint. But the Halbeck glassmakers add the compound because it makes their finished windowpanes look more nearly colorless than they otherwise would.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The compound also drives tiny air bubbles out of the molten glass, so the finished panes are clearer than they otherwise would be.
Halbeck adds the compound in quantities far too small to give its panes a purple tint that most people would notice.
Other glassworks achieve nearly colorless glass by using different compounds or more carefully purified ingredients.
Glass made from the sand that Halbeck uses is otherwise tinged yellow-green, a hue that a faint purple tint neutralizes.
A faint tint in a windowpane is often visible only when the pane is viewed edge-on rather than face-on.
questions.explanation: A tinting agent can make glass look less colored if it cancels a tint that is already there. (D) supplies that: Halbeck’s sand gives a yellow-green cast, and faint purple neutralizes it. (A) is the trap: it is about clearness (bubbles), not color. (B) and (E) only explain why the purple might go unnoticed, not why the glass looks more colorless.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: On its own the compound tints glass purple, but Halbeck adds it to make its panes look more colorless.

breakdown.analysis: How can adding color take color away? Only if there’s already a color for it to cancel. Note the stimulus’s careful phrase: “nothing else that colors glass.” That’s the hint that Halbeck’s glass might have something else. We need an answer that gives the glass a pre-existing tint that purple offsets.

choices.note: Tempting, because it says the compound makes panes “clearer.” But bubbles are about transparency, not color. The puzzle is about looking colorless. Wrong dimension.
This shows the purple might not be noticed, which at best gets you to “no worse.” It doesn’t explain why the panes look MORE colorless with the compound.
What other glassworks do doesn’t explain Halbeck’s result. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. Halbeck’s glass starts out yellow-green, and a faint purple cancels that hue. Adding a tint removes the visible tint.
Like (B), this only says a faint purple would be hard to see. It doesn’t make the glass look less colored than it would without the compound.

questions.stimulus: Graylock jays hide food in autumn and retrieve it during the winter. Jays that spread their food among many small caches later recover a smaller percentage of what they hid than do jays that use a few large caches. Even so, jays of the first kind are more likely to survive the winter than jays of the second kind.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Remembering the locations of many small caches places greater demands on a jay’s memory than remembering a few large ones does.
Jays that use many small caches typically gather several times as much food each autumn as other jays do.
Most of the food that jays fail to recover from small caches is taken by squirrels rather than simply forgotten.
In mild winters, Graylock jays of both kinds supplement the food they retrieve from their caches with insects.
Some Graylock jays hide part of their food in small caches and hide the rest in a few large ones.
questions.explanation: A smaller percentage of a much larger store can still be more food. If scattering jays gather several times as much, they end up with more to eat even though they recover a lower share. That is (B). (A) and (C) explain why the percentage is low, not why those jays survive better.

setup.label: Paradox
