setup.text: Jays with many small caches recover a smaller percentage of their food, but they survive the winter more often.

breakdown.analysis: Percentage isn’t amount. Recovering 50% of 1,000 seeds beats recovering 90% of 200. We need an answer that says the scattering jays start with more food, or otherwise end up eating more. Watch for answers that explain why the percentage is low; that side of the puzzle doesn’t need explaining.

choices.note: This explains why scattering jays recover a smaller share. But that fact isn’t the puzzle; their better survival is. Explains the wrong side.
CORRECT. Several times as much food, recovered at a lower rate, can still leave the scattering jays with more to eat. Rate versus amount.
Tempting, since it says where the lost food goes. But theft versus forgetting doesn’t change how much food the jay ends up with. It doesn’t touch survival.
It applies to both kinds of jays, so it can’t explain a difference between them.
A few mixed jays don’t explain why the pure scatterers beat the pure hoarders. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Arts administrator: Four years ago the Lisle Symphony began giving free tickets to any concertgoer under twenty-five, hoping to build a new paying audience. Since then, the symphony’s annual revenue from ticket sales has risen by 30 percent. Hence the free-ticket program has enlarged the symphony’s paying audience.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the arts administrator’s argument?
choices: Many people under twenty-five who obtained free tickets to Lisle Symphony concerts did not actually attend the concerts.
In the years just before the free-ticket program began, the symphony’s ticket revenue had been falling steadily.
Several orchestras in nearby cities that offer no free tickets have seen their revenue from ticket sales stay flat.
Over those four years the symphony raised subscription prices by about half, and few subscribers canceled.
Some concertgoers who first attended on free tickets have since bought tickets to concerts after turning twenty-five.
questions.explanation: Revenue measures dollars, not people. If the symphony raised subscription prices by about half and kept nearly all its subscribers, revenue could rise 30 percent with no larger paying audience at all, and no help from the program. That is (D). (B) is tempting, but a rise after a decline makes the program look better, not worse; (C) and (E) strengthen.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The free-ticket program has enlarged the symphony’s paying audience.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since the program began four years ago, ticket revenue has risen 30 percent.

breakdown.analysis: Does more revenue mean more paying customers? Not if each customer pays more. The evidence is a dollar figure; the conclusion is about headcount and about the program’s effect. We need an answer that explains the revenue rise some other way, ideally one that involves no new payers.

choices.note: No-shows among free-ticket holders don’t affect paid revenue or the paying audience. Irrelevant.
Tempting, because it mentions the trend before the program. But a turnaround from falling to rising revenue right when the program began, if anything, makes the program look more effective.
Flat revenue at orchestras without the program suggests the program made the difference. That strengthens.
CORRECT. A price rise of about half with few cancellations raises revenue by itself, so the 30 percent gain may come from the same people paying more. The paying audience need not have grown at all.
Free-ticket users turning into paying customers is exactly what the administrator claims. That supports the argument.

questions.stimulus: Over the past twenty-five years, the number of known asteroids whose orbits bring them near Earth has increased more than tenfold. Over the same period, astronomers’ estimate of the probability that a large asteroid will strike Earth within the next century has fallen substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Earlier estimates allowed for large asteroids not yet found; most such asteroids have since been tracked, on harmless orbits.
Most of the near-Earth asteroids discovered in the past twenty-five years are too small to cause serious damage if they struck Earth.
Telescopes used to search for asteroids can now detect objects far fainter than those detectable twenty-five years ago.
An asteroid’s orbit can be altered unpredictably when the asteroid passes close to a massive planet such as Jupiter.
Estimates of how much damage a large asteroid strike would cause have risen sharply over the past twenty-five years.
questions.explanation: An estimate of risk depends on what is unknown as well as what is known. Earlier estimates had to assume undiscovered large asteroids might be on a collision course; finding most of them and confirming safe orbits removes that uncertainty, so the estimate falls even as the count of known asteroids rises. That is (A). (B) is the near-miss: it explains why the new discoveries needn’t raise the estimate, but not why it fell.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Ten times as many near-Earth asteroids are known, but the estimated chance of a large one hitting Earth has dropped.

breakdown.analysis: Why would finding more asteroids make us feel safer? Because a risk estimate covers what you haven’t found yet. It’s like a building inspector who’s more worried about the rooms she hasn’t checked than the ones she has. Once she checks them and they’re fine, her risk estimate drops even though her list of known rooms got longer. We need an answer that turns discoveries into resolved uncertainty. Beware the answer that only neutralizes the new discoveries.

choices.note: CORRECT. The old estimate included large asteroids that hadn’t been found but might be dangerous. Now most have been found and they’re on safe orbits, so that unknown risk is gone. More known asteroids, lower estimated risk.

Tempting, and the most popular wrong answer. Small discoveries explain why the tenfold increase didn’t RAISE the large-asteroid risk. But the estimate FELL. Something has to push it down, and this doesn’t.
Better telescopes explain why more asteroids are known. That’s one side of the puzzle, and it’s not the side that needs explaining.
Unpredictable orbits would make the risk harder to rule out, if anything. Deepens the puzzle.
Damage is a different question from the probability of a strike. Wrong dimension.

questions.stimulus: Town engineer: Calcium chloride melts ice faster than rock salt does and keeps working in conditions in which rock salt fails. Last winter our town switched from rock salt to calcium chloride, and ice-related traffic accidents on town roads fell by a third compared with the winter before. Thus the switch prevented many accidents.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the town engineer’s argument?
choices: Calcium chloride, like rock salt, gradually corrodes the bodies of cars and damages concrete road surfaces and bridges.
Calcium chloride costs the town considerably more per ton than did the rock salt it replaced on town roads.
Several nearby towns that kept using rock salt last winter saw almost no change in their numbers of ice-related accidents.
Some of last winter’s ice-related accidents occurred on stretches of road that had already been treated with calcium chloride.
The winter before last brought an unusual number of freezing-rain storms, which glaze roads faster than any de-icer can be spread.
questions.explanation: The comparison is with a single prior winter. If that winter had unusually many freezing-rain storms that no de-icer could keep up with, its accident count was abnormally high, and a drop the next year is expected whatever the town spread. That is (E). (C) is the opposite-direction trap: it supports the engineer, since towns that kept salt saw no drop.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching to calcium chloride prevented many accidents.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Calcium chloride works faster and in more conditions; after the switch, ice-related accidents fell by a third compared with the previous winter.

breakdown.analysis: Fell by a third compared with what? One winter. What if that winter was unusually bad? A before/after comparison is only as good as its “before.” We need an answer that makes the earlier winter an abnormal baseline, or that gives another reason accidents dropped.

choices.note: Damage to cars and roads is a different issue from accidents. Irrelevant.
Cost doesn’t bear on whether accidents were prevented. Wrong dimension.
Tempting, because it’s about the right outcome. But it points the wrong way: towns that kept rock salt saw no drop, which suggests the switch made the difference. That strengthens.
No de-icer prevents every accident. A drop by a third is consistent with some accidents still happening on treated roads. Doesn’t weaken.

CORRECT. Freezing rain glazes roads faster than any de-icer can be spread, so the earlier winter’s count was inflated by storms no product could handle. A drop the next winter is what you’d expect anyway.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, the average amount that a Corvin taxi driver collects in fares per shift has nearly doubled, even though surveys show that the total number of taxi trips taken in Corvin each year has not increased.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: The average distance traveled per taxi trip in Corvin, on which fares are partly based, has grown considerably over the decade.
Many drivers have left the Corvin taxi fleet over the decade, so the remaining drivers share the city’s trips among fewer people.
Passengers in Corvin now tip their taxi drivers far more generously, on average, than passengers did ten years ago.
Corvin’s taxi drivers now work fewer shifts per week than they once did, but each shift is several hours longer.
The city has twice raised the regulated rate per kilometer that Corvin taxis charge their passengers.
questions.explanation: Fare money per shift can double with no more trips if each trip brings in more fare (A, E) or each shift gets a larger share of the trips (B, D). (C) is about tips, which are not fares, so it explains a rise in drivers’ income but not in fares collected. It is the one that does not help.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Fares collected per shift have nearly doubled, but the total number of taxi trips hasn’t increased.

breakdown.analysis: EXCEPT question: four answers explain, one doesn’t. Fares per shift = trips per shift × fare per trip. So the explainers either raise the fare per trip or give each shift more of the same trips. The LSAT is ultra specific here: the stimulus measures FARES. Anything that raises drivers’ pay some other way is the odd one out.

choices.note: Longer trips mean bigger fares per trip, so each shift collects more without more trips. Explains.
Fewer drivers splitting the same trips means more trips per driver per shift. Explains.

CORRECT. Tips aren’t fares. More generous tipping raises what drivers take home, but the stimulus is about the amount collected in fares, and this doesn’t touch that. It’s the tempting one to skip past because it sounds like “drivers earn more.”
Fewer, longer shifts covering the same total trips means more trips, and so more fares, in each shift. Explains.
A higher rate per kilometer raises the fare on every trip. Explains.

questions.stimulus: Entomologist: Colonies of desert harvester ants that forage only in the cool early morning gather less seed per day than colonies that forage throughout the day, but in drought years the two kinds of colonies survive at the same rate. Evidently, the amount of seed a colony gathers has little effect on whether it survives a drought.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the entomologist’s argument?
choices: Harvester ant colonies that have stored more seed are more likely than other colonies to survive an unusually cold winter.
Midday heat kills many foragers, so all-day colonies spend much of their extra seed raising replacement workers.
Morning-only colonies and all-day colonies are found side by side throughout the same desert regions.
In years without drought, all-day colonies produce more new queens, and thus more daughter colonies, than morning-only colonies do.
Droughts severe enough to threaten harvester ant colonies have become more frequent in recent decades.
questions.explanation: The argument treats the all-day colonies’ extra seed as extra food in reserve. If midday heat kills foragers and that extra seed goes into replacing them, the all-day colonies end up no better stocked, so equal survival says nothing about whether seed matters. That is (B). (A) is the trap: it shows stored seed matters for a different threat, cold, not drought.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: How much seed a colony gathers has little effect on whether it survives a drought.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All-day colonies gather more seed per day than morning-only colonies, but both survive droughts at the same rate.

breakdown.analysis: Equal survival despite unequal gathering looks like seed doesn’t matter. But is the extra seed really extra? What if the all-day colonies have to spend it on something? Then both kinds of colonies could have the same usable reserve, and seed could still matter a lot. We need an answer that shows the gathering gap isn’t a real surplus.

choices.note: Tempting, because it says stored seed helps colonies survive. But the argument is only about droughts. Cold winters are a different threat. Wrong scope.

CORRECT. The extra seed is used up replacing workers killed by the heat, so all-day colonies don’t end up with a bigger reserve. Equal survival is just what you’d expect if seed DOES matter and the effective amounts are equal.
Sharing the same regions rules out a difference in surroundings, which, if anything, strengthens the comparison.
Producing queens in good years is a different outcome from surviving drought. Irrelevant.
More frequent droughts don’t tell us what affects survival in one. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Since the sewage treatment plant serving Delby Harbor was upgraded three years ago, average bacteria levels in the harbor’s water have fallen by 70 percent. Surprisingly, in each of those three years the harbor’s clam beds were closed because of bacterial contamination on more days than in any year before the upgrade.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Heavy rains still sometimes wash bacteria from farm fields into Delby Harbor, briefly raising bacteria levels over the clam beds.
The upgraded plant releases its treated water at a point farther from the clam beds than the old plant did.
Clams take in bacteria from the water as they feed and can retain those bacteria for some time afterward.
Demand for Delby Harbor clams has grown since the upgrade, and more people now harvest clams there each season.
After storms, the upgraded plant releases stored overflow in brief surges that push bacteria over the beds to record levels.
questions.explanation: An average can fall while the peaks rise. Closures are triggered by spikes, not averages; if the new plant releases storm overflow in brief surges that drive bacteria over the beds to record highs, the beds close more often even as average levels fall. That is (E). (A) is the trap: farm runoff causes spikes, but it happened before the upgrade too, so it cannot explain the increase.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Average bacteria levels have fallen 70 percent since the upgrade, but the clam beds are closed for contamination more often than ever.

breakdown.analysis: Lower average, more closures. Can both be true? Sure, if closures depend on spikes and the spikes got worse. It’s like a river whose average level drops but that floods more often because the dam now releases water in bursts. We need something new since the upgrade that produces higher peaks. “Still” is a red flag: anything that was already true before the upgrade can’t explain a change.

choices.note: Tempting, because spikes are the right idea. But the rains “still” happen: they happened before the upgrade too. That explains closures in general, not why there are MORE of them now.
Moving the outflow away from the beds should mean fewer closures. Deepens the puzzle.
This is true of clams in general and was true before the upgrade. It doesn’t explain a change.
More harvesters doesn’t make the water more contaminated or trigger more closures. Irrelevant.
CORRECT. The upgrade changed HOW sewage reaches the harbor: less overall, but in occasional surges that push bacteria to record levels. Average down, peaks up, closures up.

questions.stimulus: School board member: The schools in our district that employ the most reading specialists also have the district’s lowest reading scores. One might reply that the specialists were sent to the schools whose scores were already lowest. But those schools still have the lowest scores five years after the specialists arrived. So the specialists have done little to improve students’ reading.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the school board member’s argument?
choices: Average reading scores at those schools are much closer to the district average now than they were before the specialists arrived.
The district assigned reading specialists to its schools mainly on the basis of how low each school’s reading scores had been.
Reading specialists in the district spend part of their working time on paperwork and meetings rather than with students.
Reading scores have been rising across the district, including at schools that employ no reading specialists at all.
Several schools that employ only one reading specialist have reading scores well above the district average.
questions.explanation: The board member infers “little improvement” from the fact that the schools are still ranked lowest. But a school can stay last while improving a great deal. (A) says the gap between those schools and the district average has narrowed sharply since the specialists arrived, which is real improvement. (B) is the main trap: it restates the objection the argument already answers.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reading specialists have done little to improve students’ reading.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Schools with the most specialists have the lowest scores; the objection that specialists went to already-low schools is answered by noting the schools are still lowest five years later.

breakdown.analysis: Still last isn’t the same as not improving. A runner can stay in last place while cutting a minute off her time. The board member slides from a ranking (lowest) to an absolute claim (little improvement). We need an answer that shows the specialist schools improved even though they kept their rank. Watch for the answer that just repeats the objection the board member already dealt with.

choices.note: CORRECT. If those schools are now much closer to the district average than before, they gained ground on everyone else. That’s improvement, and it’s fully consistent with their still being lowest. It’s phrased as a gap, so you have to see that a shrinking gap means the scores rose relative to the rest.

Tempting, and the most popular wrong answer. But the board member already grants this possibility (“One might reply…”) and answers it with the five-year point. Confirming the objection doesn’t touch the answer to it.
If anything, time lost to paperwork would help explain why specialists did little. Doesn’t weaken.
A district-wide rise, including at schools without specialists, suggests something other than specialists is lifting scores. Neutral at best; it doesn’t show the specialists helped.
Schools with one specialist doing well doesn’t tell us whether specialists improved the low-scoring schools. Irrelevant.

questions.stimulus: Twelve years ago, the nation of Ardeth banned the manufacture and sale of PBX, a flame retardant once widely added to foam cushions and mattresses. People absorb PBX mainly from household dust. Nonetheless, the average level of PBX in the blood of Ardeth’s residents is higher now than it was when the ban took effect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many homes in Ardeth still contain cushions and mattresses that were treated with PBX before the ban took effect.
Several other nations banned PBX at about the same time as Ardeth did, and their residents’ PBX levels have since fallen.
Cushions made since the ban contain a different flame retardant, one that people also absorb from dust and that lingers in the body.
PBX-treated foam gives off the chemical far more readily once it begins breaking down with age than when new.
Researchers who measure PBX in blood today use the same methods that were used when the ban took effect.
questions.explanation: People get PBX from dust, so blood levels track how much PBX old foam is shedding. If foam releases far more PBX as it ages, the foam made before the ban is now shedding more than it did twelve years ago, and levels can rise even with no new PBX. That is (D). (A) is the trap: it explains why PBX exposure continues, not why it increased.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: PBX was banned twelve years ago and people absorb it mainly from household dust, but average blood levels are higher now than when the ban began.

breakdown.analysis: The ban stopped new PBX, so the PBX people absorb must come from foam made before the ban. That explains why exposure continues. But why would it go UP? Only if the old foam is releasing more now than it did then. We need an answer about the rate of release, not just the presence of old foam.

choices.note: Tempting, and the answer most people pick. Old PBX foam still in homes explains why levels haven’t dropped to zero. But the puzzle is an increase. Furniture that’s still there, releasing at the same rate as before, gives you steady levels at best.
Other nations’ falling levels make Ardeth’s rise more puzzling. Deepens it.
A different chemical would raise blood levels of THAT chemical, not of PBX. Wrong substance.

CORRECT. Foam sheds far more PBX as it breaks down, and the pre-ban foam is now twelve years older. So the same furniture puts more PBX into dust now than it did when the ban began. It’s the hard-to-like answer because it never says the foam is still around; the stimulus already tells you PBX is still being absorbed from dust.
Same methods means the rise is real, not an artifact. That confirms the puzzle instead of resolving it.

questions.stimulus: Water utility spokesperson: Three years ago we began adding orthophosphate to the city’s water; the compound forms a coating inside lead pipes that keeps lead from dissolving. Since then, lead levels in tap-water samples from homes have averaged 60 percent lower than in the preceding three years. This shows that the orthophosphate is what reduced the lead in residents’ tap water.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the spokesperson’s argument?
choices: Orthophosphate takes several weeks after it is first added to a city’s water to form a complete coating inside lead pipes.
Samples from a few homes with especially old pipes still show lead levels above the recommended safety limit.
Most of the city’s lead service lines were dug up and replaced during the three years before orthophosphate was first added.
Some homes in the city are served entirely by newer copper or plastic pipes that contain no lead at all.
Many other cities with aging lead pipes add orthophosphate to their water supplies for this same reason.
questions.explanation: The comparison is between two three-year averages. If most lead service lines were replaced during the earlier three years, that period’s average includes high readings from before the replacements, while the later period has far fewer lead lines left. The drop could come from the replacements, not the orthophosphate. That is (C). (A) is the trap: a few weeks’ delay is trivial over three years.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Orthophosphate is what reduced lead in residents’ tap water.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: It coats lead pipes; lead levels in the three years since it was added averaged 60 percent lower than in the three years before.

breakdown.analysis: What else changed between the two periods? The answer won’t look like it’s in the after-period at all. If the city was ripping out lead lines during the BEFORE period, the before-average contains the old high readings and the after-period starts with most of the lead gone. Students often dismiss an event that happened “before” the treatment as irrelevant. Here it’s exactly the alternative cause.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s about orthophosphate’s timing. But a few weeks is nothing against a three-year average. It doesn’t threaten the comparison.
No treatment gets every home safe. A few high readings are consistent with a 60 percent average drop. Doesn’t weaken.

CORRECT. Replacing most lead lines during the earlier period means the later period has far less lead pipe to leach from. That alone could account for the lower average, with orthophosphate doing little.
Homes without lead pipes were in both periods, so they don’t explain a change between them.
Other cities using the same treatment says nothing about what caused this city’s drop. At most it mildly supports the spokesperson.

questions.stimulus: Of the planets that the Arkady survey has detected orbiting other stars, most orbit their stars more closely than Mercury orbits the Sun. But the survey’s own scientists, relying on these same detections, estimate that most planets orbiting such stars lie farther from their stars than Mercury lies from the Sun.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Many astronomers believe that planets often form far from their stars and then gradually migrate inward over millions of years.
The survey registers only planets whose orbits lie nearly edge-on to Earth, an alignment that becomes rarer as orbits widen.
Most of the planets that the survey has detected are considerably larger and more massive than Earth is.
The scientists’ estimate takes into account the planets that, in their view, the survey has probably missed.
Planets orbiting close to their stars are no easier for the survey to detect than equally large planets orbiting farther out.
questions.explanation: If the survey sees only planets whose orbits happen to be edge-on to Earth, and that alignment is rarer for wide orbits, then the survey misses a larger share of distant planets. Correcting for that bias, the scientists can conclude that most planets are actually farther out. That is (B). (D) is the trap: it says the scientists adjust for missed planets but not why the missed planets would be the distant ones. (E) deepens the puzzle.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Most detected planets are closer in than Mercury, but the scientists, using those detections, estimate most planets are farther out.

breakdown.analysis: How can your data say “mostly close” and your estimate say “mostly far”? If your detector favors close planets. Then the raw count overstates close ones, and a corrected estimate flips. We need an answer that says the survey is biased toward close-in planets, with a reason.

choices.note: Inward migration would, if anything, put more planets close in. It doesn’t explain why the estimate says most are farther out.
CORRECT. Wide orbits are less likely to be lined up edge-on, so the survey catches a smaller fraction of distant planets. Adjust for that, and the distant planets turn out to be the majority.
Planet size doesn’t bear on orbital distance here. Irrelevant.

Tempting, because it describes exactly what the scientists did: adjust for missed planets. But it never says WHY the missed planets would mostly be distant ones. It restates the puzzle instead of explaining it.
If close and distant planets are equally easy to detect, the detected sample should mirror reality. That deepens the puzzle.

questions.stimulus: Legal analyst: Since Merrow’s police officers began wearing body cameras five years ago, formal complaints against them have fallen by 40 percent. Skeptics say that people now simply avoid filing complaints a recording might contradict. But complaints later upheld as justified have fallen by the same proportion as all the rest. It follows that the cameras have improved officers’ conduct.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the legal analyst’s argument?
choices: Before the cameras were introduced, most formal complaints filed against Merrow police officers were found to be unjustified.
People who know that an encounter with the police was recorded are less likely to file a complaint they know to be false.
Police departments in nearby cities that have not adopted body cameras have seen complaints against officers rise.
Several Merrow officers have been disciplined on the basis of footage recorded by their own body cameras.
The law that mandated the cameras also requires anyone filing a complaint to appear in person and give sworn testimony.
questions.explanation: The analyst rules out one alternative (people dropping complaints a recording might contradict) by noting that justified complaints fell too. But a new burden on ALL complainants, such as appearing in person to give sworn testimony, would cut justified and unjustified complaints alike, and so fits the evidence without any change in officers’ conduct. That is (E). (B) is the trap: it supports the skeptics’ alternative, which the analyst has already answered.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The body cameras have improved officers’ conduct.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Complaints fell 40 percent after cameras arrived; the skeptics’ explanation is rejected because justified complaints fell by the same proportion as the rest.

breakdown.analysis: The analyst’s rebuttal works against an alternative that would hit only unjustified complaints. So what alternative would hit justified and unjustified complaints equally? Anything that makes complaining harder for everyone. We need a cause, other than better conduct, that came in with the cameras and cuts all complaints across the board. Don’t re-argue the skeptics’ point; the analyst already handled it.

choices.note: Knowing the old mix of complaints doesn’t tell us why both kinds fell. Irrelevant.

Tempting, and the most popular wrong answer. It backs the skeptics’ view. But the analyst already answered that: if only false complaints were deterred, justified ones wouldn’t have fallen as much. This doesn’t touch the rebuttal.
Rising complaints where there are no cameras makes the cameras look effective. That strengthens.
Discipline based on footage shows the cameras are used, and if anything suggests they matter. Doesn’t weaken.

CORRECT. A sworn, in-person requirement arrived at the same time as the cameras and discourages every complainant, justified or not. That explains an across-the-board 40 percent drop without any improvement in conduct.

sections.title: Skill Builder: Hard Evaluate & Strengthen II

questions.stimulus: A city ordinance permits the municipal zoo to waive its admission fee one day each week only if doing so raises the zoo's total weekly attendance by at least 500 visitors. Since the zoo began admitting visitors free on Wednesdays, Wednesday attendance has averaged 1,400 visitors, up from 450. So the zoo is complying with the ordinance.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether most of the people who now visit the zoo on Wednesdays live within the city's limits
whether attendance at the zoo on the other six days of the week has changed since the free Wednesdays began
whether the admission revenue the zoo gives up on Wednesdays is made up by higher sales at its food stands and gift shop
whether other zoos that waive their fees one day each week have seen attendance on that day rise by a similar amount
whether many of the people who now visit on Wednesdays had never been to the zoo before the free Wednesdays began
questions.explanation: The ordinance cares about total weekly attendance, but the evidence covers Wednesdays only. If people who used to pay on other days now just come on Wednesday, the 950-visitor jump could add little or nothing to the week. (B) asks exactly that: a drop on other days hurts the argument, no change helps it. (E) is the strongest trap, but it only helps in one direction: repeat visitors could be making extra trips rather than switching days. (C) is about money, which the ordinance never mentions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The zoo is complying with the ordinance (its free day raises total weekly attendance by at least 500).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Wednesday attendance rose from 450 to 1,400 after Wednesdays became free.

breakdown.analysis: Did the zoo gain 950 visitors a week, or did it just move them? The ordinance is about the week's total, and the evidence is about one day. Picture a bakery that gives away bread on Mondays and sees Monday traffic triple: if Tuesday through Sunday empty out, it hasn't gained a single customer. We need the answer that tells us what happened on the other days. Watch (E): first-time visitors would help the argument, but a 'no' doesn't hurt it, since regulars might be coming more often.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The ordinance counts visitors, not where they live. Either answer leaves the weekly total unknown.

CORRECT. If attendance on the other days fell by roughly the Wednesday gain, the free day has only shifted visits and the zoo may be out of compliance. If the other days held steady, the 950 extra Wednesday visitors are a real addition, well over 500. Two answers, two directions.
Wrong dimension. The ordinance turns on attendance, not revenue. Whether the zoo makes up the lost fees tells you nothing about the weekly total.
Tempting, since it seems to confirm the result. But it only backs up the Wednesday jump, which the argument already reports. Other zoos' one-day numbers say nothing about this zoo's weekly total.

Tempting. A 'yes' would help, because first-timers can't have switched from another day. But a 'no' doesn't hurt: returning visitors might be making extra trips rather than shifting days. It works in only one direction.

questions.stimulus: Historian: Among the surviving letters that soldiers in one Union regiment sent home during the 1862 campaign, complaints about food far outnumber complaints about any other hardship, including the dangers of battle. Hence, to these soldiers, poor rations were a heavier burden than the risk of being killed or wounded.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the historian's argument?
choices: whether the regiment's rations that year were smaller or of poorer quality than those issued to the other Union regiments in its army
whether the regiment suffered more casualties during the 1862 campaign than during any of its later campaigns
whether some of the regiment's soldiers were unable to write and so sent no letters home at all
whether soldiers of that era generally avoided writing about the dangers of combat so as not to alarm their families
whether the letters that survive were preserved mostly by families living in a few neighboring counties
questions.explanation: The historian treats what soldiers wrote home about as a measure of what weighed on them most. (D) tests that link: if soldiers routinely kept the dangers of battle out of their letters to spare their families, the count of complaints says little about which hardship was heavier; if they didn't, the letters are better evidence. (A) is the main trap: worse-than-average rations would show the food was bad, not that hunger outweighed fear. (C) mentions only some soldiers, so it can't change the picture much.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: To these soldiers, poor rations were a heavier burden than the risk of being killed or wounded.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In the regiment's surviving letters home, complaints about food far outnumber complaints about anything else, including battle.

breakdown.analysis: Is what you write home the same as what you fear most? A soldier writing to his mother might grumble about hardtack and keep quiet about the man who died next to him. The argument needs the letters to be a fair picture of what the men felt. We want a question whose answer tells us whether danger was left out of the letters for some other reason. Most students drawn to a wrong answer pick (A): bad rations make the food complaints believable, but the issue is the comparison with danger, not whether the food was bad.

choices.note: Tempting. If the rations were worse than other regiments', the complaints make sense. But that doesn't tell us food weighed on the men more than the risk of death. And if the rations were ordinary, the food could still have been their main burden. Neither answer settles the comparison.
Irrelevant comparison. How 1862 compares with later campaigns says nothing about how the men weighed food against danger in 1862.
Too weak. 'Some' soldiers not writing doesn't make the letters unrepresentative. A handful of missing voices doesn't change which complaint dominates.

CORRECT. If soldiers commonly kept the dangers of battle out of their letters, the scarcity of such complaints reflects tact, not feeling, and the argument collapses. If they didn't, the letters are a fair window into what bothered them, and the argument is stronger.
So? Where the letters were kept has no clear bearing on whether they mention food more than danger. Families in a few counties are no more likely to have saved food complaints than battle accounts.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, university life-science research groups that work with the newest laboratory equipment have published papers that are cited far more often than those of groups working with older equipment. Therefore, a university that wants its life-science researchers to produce more frequently cited work should replace their older equipment.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Is new laboratory equipment usually paid for by grants that are awarded on the basis of a research group's past publications?
Does the newest laboratory equipment cost more to maintain each year than the older equipment it would replace?
Do research groups in the physical sciences that use the newest equipment also publish papers that are cited unusually often?
Have some research groups that work with the newest equipment published no frequently cited papers at all?
Are papers in the life sciences cited more often, on average, than papers in most other scientific fields?
questions.explanation: The argument assumes the equipment produces the citations. (A) raises the reverse possibility: if new equipment is usually funded by grants that go to groups with strong publication records, then success brings the equipment, and buying it for weaker groups may not help. A 'no' makes that reversal unlikely. (C) is the main trap; it repeats the same correlation in another field, which doesn't tell us which way the causation runs. (B) is about cost, not whether the plan works.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A university wanting more frequently cited life-science work should replace its researchers' older equipment.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Groups with the newest equipment publish papers that are cited far more often than groups with older equipment.

breakdown.analysis: Which came first, the equipment or the success? If the best-cited groups are the ones who win grants, and grants buy new machines, then the correlation runs backward: success gets you equipment. It's like noticing that star athletes wear expensive shoes and concluding the shoes made them stars, when sponsors hand shoes to people who are already stars. We need the question that tells us whether equipment follows success. Watch (C): it repeats the pattern somewhere else, which doesn't decide the direction.

choices.note: CORRECT. Yes: equipment is handed to groups that already publish well-cited work, so the correlation may reflect success causing equipment, and the plan could fail. No: that reversal is ruled out and the plan looks better. The answer moves the argument either way.
Wrong dimension. Upkeep cost bears on whether the plan is affordable, not on whether new equipment would make papers more cited.
Tempting. Finding the same correlation in another field feels like confirmation. But the same reversal could explain it there too. A yes or a no leaves the direction of causation open.
Too weak. 'Some' groups with new equipment doing poorly is expected even if equipment helps on average. Either answer leaves the argument unchanged.
Irrelevant comparison. How life-science citations compare with other fields says nothing about whether newer equipment raises citations within the life sciences.

questions.stimulus: At Linwell Hospital, heart-surgery patients who chose to join an optional walking program after their operations were only half as likely as other heart-surgery patients to be readmitted within six months. The hospital's administrators conclude that enrolling every heart-surgery patient in the program would substantially reduce the hospital's readmission rate for such patients.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the administrators' conclusion?
choices: whether walking is the form of exercise that cardiologists most often recommend to patients recovering from heart surgery
whether enrolling every heart-surgery patient in the walking program would require the hospital to hire additional staff
whether surgeons often advised patients who had suffered complications during surgery not to join the program
whether most readmissions of heart-surgery patients at Linwell Hospital are for problems involving the heart
whether some of the patients who joined the walking program stopped taking part in it after a few weeks
questions.explanation: The walkers chose to join, so they may have differed from non-walkers before the program began. (C) gets at that indirectly: if surgeons steered patients with surgical complications away from the program, the walkers were a healthier group to start with, and their low readmission rate may owe little to walking. If surgeons did not, that explanation fades. (B) is about cost, (A) about popularity of walking, and (E) concerns only some patients.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Enrolling every heart-surgery patient in the walking program would substantially cut readmissions.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Patients who chose to join the program were half as likely to be readmitted within six months as other patients.

breakdown.analysis: Who joins an optional walking group right after heart surgery? Probably the patients who feel up to it. If the walkers were healthier from the start, they'd be readmitted less even if walking did nothing, and making the sicker patients walk wouldn't copy their results. We want a question that tells us whether the two groups started out different. The answer here doesn't say 'healthier'; it describes one way the groups could have been sorted, which is why it's easy to skip.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Doctors recommending walking doesn't tell us whether this program caused the lower readmission rate or whether the walkers were healthier to begin with.
Wrong dimension. Staffing bears on whether the plan is practical, not whether it would lower readmissions.

CORRECT. If surgeons kept patients with complications out of the program, the walkers were a lower-risk group from the start, and their lower readmission rate could have nothing to do with walking. If surgeons didn't, that explanation is weakened and the conclusion looks better.

So? Whether readmissions involve the heart or something else, we still don't know whether the program caused the walkers' advantage. Neither answer separates the program from the patients who chose it.
Too weak. Some dropouts are normal in any program. Knowing that some walkers quit doesn't tell us whether the program or the patients' prior health explains the gap.

questions.stimulus: Legislator: Two years ago our state tripled the fine for driving with a suspended license. Since then, the number of people convicted of that offense each year has fallen by about a third. Evidently, the harsher fine has persuaded many people whose licenses are suspended to stay off the road.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the legislator's argument?
choices: Several other states that raised their fines for driving with a suspended license have also seen yearly convictions for that offense decline.
The state's fine for driving with a suspended license is now higher than the corresponding fine in any neighboring state.
Since the fine was raised, prosecutors have more often allowed people charged with the offense to plead guilty to lesser charges.
Random checks by state police have turned up drivers whose licenses are suspended far less often since the fine was raised.
The fine for driving with a suspended license had not been changed for more than twenty years before it was tripled.
questions.explanation: The evidence is about convictions; the conclusion is about how many suspended drivers are actually on the road. Fewer convictions could mean fewer offenders, or just fewer cases ending in a conviction for that charge. (D) bridges the gap with a measure of the behavior itself: random checks find suspended drivers less often. (A) is the main trap: it shows other states' convictions fell too, which repeats the same conviction evidence without connecting it to driving. (C) weakens.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The harsher fine has persuaded many people with suspended licenses to stop driving.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The fine was tripled two years ago; yearly convictions for the offense have since fallen by about a third.

breakdown.analysis: Convictions aren't driving. A tougher fine can cut convictions without changing anyone's behavior: prosecutors may charge something lighter, or defendants may fight harder. So the argument jumps from 'fewer people convicted' to 'fewer people driving.' We want an answer that measures the driving directly. Watch (A): it feels like support, but it's more conviction data, and it has the same gap.

choices.note: Tempting. More states, same pattern. But it's still conviction numbers, which don't show that fewer suspended drivers are on the road. It repeats the gap instead of closing it.
Irrelevant comparison. Having the highest fine in the area doesn't show that the fine changed anyone's driving.
Weakens. Plea deals to lesser charges would cut convictions for this offense even if just as many suspended drivers were on the road.

CORRECT. Random checks sample drivers on the road, not cases in court. If they find suspended drivers much less often since the fine went up, fewer such people are driving, which is exactly what the conclusion claims.
So? How long the old fine went unchanged has no bearing on whether the new one kept suspended drivers off the road.

questions.stimulus: About 80 percent of the Bronze Age swords that archaeologists have recovered from the rivers of a certain region are of a long, slender type, and many of these swords were deliberately bent before they entered the water, a sign that they were placed there as offerings. It follows that when people of the region offered swords to the rivers, they chose the long type out of proportion to how common it was among the swords they owned.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether swords of other types recovered from the rivers were also deliberately bent before they entered the water
whether long swords required considerably more bronze and more skill to make than shorter swords of the period did
whether Bronze Age swords of the long, slender type have also been recovered from rivers in neighboring regions
whether the people who placed swords in the rivers as offerings also placed bronze spearheads and axes there
whether the long type is similarly predominant among the region's Bronze Age swords that have been found in graves and settlements
questions.explanation: 'Favored' means chosen more often than you'd expect from the swords available. If long swords were about 80 percent of all swords in use, finding them 80 percent of the time in rivers shows no preference at all. (E) supplies that base rate: if long swords also dominate in graves and settlements, the river figure is just what was available; if not, the rivers really do over-represent them. (B) is the main trap: costlier swords would give a motive to prefer them, but it doesn't show they were preferred. (A) concerns whether other types were offerings, which doesn't change the proportions.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: When people of the region offered swords to the rivers, they favored the long type over other types.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: About 80 percent of swords recovered from the region's rivers are long and slender; many were bent first, a sign they were offerings.

breakdown.analysis: Eighty percent sounds like a lot, but compared with what? If nearly every sword in the region was long, people would toss long swords into rivers 80 percent of the time without favoring them at all. It's like noticing that most cars in a church parking lot are sedans and concluding churchgoers prefer sedans, without checking what most people in town drive. We need the comparison number: how common were long swords overall? Most students who miss this pick (B), because a costlier sword sounds like a better gift. But a reason people might have preferred long swords isn't evidence that they did.

choices.note: Tempting, because it reuses the bending detail. But if other types were bent too, they were offerings too, which tells us nothing about whether long swords were chosen more often than their numbers predict.

Tempting. Costlier swords would make a fitting offering, so a yes sounds supportive. But it gives only a possible motive. Without knowing how common long swords were, we can't tell whether the 80 percent reflects preference. And a no doesn't hurt the argument.
Irrelevant. Swords in other regions' rivers say nothing about the proportions in this region.
So? Offering spearheads and axes too doesn't tell us whether long swords were picked out of proportion to their numbers.

CORRECT. This is the base rate. If long swords also make up about 80 percent of swords found in graves and settlements, the river share just mirrors what people owned, and there's no sign of preference. If they're much rarer there, the rivers over-represent them and the conclusion gains real support.

questions.stimulus: A museum's south gallery receives direct afternoon sunlight through large windows, while its north gallery receives none. Over the past fifty years, paintings in the south gallery have faded far more than those in the north gallery. The museum's conservator therefore argues that coating the south gallery's windows with a film that blocks ultraviolet light would largely halt the fading there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the conservator's argument?
choices: Paintings near the one south-gallery window fitted decades ago with ultraviolet-blocking glass have faded little more than north-gallery paintings.
Films that block ultraviolet light reduce the amount of visible light passing through a window by only a small fraction.
Coating the south gallery's windows with the film would cost less than restoring even one badly faded painting.
Before the museum was renovated thirty years ago, paintings in the south gallery also faded faster than those in the north gallery.
Because of the afternoon sun, the south gallery is several degrees warmer than the north gallery for much of the year.
questions.explanation: The evidence implicates sunlight; the plan blocks only one part of it, ultraviolet light. If visible light or the sun's heat is doing the damage, the film won't help. (A) separates the factors: near a window that blocks ultraviolet but still admits visible light and heat, paintings have barely faded. (D) is the main trap: it confirms that sunlight correlates with fading, which the argument already grants. (B) seems helpful but actually leaves visible light in place, and (E) points to heat as a rival cause.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Coating the south gallery's windows with ultraviolet-blocking film would largely halt the fading there.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The sunlit south gallery's paintings have faded far more over fifty years than the unlit north gallery's.

breakdown.analysis: Sunlight is a package: ultraviolet, visible light, and heat. The evidence shows the package fades paintings; the plan removes only one item from it. What if it's the visible light or the warmth? We need evidence that blocking just the ultraviolet makes the difference. Most students tempted by a wrong answer pick (D), since it shows the south gallery fading faster in an earlier era too. But that's the same sunlight correlation the argument starts with; it doesn't tell us which part of the sunlight matters.

choices.note: CORRECT. That window lets in visible light and heat but not ultraviolet, and the paintings near it have barely faded. So ultraviolet is what's doing the damage, and a film that blocks it should work. It's a small natural experiment for the plan.

Tempting, because it sounds like good news about the film. But if visible light helps cause the fading, a film that leaves visible light alone won't halt it. This fact doesn't help the plan; if anything it raises a worry.
Wrong dimension. Cheapness bears on whether the plan is worth trying, not on whether it would work.
Irrelevant corroboration. It shows sunlight and fading went together before, too. The argument already grants that. It doesn't show that ultraviolet, rather than other parts of sunlight, is to blame.
Weakens. If the south gallery is warmer, heat might be causing the fading, and blocking ultraviolet light wouldn't change the temperature.

questions.stimulus: Wildlife biologist: Reported sightings of the eastern box turtle in our state have more than doubled since a smartphone app for reporting sightings was released three years ago. Some say this merely reflects how easy the app makes reporting. But the state's volunteer turtle survey, which has covered the same routes every year for two decades, has also recorded far more box turtles in the past three years. Hence the species' population is rising.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the wildlife biologist's argument?
choices: whether most of the sightings reported through the app came from people who had never before reported seeing any reptile
whether the survey volunteers have spent more time covering each route in the past three years than they did in earlier years
whether box turtles are more likely to be seen near the survey's routes than in other parts of their habitat
whether the eastern box turtle is classified as a threatened species in any of the neighboring states
whether some of the turtles recorded by the survey's volunteers were counted more than once in the same year
questions.explanation: The biologist concedes the app's numbers may be inflated and rests the case on the survey, whose routes haven't changed. But a fixed route isn't a fixed effort: more searching on the same routes would turn up more turtles without any rise in the population. (B) checks that. (A) is the main trap: it targets the app data, which the argument has already set aside. (C) concerns whether the routes are typical habitat, which doesn't matter for a year-to-year comparison on the same routes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The eastern box turtle's population in the state is rising.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: App-reported sightings have doubled (possibly just because reporting got easier); the volunteer survey, on unchanged routes, has also recorded far more turtles in the past three years.

breakdown.analysis: The biologist has a good answer to the app objection: the survey uses the same routes as always. But are the volunteers doing the same amount of looking? Same route, twice the hours, twice the turtles, and the population could be flat. It's like a fisherman who fishes the same pond every year and catches more this year because he stayed out twice as long. We need to know whether the search effort changed. Most students pick (A) because it attacks the app data, but the biologist has already conceded that point and doesn't rely on it.

choices.note: Tempting, and it's the trap. It attacks the app numbers, but the biologist already concedes they might be inflated and leans on the survey instead. Knowing who used the app doesn't touch the survey evidence.

CORRECT. If volunteers have been searching longer on the same routes, more turtles would be counted even if the population hasn't grown, and the survey stops supporting the conclusion. If effort hasn't changed, the survey rise is much better evidence of a real increase.
Doesn't matter for a trend. Whether or not the routes are typical habitat, they're the same routes each year, so the comparison over time is unaffected.
Irrelevant. Status in other states says nothing about whether the population here is rising.
Too weak. Some double counting happens in any survey, and unless it increased recently it wouldn't create a rise. 'Some' doesn't tell us that.

questions.stimulus: Because people with little schooling tended to spell words as they pronounced them, historians of English treat the spellings in such people's private letters as evidence of pronunciation. In a large collection of these letters from the early 1700s, "join" is usually spelled "jine." Historians conclude that most English speakers of that time, whether educated or not, pronounced "join" to rhyme with "line."
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historians' argument?
choices: Writers with little schooling in the early 1700s also spelled many other words in ways that reflected how they pronounced them.
Dictionaries published in the early 1700s spelled "join" the same way it is spelled today.
Many of the letters in the collection were written by servants and laborers who had moved to cities from the countryside.
In some rural dialects of English, "join" is still pronounced to rhyme with "line."
University-educated poets of the early 1700s often rhymed "join" with words such as "line" and "design."
questions.explanation: The letters show how less-schooled writers spoke; the conclusion covers most speakers, educated ones included. (E) shows the educated pronounced it the same way, since poets rhyme by sound, so the sample's pattern holds beyond the group it came from. (A) is the main trap: it backs the premise that such spellings reflect pronunciation, which only confirms what the less-schooled said. (B) confuses spelling standards with speech, and (D) is about rural speech today.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most English speakers of the early 1700s, educated or not, pronounced "join" to rhyme with "line."

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Less-schooled writers spelled as they spoke; in their letters from that time, "join" is usually spelled "jine."

breakdown.analysis: The letters can only tell us how one group talked: people with little schooling. The conclusion speaks for everyone, including the educated, who spelled by the book and so left no such clues. Maybe the educated said 'join' the modern way. We want evidence that the educated pronounced it like 'line' too. The right answer comes in sideways through poetry, since a rhyme is a record of sound. Watch (A): it strengthens the idea that these spellings track speech, but only for the group we already have evidence about.

choices.note: Tempting. It supports the method: these writers really did spell by ear. But that just confirms how the less-schooled pronounced 'join.' It says nothing about educated speakers, which is where the gap is.
Spelling isn't speech. Dictionaries record standard spelling, which can stay fixed while pronunciation varies. This doesn't tell us how anyone said the word.
If anything this weakens. It suggests the letters reflect regional speech brought in from the countryside, which makes them a shakier guide to how most speakers talked.
Tempting, since it shows the pronunciation existed. But a few rural dialects today don't show that most speakers, including the educated, used it three centuries ago.

CORRECT. Poets rhyme by sound, so educated poets pairing 'join' with 'line' shows that the educated pronounced it that way too. The letters' pattern isn't limited to the less-schooled group they come from.

questions.stimulus: Nearly every house still standing in the town of Bramford that was built before 1850 is structurally sound, whereas inspectors have found serious structural defects in many of the town's houses built since 1970. This suggests that the builders who worked in Bramford before 1850 were, as a group, more careful than those who have worked there since 1970.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether builders in Bramford before 1850 generally learned their trade through long apprenticeships rather than in schools
whether the pre-1850 houses still standing in Bramford are far too few to have housed its 1850 population
whether the houses built in Bramford since 1970 are, on average, larger than the houses built there before 1850
whether most of the defects found in the houses built since 1970 could be repaired at modest cost
whether some of the town's pre-1850 houses have been extensively restored by their present owners
questions.explanation: The old houses being compared are only the ones still standing, and badly built ones would long since have fallen down or been torn down. (B) tests how much has been lost: if the survivors couldn't possibly have housed the 1850 town, many old houses have disappeared and the sound survivors may be a select few. If they could have, few were lost and the comparison is fairer. (A) is the main trap: apprenticeships sound like evidence of skill but don't show the houses were better built. (E) mentions only some houses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bramford's builders before 1850 were, as a group, more careful than those working there since 1970.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Nearly every pre-1850 house still standing is sound; many houses built since 1970 have serious defects.

breakdown.analysis: Notice the phrase 'still standing.' The old houses that were badly built aren't around to be inspected. Only the survivors get compared with every new house, good and bad. It's like judging old music by the songs still on the radio: the forgettable ones dropped out long ago. So how many old houses have vanished? The right answer gets at that indirectly, through population: if the surviving houses are far too few for the town's 1850 population, lots of houses are gone. Most students who miss this choose (A), because it sounds like evidence of skill. But how builders were trained doesn't tell us how well the houses were built.

choices.note: Tempting. Long apprenticeships sound like a reason for better work. But training methods don't show the houses were sounder, and a no wouldn't hurt the argument either. It doesn't address the real gap.

CORRECT. If the surviving pre-1850 houses are far too few to have housed the 1850 population, many old houses have disappeared, probably the weaker ones, and the survivors are a filtered sample. If not, few were lost and the comparison stands up better. The answer cuts both ways.
So? Size doesn't tell us whether builders were careful. Either answer leaves the comparison where it was.
Wrong dimension. Cheap repairs don't change how carefully the houses were built.
Too weak. 'Some' restored houses could explain only a few sound survivors, not nearly all of them. A yes barely moves the argument.

questions.stimulus: In a survey of northern lakes, those on which loons nest were found to have much clearer water than lakes on which no loons nest. Loons eat large numbers of minnows, and minnows feed on the tiny animals that graze on algae. Ecologists therefore conclude that by keeping minnow numbers down, nesting loons help keep lakes clear of algae.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ecologists' argument?
choices: Minnows make up a large part of the diet of several other fish-eating birds that nest on northern lakes.
Loons generally return to nest on the same lake year after year once they have nested there.
Loons hunt by sight and catch prey more easily in clear water than in cloudy water.
On some lakes on which no loons nest, the water is as clear as it is on lakes where loons nest.
Lakes on which loons have just begun nesting are typically no clearer than nearby lakes without loons.
questions.explanation: The survey links loons with clear water, but the link might run the other way: loons could simply choose clear lakes. (E) rules that out: lakes are no clearer when loons first arrive, so the clarity comes after the loons, not before. (C) is the main trap: it mentions loons and clear water together, but it gives loons a reason to choose clear lakes, which supports the reverse explanation and weakens. (B) is consistent with either direction.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: By keeping minnow numbers down, nesting loons help keep lakes clear of algae.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lakes where loons nest have much clearer water; loons eat minnows, and minnows eat the tiny animals that graze on algae.

breakdown.analysis: The food chain makes the story sound tight: loons eat minnows, fewer minnows means more grazers, more grazers means less algae. But do loons make lakes clear, or do they pick lakes that are already clear? The correlation alone can't say. We want an answer that shows the clarity comes after the loons. The right answer doesn't mention minnows or algae at all, which is why it's easy to skip. Most students who go wrong pick (C), since it ties loons to clear water. Read it again: it explains why loons would choose clear lakes, so it supports the reverse explanation.

choices.note: Tempting, but it cuts the wrong way if anything. If other birds also eat lots of minnows, the clear water could be their doing, not the loons'. It doesn't help single out loons.
Consistent with both explanations. Loons that returned to a lake they'd chosen for its clarity would behave the same way. It doesn't tell us which came first.
Weakens, and it's the trap. If loons hunt better in clear water, they have a reason to settle on lakes that are already clear. That's the reverse explanation.
Too weak, and if anything a slight weakener. Other factors can make a lake clear. 'Some' clear loon-free lakes don't show anything about what loons do.

CORRECT. If lakes are no clearer than their neighbors when loons first move in, loons aren't selecting clear lakes. The clarity found in the survey comes after the loons arrive, which fits the claim that loons cause it.

questions.stimulus: The nation's highest court has never overturned one of its own precedents unless that precedent had first drawn at least two published dissents urging that it be abandoned. Last month, the court's precedent in Harlow v. Dane drew its second such dissent. Court observers have concluded that Harlow is now likely to be overturned.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions most helps in evaluating the argument?
choices: Did the dissents criticizing Harlow v. Dane argue that the case had been wrongly decided from the start?
Were the precedents that the court overturned usually overturned within a few years after drawing their second such dissent?
How many of the court's precedents that have drawn two or more such dissents remain in force today?
Have any of the court's precedents been nullified by legislation rather than overturned by the court itself?
Has the court ever overturned a precedent that it had expressly reaffirmed only a few years earlier?
questions.explanation: The premise gives a necessary condition: no precedent is overturned without two dissents. The observers treat it as if it made overturning likely. Whether that's right depends on how often precedents with two dissents actually get overturned. (C) asks exactly that: if many such precedents still stand, two dissents predict little; if few do, the prediction gains support. (B) is the main trap: timing would matter for a 'within a few years' prediction, but the observers name no time frame, and the answer leaves the base rate untouched.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Harlow v. Dane is now likely to be overturned.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The court has never overturned a precedent unless it first drew at least two dissents urging its abandonment; Harlow has just drawn its second.

breakdown.analysis: Spell out the rule: overturned → drew 2+ dissents. The observers run it backward: drew 2+ dissents → likely overturned. That only works if most precedents with two dissents end up overturned. Imagine that every Olympic champion trained for years; that doesn't mean most people who train for years win gold. What we need is the hit rate: of the precedents that reached two dissents, how many fell? Many students choose (B) because it seems to test the pattern. But the observers say nothing about timing, and how quickly the overturned precedents fell says nothing about how many with two dissents survived.

choices.note: Tempting, because it digs into the Harlow dissents. But the observers' reasoning rests only on the count of dissents. What the dissents argued doesn't tell us how often two dissents lead to overturning.

Tempting, and the most popular trap. It would matter if the observers had predicted when Harlow would fall, but they didn't. And it looks only at precedents that were overturned, so it can't tell us how many with two dissents were left alone.

CORRECT. This is the hit rate. If many precedents with two or more dissents are still in force, reaching two dissents is common and predicts little, so the conclusion fails. If almost none survive, two dissents really do signal trouble and the prediction is well founded.
Irrelevant. Legislative nullification is a different route; the question is whether the court itself will overturn Harlow.
Irrelevant. Whether the court has reversed a recently reaffirmed precedent tells us nothing about how often two dissents lead to overturning.

questions.stimulus: Seismologist: Of the 40 moderate earthquakes recorded in the Kessel Basin since 1990, 31 began within a month after a week in which more than 10 centimeters of rain fell there. Water from such heavy rain seeps down into the basin's faults, raising the pressure within them. Thus, heavy rain makes moderate earthquakes in the basin more likely.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the seismologist's argument?
choices: Since 1990, only about one day in five in the basin has come within a month after such a week.
Most weeks since 1990 with more than 10 centimeters of rain in the basin were not followed within a month by a moderate earthquake.
The moderate earthquakes that followed weeks of heavy rain were no stronger, on average, than those that did not.
Moderate earthquakes have often been recorded within a month after heavy rains in several mountain regions far from the basin.
Records of rainfall in the basin before 1990 are too incomplete to show which weeks had more than 10 centimeters of rain.
questions.explanation: Thirty-one of 40 quakes in the month after heavy rain means something only if such months are a small share of all time. If heavy rain is so common that most days fall within a month of it, quakes would land there by chance. (A) supplies the base rate: only about 20 percent of days are in that window, yet about 78 percent of quakes were, so the rain window is far over-represented. (B) is the main trap: it sounds like a weakener, but 'more likely' doesn't require most heavy rains to trigger quakes. (D) offers the same kind of uncontrolled correlation from other places.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Heavy rain makes moderate earthquakes in the Kessel Basin more likely.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 31 of 40 moderate quakes since 1990 began within a month after a week with more than 10 cm of rain; such water raises pressure in faults.

breakdown.analysis: 31 out of 40 sounds damning. But how much of the calendar sits within a month of a heavy-rain week? In a rainy basin it could be most of it, and then quakes would land in those windows by pure chance. Think of a fan who notices his team wins most games played on weekdays; that's meaningless if most games are played on weekdays. We need the base rate. The key just gives a fraction of days and doesn't mention earthquakes, which makes it easy to skip. Many students choose (B), reading it as a weakener; but a factor can raise the odds of something without causing it most of the time, so (B) is neither a strengthener nor a real threat.

choices.note: CORRECT. If only about 20 percent of days fall in the month after a heavy-rain week, yet about 78 percent of the quakes (31 of 40) began in that window, quakes are about four times as frequent there as chance would predict. That's what makes the correlation evidence that rain raises the risk.

Tempting as a weakener, and the trap. But the conclusion is only that heavy rain makes quakes more likely, not that it usually causes one. Most rainy weeks being followed by no quake is compatible with that. It doesn't strengthen, and it doesn't really weaken either.
So? Whether rain-linked quakes are stronger has no bearing on whether rain makes quakes more likely in the first place.
Tempting, since it seems to show a general pattern. But it's the same kind of evidence with the same gap: without knowing how often heavy rains occur there, quakes after rain could be coincidence.
Irrelevant. Missing records before 1990 neither help nor hurt an argument built on data since 1990.

questions.stimulus: Two years ago, the 40 public schools in the state with the lowest average reading scores that year were each assigned a full-time reading coach for the following school year. In that year, average reading scores at those 40 schools rose by 11 points, while scores at the state's other schools rose by 2 points. So the coaches account for most of the improvement at the schools to which they were assigned.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: whether the reading coaches assigned to the 40 schools had previously taught in schools with low reading scores
whether the state spent more on the coaching program than it spends each year on new reading textbooks
whether the reading test given in the year the coaches worked at the schools was easier than the one given the year before
whether schools ranked near the bottom in reading one year typically gain far more than other schools the next year
whether some teachers at the 40 schools would have preferred additional classroom aides to a reading coach
questions.explanation: The 40 schools were picked because their scores were the lowest in one year, and an unusually bad year is often followed by a better one regardless of what happens in between. (D) asks whether bottom-ranked schools ordinarily jump the next year anyway: if so, much of the 11-point gain would have happened without coaches; if not, the coaches look responsible. (C) is the main trap: an easier test would raise scores, but it would raise them at every school, and the comparison with the other schools' 2-point gain already accounts for that. (A) is about the coaches' background, which doesn't separate the coaches from other causes.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The coaches account for most of the improvement at the 40 schools.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The 40 schools were chosen for having the lowest scores in one year; the next year, with coaches, their scores rose 11 points versus 2 points elsewhere.

breakdown.analysis: How were these schools picked? For having the worst scores in one particular year. Some of that year's low scores were probably bad luck: a rough cohort, a flu outbreak on test day. Schools picked at their low point tend to bounce back the next year with no help at all. It's like a golfer who signs up for lessons right after the worst round of his life; his next round will probably be better even if the lessons are useless. So we need to know how much bottom-ranked schools usually rebound by themselves. Many students choose (C), since an easier test would inflate scores. But every school took the same test, and the other schools gained only 2 points, so test difficulty can't explain the gap between them.

choices.note: Tempting. Experience in low-scoring schools makes the coaches sound effective, so a yes feels supportive. But it doesn't tell us whether the 11 points came from the coaches or would have come anyway. A no doesn't hurt the argument either.
Wrong dimension. Cost bears on whether the program is a good use of money, not on whether the coaches caused the gain.

Tempting, and the most common wrong pick. But all schools took the same test. An easier test would have lifted the other schools too, and they rose only 2 points. The argument's comparison already takes care of this.

CORRECT. Schools chosen for one year's low scores tend to rebound the next year on their own. If bottom schools typically gain far more than others the following year, much of the 11 points would have come without coaches. If they don't, the coaches look responsible. Two answers, two directions.
Irrelevant. Teachers' preferences say nothing about whether the coaches produced the improvement.

questions.stimulus: Paleontologist: In our region, fossils of small mammals are far scarcer in rock from the last million years of the Cretaceous period than in rock from the first million years of the period that followed. Admittedly, small bones are more easily destroyed before they can fossilize than large bones are, so fossil counts understate the abundance of small animals. Even so, the contrast shows that small mammals became much more abundant in the region once the Cretaceous ended.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the paleontologist's argument?
