choices: Small bones are more likely to be destroyed before fossilizing when they are buried by fast-moving water than when they settle in still water.
Many of the small-mammal species found in the later rock have no close relatives among those found in the earlier rock.
The rock from both periods formed from the same kind of sediment, laid down under similar conditions.
Some of the mammal species found in the later rock were considerably larger than any mammal found in the earlier rock.
Fossil counts understate the abundance of small reptiles and amphibians just as they do that of small mammals.
questions.explanation: The paleontologist concedes that small bones are often destroyed before they fossilize, then compares counts from two rock layers. That comparison works only if the destruction was about as severe in both layers; if the older rock formed under harsher conditions, small bones would be scarcer there even with no change in the animals. (C) secures that: similar sediment and conditions mean similar losses, so the contrast reflects real abundance. (A) is the main trap: it explains how destruction varies but doesn't say which layer had it worse. (B) shows new species, not more animals.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Small mammals became much more abundant in the region once the Cretaceous ended.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Small-mammal fossils are far scarcer in the last million years of Cretaceous rock than in the first million years of the following rock; small bones are often destroyed before fossilizing (conceded).

breakdown.analysis: The paleontologist admits the measuring tool is biased: small bones get lost. A biased tool can still compare two things fairly, but only if the bias is the same for both. What if the older rock formed in rough conditions that destroyed small bones, and the younger rock in calm ones that preserved them? Then the counts would differ even if the mammals didn't. It's like comparing two nets' catches when one net has bigger holes. We want an answer that says the 'nets' were the same. The key sounds like dry geology, so many students skip it. Most of them pick (A), which repeats the concession's idea about how bones get destroyed. But (A) never says which layer was laid down in which kind of water, so it can't tell us whether the losses were equal.

choices.note: Tempting, and the trap. It fleshes out the concession by saying when bones are destroyed. But it doesn't tell us whether either layer was laid down by fast or still water, so it can't show that the losses were the same in both.
Diversity isn't abundance. New kinds of small mammals could appear without their total numbers rising. It sounds like a mammal boom but doesn't support the conclusion as stated.

CORRECT. If both layers formed from the same kind of sediment under similar conditions, small bones were destroyed at about the same rate in each. The bias the paleontologist concedes then affects both counts alike, so the contrast reflects a real change in abundance.

Irrelevant to the count. The conclusion is about small mammals; larger mammals in the later rock tell us nothing about whether small ones became more abundant. It plays on a familiar 'mammals took over' story.
So? This widens the concession to other small animals. It doesn't tell us whether the bias was the same in the two layers, which is what the comparison needs.

passages.title: The Crystal Palace
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When the commission organizing the Great Exhibition of 1851 invited designs for a building to house it in London’s Hyde Park, it received nearly two hundred and fifty entries and adopted none of them. The design eventually chosen came from Joseph Paxton, who was not an architect but the head gardener at Chatsworth, the Duke of Devonshire’s estate, where he had spent years building glasshouses. His building, soon nicknamed the Crystal Palace, was assembled from cast-iron columns and girders, wooden glazing bars, and some three hundred thousand panes of glass, and it was completed in less than a year. Visitors marveled at its scale and its light, but many critics doubted that it belonged to the art of architecture at all, as distinct from the practical business of engineering.

What set the building apart was less its appearance than the way it was conceived. Paxton did not design a form and then work out how to construct it; he devised a small repertory of standard parts, each sized to a common grid, and the building was in effect whatever those parts, repeated, could enclose. Because every column, girder, and gutter was interchangeable with every other of its kind, components could be produced in quantity at separate works while the site was being prepared, and one section could be raised while another was still being glazed. Several parts served more than one purpose: the roof’s gutters, part of a ridge-and-furrow glazing system Paxton had developed for his glasshouses, drained into the hollow iron columns, which thus acted as downpipes as well as supports. The same logic made the building portable. After the exhibition closed, it was taken apart and re-erected, enlarged, at Sydenham in south London, where it stood until a fire destroyed it in 1936.

This may explain why later historians have found the Crystal Palace easier to admire than to place. Writers in the early twentieth century, searching for ancestors of an architecture of glass and steel, claimed it as a forerunner of modernism, and the resemblance is genuine. Yet the comparison rests on the building’s look, its transparent skin and exposed frame, and the look was arguably a by-product: glass and slender iron were simply what a structure raised quickly from light, factory-made parts would be made of. The building’s more lasting significance lies in the method that produced that look, the idea that a large structure could be specified as a set of standardized components to be manufactured elsewhere and assembled on site. That idea took generations to find wide application, but much modern construction, from prefabricated housing to the steel-framed office tower, now depends on it.

passages.title: Ford’s five-dollar day
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In January 1914 the Ford Motor Company announced that it would pay qualifying workers at its Highland Park plant five dollars for an eight-hour day, roughly twice what most had been earning for a nine-hour one. The announcement drew national attention, and thousands of job seekers gathered at the plant’s gates soon afterward. Why a firm that could already hire all the workers it wanted should choose to pay double has been debated ever since.

The explanation most often given by economists starts from a problem Ford had created for itself. The moving assembly line, introduced at Highland Park in 1913, had made the work faster and far more monotonous, and workers left in great numbers: during that year the company had to hire several times as many people as it employed at any one time, and absences were frequent. On this view the higher wage was a means of cutting these costs: a worker earning far more than he could get elsewhere had reason to stay, to show up, and to keep pace with the line, and the savings in hiring and training could offset much of what the wage cost.

Some labor historians have proposed a different motive. Organizers from the Industrial Workers of the World had been active in Detroit’s automobile plants during 1913, and a wage far above the prevailing rate, these historians argue, was the surest way to make a union unattractive to Ford’s workers. Others see the wage as an instrument of control. Much of the five dollars was paid as a share of profits, which a worker received only if investigators from the company’s Sociological Department, after visiting his home, judged his habits and household acceptable.

These accounts are not mutually exclusive, and the evidence usually cited in the debate does little to choose among them. Turnover and absenteeism at Highland Park fell sharply after the raise, but a wage that kept workers out of a union or made them more compliant would be expected to have much the same result. Nor does the crowd at the gates settle anything; it shows that the wage was well above what workers could earn elsewhere, which every account presupposes.

More telling is a feature of the plan that has drawn less notice than the home visits: new employees were not eligible for the higher pay until they had worked for the company for six months. A measure aimed chiefly at forestalling a union would have had little reason to withhold its benefits from recent hires, who could join a union as readily as anyone, and one aimed chiefly at reshaping workers’ habits could as easily have applied from the first day. A measure meant to reduce turnover, by contrast, would do exactly this, rewarding those who stayed and giving new hires a reason to stay long enough to qualify. The waiting period does not show that other motives were absent, but it suggests which problem the plan’s designers were most concerned to solve.

passages.title: The rule of lenity
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Under the rule of lenity, when a criminal statute is ambiguous, a court is to adopt the reading more favorable to the defendant. Few principles of statutory interpretation are older, and few are applied so unpredictably. American courts agree that lenity has some role to play but disagree about when it comes into play. Some invoke it whenever a statute’s words reasonably admit a narrower reading; others, including the United States Supreme Court in many of its opinions, reserve it for cases in which a grievous ambiguity remains after every other interpretive resource, including the statute’s evident purpose, has been exhausted. Under the second approach the rule seldom decides anything, since some purpose can almost always be found to tip the balance.

Much of this confusion, the legal scholar Teodor Vasko has argued, stems from the justification usually offered for the rule. Lenity is commonly defended on the ground of fair notice: no one should be punished for conduct that the law did not clearly forbid. But few people read criminal statutes before acting, and fewer still read the appellate opinions that settle what those statutes mean, so the notice the rule protects is largely notional. A rule resting on so thin a rationale invites courts to treat it as a tiebreaker of last resort, to be consulted only when nothing weightier is at hand.

Vasko proposes that the rule be grounded instead in a principle courts already accept for other purposes: that the power to define crimes belongs to the legislature. When a court resolves an ambiguity in a criminal statute by inferring what the statute was for, it decides for itself whether conduct the legislature did not clearly address shall be punished, which is just the decision that principle withholds from courts. So understood, lenity would apply after a court has read a statute’s text in light of its structure and its relation to other provisions, but before the court turns to purpose, because inferring a purpose in order to extend criminal liability is the very step the rule exists to forbid. The rule would also place the burden of clarity where it can be discharged: a legislature displeased by a lenient reading can amend the statute, whereas a defendant convicted under a harsh one has no comparable recourse.

The proposal has been attacked as an invitation to acquit the guilty on technicalities. The charge mistakes its effect. Lenity on Vasko’s account does not license a court to adopt any reading a statute’s words might bear, only to decline to extend liability beyond what text and structure establish, and the cost of the occasional lenient reading falls on a body equipped to remedy it. What the proposal would eliminate is not punishment for clearly forbidden conduct but the anomaly of a rule that is cited constantly and decides almost nothing.

passages.title: Benefit of clergy
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
For centuries English law made nearly every felony, from murder to the theft of goods worth more than a few pence, punishable by death. Yet many of those convicted of felony were never hanged, and one reason was a privilege known as benefit of clergy. Originally the privilege allowed a cleric accused of felony to be handed over to the church’s courts, which could not impose death. Because clerics were among the few who could read, the royal courts came to accept the ability to read a verse of scripture as proof of clerical status, and by the fifteenth century almost any man who could read could claim the privilege. The passage usually set was the opening verse of the fifty-first psalm, which came to be known as the neck verse.

Earlier legal historians treated the privilege as an embarrassment, a medieval anomaly that let literate criminals escape the gallows on a technicality. The historian Ruth Danbury has argued instead that by the sixteenth century it had become a deliberate instrument of mitigation. Parliament, she notes, withdrew the privilege from the gravest offenses while leaving it available for lesser ones, and a statute of 1489 provided that a layman could claim it only once, branding him on the thumb so that a second claim could be detected. The result, Danbury argues, was a graded system within a law that otherwise knew a single penalty: first offenders convicted of lesser felonies were spared, while repeat and grave offenders were not.

Whether anyone meant the privilege to work this way is a separate question, and on it Danbury’s evidence is thinner than her conclusion. The statutes she cites were passed piecemeal, over more than two centuries, by legislators responding to particular crimes; none of them describes the privilege as a scheme of graded punishment, and several were plainly aimed at closing what their framers regarded as abuses. A system of mitigation can arise from such measures without anyone having designed it. The privilege is perhaps better understood as an institution that acquired a function no one set out to give it, one that judges and juries learned to exploit because Parliament had trimmed the privilege, for reasons of its own, into a usable shape.

Nor did the mitigation fall evenly. So long as the reading test survived, the privilege favored those who could read, and an illiterate laborer could be hanged for a theft for which a literate defendant would be branded and released. Only when Parliament abolished the reading test in 1706 did the privilege become available to eligible offenders regardless of their schooling, and even then it remained unavailable for the many offenses that Parliament had by that time declared to be without benefit of clergy.

passages.title: Condensates and cellular function
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Some of the cell’s internal compartments, such as the nucleolus, where the components of ribosomes are assembled, have no membrane around them, and how such structures hold together and keep their contents distinct without a boundary was long unclear. In 2009 researchers studying embryos of the worm Caenorhabditis elegans reported that certain granules in them behave like liquid droplets, fusing when they touch and dissolving in one region of the cell while condensing in another. Since then many cell biologists have come to regard membraneless compartments as condensates: assemblies that form when particular proteins and RNA molecules separate from the surrounding fluid, much as oil separates from water, and so occupy a distinct region of the cell without any wall to enclose them.

The process depends on molecules that can bind weakly to many partners at once. Many condensate-forming proteins contain long stretches that lack a fixed three-dimensional shape and carry repeated short motifs, each able to stick briefly to a motif on another molecule. Below a threshold concentration such molecules remain dispersed; above it, the many weak contacts favor a separate phase in which the molecules are densely packed yet still free to move, exchanging continually with those outside. Because the threshold itself depends on conditions, a cell can create or dissolve a condensate without making or destroying any molecule: adding a phosphate group to a protein can weaken its contacts and dissolve a droplet, and a shift in temperature or acidity can make a protein condense where it had not. Proponents suggest that cells exploit this in two ways. A condensate can gather an enzyme and its substrates into a small volume and so speed a reaction, and it can sequester molecules, holding them out of action until conditions change.

Showing that a given condensate actually does either of these things inside a living cell has proved considerably harder than showing that the condensate forms at all. Many proteins have been made to form droplets in a test tube, often at concentrations far above those found in living cells, and droplets that appear only under such conditions may say more about the experiment than about the cell. The test that many researchers now regard as the most telling is genetic: alter a protein so that it can no longer condense while leaving intact its ability to bind its partners, then ask whether the cell loses the capacity attributed to the condensate. Where that test has been carried out, in yeast and in other organisms, the results have varied from protein to protein, which suggests that condensation is less a single key to cellular organization than a mechanism whose role must be established case by case.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: trace the influence that the Crystal Palace exerted on the architecture of glass and steel that emerged in the early twentieth century
argue that a celebrated structure mattered chiefly for the way it was conceived and assembled rather than for its look
explain why critics of the 1850s were mistaken to doubt that the Crystal Palace belonged to the art of architecture
show how a gardener with no architectural training came to design the building for the Great Exhibition of 1851
contrast the methods Paxton used in his glasshouses at Chatsworth with those he used in designing the Crystal Palace
questions.explanation: The passage introduces the Crystal Palace, says in the second paragraph that what set it apart was 'less its appearance than the way it was conceived,' and closes by locating its 'more lasting significance' in that method. B says this in other words. A is the trap: the passage grants that the resemblance to modernism is genuine but never traces any influence, and it says the comparison rests on the wrong feature. D describes only the first paragraph's background.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the whole passage is trying to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Mostly the first sentence of the second paragraph and the second half of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: This is a spotlight passage: a famous building, then the author's claim about why it matters. The thesis appears twice: the building's distinction lay 'less [in] its appearance than the way it was conceived,' and its 'more lasting significance lies in the method.' We need an answer about method over look. Watch for answers that pick up the modernism discussion, which the author mentions only to redirect it.

choices.note: Tempting, because the third paragraph mentions early twentieth-century glass-and-steel architecture. But the author never says the Crystal Palace influenced it; later writers 'claimed it as a forerunner,' and the author says that comparison rests on the less important feature.

CORRECT. 'The way it was conceived and assembled' paraphrases the author's 'method'; 'rather than for its look' matches 'less its appearance.' That is the claim both the second and third paragraphs build toward.
The author reports that many critics doubted it was architecture but never says they were wrong. The passage is about why the building matters, not about whether it counts as architecture.
That Paxton was a gardener is background from the first paragraph. The passage doesn't explain how he came to be chosen, and it isn't the point.
The glasshouses come up only as the source of the ridge-and-furrow roof. Nothing contrasts the two sets of methods; the passage implies continuity, not contrast.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the hollow iron columns of the Crystal Palace
choices: were manufactured to a different standard from the girders so that the two could be produced at separate works
formed part of a glazing system that Paxton had first worked out for his glasshouses at Chatsworth
were the only components of the building that were designed to serve more than one purpose
were enlarged when the building was taken apart and re-erected at Sydenham after the exhibition
carried off water collected by the roof in addition to holding the structure up
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the roof's gutters 'drained into the hollow iron columns, which thus acted as downpipes as well as supports.' E restates that without the passage's words. B is the near-miss: the ridge-and-furrow glazing system came from the glasshouses, but the passage ties that system to the roof and gutters, not to the columns. C overstates 'several parts served more than one purpose.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the columns.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Locate the sentence: gutters 'drained into the hollow iron columns, which thus acted as downpipes as well as supports.' So the columns did two jobs: drainage and support. The right answer will say that in different words. Expect traps that move a nearby detail onto the columns.

choices.note: The passage says the opposite kind of thing: every column, girder and gutter was interchangeable with others of its kind, and parts were made at separate works. Nothing says columns and girders followed different standards.

Tempting, because it's the same sentence. But the ridge-and-furrow system is a roof-glazing system; the passage says the gutters belonged to it and drained into the columns. The columns aren't said to be part of it, let alone to come from Chatsworth.
Too strong. 'Several parts served more than one purpose'; the columns are the example given, not the only case.
The building as a whole was 'enlarged' at Sydenham. Nothing says the columns themselves were made bigger.
CORRECT. 'Downpipes as well as supports' = carrying off rainwater from the roof and holding the building up.

questions.stem: By saying that later historians have found the Crystal Palace “easier to admire than to place” (first sentence of the third paragraph), the author most probably means that these historians
choices: have had difficulty fitting the building into an account of architecture’s development, however much they esteem it
have praised the building while disagreeing about whether Paxton or the firms that made its parts deserve the credit
have valued the building chiefly for its appearance rather than for the method by which it was built
have regarded the building as a forerunner of modernism while doubting that it influenced any later building
have found its achievement easier to appreciate than that of the more conventional designs rejected in 1850
questions.explanation: 'Place' here means locate within architectural history: the next sentence shows writers trying to fit it in as 'a forerunner of modernism,' and the author says that placement rests on the wrong feature. A captures admiration plus difficulty classifying. C is the near-miss: it is the author's complaint about the modernist comparison, but it describes what historians valued, not what 'place' means. D invents a doubt about influence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what 'easier to admire than to place' means in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first two sentences of the third paragraph, and the end of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: 'Admire' is easy: they like it. 'Place' is the key word. Read on: writers 'claimed it as a forerunner of modernism,' that is, they tried to place it in a lineage, and the author thinks they placed it by the wrong feature. Remember too that critics in 1851 doubted it was architecture at all. So 'place' = situate it in the story of architecture. Prephrase: they admire it but struggle to say where it belongs.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Fitting the building into an account of architecture's development' is what 'place' means here, and 'however much they esteem it' is the 'admire' half.
Nothing in the passage raises a dispute about credit between Paxton and the manufacturers. This reads 'place' as assigning credit, which the passage never discusses.

Tempting, because the author does say the modernist comparison rests on the building's look. But that's a criticism of one placement, not the meaning of 'easier to admire than to place.' The phrase is about difficulty classifying, not about which feature they valued.
Half right: they did regard it as a forerunner. But the passage never says historians doubted it influenced later buildings; the influence question doesn't come up.
The rejected designs appear only in the first paragraph, and no historian compares them with Paxton's. The phrase compares admiring with placing, not this building with others.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the building was taken apart and re-erected at Sydenham (end of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that the building was more highly regarded after the exhibition than it had been while the exhibition was open
show that the building’s later history bore out the doubts of critics who denied that it was a work of architecture
indicate that the building’s appearance was a by-product of the light, factory-made parts from which it was raised
illustrate a consequence of the building’s having been conceived as an assembly of interchangeable standard parts
explain how later historians were able to study the building closely enough to claim it as a forerunner of modernism
questions.explanation: The Sydenham move is introduced with 'The same logic made the building portable': a structure made of interchangeable bolted parts could be dismantled and rebuilt. D names that role. C is tempting because it borrows the third paragraph's 'by-product' and 'factory-made parts,' but the move illustrates portability, a result of the method, not anything about the building's look.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the move to Sydenham.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence right before it: 'The same logic made the building portable.' 'The same logic' is the standard-parts method the paragraph has been describing. So the move is an example of what that method made possible. We want an answer like: it shows a result of building from interchangeable parts.

choices.note: Nothing compares how the building was regarded before and after the exhibition. The move is about how it was built, not its reputation.
The critics' doubts are mentioned in the first paragraph, and nothing about Sydenham bears on them. The move shows a strength of the method, not a failing.
Tempting, because it uses the third paragraph's language. But the Sydenham sentence comes after 'the same logic made the building portable'; it illustrates portability, not anything about the look.
CORRECT. 'The same logic' is the standard-parts method; being dismantled and rebuilt elsewhere is a consequence of that method.
The passage never connects the move to how historians studied the building. This invents a link between two separate parts of the passage.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author’s suggestion about the building’s appearance in the third paragraph?
choices: The writers who later claimed the building as a forerunner of modernism knew it mainly from photographs taken after its move to Sydenham.
Visitors to the exhibition wrote far more often about the building’s light and transparency than about the speed with which it had been raised.
Paxton rejected a cheaper roofing material that could have been made and installed just as quickly, on the ground that it would darken the interior.
The iron members of the building were more slender than those of most iron-framed buildings of the period, chiefly because the glass they carried was so light.
Within a few decades of 1851, buildings assembled from standardized, factory-made components had become common in several countries.
questions.explanation: The author suggests the building's look was 'arguably a by-product': glass and slender iron were 'simply what a structure raised quickly from light, factory-made parts would be made of.' C shows Paxton choosing glass over an equally quick, cheaper material for the sake of light, so the look was an aim, not a by-product. E is the main trap: it does contradict the passage, but it attacks the claim that the method 'took generations' to spread, not the claim about the look. B concerns visitors' reactions, not why the look came about.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most undermines the claim that the building's look was a by-product of its method.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: First pin down the claim. The author says the transparent skin and exposed frame were 'arguably a by-product': glass and thin iron were simply what you'd get from a quickly built structure of light factory parts. So the look wasn't a goal. To weaken that, show the look was chosen for its own sake: some option that served speed and economy just as well was turned down because of how it would look. Beware of answers that hit a different sentence of the same paragraph.

choices.note: Irrelevant. This might embarrass the modernist writers, but the author's claim is about why the building looked as it did, not about how anyone later saw it.
Tempting: it shows the look mattered to visitors. But a by-product can impress people. What visitors noticed tells us nothing about whether the look was an aim of the design.

CORRECT. If glass was chosen over a cheaper material that was just as fast to make and install, and chosen for the light, then the look wasn't simply what the method produced; it was sought. That cuts directly against 'by-product.'
This strengthens the author. It says the slender frame followed from the light materials, which fits the idea that the look fell out of the method.

Tempting, because it does contradict the passage, which says the idea 'took generations to find wide application.' But that's a different claim. The question asks about the suggestion concerning the building's appearance.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: The critics of the 1850s who doubted that the Crystal Palace was architecture were proved wrong when its method was taken up in later construction.
The writers who claimed the Crystal Palace as a forerunner of modernism were mistaken in seeing any real resemblance between it and later buildings.
The Crystal Palace would not have influenced later construction had it not been dismantled and re-erected after the exhibition.
The Crystal Palace was a greater achievement than any of the glass and steel buildings of the early twentieth century that resemble it.
A building that reproduced the Crystal Palace’s transparent skin and exposed frame by conventional means would lack what most distinguished the original.
questions.explanation: Combine the second paragraph (the building's distinction was 'less its appearance than the way it was conceived') with the third (its 'more lasting significance lies in the method'). A building that copies only the look while being built conventionally would lack exactly that. B is the strongest trap for readers who expect the author to reject the modernists outright; the author says 'the resemblance is genuine.' A credits the author with a verdict on the 1850s critics that is never given.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's views support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph and the last three sentences of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so test each choice against two things the author commits to: (1) what distinguished the building was the method (standard parts, made elsewhere, assembled), not the look; (2) the modernist resemblance is real but rests on the look. Watch for choices that turn the author's redirection into a rejection, or that add a verdict the author never gives.

choices.note: The author reports the critics' doubts but never says they were wrong, and later use of the method wouldn't settle whether the building was 'architecture' anyway.
Tempting if you expect the author to reject the modernists. But the author says 'the resemblance is genuine'; the complaint is that the comparison rests on the less important feature.
Nothing links the Sydenham move to later influence. The move illustrates portability; it isn't offered as a cause of anything.
No comparison of greatness appears anywhere. The author says only where the building's significance lies.

CORRECT. The author locates the building's distinction in its method, not its appearance. A copy of the look built by conventional means would have the less important feature and lack the more important one.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Ford’s five-dollar day was adopted primarily to keep a union out of the Highland Park plant, though it also reduced turnover and absenteeism there.
The sharp fall in turnover and absenteeism at Highland Park after 1914 shows that Ford’s higher wage paid for itself, as efficiency-wage reasoning predicts.
While the evidence usually cited cannot settle why Ford doubled pay, the plan’s terms point to turnover as the company’s main concern.
Because several motives may have been at work, it is impossible to determine why the Ford Motor Company adopted the five-dollar day in 1914.
The five-dollar day was less a wage than an instrument of control, since much of the money depended on investigators’ judgments of workers’ private lives.
questions.explanation: The passage lays out three explanations, says the usual evidence 'does little to choose among them,' then argues that the six-month waiting period 'suggests which problem the plan's designers were most concerned to solve': turnover. C has both halves, with the author's hedge ('point to'). D is the near-miss: the author grants the motives aren't exclusive but does not say the question is unanswerable; the last paragraph offers a way to favor one. A and E are rival explanations the author reports but doesn't adopt.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the author's main conclusion.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth and fifth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Phenomenon, then competing explanations, then an evaluation. Where does the author land? Paragraph 4: the usual evidence can't decide. Paragraph 5: a neglected feature, the six-month wait, favors the turnover explanation, though it doesn't rule out the others. So the main point has two parts: the common evidence is inconclusive, but the plan's terms favor turnover.

choices.note: This is the labor historians' view from the third paragraph. The author argues that the waiting period fits a union motive poorly.

The author says the fall in turnover would be expected under every explanation, so it can't show what the efficiency view predicts over the others. And the passage never says the wage paid for itself.
CORRECT. 'Evidence usually cited cannot settle' = the fourth paragraph; 'the plan's terms point to turnover' = the fifth. 'Point to' keeps the author's caution ('suggests').
Tempting, because the author does say the accounts aren't mutually exclusive. But the author then argues that one feature tips the balance. 'Impossible to determine' contradicts the final paragraph.
This is the control explanation from the third paragraph, stated as fact. The author treats it as one account among three and argues the waiting period fits it less well.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in 1913 the Ford Motor Company
choices: had to keep replacing workers so often that its hiring over the year far exceeded the size of its workforce
began paying a share of its profits to workers whose households were judged acceptable by its investigators
faced a strike at Highland Park organized by the Industrial Workers of the World in protest against the assembly line
required new employees to work for six months before they received any wage above the prevailing rate
paid its workers more for a nine-hour day than most of its competitors paid for an eight-hour one
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that in 1913 'the company had to hire several times as many people as it employed at any one time.' A paraphrases that. C is the near-miss: the passage says IWW organizers were 'active in Detroit's automobile plants during 1913,' not that they struck Ford. B and D describe the 1914 plan, not 1913.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about Ford in 1913.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second sentence of the second paragraph; also the first sentence of the third.

breakdown.analysis: Two sentences mention 1913: the assembly line arrived and turnover soared (paragraph 2), and IWW organizers were active in Detroit (paragraph 3). The answer will paraphrase one of them. Watch the dates: the profit-sharing, home visits and six-month rule all belong to the 1914 plan.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Hire several times as many people as it employed at any one time' = hiring over the year far exceeded the workforce.
The profit-sharing and home visits were part of the plan announced in January 1914, not 1913.
Tempting, because the IWW was active in 1913. But the passage says only that organizers were 'active in Detroit's automobile plants.' No strike at Ford is mentioned.
The six-month rule was part of the 1914 plan, and it governed eligibility for the higher pay, not for 'any wage above the prevailing rate' before then.
The passage never compares Ford's pre-1914 pay with competitors'. It says only that the new wage was roughly double what most Ford workers had earned.

questions.stem: The author’s discussion of the crowd of job seekers in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to
choices: support the claim in the first paragraph that Ford could already hire all the workers it wanted
dismiss a piece of evidence as unable to favor any one of the proposed explanations over the others
suggest that the new wage was not in fact far above what workers could earn at other plants
show that the explanation most often given by economists rests on an assumption the other explanations reject
indicate that public reaction to the five-dollar day was more favorable than the company had expected
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the crowd 'shows that the wage was well above what workers could earn elsewhere, which every account presupposes.' Evidence that every account assumes can't favor one of them, so the author sets it aside: B. A is tempting because the crowd does bear on that first-paragraph remark, but in the fourth paragraph the author's point is that the crowd is useless for choosing among explanations. D reverses 'every account presupposes.'

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the crowd does in the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence: 'Nor does the crowd at the gates settle anything; it shows that the wage was well above what workers could earn elsewhere, which every account presupposes.' So the crowd proves something all three explanations already take for granted. That makes it worthless as a tiebreaker. Prephrase: it's set aside as evidence that can't discriminate.

choices.note: Tempting, because a crowd of applicants does suggest Ford could hire whom it wanted. But that isn't the role in the fourth paragraph, which is about whether evidence can decide among the explanations.
CORRECT. Evidence that 'every account presupposes' can't count for one account over another. That's why the author says it doesn't 'settle anything.'
This reverses the passage. The crowd shows the wage was well above what workers could earn elsewhere.
The author says every account presupposes what the crowd shows, so no explanation rejects it.
Neither public reaction nor the company's expectations come up in the fourth paragraph. The crowd is treated as evidence about the wage, not about public opinion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, those who regard the five-dollar day as an instrument of control point to the fact that
choices: new employees had to work for the company for six months before they became eligible for the higher pay
a wage far above the prevailing rate made a union unattractive to workers who might otherwise have joined one
the moving assembly line had made work at Highland Park both faster and far more monotonous than before
a large part of the money depended on the company’s approval of how a worker lived outside the plant
investigators from the Sociological Department visited the homes of workers who had left the company
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives the control view's evidence: much of the five dollars was a profit share paid 'only if investigators ... after visiting his home, judged his habits and household acceptable.' D paraphrases that. A is the strongest trap: the six-month rule is the author's own evidence in the fifth paragraph, and the author uses it against the control view. B is the union historians' argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the evidence the passage attributes to the control explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three explanations, three bodies of evidence: turnover (economists), IWW activity (labor historians), home visits tied to profit-sharing (control). The control evidence is that much of the pay was conditional on investigators approving the worker's habits and household. Watch for evidence that belongs to someone else.

choices.note: Tempting, because it's a real feature of the plan. But the author raises it in the fifth paragraph, and argues that it fits the control explanation poorly, since such a measure 'could as easily have applied from the first day.'
This is the reasoning of the labor historians who stress the union, not of the control camp.
This is the economists' starting point in the second paragraph.
CORRECT. The profit share depended on investigators judging a worker's 'habits and household acceptable,' that is, on approval of his life outside the plant.
The investigators visited workers' homes to decide whether they qualified for the profit share. Nothing says they visited former workers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A business decision is described; an explanation of it is presented; two objections to that explanation are raised; the explanation is defended by appeal to a feature of the decision that the objections overlook.
A business decision is described; three explanations of it are presented; each is shown to conflict with some of the evidence; a combination of the three is proposed as the best account.
A business decision and the reaction to it are described; two explanations are compared; the evidence is found to favor neither; a third explanation is offered in place of both.
A business decision is described; three explanations are presented; the most widely accepted is rejected on the basis of new evidence; one of the remaining two is shown to be better supported.

A business decision is described; three explanations of it are presented; the evidence commonly cited is shown not to discriminate among them; a less noticed feature of the decision is offered as favoring one.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: Ford doubles pay. Paragraphs 2–3: three explanations (turnover, union, control). Paragraph 4: the usual evidence doesn't choose among them. Paragraph 5: the overlooked six-month rule favors turnover. That is E. A is the near-miss: it treats the union and control accounts as 'objections' to the economists' view, but the passage presents them as rival explanations, which the author says are not even mutually exclusive. D reverses the outcome: the economists' account is the one favored.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the passage's paragraph-by-paragraph structure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole passage; the first sentence of each paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Outline it first. (1) The decision. (2) Economists: turnover. (3) Historians: union; others: control. (4) The usual evidence fits all three. (5) The six-month wait favors turnover. One wrong element kills an organization answer, so check every clause.

choices.note: Tempting: its last clause sounds like paragraph 5. But the third paragraph offers 'a different motive' and another view; these are rival explanations, not objections to the first, and paragraph 5 doesn't defend against anything the alternatives 'overlook.'
No explanation is shown to conflict with the evidence; the problem in paragraph 4 is that the evidence fits all of them. And the author favors one account rather than proposing a combination.
There are three explanations, not two, and the evidence that fails to discriminate is followed by evidence favoring one of them, not by a new explanation.
The most widely given explanation, the economists', is the one the author ends up favoring. Nothing is rejected.
CORRECT. Each clause matches a stage: decision, three accounts, inconclusive common evidence, and the neglected six-month rule tipping the balance.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?
choices: Had the higher pay been offered from a worker’s first day, the plan’s terms would give less reason to single out turnover as the problem it chiefly addressed.
The fall in turnover after 1914 shows that the higher wage recovered most of what it cost, even if it does not reveal why the wage was adopted.
The home visits by the Sociological Department’s investigators were intended chiefly to identify workers who were likely to join a union.
The six-month waiting period shows that Ford’s managers were not concerned about the possibility that their workers would join a union.
The crowd at the gates makes the economists’ explanation more plausible than the explanation that emphasizes control of workers’ habits.
questions.explanation: The author's case for turnover rests on the waiting period: a turnover measure 'would do exactly this,' while the other aims 'could as easily have applied from the first day.' Remove the waiting period and that discriminating evidence disappears, so A follows, with the author's own caution. D is the strongest trap; the author explicitly says the waiting period 'does not show that other motives were absent.' B adds a cost-recovery claim the passage never makes, and E contradicts the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the author's reasoning supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fifth paragraph, read with the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Ask what the author's argument depends on. The turnover explanation wins only because of one feature, the six-month wait, which the other motives give 'little reason' to include. So imagine that feature gone: the plan would look the same under all three accounts, and the author's reason for singling out turnover would vanish. That's a counterfactual, phrased cautiously. Hard to spot because it doesn't echo any one sentence.

choices.note: CORRECT. The waiting period is the author's only evidence that separates turnover from the other motives. Without it, the terms would no longer point to turnover in particular; the fourth paragraph already says the rest of the evidence fits all three.

The second paragraph says savings 'could offset much of what the wage cost,' as part of the economists' view. The author never says the fall in turnover shows the wage paid for itself, and in the fourth paragraph says that fall fits every account.
The passage ties the home visits to the control explanation, not the union one. Nothing suggests they were aimed at finding union sympathizers.

Tempting, because the author says the waiting period fits a union motive poorly. But that's too strong: the author adds that it 'does not show that other motives were absent.' Weaker evidence for a motive isn't proof that managers didn't care.
The fourth paragraph says the crowd shows only what 'every account presupposes,' so it can't favor the economists over anyone.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The rule of lenity should be abandoned, because the fair notice it is said to protect is largely a fiction and courts apply it unpredictably.
Courts should invoke the rule of lenity only when a grievous ambiguity remains after every other interpretive resource has been exhausted.
Although a proposal to reground lenity would make the rule more predictable, it would allow too many guilty defendants to escape conviction.
Grounding lenity in the legislature’s sole power to define crimes, rather than in fair notice, would give the rule a definite, earlier place in courts’ reasoning.
The rule of lenity is better defended by the principle of fair notice than by the principle that only the legislature may define crimes.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out a problem (lenity is applied unpredictably), traces it to the thin fair-notice rationale, presents Vasko's remedy (ground the rule in legislative power, so it applies before purpose), and defends that remedy against its main objection. D states the remedy and its payoff. A misreads the critique of fair notice as a call to abandon the rule; B is the Supreme Court approach the passage criticizes; C is the objection the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the passage's main point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph and the whole fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Problem → diagnosis → proposed solution → defense of the solution. The author sides with the proposal: the objection 'mistakes its effect.' So the main point is the proposal and what it achieves: base lenity on legislative primacy, which fixes where it applies (after text and structure, before purpose).

choices.note: Vasko criticizes the fair-notice rationale, not the rule. His proposal keeps lenity and gives it a stronger footing.
This is the Supreme Court approach in the first paragraph, which the passage says makes the rule decide almost nothing.
This is the objection from the fourth paragraph, which the author says 'mistakes its effect.' The author endorses the proposal without this reservation.

CORRECT. 'Legislature's sole power to define crimes' = the principle in the third paragraph; 'definite, earlier place' = after text and structure but before purpose. That's the proposal the author defends.
This reverses the passage, which calls fair notice 'so thin a rationale' and favors the legislative-power grounding.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that Vasko holds that the fair-notice rationale contributes to the unpredictable application of lenity chiefly because that rationale
choices: conflicts with the principle that the power to define crimes belongs to the legislature rather than to the courts
requires a court to determine whether a particular defendant actually read the statute before acting
is too weak to give courts a reason to apply the rule ahead of any other interpretive consideration
has been rejected by the Supreme Court in favor of a standard based on grievous ambiguity
leads some courts to apply the rule whenever a statute’s words reasonably admit a narrower reading
questions.explanation: Vasko says 'a rule resting on so thin a rationale invites courts to treat it as a tiebreaker of last resort, to be consulted only when nothing weightier is at hand' (end of the second paragraph). A weak rationale gives courts no reason to put lenity first: C. E is the near-miss; it describes one side of the inconsistency, but Vasko's complaint is that the weak rationale pushes lenity to the end, not that it makes courts apply it broadly. A borrows the third paragraph's principle in a relation the passage never states.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out why, on Vasko's view, the fair-notice rationale makes lenity unpredictable.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last two sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Vasko's chain: (1) fair notice is mostly fictional, because few people read statutes; (2) a rule with 'so thin a rationale' gets treated as a last-resort tiebreaker. The answer should say the rationale is too weak to justify using lenity early. Note it's not stated in those words, so it's an inference.

choices.note: Tempting because it uses the third paragraph's principle. But Vasko never says fair notice conflicts with legislative power; he offers that principle as a better foundation, not as a rival the old one contradicts.
Nothing says the rationale requires courts to check whether a defendant read the statute. Vasko's point is that few people do, which makes the protected notice 'largely notional.'
CORRECT. 'So thin a rationale' that it gets used only 'when nothing weightier is at hand' = too weak to justify putting the rule ahead of other considerations.
The passage never says the Supreme Court rejected fair notice. It describes the Court's last-resort approach, which Vasko attributes to the weakness of the rationale.
Tempting: some courts do this, per the first paragraph. But Vasko blames the thin rationale for the last-resort treatment, not for broad application.

questions.stem: The primary function of the fourth paragraph is to
choices: respond to a criticism of the proposal described in the third paragraph by clarifying what that proposal would and would not permit
concede that the proposal described in the third paragraph carries a cost that its advocates have so far failed to acknowledge
offer further evidence that the fair-notice rationale has led courts to apply the rule of lenity unpredictably
propose a modification of Vasko’s proposal that would meet the objections raised against it by its critics
explain why the Supreme Court has reserved the rule of lenity for cases in which a grievous ambiguity remains
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph states the objection that the proposal invites acquittals 'on technicalities,' says the charge 'mistakes its effect,' and explains that lenity would only stop courts from extending liability beyond text and structure. That is A. B is tempting because the paragraph mentions 'the cost of the occasional lenient reading,' but the author treats that cost as acceptable and places it on the legislature; it isn't a concession that advocates overlooked anything.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the role of the last paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Objection, then reply. The objection: acquittals on technicalities. The reply: that misreads what the proposal does; lenity only refuses to stretch liability past text and structure, and the legislature can fix lenient readings. So the paragraph defends the proposal by clarifying its scope.

choices.note: CORRECT. The paragraph answers the 'technicalities' charge by spelling out what lenity on Vasko's account allows (declining to extend liability) and doesn't (adopting any reading the words might bear).
Tempting, because a cost is mentioned. But the author mentions it to show it lands on a body that can remedy it, as part of the defense. Nothing suggests advocates failed to acknowledge it.
The fair-notice rationale is discussed in the second paragraph; the fourth doesn't return to it.
The paragraph defends the proposal as it stands. No change to it is suggested.
The Supreme Court's approach appears in the first paragraph. The fourth paragraph doesn't explain it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles most closely underlies the reasoning in the last sentence of the third paragraph?
choices: Where the law is uncertain, the uncertainty should be resolved in favor of whichever party would suffer the greater harm from an adverse resolution.
When an uncertainty in the law must be resolved against one of two parties, it should be resolved against the party able to remove it for the future.
A party responsible for creating an ambiguity in a legal text should not be permitted to benefit from that ambiguity in a later dispute.
Courts should defer to the legislature’s judgment about which reading of a statute best serves the purpose the statute was meant to achieve.
No one should be punished for conduct that the law did not clearly forbid at the time the conduct took place.
questions.explanation: The sentence says lenity 'would also place the burden of clarity where it can be discharged': a legislature displeased by a lenient reading 'can amend the statute,' while a convicted defendant 'has no comparable recourse.' The principle is about which side can cure the problem: B. A is the main trap; the defendant surely suffers more, but the sentence's reason is ability to remedy, not size of harm. C sounds right because legislatures draft statutes, but the sentence never mentions who created the ambiguity. E is the fair-notice rationale the passage calls thin.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the principle behind the 'burden of clarity' sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Read the reason given: the legislature 'can amend'; the defendant 'has no comparable recourse.' So the burden goes to the party that can fix things. A principle answer must use that same reason. Traps will offer other plausible reasons for siding with the defendant: greater harm, fault for drafting, fair notice.

choices.note: Tempting, because a defendant facing prison does stand to lose more. But the sentence never weighs harms; it turns on who 'can amend' and who 'has no comparable recourse.'
CORRECT. 'Place the burden of clarity where it can be discharged' = resolve the uncertainty against the party that can fix it going forward, the legislature.

Tempting, since legislatures write statutes. But the sentence's reason is the legislature's power to amend, not its responsibility for the ambiguity. This is a fault-based principle; the passage's is capacity-based.
This is close to the opposite of the proposal, which forbids courts to use inferred purpose to extend liability.
This is the fair-notice rationale, which the second paragraph calls 'so thin' and which the proposal replaces.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Vasko’s proposal is most accurately described as
choices: cautious approval, tempered by doubt about whether courts could reliably separate reading a statute’s structure from inferring its purpose
reluctant acceptance, on the ground that although it rests on a weak rationale it is still preferable to the Supreme Court’s approach
skepticism, since the proposal would leave the rule of lenity as unpredictable as reliance on fair notice has already made it
neutrality, since the passage presents both the proposal and the chief criticism of it without choosing between them
approval, combined with the view that the main objection to it misunderstands what it would actually do
questions.explanation: In the fourth paragraph the author says the 'technicalities' charge 'mistakes its effect' and closes by praising what the proposal would eliminate. No reservation appears, so E fits. A is the trap for readers who expect every LSAT author to hedge: it invents a doubt the passage never raises. D ignores that the author answers the criticism. B attributes a weak rationale to the proposal, when the weak rationale is the one it replaces.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Characterize the author's attitude toward the proposal.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Look for the author's own voice. It appears in the fourth paragraph: the objection 'mistakes its effect,' and the proposal would eliminate 'the anomaly of a rule that is cited constantly and decides almost nothing.' That's endorsement. Is there any reservation? Search the passage: none. Don't add a hedge just because LSAT authors often have one.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'cautious approval' is a common LSAT key. But the passage never doubts that courts can separate structure from purpose. The reservation is invented.
The proposal doesn't rest on a weak rationale; it replaces the weak one (fair notice) with legislative power. And 'reluctant' doesn't fit an author who rebuts the main objection.
The author says the proposal would end the anomaly of a rule that decides nothing, the opposite of leaving it unpredictable.
The author does choose: the criticism 'mistakes its effect.' That isn't neutral.
CORRECT. The author endorses the proposal and says its main objection 'mistakes its effect,' which is misunderstanding what it would do.

questions.stem: Suppose that a criminal statute’s words admit two readings, that another provision of the same statute makes sense only if the harsher reading is adopted, and that the statute’s evident purpose also favors the harsher reading. Based on the passage, a court following Vasko’s proposal would most likely
choices: adopt the harsher reading, but only because the statute’s purpose may be consulted once lenity has been considered and found inapplicable
adopt the more lenient reading, since inferring a statute’s purpose in order to extend criminal liability is the step lenity exists to forbid
adopt the harsher reading, since the statute’s structure resolves the ambiguity before any question of its purpose arises
adopt the more lenient reading, since the defendant cannot have received fair notice of what the harsher reading forbids
decline to apply the statute until the legislature has made clear which of the two readings it intended
questions.explanation: Under Vasko's proposal, lenity 'would apply after a court has read a statute's text in light of its structure and its relation to other provisions, but before the court turns to purpose.' Here another provision of the same statute settles the matter, so no ambiguity is left for lenity, and purpose never comes into it: C. B is the strongest trap: it applies the rule's ban on purpose correctly but forgets that structure is consulted first. A reaches the right result for the wrong reason, describing the last-resort approach Vasko rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Vasko's sequence to a new statute.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Vasko's order of operations: (1) text read with structure and related provisions; (2) if still ambiguous, lenity; (3) purpose never gets used to extend liability. In the case, step 1 already resolves it: the related provision works only on the harsher reading. So lenity is never reached. The purpose fact is a decoy that pulls you toward lenity's ban on purpose.

choices.note: Right result, wrong reason. Under Vasko's proposal purpose is never used to extend liability, and lenity isn't 'considered and found inapplicable' first. This describes something closer to the last-resort approach.
Tempting: it quotes the core of the proposal. But lenity comes in only if the ambiguity survives text and structure. Here a related provision resolves it, so the ban on purpose never matters.

CORRECT. The other provision is the statute's structure and 'relation to other provisions,' which Vasko consults before lenity. It settles the ambiguity, so the harsher reading stands without any appeal to purpose.
Fair notice is the rationale Vasko rejects, and lenity on his account is triggered by ambiguity remaining after text and structure, not by lack of notice.
Nothing in the passage permits a court to refuse to decide. And the ambiguity is resolved here anyway.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Benefit of clergy was a medieval anomaly that let literate criminals escape the gallows on a technicality until Parliament abolished the reading test in 1706.
By the sixteenth century Parliament had deliberately reshaped benefit of clergy into a graded system that spared first offenders convicted of lesser felonies.
Benefit of clergy, originally a protection for clerics, was extended by means of a reading test to almost any man who could read.
Danbury misdescribes how benefit of clergy worked in practice, though she is right that the statutes restricting it were aimed at abuses.
The privilege did come to soften a harsh law, though apparently not by design, and for long its relief depended on a skill many lacked.
questions.explanation: The author accepts that the privilege came to work as mitigation (second paragraph), doubts that anyone designed it so (third), and adds that the relief was uneven while the reading test lasted (fourth). E carries all three, keeping the author's tentativeness ('perhaps better understood') in 'apparently.' B is Danbury's view, which the author rejects in its claim of deliberate design. D reverses what the author accepts and doubts. C is only the first paragraph's background.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify the main point of the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third and fourth paragraphs, read against Danbury's view in the second.

breakdown.analysis: Separate the views. Earlier historians: an embarrassing anomaly. Danbury: a deliberate instrument of mitigation. Author: it did mitigate, but nobody clearly designed it to, and the mitigation favored the literate. A main point answer needs the author's position, not Danbury's or the earlier historians'.

choices.note: This is the earlier historians' view. The author agrees the privilege functioned as mitigation, which is more than a technicality.
This is Danbury's view. The author's main disagreement is with 'deliberately': no statute 'describes the privilege as a scheme of graded punishment.'
True, but it's the first paragraph's background, not the point the passage argues.
Reversed. The author accepts Danbury's account of how the privilege worked and doubts her account of its purpose. The abuse-closing statutes are the author's evidence, not Danbury's.

CORRECT. 'Did come to soften a harsh law' = it functioned as mitigation; 'apparently not by design' = the third paragraph's doubt about intent; 'depended on a skill many lacked' = the reading test in the fourth.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the statute of 1489
choices: withdrew benefit of clergy from the gravest felonies while leaving it available for lesser ones
described benefit of clergy as one element of a scheme of graded punishment for felony
required that every person who claimed benefit of clergy be branded on the thumb
provided a means of identifying laymen who had already claimed the privilege once
was one of the statutes that the author says were plainly aimed at closing abuses
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the 1489 statute let a layman claim the privilege only once, 'branding him on the thumb so that a second claim could be detected.' D paraphrases that purpose. C is the near-miss: branding applied to laymen, not to 'every person' who claimed the privilege, clerics included. A describes a separate set of measures in the same sentence; E credits the author with a claim about this statute that the passage never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the 1489 statute.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence packs in two things Parliament did: it withdrew the privilege from grave offenses (no date given), and a statute of 1489 limited laymen to one claim, with branding to detect a second. Keep them apart, and notice the word 'layman.'

choices.note: This is the other measure in the same sentence, which the passage doesn't date or attribute to the 1489 statute.
The author says none of the statutes Danbury cites describes the privilege this way.
Tempting, but too broad. The statute concerned laymen: 'a layman could claim it only once, branding him.' Clerics aren't covered by 'him.'
CORRECT. The branding existed 'so that a second claim could be detected,' a way of spotting laymen who had used the privilege before.
The author says 'several' of the statutes targeted abuses but never says which. You can't place the 1489 statute in that group from the passage.

questions.stem: In saying that Parliament had “trimmed the privilege, for reasons of its own, into a usable shape” (last sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that
choices: Parliament’s limits on the privilege, whatever their aim, left it in a form suited to distinguishing among offenders
Parliament deliberately reshaped the privilege so that judges and juries could use it to grade the punishment of felons
Parliament restricted the privilege until it was so rarely available that it made little difference in practice
Parliament simplified the procedure by which an accused felon could claim the privilege in the royal courts
Parliament designed its limits on the privilege so that they would be easy for judges to apply in particular cases
questions.explanation: 'For reasons of its own' signals that Parliament wasn't aiming at mitigation; 'usable shape' means the result was something judges and juries could use to separate offenders. A says both. B and E are the traps: each turns Parliament's trimming into a deliberate design, which is Danbury's claim and exactly what the author denies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Interpret the quoted phrase in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two pieces. 'For reasons of its own' = not for the purpose of mitigation (the paragraph's whole point). 'Trimmed ... into a usable shape' = the restrictions left a form that judges and juries 'learned to exploit.' So: restrictions made for other reasons happened to leave a tool for grading offenders.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Whatever their aim' = 'for reasons of its own'; 'suited to distinguishing among offenders' = the usable shape judges and juries exploited.
Tempting, but 'deliberately reshaped ... so that' is Danbury's claim of design, the very thing 'for reasons of its own' denies.
'Usable' means the opposite: it remained something judges and juries could put to work.
Nothing in the passage concerns simplifying procedure. This reads 'trimmed' as streamlining.
Again assigns Parliament a purpose, here ease of application. 'For reasons of its own' tells us its purposes were something other than making the privilege usable.

questions.stem: The author’s statement that several of the statutes “were plainly aimed at closing what their framers regarded as abuses” (second sentence of the third paragraph) functions primarily to
choices: lend support to the earlier historians’ view that the privilege let criminals escape the gallows on a technicality
show that the privilege did not in fact operate as a means of sparing some felons from death
call into question the purpose that Danbury attributes to the legislators who restricted the privilege
explain why judges and juries eventually came to use the privilege as a way of distinguishing among offenders
indicate that Parliament regarded first offenders convicted of lesser felonies as undeserving of mercy
questions.explanation: The third paragraph asks 'whether anyone meant the privilege to work this way.' Statutes aimed at closing abuses were not written to build a system of mercy, so the remark casts doubt on Danbury's claim of deliberate design: C. A is tempting because 'abuses' echoes the earlier historians, but the author doesn't adopt their view. D describes the paragraph's last sentence, not this one, and B contradicts the author's acceptance that the privilege did spare felons.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the quoted remark does in the argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first three sentences of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph's question is intent: did anyone mean the privilege to work as mitigation? The evidence: the statutes never call it graded punishment, and several aimed to close abuses. Legislators closing abuses weren't designing mercy. So the remark is evidence against Danbury's account of purpose.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'abuses' sounds like the earlier historians' 'technicality.' But the author uses the point against Danbury's claim of design, and elsewhere accepts that the privilege worked as real mitigation.
The author accepts that the privilege functioned as mitigation. The question is only whether anyone intended that.
CORRECT. Danbury says Parliament made the privilege 'a deliberate instrument of mitigation.' Statutes aimed at abuses suggest a different aim.
That's the job of the paragraph's last sentence (judges and juries 'learned to exploit' it). The abuses remark concerns what legislators intended.
Nothing says Parliament thought first offenders undeserving. Closing abuses doesn't imply denying mercy to that group.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the development that the author describes in the third paragraph?
choices: A legislature, hoping to reduce the use of a harsh penalty, enacts a schedule of milder penalties to be imposed on first offenders.
A city passes separate parking rules over many years, each aimed at a particular nuisance, and officials come to use them together to ration scarce space downtown.
A rule meant to protect a small group is extended to a much larger one because the test used to identify members of the group is easy to pass.
An exemption granted for good reasons is exploited by people for whom it was never intended, until the legislature finally abolishes it.
Officials adopt an informal practice for sorting cases by seriousness, which a legislature later enacts into a formal system of graded penalties.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph describes measures 'passed piecemeal' for particular purposes that together left an institution in 'a usable shape,' which judges and juries then exploited for a function 'no one set out to give it.' B matches every element: separate rules with their own aims, combined use for an unintended purpose. A is Danbury's deliberate design. C matches the first paragraph's development (clergy to all literates), not the third's. D is the earlier historians' picture.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of the third paragraph's account to a new case.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third paragraph, especially its last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: List the elements: (1) many separate measures over time, (2) each with its own aim, not the eventual one, (3) together they leave something usable, (4) practitioners exploit it for a function nobody designed. The right answer needs all four. Check the traps against the other paragraphs: each one maps onto a different part of the passage.

choices.note: This is deliberate design, Danbury's account, which the author rejects. Element (2) fails.
CORRECT. Piecemeal rules with separate aims, then officials using them together for an unintended purpose: the same pattern as Parliament's trimming and the use judges and juries made of it.

Tempting: this is the passage's own first-paragraph story, clerical privilege spreading through the reading test. But the question asks about the third paragraph's development, which is about unplanned function, not widening eligibility.
This is the earlier historians' picture of abuse. The author's development is about restrictions creating a useful tool, not misuse ending in abolition.
Reversed sequence: informal practice first, deliberate legislation later. The passage has legislation for other reasons first, then unplanned use.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship of the fourth paragraph to the third paragraph?
choices: The fourth paragraph provides further evidence for the third paragraph’s claim that the privilege was never designed by anyone as a means of mitigation.
The third paragraph accepts one part of an account and doubts another, and the fourth qualifies the part that the third accepts.
The fourth paragraph withdraws a concession made in the third and concludes that the privilege did not in fact mitigate punishment.
The third paragraph criticizes Danbury’s account, and the fourth defends the earlier historians’ view of the privilege against that criticism.
The fourth paragraph describes a later development that confirms the account of the privilege’s purpose rejected in the third.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph grants that the privilege worked as mitigation but doubts that anyone designed it to. The fourth ('Nor did the mitigation fall evenly') limits the mitigation itself, the part already accepted. That is B, stated abstractly. A is the main trap: the fourth paragraph isn't about design at all. C overreads 'Nor did the mitigation fall evenly' as denying mitigation.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the last paragraph relates to the one before it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the third paragraph and the first sentence of the fourth.

breakdown.analysis: Map it. Danbury's account has two parts: how the privilege worked (mitigation) and why (design). The third paragraph keeps the first and doubts the second. The fourth opens 'Nor did the mitigation fall evenly': it narrows the mitigation claim, the kept part. The right answer is abstract, so translate it back to these parts before choosing.

choices.note: Tempting, because the fourth paragraph also cuts against Danbury. But it addresses who benefited, not whether anyone designed the privilege. It's not evidence about intent.
CORRECT. Part accepted: the privilege worked as mitigation. Part doubted: it was designed so. The fourth paragraph qualifies the accepted part by showing the mitigation favored the literate.
Too strong. The fourth paragraph says the mitigation was uneven, not that there was none.
The fourth paragraph doesn't defend the 'technicality' view; it assumes the privilege did spare some felons.
The 1706 change isn't offered as evidence of anyone's purpose, and it doesn't confirm Danbury's claim of design.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that most of the condensates reported so far are probably artifacts of the unnatural conditions under which they were observed
