explain why the discovery of liquid-like granules in the embryos of worms changed biologists’ understanding of the nucleolus
compare two rival explanations of how compartments that lack membranes manage to hold together inside cells
explain how certain cell structures are thought to form and act, and what would show that a given one has a function
defend the view that condensation is the general mechanism by which cells organize their internal chemistry
questions.explanation: The first two paragraphs explain the condensate model and the mechanism behind it; the third explains why function is harder to show and what test is regarded as decisive. D covers both. A overstates the third paragraph's caution ('may say more about the experiment'). E overstates in the other direction; the author ends by calling condensation 'less a single key' than a mechanism to be established case by case. C invents a debate between two explanations.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the passage as a whole sets out to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole passage, especially the first sentence of each paragraph and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: This one is mostly exposition: what condensates are (paragraph 1), how they form and what they might do (paragraph 2), and how to tell whether a given one does anything (paragraph 3). The author's only real judgment comes at the end, and it's moderate: decide case by case. So look for a purpose that's descriptive and covers both formation and the function test, with no strong verdict either way.

choices.note: Too strong. The third paragraph says test-tube droplets 'may say more about the experiment than about the cell,' and that results of the decisive test vary. It never says most condensates are artifacts.
The worm granules appear as the 2009 finding that launched the view, and the nucleolus as an example. The passage doesn't trace how one changed understanding of the other.
There's only one account of how such compartments hold together. The passage doesn't set up two rival explanations.
CORRECT. 'How certain cell structures are thought to form and act' = paragraphs 1–2; 'what would show that a given one has a function' = the genetic test in paragraph 3.
Tempting, since proponents hold something like this. But the author concludes that condensation is 'less a single key to cellular organization' than a mechanism to be checked case by case.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the molecules within a condensate
choices: are held in place by a small number of strong bonds that form only above a threshold concentration
are present at a concentration lower than the threshold at which such molecules would remain dispersed
are separated from the surrounding fluid by a thin layer of molecules that functions much as a membrane does
remain free to move and are continually trading places with molecules of the same kind outside the condensate
bind to one another only after a phosphate group has been added to at least one of the proteins involved
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the molecules in the separate phase are 'densely packed yet still free to move, exchanging continually with those outside.' D paraphrases that. A reverses 'the many weak contacts.' C turns the oil-and-water comparison into a membrane, though such compartments 'have no membrane.' E reverses the phosphate example, which dissolves droplets.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about molecules inside a condensate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The key sentence: above the threshold, weak contacts favor 'a separate phase in which the molecules are densely packed yet still free to move, exchanging continually with those outside.' So: crowded but mobile, constantly swapping with the outside. Watch for answers that turn 'weak' into 'strong' or the oil comparison into a boundary.

choices.note: Reversed. The passage stresses 'many weak contacts,' not a few strong bonds.
Reversed. Below the threshold the molecules stay dispersed; a condensate forms above it.
Tempting, because of 'much as oil separates from water.' But the whole point is that these compartments 'have no membrane around them.' No boundary layer is mentioned.
CORRECT. 'Free to move' and 'exchanging continually with those outside' = mobile and constantly trading places with molecules outside.
The phosphate example works the other way: adding a phosphate 'can weaken its contacts and dissolve a droplet.'

questions.stem: The primary function of the second paragraph is to
choices: present evidence that condensates form in living cells at normal concentrations and not merely in the test tube
describe the experiments by which researchers showed that condensates speed up chemical reactions inside living cells
explain what drives the process introduced in the first paragraph and what cells are thought to gain from it
offer an alternative to the account of membraneless compartments that is given in the first paragraph of the passage
explain why the nucleolus forms only when the proteins that compose it exceed a threshold concentration
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains why the molecules separate (many weak contacts, a threshold concentration that depends on conditions) and closes with what proponents 'suggest' cells do with condensates. C covers both. B is the near-miss: the paragraph says a condensate 'can' speed a reaction as a proponents' suggestion, but describes no experiments; showing function is the third paragraph's problem. A also belongs to the third paragraph's concerns.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the second paragraph does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Summarize the paragraph in a phrase: the mechanism (weak multi-partner binding, threshold, conditions) plus the proposed uses (speeding reactions, sequestering). Nothing in it is evidence or experiment. The answer should say 'how it works and what it might be for.'

choices.note: The test-tube problem is raised in the third paragraph. The second paragraph offers no evidence about living cells.

Tempting, because the paragraph says condensates can speed reactions. But that's what 'proponents suggest'; no experiments appear, and the third paragraph says showing such functions 'has proved considerably harder.'
CORRECT. Weak contacts, threshold and conditions = what drives the process; speeding reactions and sequestering = what proponents think cells gain.
The second paragraph builds on the first paragraph's account; it doesn't offer a rival one.
The nucleolus is only an example in the first paragraph. The second paragraph doesn't single it out.

questions.stem: The author mentions that adding a phosphate group to a protein can dissolve a droplet (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: show that condensates are artifacts that appear only when proteins are present at unnatural concentrations
give an example of a condensate whose function has been established by the genetic test the author describes
support the suggestion that condensates allow cells to hold molecules out of action until conditions change
explain how a condensate speeds a reaction by gathering an enzyme and its substrates into a small volume
illustrate how a cell can create or end a condensate without changing the amounts of its components
questions.explanation: The example follows the claim that 'because the threshold itself depends on conditions, a cell can create or dissolve a condensate without making or destroying any molecule.' A phosphate group changes conditions, not quantities: E. C is the main trap: sequestering molecules 'until conditions change' comes two sentences later as one of the uses proponents propose, but the phosphate example illustrates the claim before the colon, not that later suggestion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the phosphate example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth sentence of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Look at the colon. Before it: a cell can create or dissolve a condensate 'without making or destroying any molecule,' because the threshold depends on conditions. After it: phosphate and temperature examples. So the examples illustrate control of condensates through conditions rather than through amounts. The uses (speeding reactions, sequestering) come afterward as a separate point.

choices.note: The test-tube worry is in the third paragraph, and the phosphate example concerns dissolving droplets in cells, not artifacts.
The genetic test comes in the third paragraph, and no example of its results is given.

Tempting, because both involve changing conditions. But the phosphate example is attached to the claim that cells can switch condensates on and off without changing amounts. The sequestering use is introduced afterward as something proponents 'suggest.'
That's the other proposed use, and the phosphate example doesn't involve enzymes or substrates.

CORRECT. The sentence's claim is that a cell can create or dissolve a condensate 'without making or destroying any molecule'; adding a phosphate group is how one is dissolved without changing amounts.

questions.stem: By the standard the author describes as decisive, which one of the following findings about a yeast protein that forms condensates during heat stress would provide the strongest evidence that the protein’s condensing helps cells survive heat?
choices: Cells altered so that the protein cannot condense, though it still binds its usual partners normally, fail to recover from heat.
In heated cells, the protein forms droplets at concentrations no higher than those at which it is normally present in unheated cells.
Cells in which the protein has formed droplets during heat stress recover, while cells in which it has not formed droplets do not.
Cells altered so that the protein can neither condense nor bind the molecules it usually binds fail to recover from heat.
In a test tube, the protein forms droplets only at temperatures within the range at which yeast cells are damaged by heat.
questions.explanation: The decisive test is to 'alter a protein so that it can no longer condense while leaving intact its ability to bind its partners, then ask whether the cell loses the capacity.' A is that experiment with a positive result. D is the strongest trap: it removes condensing and binding together, so a failure could be due to lost binding. C is a correlation, not the genetic test; something else could cause both droplets and recovery. B shows only that the protein condenses in the cell, not that condensing does anything.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author's 'decisive' test to a new protein.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The third sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The test has two parts: (1) knock out condensing, (2) keep binding intact, then see whether the capacity disappears. Each trap breaks one part. A finding that drops condition (2) can't separate condensing from binding. A finding with no alteration at all is just correlation. A finding about where or when droplets form tells you the protein condenses, not that condensing helps.

choices.note: CORRECT. Condensing removed, binding kept, capacity lost. That's the test the third paragraph calls decisive, with the result that ties the function to condensing.
Tempting, because it answers the test-tube worry: the droplets are real in cells. But the passage separates showing that a condensate forms from showing that it does anything.
Tempting: it links droplets with survival. But it's an observed correlation, not the genetic test. Cells that form droplets might differ in other ways that explain their recovery.

Tempting, because it looks like the genetic test. But binding is lost too, so the failure might come from losing binding, not condensing. The test requires 'leaving intact its ability to bind its partners.'
A test-tube result, the kind of evidence the third paragraph says 'may say more about the experiment than about the cell.'

passages.title: Promises to the dead
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
Most accounts of promising hold that a promise binds because it gives the person to whom it is made an assurance on which he or she may rely, and that the obligation ends if that person releases the promisor. Taken together, these claims raise a puzzle about promises made to people who have since died. A dead promisee can neither rely on anything nor release anyone. Yet a person who has promised a dying parent to keep the family farm, or to see that a manuscript is burned unread, does not ordinarily feel released by the death, and someone who breaks such a promise is generally thought to have done wrong, even if no one else ever learns of the breach.

The philosopher Edda Haske has offered the most influential attempt to vindicate this ordinary judgment. Haske argues that some of a person’s interests outlast the person. We have interests in how our reputations fare, in whether projects we began are completed, and in whether our wishes about our property are respected, and these interests can be set back after we die even though we will never learn of the setback. A promise to the dead remains binding, on Haske’s view, because breaking it defeats one of these surviving interests.

Haske’s account has the merit of explaining why such promises carry any weight at all, and why their weight does not depend on anyone’s learning that they were broken, but it explains too much. If the obligation derives from the dead person’s surviving interests, then the promise itself contributes nothing to it. A stranger who happened to learn of the dead person’s wish that the manuscript be burned would be under the same obligation as the friend who swore to burn it, provided the stranger could act at no greater cost. Yet no one thinks that a stranger who declines to act has broken faith with anyone. Haske’s view thus makes the promise merely the occasion on which the promisor learned of an obligation that existed independently of it.

A better account would locate the obligation in the exchange that took place while both parties were alive. In accepting the promise, the promisee relied on it, and often forwent other arrangements, such as asking someone else or adding a provision to a will, that might have secured the same end. Death does not undo that reliance; it only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal. On this account, the promisee’s inability to release the promisor is not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it: the only person who could have waived the obligation is the one whose reliance created it, and that person is gone.

passages.title: Aligned spins in the Koronis family
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
When a collision shatters a large asteroid, the fragments continue to orbit the Sun on similar paths, and astronomers call such a group a family. Because a shattering collision sets each fragment tumbling on its own, the spin axes of a family’s members were expected to point every which way. It was therefore a surprise when, in 2002, the astronomer Stephen Slivan reported that among ten large members of the Koronis family, the four spinning in the same direction as their orbital motion had nearly parallel spin axes and similar rotation periods. The six spinning in the opposite direction showed no such alignment; their periods instead clustered near the extremes, either very fast or very slow.

One early suggestion was that the alignment was inherited: if the parent body broke apart gently, its fragments might have retained much of its original spin. But the Koronis family is thought to be some two to three billion years old, and over so long a span collisions and other disturbances would probably have erased whatever spin the fragments inherited. Nor can inheritance explain why only the members spinning in one direction are aligned, since all ten emerged from the same breakup.

A more successful account, developed by David Vokrouhlický and his colleagues, appeals to an effect of sunlight. An asteroid reradiates absorbed sunlight as heat, and the departing heat gives the body a slight recoil. On a symmetrical body these recoils would produce no net twist, but on an irregularly shaped one they produce a tiny torque. The torque differs from a related effect: because a rotating asteroid’s surface is warmest some hours after local noon, its heat also nudges the body along or against its direction of travel, altering its orbit rather than its spin. Over hundreds of millions of years or more, the torque can change both how fast an asteroid spins and how its axis is tilted. Acting alone, it would push spin axes toward extreme tilts, not toward a common direction. But as the torque alters an asteroid’s spin, the slow wobble of its axis can come to match a periodic shift in the orientation of its orbit caused by the giant planets’ gravity. An asteroid caught in this resonance has its axis held near one particular orientation, which all asteroids so caught come to share. Only asteroids spinning in the direction of their orbital motion can be caught; the others are driven instead toward the fast and slow extremes.

The account has implications its rival lacks. Because the torque acts more strongly on small bodies than on large ones, a family’s smaller members should, if anything, be aligned more fully than the large ones studied. And a family too young for the torque to have had much effect should show little alignment of this kind. Neither is easily checked, since the asteroids involved are mostly small and faint; for now, the account’s advantage lies more in what it explains than in what has been confirmed.

passages.title: Seaward and landward in Mavuro
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Speakers of Mavuro, a language of the fishing villages along the coast of Ambra Island, have no words that locate objects to a person’s left or right. A Mavuro speaker says that a cup stands seaward of a plate, or that a door is on the landward side of a room, even indoors. In the 1990s the linguist Ruth Abernell asked whether this habit of speech affects how speakers remember spatial arrangements. She showed participants a row of three toy animals on one table, turned them around to face a second table, and asked them to set out the same row again. Mavuro speakers tended to rebuild the row so that the animal that had been seaward remained seaward, reversing its left-to-right order, while speakers of the island’s official language, which has words for left and right, tended to preserve the left-to-right order. Abernell concluded that a language’s habitual frame of reference shapes how its speakers encode space even when they are silent.

Abernell’s critics replied that her two groups differed in more than language. The Mavuro speakers lived where the sea is nearly always visible and were tested outdoors; the speakers of the official language lived in the island’s inland capital and were tested in an office. People who spend their days oriented to a single prominent landmark, the critics argued, will come to remember arrays by reference to it whatever language they speak; the Mavuro way of talking is a symptom of that orientation, not its cause.

The objection is a fair one against Abernell’s study, which could not separate language from setting. It does not follow, however, that language plays no role, and a later study by Tomas Iver suggests otherwise. Iver tested children in the village of Pelloc whose families had moved there from inland. Some of these households had adopted Mavuro at home; others continued to speak the official language. The children all attended the same school and played on the same shore, yet those raised in Mavuro-speaking homes rebuilt the rows seaward, while the others preserved left and right. Iver’s result does not settle the matter, since a family’s choice of home language may go along with other habits, such as whether its members fish, that also direct attention to the sea. But it changes what the critics must show: they now need to name some feature of these households, other than language, that differs along with it.

Both sides of this dispute have assumed that language and surroundings are rival explanations, so that whatever is credited to one must be subtracted from the other. Iver’s findings suggest a different picture, in which a language is one of the means by which a community teaches its children which features of their surroundings to keep track of.

passages.title: Sunset provisions
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Sunset provisions, which cause a statute to expire on a set date unless the legislature reenacts it, are usually defended as a way of forcing legislators to ask whether a law has done what it was meant to do, rather than leaving it in force by default. The record of such provisions is disappointing, for three reasons.

First, renewal rarely involves review. A legislature facing dozens of expiring provisions in a single session tends to extend them together, often in one bill passed in the last days before the deadline, and few legislators examine any particular law in the process. Indeed, the more laws carry sunset dates, the less attention each renewal can receive. Second, a sunset date gives the interests that benefit from a law a recurring occasion to press their case. Because those interests are organized and the general public is not, the renewal debate, when there is one, more often becomes an occasion to enlarge the law than to scrutinize it, and a law meant to be temporary emerges from each renewal broader than before.

Third, the people who must comply with a law cannot plan around a rule that may vanish. Businesses deciding whether to invest and agencies deciding whether to hire must discount for the chance that the law will lapse, and they bear that cost even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt.

Review of whether laws work is worth having. But legislators can obtain it by requiring agencies to report on a law’s effects and by holding hearings on those reports, without staking the law’s survival on a vote that may never receive real attention.

Passage B

Legislative inertia ordinarily favors whatever is already law. A statute stays in force until a majority agrees to repeal it, so a law that has outlived its rationale can survive for decades if those who benefit from it can keep such a majority from forming. Opponents of a law, by contrast, gain nothing from delay; every session in which they fail to agree is a session in which the law continues. A sunset provision reverses this default for the laws to which it is attached: the law lapses unless a majority affirmatively wants to keep it.

The reversal matters most for measures adopted quickly under pressure, such as emergency powers or experimental programs, where legislators acted on predictions they had no way to check. If the predictions fail, the law should not need a fresh coalition to end it. Critics observe that renewal votes are often perfunctory. Perhaps so; but even a perfunctory vote must be taken, and the requirement guarantees any legislator who has doubts about the law a moment at which the law’s defenders, not its opponents, must assemble a majority.

Reporting requirements, which critics of sunset provisions often recommend instead, offer no such moment. They produce documents that no one is obliged to read, let alone act on.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Promises made to people who have since died do not bind the promisor, since a dead promisee can neither rely on a promise nor release anyone from it.
Haske is right that some interests outlast the person who has them, but such interests can ground obligations only for those who have made a promise.
The puzzle about promises to the dead shows that the standard account of promising, which ties a promise’s force to reliance, must be abandoned.
Haske’s explanation of why promises to the dead still bind leaves the promise no role; the obligation is better traced to the promisee’s reliance while alive.
Because some of a person’s interests survive death, breaking a promise to the dead wrongs the promisee in the same way as breaking a promise to the living.
questions.explanation: The author grants Haske’s account a merit but says it ‘explains too much’ because ‘the promise itself contributes nothing’ (third paragraph), then offers ‘a better account’ that locates the obligation in the promisee’s reliance (fourth paragraph): D. C is the main trap: the author says the puzzle is ‘not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it,’ so the theory is kept, not abandoned. A is the conclusion the puzzle seems to force, which the author rejects, and E is Haske’s view without the author’s objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on promises to the dead.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (‘it explains too much’) and fourth paragraph (‘A better account would locate the obligation…’).

breakdown.analysis: Three things happen: a puzzle (promises bind through reliance and end on release, but the dead can do neither), Haske’s fix (surviving interests), and the author’s verdict (Haske proves too much; reliance while alive is the better answer). So is the author against Haske? Partly. Against the standard view? No, the last paragraph rescues it. We need an answer with both halves: Haske’s account fails for a specific reason, and reliance does the job instead.

choices.note: The puzzle seems to push toward this, but the whole passage defends the ordinary judgment that such promises still bind. Opposite of the author’s view.

Half right. The author never denies that interests outlast the person, but nothing in the passage says those interests bind only promisors. The author’s point is that the obligation comes from the promise, not from the interests.

Tempting, because the puzzle does put pressure on the standard account. But the last paragraph says the dead promisee’s inability to release is ‘not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it.’ The author saves the theory.
CORRECT. Haske’s view ‘makes the promise merely the occasion’ for an obligation that exists anyway, and the author’s ‘better account’ grounds the obligation in reliance during the exchange.
This is Haske’s position, and even Haske doesn’t say ‘in the same way.’ The author argues against grounding the obligation in surviving interests.

questions.stem: Haske’s view, as it is described in the passage, commits Haske to which one of the following?
choices: A promise to the dead binds only if the promisee gave up some other means of securing the promised end.
A person can be made worse off in some respect by an event that the person never experiences.
A stranger who learns of a dead person’s wishes is under no obligation to see that they are honored.
A promise made to a person who has since died can be broken only by the person who made it.
The interests that survive a person’s death carry less weight than those the person had while alive.
questions.explanation: Haske holds that some interests ‘can be set back after we die even though we will never learn of the setback’ (second paragraph), so a person can be worse off in some respect through an event the person never experiences: B. A is the main trap: forgoing other arrangements belongs to the author’s reliance account in the fourth paragraph, not to Haske. C and D are the reverse of what Haske’s view implies (the third paragraph says a stranger would be equally bound), and E is never said.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim that Haske’s position requires.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (Haske’s view) and third paragraph (what follows from it).

breakdown.analysis: Haske’s move is that interests outlast the person, and they ‘can be set back after we die even though we will never learn of the setback.’ So what does Haske have to believe? That being harmed doesn’t require feeling or knowing anything. We need an answer that states that commitment in general terms. Watch for answers that hand Haske the author’s ideas (reliance, forgone arrangements) or deny what the third paragraph says Haske’s view implies.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a careful theory of promises to the dead. But it’s the author’s account (‘often forwent other arrangements’), not Haske’s, and even the author doesn’t make it a condition.

CORRECT. Haske says surviving interests can be set back after death, when the person can no longer learn of or experience anything. That commits Haske to harm without experience, stated here abstractly.
Reversed. The third paragraph argues that Haske’s view puts the stranger under ‘the same obligation as the friend.’ Haske is committed to the opposite of this.
This is the author’s intuition that only the promisor breaks faith. On Haske’s view, anyone who defeats the surviving interest does the same wrong, which is the author’s complaint.
Nothing compares the weight of surviving interests with the interests of the living. Unstated.

questions.stem: In saying that the promisee’s inability to release the promisor is “not an embarrassment for the theory of promising but a consequence of it” (last sentence of the passage), the author most likely means that
choices: the standard theory of promising must be given up, since it cannot explain why a dead promisee is unable to release anyone
Haske’s account, once properly understood, already explains why only the promisee can waive a promise
the difficulty the puzzle raises is genuine but arises in too few cases to count against an otherwise sound theory
a dead promisee’s inability to release the promisor shows that the promisee’s surviving interests cannot be waived
a feature that seemed to count against the theory in fact follows from a correct version of it
questions.explanation: The first paragraph presents the inability to release as the source of the puzzle; the last paragraph shows that on a reliance account only the promisee could waive the obligation, so the inability follows from the theory: E. B is the main trap: the explanation the author praises is the author’s own reliance account, not Haske’s, which the author criticizes. A reverses the author’s claim, C keeps the inability as a small problem rather than a consequence, and D brings in Haske’s surviving interests.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain what the author means by calling the inability to release ‘a consequence’ of the theory rather than ‘an embarrassment.’

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the two claims and the puzzle) and the last sentence of the fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Back in the first paragraph, the fact that a dead person can’t release anyone looked like trouble for the theory: if release ends a promise and reliance grounds it, what happens when the promisee dies? The author flips it. If reliance created the obligation, only the person who relied could waive it; that person is gone, so no one can. The awkward fact is now a prediction of the theory. We need an answer that says ‘what looked like a problem for the theory actually follows from it.’

choices.note: Opposite. ‘Not an embarrassment’ is the author saying the theory survives.

Tempting, because Haske is the other account in play and the sentence is about explaining the puzzle. But the account doing the explaining here is the author’s ‘better account,’ built on reliance. The author thinks Haske’s view ‘explains too much.’

Tempting, because it also says the puzzle doesn’t sink the theory. But the author’s reason isn’t that the case is rare. The author says the inability to release follows from the theory: ‘a consequence of it.’ This answer keeps the inability as a problem, just a small one.
Mixes in Haske. The last paragraph is about reliance, not surviving interests, and says nothing about waiving interests.
CORRECT. The feature that generated the puzzle turns out to be implied by the reliance version of the theory.

questions.stem: According to the account the author favors, the death of a promisee changes
choices: the promisee’s reliance on the promise, though not the promisor’s obligation to keep it
who holds the power to waive the obligation, which passes to those who inherit the promisee’s property
whether the obligation binds at all, in those cases in which the promisee forwent no other arrangements
the source of the obligation, which then rests on the promisee’s surviving interests rather than on reliance
whether a breach could be made good to the person wronged, but not the reliance on which the obligation rests
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says ‘Death does not undo that reliance; it only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal’: E, which restates both halves in other words. A is the main trap: it gets the reliance half backward, since death ‘does not undo’ it. B and C are never said, and D folds Haske’s surviving interests into the author’s account.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what, on the author’s reliance account, death does and doesn’t change.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence carries this: ‘Death does not undo that reliance; it only removes any chance of compensating the promisee for its betrayal.’ So two things: the reliance (and the obligation built on it) survives; the chance to make it up to the promisee doesn’t. We need an answer with both halves, in other words. Expect a trap that flips which half survives.

choices.note: Reversed. The passage says death ‘does not undo that reliance.’ The reliance stays.
Nothing about heirs. The author says the only person who could waive the obligation ‘is gone,’ which suggests no one else gets that power.
The author says promisees ‘often’ forwent other arrangements, not that the obligation depends on it. Death isn’t said to cancel anything.
That’s Haske’s ground, which the author rejects. On the author’s account the obligation still rests on the reliance.
CORRECT. ‘Compensating the promisee’ becomes ‘made good to the person wronged,’ and ‘Death does not undo that reliance’ becomes the reliance staying in place.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: Two widely held claims about promising are stated; a philosopher’s argument against both claims is summarized; the author defends one of the claims against that argument.
A puzzle is stated; two rival solutions to it are described; the author argues that both solutions fail for the same reason; a restatement of the puzzle is proposed.
A puzzle arising from two widely held claims is posed; a solution is proposed and then objected to; an alternative treats a source of the puzzle as an implication.
A puzzle arising from two widely held claims is posed; a proposed solution is described and defended against an objection; the solution is then extended to a further class of cases.
A common judgment is called into question; a philosopher’s defense of that judgment is described; the author concludes that the judgment cannot be defended and should be given up.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph derives a puzzle from two claims about promising, the second gives Haske’s solution, the third objects that it ‘explains too much,’ and the fourth offers a reliance account on which the inability to release is ‘a consequence’ of the theory: C. D is the main trap: its first two steps match, but the author raises the objection against Haske rather than defending Haske from it, and nothing is extended. A misdescribes Haske as attacking the two claims, B invents a second solution, and E has the author abandon a judgment the author defends.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match each paragraph to a step in the answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Whole passage: paragraph 1 (puzzle), 2 (Haske), 3 (objection), 4 (author’s alternative).

breakdown.analysis: Map it first: 1. Two claims (promises bind through reliance; release ends them) plus dead promisees = puzzle. 2. Haske’s solution: surviving interests. 3. Objection: it explains too much (the stranger). 4. The author’s alternative: reliance during the exchange, which makes the inability to release a consequence. Organization answers are long chains; one wrong link kills the answer, so check every step.

choices.note: Haske doesn’t argue against the two claims; Haske tries to defend the ordinary judgment the puzzle threatens.
There is only one proposed solution (Haske’s), and the author ends with a new account, not a restatement of the puzzle.
CORRECT. Every link matches, including the last: the inability to release, which generated the puzzle, becomes a consequence of the author’s account.

Tempting, because the first two links are perfect. But the objection in the third paragraph is the author’s objection TO Haske, not a defense of Haske, and the last paragraph replaces the solution rather than extending it.
The author defends the common judgment that promises to the dead bind; only Haske’s defense of it is rejected.

questions.stem: The author discusses a stranger who learns of a dead person’s wish (third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the claim that a person’s interests can be defeated even by those who never made that person any promise at all
argue that people who have made no promise are never under any obligation concerning the wishes of the dead
show that Haske’s account cannot explain why breaking a promise to the dead is generally and rightly thought to be wrong
suggest that a promisor’s obligation to a dead promisee is weaker than Haske’s account implies
bring out an implication of Haske’s view that conflicts with a judgment the author takes to be widely shared
questions.explanation: The stranger shows what follows from Haske’s view (the stranger would have ‘the same obligation as the friend’) and then sets it against a common judgment (‘no one thinks that a stranger who declines to act has broken faith’): E. C is the main trap: the author grants that Haske’s account explains ‘why such promises carry any weight at all,’ so the complaint is that it explains too much, not that it fails to explain the wrong. A is a premise of Haske’s view rather than the point of the example, B overstates the author’s claim, and D is never suggested.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the stranger example is in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, especially its first and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Ask what the stranger is doing to Haske. Haske’s view: the obligation comes from the dead person’s interests. Then anyone who knows of those interests, like the stranger, is equally bound. But nobody thinks the stranger broke faith. So Haske’s view produces an obligation where we see none: it ‘explains too much.’ Notice what the author does NOT say: that Haske fails to explain why breaking the promise is wrong. The author explicitly credits Haske with explaining that. We need an answer that says ‘draws out a consequence of Haske’s view that clashes with common opinion.’

choices.note: The stranger example does involve someone who made no promise, but its job isn’t to illustrate Haske’s claim about interests; it’s to show that the claim proves too much.
Too strong. The author says only that we don’t think the stranger ‘has broken faith with anyone.’ ‘Never under any obligation’ goes far beyond that.

Tempting, because the example does attack Haske. But the author says Haske’s account ‘has the merit of explaining why such promises carry any weight at all.’ The complaint is overreach: the account explains the promisor’s obligation and also gives one to the stranger.
Nothing in the passage says the obligation is weaker than Haske thinks. The author’s point is about where the obligation comes from and who has it.
CORRECT. Haske’s view implies the stranger is as bound as the friend; ‘no one thinks’ the stranger has broken faith. Implication vs. shared judgment.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the author’s objection to Haske’s account?
choices: On Haske’s view, making a promise can itself give the promisee a further interest that survives death and that only the promisor is in a position to defeat.
Promisees often do not forgo any other arrangements when they accept a promise concerning what is to happen after their death.
Some interests, such as an interest in how one’s reputation fares, can be set back after death even if no one ever learns of the setback.
A stranger who learns of a dead person’s wish can seldom act on it at no greater cost than the person who promised to carry it out.
Some people feel bound by a promise to the dead only when others are likely to find out whether the promise has been kept.
questions.explanation: The author’s objection (third paragraph) is that on Haske’s view ‘the promise itself contributes nothing,’ so a stranger would be as bound as the promisor. If the promise creates a further surviving interest that only the promisor can defeat, Haske’s view gives the promise a role after all and the stranger is not equally bound: A. B is the main trap: it weakens the author’s own alternative in the fourth paragraph, not the objection to Haske. D attacks a case the author has already stipulated away (‘provided the stranger could act at no greater cost’), C supports a premise the author concedes, and E bears on the ordinary judgment, not on the objection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that would most damage the author’s argument against Haske.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the objection); compare the fourth paragraph (the author’s own account).

breakdown.analysis: Pin down the objection first. 1. On Haske’s view, the obligation comes from the dead person’s surviving interests. 2. So the promise adds nothing. 3. So a stranger who knows the wish is as bound as the promisor. 4. But nobody thinks the stranger broke faith. Which step is soft? Step 2. If Haske can show that the promise itself creates something only the promisor can betray, the promise does contribute and the stranger drops out. We need an answer that gives Haske a way for the promise to matter. Most students pick (B) or (D): (B) hits the wrong target, the author’s alternative, and (D) fights a hypothetical the author built to avoid that very point.

choices.note: CORRECT. If promising creates a surviving interest that only the promisor can defeat, then on Haske’s own terms the promise contributes something, and a stranger who declines to act hasn’t defeated that interest. The step ‘the promise itself contributes nothing’ fails.

Tempting, because it hurts the author. But it hurts the author’s own account in the fourth paragraph, and even there the author says only that promisees ‘often’ forgo other arrangements. The objection to Haske doesn’t depend on it.

So? The author grants that such interests exist; the objection is that Haske’s view ‘explains too much,’ not that surviving interests are unreal. Support for a conceded premise doesn’t weaken the objection.

Tempting, because it seems to make the stranger case unrealistic. But the author’s argument stipulates ‘provided the stranger could act at no greater cost.’ How often that condition holds in practice doesn’t matter to a point about what Haske’s view implies.
This bears on how widely the ordinary judgment is shared, which is about the puzzle in the first paragraph, not about whether Haske’s view gives the stranger the promisor’s obligation.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: argue that collisions among asteroids are much rarer than astronomers had generally assumed
explain how the heat an asteroid reradiates can alter both its rate of spin and its orbit over long periods
describe an unexpected pattern among members of an asteroid family and show why one account of it is preferable to another
present two explanations of a puzzling observation and argue that neither can be assessed until fainter asteroids are measured
show that a recently confirmed account of an asteroid family’s spins has settled how such families are formed
questions.explanation: The first paragraph reports the surprising alignment, the second rejects the inheritance suggestion, and the third and fourth present ‘a more successful account’ and what it implies: C. D is the main trap: the author does say the implications are hard to check, but has already judged one account more successful, so the passage doesn’t leave both unassessed. B describes part of the third paragraph only, E overstates (‘confirmed,’ ‘settled’), and A is never argued.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage as a whole sets out to do.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the surprise), the start of the second and third paragraphs, and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Structure: a surprising finding (aligned spins), a first explanation that fails (inheritance), a better one (the thermal torque plus resonance), and what that one implies, with a hedge that it hasn’t been confirmed. So the job is ‘puzzle, then why one explanation beats another.’ Watch for answers that inflate the hedge into ‘neither can be judged’ or deflate it into ‘confirmed.’

choices.note: The passage mentions collisions only to say they would have erased inherited spin. Nothing says they’re rarer than thought.
Half right. The heat effects are explained, but only as part of an account of the alignment. That’s a piece of the third paragraph, not the passage’s purpose.
CORRECT. The unexpected pattern is the alignment of the four members; the passage rejects inheritance and calls the torque account ‘more successful.’
Tempting, because of the last sentence. But the author already prefers one account; the hedge is only that its advantage lies ‘more in what it explains than in what has been confirmed.’
Too strong. The last sentence says the account’s implications haven’t been confirmed, and the passage isn’t about how families form.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, on the account developed by Vokrouhlický and his colleagues, the six Koronis members that spin opposite to their orbital motion
choices: were caught in the resonance but have been held there at a variety of orientations
will eventually come into alignment once the torque has acted on them long enough
have had their rotation periods shaped largely by the torque that brought the other four into the resonance
retain, for the most part, the rotation periods that they inherited from the family’s parent body
have been affected less by the torque than the other four were, since the six are on the whole larger bodies
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the six have periods ‘either very fast or very slow’; the third says the torque alters spin and that asteroids that cannot be caught in the resonance ‘are driven instead toward the fast and slow extremes.’ So the torque that brought the four into the resonance also produced the six’s extreme periods: C. E is the main trap: the torque does depend on size, but nothing says the six are larger. A and B contradict ‘Only asteroids spinning in the direction of their orbital motion can be caught,’ and D is the rejected inheritance idea.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the torque account says about the six members that aren’t aligned.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph (the six’s periods) and the end of the third paragraph (‘the others are driven instead…’).

breakdown.analysis: Connect two spots. Paragraph 1: the six spin backward and have very fast or very slow periods. Paragraph 3: the torque changes spin; the forward spinners can get caught in the resonance; ‘the others are driven instead toward the fast and slow extremes.’ Driven by what? The torque. So the same torque explains both groups; only the resonance differs. We need an answer saying the six’s periods come from that torque.

choices.note: Contradicted. Only asteroids spinning in the direction of their orbital motion can be caught at all.
Contradicted for the same reason. Backward spinners are driven toward the extremes, not into alignment.
CORRECT. The torque that changed the four’s spins until they were caught in the resonance is what drives the uncaught six toward very fast or very slow rotation.
That’s the inheritance idea the second paragraph rejects, and the stem asks about the other account.

Tempting, because the fourth paragraph says the torque acts more strongly on small bodies. But the passage gives no sizes for the six versus the four, and on the account the six were plainly affected: their periods were driven to the extremes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the torque described in the third paragraph differs from the related effect mentioned there in that the torque
choices: arises because an asteroid’s surface is at its warmest some hours after local noon
would not arise at all on an asteroid whose shape was perfectly regular
gradually alters the path along which an asteroid travels around the Sun
acts more strongly on large asteroids than it does on small ones
does not depend on the asteroid’s absorbing and reradiating sunlight
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the recoils ‘would produce no net twist’ on a symmetrical body and a torque only on an irregularly shaped one; the related effect instead comes from the surface being ‘warmest some hours after local noon’ and alters the orbit: B. A is the main trap: it reuses the passage’s words but attaches the related effect’s cause to the torque. C is the related effect’s result, D reverses the fourth paragraph’s size claim, and E contradicts the torque’s origin in reradiated sunlight.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says distinguishes the spin-changing torque from the other heat effect.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third and fourth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two effects of reradiated heat. The torque: recoils cancel on a symmetrical body, so only an irregular shape produces a twist, and it changes spin. The related effect: comes from the afternoon temperature lag and changes the orbit, ‘rather than its spin.’ We need the torque’s side of that contrast. Expect traps that swap the two effects’ causes or results.

choices.note: Tempting, because these words are right there. But they explain the related effect, the one that ‘nudges the body along or against its direction of travel.’ Wrong effect.
CORRECT. ‘On a symmetrical body these recoils would produce no net twist’: the torque depends on irregular shape, which the related effect is not said to need.
Reversed. Altering the orbit is what the related effect does, ‘rather than its spin.’
Reversed. The fourth paragraph says the torque acts more strongly on small bodies.
Both effects come from sunlight reradiated as heat. The torque starts there: ‘An asteroid reradiates absorbed sunlight as heat.’

questions.stem: The author mentions that the Koronis family is thought to be some two billion years old (second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: explain why the torque has had enough time to bring some of the family’s members into the resonance
contrast the family with younger families in which the predicted absence of alignment has been observed
support the suggestion that the family’s parent body broke apart gently rather than violently
suggest that the family’s members have been struck so often that their spins cannot be measured reliably
question whether a feature of the fragments could have lasted long enough to produce what was observed
questions.explanation: Right after the inheritance suggestion, the author says ‘But’ the family is some two billion years old, over which span collisions and other disturbances ‘would probably have erased whatever spin the fragments inherited’: the age tells against an inherited spin lasting to the present, E. A is the main trap: the family’s age does matter to the torque account, but the sentence appears as an objection to inheritance, before the torque is introduced. B claims observations the passage never reports, C reverses the point, and D is never said.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the family’s age is brought up where it is.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Look at what comes just before: ‘the alignment was inherited.’ Then ‘But’ the family is two billion years old, and over that span collisions would probably have erased inherited spin. So the age is evidence against inheritance: a property from the breakup wouldn’t last that long. The right answer will describe that job, likely in abstract terms (‘a feature of the fragments,’ ‘lasted long enough’).

choices.note: Tempting, because the torque does need hundreds of millions of years, so the age fits that account. But in the second paragraph the age is used against inheritance, and the torque hasn’t even been introduced yet. Right fact, wrong job.
The passage reports no observations of young families. The fourth paragraph only says what such families should show and that this isn’t easily checked.
Reversed. The age undercuts the inheritance hypothesis, which is the one that relies on a gentle breakup.
Nothing says the spins can’t be measured; Slivan measured them.
CORRECT. The ‘feature of the fragments’ is the spin inherited from the parent body; the age makes it doubtful that the inherited spin survived to produce the alignment seen today.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following about the resonance described in the third paragraph?
choices: It arises from the uneven way in which an irregularly shaped asteroid reradiates the sunlight it has absorbed.
It can catch asteroids spinning in either direction, though it holds only some of them at a fixed orientation.
It pushes the spin axes of the asteroids caught in it toward extreme tilts over very long periods.
Whether an asteroid enters it depends in part on a change in spin brought about by a different influence.
It has acted on every member of the Koronis family, though with different results for different members.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that ‘as the torque alters an asteroid’s spin, the slow wobble of its axis can come to match’ the shift in its orbit; so whether an asteroid is caught depends partly on the torque’s effect on its spin: D. A is the main trap: uneven reradiation produces the torque, not the resonance, which is caused by the giant planets’ gravity. B contradicts ‘Only asteroids spinning in the direction of their orbital motion can be caught,’ C is what the torque would do ‘acting alone,’ and E is never said.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the resonance itself, as distinct from the torque.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last four sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Keep the two mechanisms apart. Torque: from uneven reradiation; changes spin rate and tilt; alone, pushes axes to extremes. Resonance: the axis wobble matches a periodic shift in the orbit caused by the giant planets; a caught asteroid’s axis is held near one orientation. How do they connect? The torque changes the spin until the wobble matches. So entry into the resonance depends on the torque. That link, stated abstractly, is the answer.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s an accurate description of the torque. But the stem asks about the resonance, which comes from the giant planets’ gravity matching the axis’s wobble.
Contradicted. Only forward spinners can be caught at all.
That’s what the torque would do ‘acting alone.’ The resonance does the opposite: it holds caught axes near one orientation.
CORRECT. The ‘different influence’ is the torque: as it alters the spin, the wobble can come to match the orbit’s shift, and only then is the asteroid caught.
Only the four forward spinners are said to be caught; the six are driven toward the extremes instead. ‘Every member’ goes beyond the passage.

questions.stem: The passage most strongly suggests that the inheritance hypothesis, unlike the account developed by Vokrouhlický and his colleagues, would lead one to expect that
choices: whatever alignment a family’s members display would be most pronounced soon after the family formed
a family’s smaller members would, if anything, be aligned more fully than its larger members
alignment would be found mainly in families whose members had been struck repeatedly by other asteroids
no family’s members would show any alignment once the family was more than a few hundred million years old
alignment would be found only in families whose parent bodies broke apart violently
questions.explanation: On the inheritance hypothesis the alignment is left over from the breakup, and the second paragraph says collisions and other disturbances erase inherited spin over time; so the alignment should be strongest early and fade. The torque account, by contrast, expects ‘little alignment’ in a family too young for the torque to act (fourth paragraph): A. B is the main trap: it is the torque account’s own prediction, word for word. D turns ‘erased over two billion years’ into a specific cutoff the passage never gives, and C and E reverse the hypothesis’s conditions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what the rival hypothesis predicts about how alignment changes as a family ages.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (inheritance and why it fails) and fourth paragraph (the torque account’s implications).

breakdown.analysis: The passage never states the inheritance hypothesis’s prediction; you have to build it. 1. Alignment comes from spin retained at a gentle breakup. 2. Over time, collisions and disturbances erase inherited spin. So alignment starts strong and fades. The torque account says the opposite about age: a young family should show little alignment, because the torque hasn’t had time. We need the inheritance side of that contrast. Most students reach for (B) because it’s in the passage; it’s the wrong account’s prediction.

choices.note: CORRECT. Inherited alignment is greatest at the breakup and is erased over time, so it should be most pronounced in a young family; that is the reverse of what the torque account expects.

Tempting, because it quotes the fourth paragraph. But that’s the torque account’s implication, based on the torque acting more strongly on small bodies. Inheritance gives no reason to favor small members.
Reversed. Collisions erase inherited spin; repeated strikes would destroy inherited alignment, not produce it.
Too strong. The passage says only that two billion years would probably erase inherited spin. ‘A few hundred million years’ and ‘no family… any alignment’ are invented precision.
Reversed. The hypothesis requires that the parent body ‘broke apart gently.’

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the account developed by Vokrouhlický and his colleagues?
choices: The smaller Koronis members that spin with their orbital motion turn out to be aligned about as closely as the large members studied.
For bodies as large as those studied, no torque-driven change in spin could make the axis’s wobble keep pace with the orbit’s shift.
Collisions among members of the Koronis family turn out to have been far less frequent than astronomers had believed.
Several of the six Koronis members that spin opposite to their orbital motion turn out to have spin axes tilted at extreme angles.
The parent body of the Koronis family is found to have broken apart violently rather than gently.
questions.explanation: On the account, the four large members are aligned because the torque altered their spins until the axis’s wobble matched the shift in the orbit, trapping them in the resonance (third paragraph). If no torque-driven change could produce that match for bodies their size, the mechanism could not have aligned them: B. A is the main trap: the fourth paragraph says smaller members should be aligned more fully only ‘if anything,’ so equal alignment is consistent with the account. C and E bear on the rival inheritance hypothesis, not on this account, and D fits the account’s claim that the torque alone drives axes toward extreme tilts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the discovery that would most damage the torque-and-resonance explanation of the alignment.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (the mechanism) and fourth paragraph (its implications).

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the mechanism as a chain: torque changes the spin → the axis’s wobble comes to match the orbit’s periodic shift → the asteroid is caught → its axis is held at the shared orientation. Break any link and the account can’t explain the four aligned members. Which choice breaks a link? Don’t go hunting for the account’s ‘predictions’ first; the passage hedges them. The hard-to-like answer attacks the middle link in technical-sounding terms. Most students pick (A) because it seems to contradict the size prediction, or (C) because it helps the rival.

choices.note: Tempting, because it echoes the size prediction. But the passage says smaller members should ‘if anything’ be aligned more fully; that hedge means ‘at least as fully.’ Equal alignment fits.

CORRECT. The account needs the torque to bring the wobble into step with the orbit’s shift; if that can’t happen for bodies the size of those studied, the account can’t explain why those four are aligned.

This would rescue part of the inheritance hypothesis, whose problem was that collisions erase inherited spin. But helping a rival isn’t the same as showing this account is wrong, and the rival still can’t explain why only forward spinners are aligned.
This fits the account. The torque ‘acting alone’ pushes axes toward extreme tilts, and the six can’t be caught in the resonance.
This hurts the inheritance hypothesis, which needed a gentle breakup. The torque account doesn’t depend on how the parent body broke apart.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Iver’s study has shown that the language people speak, rather than the surroundings in which they live, determines how they remember spatial arrangements.
Abernell’s critics were wrong to claim that her study failed to separate the influence of language on spatial memory from the influence of setting.
Mavuro speakers remember arrays by reference to the sea because the sea is almost always visible to them, and their way of speaking merely reflects this.
Since a family’s home language may vary with its other habits, no study can determine whether language affects how people remember spatial arrangements.
Though a fair objection undercuts Abernell’s study, later evidence suggests that language does affect spatial memory, perhaps as one way communities direct attention.
questions.explanation: The author calls the critics’ objection ‘a fair one against Abernell’s study’ but says Iver’s study suggests language plays a role, then proposes that language is one means by which a community teaches attention to surroundings (third and fourth paragraphs): E. A is the main trap: it treats Iver as having settled the matter, though the author says his result ‘does not settle the matter,’ and its ‘rather than’ is the either-or framing the last paragraph rejects. B contradicts the author’s concession, C is the critics’ view, and D overstates the author’s caution.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall position on the Mavuro dispute.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (‘The objection is a fair one… It does not follow, however…’) and fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Three parties: Abernell (language shapes spatial memory), the critics (it’s the surroundings; language is a symptom), the author. The author grants the critics’ point against Abernell’s study, uses Iver to say language does matter after all, and then says the either-or framing is wrong. So the main point has a concession, a claim, and a hedge (‘suggests’). Watch for answers that drop the hedge.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sides with language as the author does. But the author says Iver’s result ‘does not settle the matter,’ and the last paragraph rejects treating language and surroundings as rivals, which is exactly what ‘rather than’ does. Too strong, and the wrong framing.
The author says the opposite: the objection ‘is a fair one against Abernell’s study, which could not separate language from setting.’
This is the critics’ position from the second paragraph, which the author argues does not follow.
Too strong. The author says Iver’s result doesn’t settle it, not that no study can. The author even says what the critics now need to show, which implies further evidence could decide the matter.

CORRECT. Concession (a fair objection to Abernell’s study), claim (language does affect spatial memory), and the last paragraph’s picture (language as a way of directing attention), with the author’s hedge intact.

questions.stem: Abernell’s critics, as described in the passage, would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?
choices: The Mavuro way of describing space is what leads Mavuro speakers to attend closely to the sea.
Abernell’s results would have been reversed had both of her groups been tested in an office.
The children in Iver’s study who preserved left-to-right order were tested in a different setting from the others.
Speakers of the island’s official language whose daily lives were oriented to the sea would tend to rebuild the rows seaward.
A language’s habitual way of describing space has no effect on any aspect of how its speakers think.
questions.explanation: The critics hold that people who spend their days oriented to a single prominent landmark ‘will come to remember arrays by reference to it whatever language they speak’ (second paragraph); applied to official-language speakers oriented to the sea, that predicts seaward rows: D. A is the main trap: it reverses the critics’ causal claim that the Mavuro way of talking is ‘a symptom of that orientation, not its cause.’ B overstates what the critics claimed about the testing location, C contradicts the passage’s account of Iver’s study, and E goes far beyond the critics’ claim about spatial memory.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the critics’ view to a case the passage doesn’t describe.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The critics’ claim has two parts. 1. Orientation to a landmark, not language, makes people remember arrays by that landmark, ‘whatever language they speak.’ 2. So the Mavuro way of talking is a symptom of that orientation. Now apply part 1 to a new group: speakers without a seaward vocabulary but with sea-oriented lives. The critics must expect seaward rows. Watch the causal direction in the traps.

choices.note: Reversed. The critics say the way of talking is ‘a symptom of that orientation, not its cause.’ Same words, opposite arrow.
Too strong. The critics name the testing location as one difference among others, especially where the groups lived. They never predict a full reversal in an office.
Contradicted. Iver’s children all ‘attended the same school and played on the same shore,’ and the passage doesn’t say they were tested apart.
CORRECT. ‘Whatever language they speak’: on the critics’ view, life oriented to the sea, not the Mavuro language, is what produces seaward rows.
Too strong. The critics deny that language explains Abernell’s result. They say nothing about every aspect of thought.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the objection raised by Abernell’s critics can best be described as
choices: dismissive, on the grounds that it rests on a misunderstanding of how Abernell conducted her tasks
accepting of it as a criticism of one study but unpersuaded that it supports the critics’ wider conclusion
persuaded by it that the Mavuro way of speaking is a product of the surroundings in which speakers live
persuaded that it is decisive against Abernell’s conclusion as well as against the design of her study
sympathetic to it at first but convinced by Iver’s study that it was mistaken in every respect
questions.explanation: The author says ‘The objection is a fair one against Abernell’s study’ but ‘It does not follow, however, that language plays no role’ (third paragraph): B. E is the main trap: Iver’s study is used against the critics’ broader claim, not against the objection to Abernell’s study, which the author never withdraws. D is a near-miss that stretches the author’s acceptance from the study’s design to Abernell’s conclusion, A contradicts ‘a fair one,’ and C is the critics’ conclusion the author rejects.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author regards the critics’ objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two claims in the critics’ package: (1) Abernell’s study confounded language and setting; (2) so language is just a symptom. The author accepts (1) (‘a fair one’) and rejects the move to (2) (‘It does not follow’). Attitude answers are usually mixed like this; traps overshoot in one direction.

choices.note: The author calls the objection ‘a fair one.’ Not dismissive at all.
CORRECT. Fair against Abernell’s study; but ‘it does not follow… that language plays no role.’
That’s the critics’ conclusion, which the author says doesn’t follow.

Tempting, because the author does accept the objection to her study’s design. But Abernell’s conclusion is that language shapes how speakers encode space, and the author goes on to say Iver’s study supports a role for language. Fair against the design; not decisive against the conclusion.

Tempting, because Iver’s study does push back on the critics. But it pushes back on their wider claim that language plays no role. The author never says the objection to Abernell’s study was wrong. ‘Every respect’ is the overshoot.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the children in Iver’s study who preserved left-to-right order
choices: belonged to households whose members did not fish
had moved to Pelloc more recently than the others
attended a school apart from the Mavuro-raised children
shared their everyday surroundings with children who rebuilt the rows seaward
were raised in households that had given up the official language
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says all the children ‘attended the same school and played on the same shore,’ yet those from Mavuro-speaking homes rebuilt the rows seaward while ‘the others preserved left and right’: D. A is the main trap: the author raises fishing only as a habit that ‘may go along with’ home language, and never says which households fish. C contradicts ‘the same school,’ E reverses the households, and B is never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the Iver children who kept left and right.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third through fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Who are these children? All of Iver’s children came from families that moved to Pelloc from inland. Some households switched to Mavuro; others kept the official language. The official-language children kept left and right. And all the children shared a school and a shore. That shared setting is the whole point of the study. The right answer may describe it in roundabout words.

choices.note: Tempting, because fishing comes up right after the study. But the author says only that home language ‘may go along with’ habits such as fishing. The passage never says which households fish. Possible isn’t stated.
All the families moved from inland; nothing says when, or that one group came later.
Contradicted: ‘The children all attended the same school.’
CORRECT. Same school, same shore; the children who rebuilt seaward were their schoolmates and playmates.
Reversed. These children came from households that ‘continued to speak the official language.’

questions.stem: The author’s remark that the critics “now need to name some feature of these households, other than language, that differs along with it” (last sentence of the third paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: indicate what the critics would now have to establish for their explanation to withstand Iver’s result
concede that Iver’s result is most likely explained by differences in the households’ working habits
suggest that the critics have already identified the household feature responsible for Iver’s result
argue that no feature of a household other than its language could affect how children remember arrays
show that Iver’s study suffers from the same flaw that undermined Abernell’s earlier study
questions.explanation: Iver’s result is a problem for the critics, and the sentence tells them what would answer it: a household feature other than language that varies with language and could explain the difference: A. B is the main trap: the preceding sentence says home language ‘may go along with’ other habits, a possibility, not the most likely explanation. E is tempting too, but Abernell’s flaw was a difference in setting, which Iver’s design removed; C and D are never claimed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the ‘name some feature’ sentence does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Read the two sentences together. First: Iver’s result ‘does not settle the matter,’ because home language might travel with other habits like fishing. Second: ‘But it changes what the critics must show.’ The critics used to be able to point at different surroundings. Now the surroundings are shared, so they’d need a household difference besides language. The sentence states the critics’ new burden. It does not say that such a feature exists or is likely.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critics’ explanation survives Iver only if some household feature other than language varies with it; the sentence states that requirement.

Tempting, because fishing is named as a possibility. But the author says only that home language ‘may go along with’ such habits. ‘Most likely explained by’ turns a possibility into a verdict, and the next sentence treats the question as open.
If the critics had already named such a feature, they wouldn’t ‘now need to’ name it.
Too strong. The author admits other habits might matter; that’s why the result ‘does not settle the matter.’
Tempting, but Abernell’s flaw was that her groups lived and were tested in different settings. Iver’s children shared a school and shore. Any remaining weakness is a different one.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the function of the last paragraph?
choices: It summarizes the evidence that has led the author to side with Abernell’s critics against Abernell herself.
It proposes that the dispute be resolved by testing children raised in the island’s inland capital.
It concludes that language and surroundings are rival explanations, of which Iver has shown language to be the correct one.
It identifies a flaw in Iver’s study that both Abernell and her critics failed to take into account.
It questions a supposition common to both sides of the dispute and sketches an alternative picture.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says ‘Both sides of this dispute have assumed that language and surroundings are rival explanations’ and then offers ‘a different picture’ in which language is a means of teaching attention to surroundings: E. C is the main trap: it reuses the paragraph’s own phrase ‘rival explanations,’ but as the author’s conclusion, when the paragraph rejects that framing. A, B, and D describe moves the paragraph never makes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what the last paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Two sentences: 1. Both sides assumed language and surroundings are rivals (credit one, subtract from the other). 2. Iver’s findings suggest a different picture: language is one way a community teaches attention to its surroundings. So the paragraph names a shared assumption and offers an alternative. Watch for an answer that uses the paragraph’s words but flips their role.

choices.note: The author doesn’t side with the critics; the third paragraph says their conclusion doesn’t follow.
No new test is proposed, and the inland capital belongs to Abernell’s study.

Tempting, because ‘rival explanations’ is a direct quote. But the paragraph attributes that framing to both sides and then rejects it. The author doesn’t pick a winner between rivals; the author denies they’re rivals.
The possible weakness in Iver’s study (habits like fishing) is raised in the third paragraph, not the fourth.
CORRECT. The shared supposition is that language and surroundings are rivals; the different picture is language as a means of teaching attention to surroundings.

questions.stem: Which one of the following studies would be most analogous in design to Iver’s study as described in the passage?
choices: To learn whether owning a dog leads people to walk more, a researcher compares dog owners in a rural county with people who own no dog in a large city.
To learn whether owning a dog leads people to walk more, a researcher records how much each of a group of people walks in the year before and the year after acquiring a dog.

To learn whether owning a dog leads people to walk more, a researcher studies residents of one apartment complex, all of whom moved there from elsewhere, some of whom have since acquired dogs and some of whom have not.
To learn whether owning a dog leads people to walk more, a researcher compares how much a group of dog owners walk while living in a city with how much they walk after moving to the countryside.

To learn whether owning a dog leads people to walk more, a researcher studies residents of one apartment complex, comparing dog owners who have lived there all their lives with residents without dogs who have recently moved in from elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Iver studied children who shared a school and shore, whose families had all moved in from inland, and who differed in whether their households had taken up Mavuro (third paragraph): one shared setting, a common origin, and a difference that arose after arrival. C matches every element. E is the main trap: same building, but the two groups differ in background as well as in dog ownership, the kind of second difference Iver’s design avoided. A copies Abernell’s design (two groups in different settings), B follows the same people over time, and D varies the setting rather than the factor of interest.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of Iver’s study, not its subject.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, sentences three through five.

breakdown.analysis: Strip Iver’s study to its parts. 1. Everyone shares the same present surroundings (same school, same shore). 2. Everyone has the same origin (families moved from inland). 3.
