The groups differ in one thing they took up after arriving (home language). 4. Compare outcomes. The point of the design is to answer Abernell’s critics by holding setting constant. Check every choice against all four parts; the near-miss will match most of them.

choices.note: This is Abernell’s design: two groups who differ in both the factor of interest and where they live, exactly the confound the critics complained of.
A before-and-after study of the same people. Iver compared two groups at one time.

CORRECT. Shared setting (one complex), shared origin (all moved in from elsewhere), and a difference that arose after arrival (some acquired dogs), as with the families that ‘had adopted Mavuro at home.’
This varies the surroundings while holding the dog constant, which is closer to testing the critics’ hypothesis than to Iver’s design.

Tempting, because the shared building looks like Iver’s shared shore. But the groups also differ in background (lifelong residents vs. newcomers), a second difference that travels with dog ownership. Iver’s groups all came from inland.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with
choices: whether legislatures that renew many expiring laws in a single bill examine any of those laws
whether making a statute’s survival depend on reenactment is a worthwhile legislative practice
whether reporting requirements can serve as an adequate substitute for sunset provisions
how sunset provisions affect the plans of businesses and agencies that must comply with the law
why laws adopted quickly under pressure are especially likely to outlive their original purpose
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that the record of sunset provisions ‘is disappointing,’ and passage B defends them as reversing legislative inertia, so both are about whether requiring reenactment is worthwhile: B. C is the main trap: both passages mention reporting requirements, but each does so only in its final paragraph, as a side comparison. A and D come only from passage A, and E distorts a remark in passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are mainly about.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph of each passage; last paragraph of each for the reporting requirements.

breakdown.analysis: A: sunset provisions don’t deliver the review they promise; get review another way. B: sunset provisions flip the default so defenders must win a vote; reporting does no such thing. Same practice, opposite verdicts. For ‘both… primarily concerned,’ the answer must be central to each, not merely mentioned in each.

choices.note: Only passage A makes this point, and it’s one of A’s three reasons. B mentions perfunctory votes, but not bulk renewal.
CORRECT. A says sunset provisions disappoint; B says they serve a real purpose. Both are about whether the practice is worth having.
Tempting, because both passages mention reporting requirements. But each raises them only at the end, as a side comparison. ‘Primarily concerned with’ needs the main topic.
Only passage A, and only its third reason.

Passage B says sunset provisions matter most for such laws because legislators couldn’t check their predictions. It never says these laws are more likely to outlive their purpose, and passage A doesn’t discuss them.

questions.stem: Passage A suggests which one of the following about the costs that sunset provisions impose on businesses and agencies?
choices: They are incurred whether or not the law in question ultimately lapses.
They fall most heavily on the organized interests that benefit from the law in question.
They could be avoided if renewal votes were held well before a law was due to expire.
They are the chief reason that legislatures renew expiring laws together in a single bill.
They are borne by agencies deciding whether to hire but not by businesses deciding whether to invest.
questions.explanation: Passage A’s third paragraph says those who must comply ‘must discount for the chance that the law will lapse, and they bear that cost even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt’; so the cost comes from the uncertainty itself, not from the outcome: A. B is the main trap: organized interests appear in passage A’s second objection, about renewal debates, not in the planning-cost objection. C and D are never said, and E contradicts the paragraph, which names both businesses and agencies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A implies about who bears planning costs and when.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph says compliance planning must discount for the chance of a lapse, and the cost is borne ‘even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt.’ So it doesn’t matter whether the law actually lapses: the cost is paid in advance, because of the possibility. We need that point in general terms. Traps will pull in pieces of A’s other two objections.

choices.note: CORRECT. The cost is paid when businesses and agencies plan, so it arises ‘even for laws whose renewal is never in doubt’ and, plainly, for laws that do lapse.

Tempting, because organized interests are central to passage A’s second objection. But that objection is about renewal debates. The planning costs fall on ‘businesses deciding whether to invest and agencies deciding whether to hire.’
Passage A never discusses the timing of renewal votes as a fix. The uncertainty lasts as long as the law can lapse.
Bulk renewal is the first objection, and passage A explains it by the number of expiring provisions, not by planning costs.
Contradicted. Both ‘businesses deciding whether to invest’ and ‘agencies deciding whether to hire’ are named.

questions.stem: In passage B, the author’s discussion of the observation that renewal votes are often perfunctory serves primarily to
choices: grant a criticism of sunset provisions while denying that it shows the provisions lack value
dispute the evidence on which critics rely in claiming that renewal votes are seldom substantive
show that perfunctory renewal votes occur more often for emergency measures than for other laws
suggest that a legislator who objects to a law will usually be able to prevent the law’s renewal
argue that renewal votes would receive more attention if fewer laws carried sunset dates
questions.explanation: Passage B answers the critics with ‘Perhaps so; but even a perfunctory vote must be taken,’ granting the point and then saying the required vote still makes the law’s defenders assemble a majority: A. D is the main trap: passage B says the requirement gives a doubting legislator ‘a moment’ at which defenders must assemble a majority, not that the legislator can usually block renewal. B contradicts ‘Perhaps so,’ C is never claimed, and E is passage A’s point, not passage B’s.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what passage B does with the critics’ point about perfunctory votes.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph of passage B, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Concede-and-rebut: ‘Critics observe… Perhaps so; but…’ The author doesn’t fight the fact. The author says the fact doesn’t matter much, because even a perfunctory vote forces the law’s defenders to win a majority. Note the strength of the rebuttal: it gives doubters ‘a moment,’ not a veto.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Perhaps so’ grants the criticism; ‘but even a perfunctory vote must be taken’ denies that it makes the requirement worthless.
The author doesn’t dispute the evidence; ‘Perhaps so’ accepts it.
Emergency measures come up in the sentence before, but nothing compares how perfunctory their renewal votes are.

Tempting, because the passage does say the requirement helps a doubting legislator. But what it guarantees is ‘a moment at which the law’s defenders… must assemble a majority.’ The defenders may well assemble it. A moment isn’t a veto.
This echoes passage A (‘the more laws carry sunset dates, the less attention each renewal can receive’). Passage B never says it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following legislative rules would the author of passage B be most likely to regard as securing the chief advantage that passage B attributes to sunset provisions?
choices: a rule allowing any legislator to force a vote, at any time, on whether to repeal an existing law
a rule requiring agencies to report yearly on a law’s effects to a committee that must hold hearings on each report
a rule requiring a two-thirds majority, rather than a simple majority, to repeal any emergency measure
a rule allowing any legislator to force a vote at which a law will lapse unless a majority votes to keep it
a rule requiring the sponsors of any new law to state the predictions on which it rests and what evidence would refute them
questions.explanation: Passage B values sunset provisions because they reverse legislative inertia: ‘the law lapses unless a majority affirmatively wants to keep it,’ guaranteeing a doubting legislator ‘a moment at which the law’s defenders, not its opponents, must assemble a majority.’ D gives a doubter exactly that moment. A is the main trap: it gives any legislator a vote, but on repeal, so the opponents must still assemble the majority, the very default passage B wants reversed. B is passage A’s alternative, which passage B says offers ‘no such moment,’ C strengthens the default, and E echoes passage B’s point about predictions without shifting who must win the vote.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply passage B’s reason for valuing sunset provisions to rules it never discusses.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph (inertia and its reversal) and second paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: What exactly does passage B like? Not review, not attention: the reversal of the default. Without a sunset, a law survives until opponents assemble a majority; with one, the law dies unless defenders assemble one. And the vote must happen, so a doubter is guaranteed that moment. So the rule we want must (1) give a doubting legislator a guaranteed vote and (2) make the law’s defenders, not its opponents, win it. Check both conditions. The near-miss satisfies only the first.

choices.note: Tempting, because it guarantees a vote on demand. But a repeal vote succeeds only if opponents assemble a majority; the law survives by default. That’s the inertia passage B wants reversed.
This is passage A’s recommendation. Passage B says reporting requirements ‘offer no such moment’ and produce documents ‘no one is obliged to read.’
This makes repeal harder, strengthening the default in favor of existing law, the opposite of what passage B values.
CORRECT. A doubter can force the moment, and at that moment the law lapses unless its defenders muster a majority. Both conditions of passage B’s advantage are met.
Tempting, because passage B worries about laws based on predictions legislators ‘had no way to check.’ But stating predictions doesn’t change who must assemble a majority to keep or end the law.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes a legislative practice without evaluating it, while passage B evaluates that practice and recommends its wider use.
Passage B responds in turn to each of the objections raised in passage A and concludes that none of those objections succeeds.
Passage B defends a practice that passage A criticizes, answering some but not all of passage A’s considerations.
Passage A proposes an alternative to a practice, and passage B argues that the alternative has the same defects as the practice.
Passage B presents a general principle about legislative inertia, and passage A applies that principle to one kind of statute.
questions.explanation: Passage B defends sunset provisions, answers passage A’s point about perfunctory renewal and its preference for reporting requirements, but says nothing about lobbying at renewal or the cost of uncertainty: C. B is the main trap: passage B does reply to some of passage A’s objections, but not to all of them, and it never says that all of them fail. A misdescribes passage A, D gives passage B the wrong complaint about reporting, and E reverses which passage is general.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s three reasons and last paragraph; passage B’s second and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Make a checklist of A’s points: 1. renewal is perfunctory; 2. organized interests use renewal to expand laws; 3. uncertainty costs; 4. use reporting instead. Now check B: it answers 1 (‘Perhaps so; but…’) and 4 (‘Reporting requirements… offer no such moment’). It says nothing about 2 or 3. So B is a defense that covers part of A’s case.

choices.note: Passage A clearly evaluates: ‘The record of such provisions is disappointing.’ And passage B doesn’t recommend wider use.

Tempting, because passage B does answer passage A’s points about perfunctory votes and reporting. But it ignores lobbying and uncertainty, and never says all the objections fail. ‘Each’ is too strong.
CORRECT. Opposite verdicts on the same practice; B answers points 1 and 4 of A’s case but not 2 and 3.
Passage B criticizes reporting for a different reason (no one must act on the reports), not for the defects passage A finds in sunset provisions.
Backwards. Passage B gives the general point about inertia, but passage A doesn’t apply it; A argues against the practice B defends.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles most accurately describes the content of passage A and passage B, respectively?
choices: “Sunset Provisions and the Cost of Uncertainty” and “The Case Against Legislative Reporting Requirements”
“How Organized Interests Capture Renewal Debates” and “Why Renewal Votes Are Seldom Perfunctory”
“The Hidden Benefits of Renewing Laws in Bulk” and “Emergency Powers and the Need for Expiration Dates”
“Better Ways to Review Old Laws” and “Expiration Dates for Emergency Measures”
“The Unkept Promise of Expiring Statutes” and “Expiration Dates as a Check on Legislative Inertia”
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that sunset provisions fail to deliver the review for which they are defended; passage B defends them as reversing the inertia that favors existing law: E. D is the main trap: each title names a real part of a passage (A’s last paragraph, B’s second), but neither captures the passage as a whole. A’s titles are likewise single points, B’s second title contradicts passage B’s ‘Perhaps so,’ and C’s first title reverses passage A’s complaint about bulk renewal.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the pair that captures each passage’s overall content.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, first and last paragraphs; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Summarize each passage in a phrase first. A: sunset provisions are defended as forcing review, but they don’t deliver it (three reasons), and review can be had another way. B: sunset provisions are worth having because they flip legislative inertia. A good title pair says ‘a disappointing promise’ for A and ‘reversing inertia’ for B. Both halves have to fit; titles that name one paragraph are the standard trap.

choices.note: Each title names one point: A’s third objection and B’s last paragraph. Neither is the passage’s main concern.
A’s first title names only its second objection, and B never says renewal votes are seldom perfunctory; it says ‘Perhaps so.’
Passage A presents bulk renewal as a problem, not a hidden benefit.

Tempting, because both titles name something really in the passages: A recommends reporting and hearings, and B stresses emergency measures. But A is mostly a critique of sunset provisions, and B’s argument covers any law with a sunset, emergency measures being where it ‘matters most.’

CORRECT. ‘Unkept promise’ fits A’s claim that the provisions’ record is ‘disappointing’ against the review they are said to force; ‘check on legislative inertia’ fits B’s central claim that a sunset ‘reverses this default.’

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: it is worthwhile to learn whether existing laws have achieved the aims for which they were enacted
a required vote on whether a law should survive is of value even if few legislators examine the law before voting
organized interests that benefit from a law tend to work to keep that law in force
laws adopted in emergencies should be made to expire on a set date unless they are reenacted
votes to renew expiring laws are often taken without much attention to the laws being renewed
questions.explanation: Passage A treats renewal in which ‘few legislators examine any particular law’ as a failure and objects to staking a law’s survival ‘on a vote that may never receive real attention’; passage B says ‘even a perfunctory vote must be taken’ and that the requirement guarantees a doubter a moment at which defenders must assemble a majority: B. E is the main trap: it sounds like the dispute, but passage B concedes it (‘Perhaps so’). A and C are points both authors accept, and D is addressed only by passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would accept and the other would reject.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and last paragraphs; passage B, second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. The tempting candidate is the fact about perfunctory votes, but B grants it (‘Perhaps so’). The real split is about what follows from it. A: a vote that gets no real attention delivers nothing worth the costs; review should come another way. B: even a perfunctory vote does something, since the law’s defenders must still win it. So they disagree about whether an inattentive required vote has value.

choices.note: Both agree. Passage A says ‘Review of whether laws work is worth having,’ and passage B wants laws whose predictions fail to end.

CORRECT. Passage A counts inattentive renewal as the provisions’ failure and wants review ‘without staking the law’s survival on a vote that may never receive real attention’; passage B says the perfunctory vote still forces defenders to assemble a majority.
Both agree. Passage A says beneficiaries press their case at renewal; passage B says those who benefit can keep a repeal majority from forming.
Only passage B addresses emergency measures. Passage A says nothing about them, so there is no evidence of disagreement.
Tempting, because it’s the critics’ observation that passage B answers. But passage B answers ‘Perhaps so’: it accepts the fact and disputes only its significance. Both authors agree here.

passages.title: Laclos and the novel in letters
passages.subject: humanities
passages.text:
When Pierre Choderlos de Laclos published Les Liaisons dangereuses in 1782, the novel in letters had been fashionable for four decades. Samuel Richardson’s Pamela (1740) and Clarissa (1747–1748) had made the form’s appeal plain: because each letter is written in the midst of events, before its writer knows how they will turn out, the reader seems to overhear a mind at a particular moment, a method Richardson described as “writing to the moment.” The letter, so understood, was a confession that happened to have an addressee.

Laclos kept the form and emptied it of that assumption. His two principal correspondents, the Vicomte de Valmont and the Marquise de Merteuil, write chiefly to produce effects: to seduce, to flatter, to recruit an ally or to wound one. Valmont addresses Madame de Tourvel, the devout married woman he is pursuing, in the language of reverent passion, and in one notorious letter he composes a fervent letter to her using the back of a courtesan as his writing desk, then forwards it through Merteuil, inviting her to read it first and savor its double meanings. No letter in the book can be taken at its word, and the novel can seem at first an assault on the very sincerity that had made the form popular.

Yet the access to private feeling that the form had promised is not abolished in Les Liaisons dangereuses so much as handed to someone else. The novel’s 175 letters go to many recipients, and no character reads more than a portion of them. Tourvel never sees what Valmont writes about her to Merteuil; Cécile Volanges, the convent-educated girl whom the two libertines set out to corrupt, never learns how her confidences are discussed. Only the reader holds the whole correspondence, and the discrepancies among letters disclose what no single letter states: the moments when Valmont’s reports to Merteuil grow defensive about a woman he claims merely to be conquering. Some readers find this position uncomfortable, since it so resembles the libertines’ own. The resemblance seems deliberate.

The plot bears this out. Valmont and Merteuil are formidable as long as each of them sees letters that others do not; they are ruined when that privilege passes to others. Mortally wounded in a duel with Danceny, Cécile’s young admirer, Valmont gives him a packet of Merteuil’s letters, and once their contents circulate, her standing in society collapses. The catastrophe is not simply that a deceiver is exposed—her correspondents had been deceived for months without the novel’s treating that as a disaster—but that others at last occupy the vantage the reader has held all along. Laclos does not repudiate the form’s promise of intimacy; he shows that it was always kept by the collection rather than the single letter, and makes possession of the collection the substance of power.

passages.title: Looking time and infant expectation
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Since the mid-1980s, much of what psychologists claim to know about infants’ minds has rested on one measure: how long an infant looks at something. In the violation-of-expectation method, developed largely by Renée Baillargeon and Elizabeth Spelke, infants see two outcomes of a scene, one possible and one not. In a typical study, a ball rolls behind a screen toward a solid wall; when the screen is removed, the ball rests either in front of the wall or beyond it, as though it had passed through. Infants of three or four months generally look longer at the second outcome, which many researchers take to show that they expected the ball to stop. If so, infants grasp that solid objects cannot pass through one another months before they will search for a hidden object, the behavior on which Jean Piaget based a much later timetable.

The difficulty is that a second explanation fits the same data. Infants look longer at displays that differ perceptually from those they have grown used to, and in many such studies the impossible outcome is also the less familiar display: the ball comes to rest in a position the infant has not seen it occupy. Critics in the late 1990s, Marshall Haith among them, argued that the studies credited infants with knowledge that a leaner, perceptual account did not require. On the lean account the infant registers that something looks new; on the rich account, that something is impossible.

Neither side has dislodged the other, partly because of the measure itself. Proponents of the rich account have matched the two outcomes ever more closely in position, color, and timing, controls that early studies did not think necessary, and a difference in looking time often survives. But infants do not always prefer the novel: after brief exposure to a display they often look longer at what is familiar, and only with longer exposure does the preference reverse. A perceptual account armed with both tendencies can accommodate a difference in either direction, which makes it hard to refute; but by the same token a surviving difference cannot settle the matter, since each account can claim it.

What would decide it is a measure of expectation taken before there is anything new to see. Eye-tracking allows one: researchers can record where an infant looks just before the ball reaches the wall. An infant who expects the ball to stop should glance toward the near side of the wall, where it ought to come to rest; an infant guided only by novelty has, at that moment, nothing novel to respond to. Such measures have limits, revealing expectations about where an object will be rather than about all its properties. If they confirm what looking times suggested, the rich account will have earned its conclusion. It will not have earned it from looking times alone.

passages.title: Counting the Chartist petitions
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Between 1839 and 1848 the Chartists, campaigning for the six points of the People’s Charter, among them a vote for every adult man and the secret ballot, presented three national petitions to the House of Commons. Their organizers claimed some 1.3 million signatures for the first, more than 3 million for the second, and nearly 6 million for the third. The Commons rejected the first two by large majorities, and when its clerks examined the 1848 petition they reported fewer than 2 million signatures, many of them plainly fictitious, such as “Victoria Rex” and “Punch.” For opponents the count was a vindication; for later historians sympathetic to the movement, even the reduced figures recorded a mass demand in a country where few working men could vote.

Both readings treat a signature as something like a vote, and it is doubtful that it was one. Signatures were gathered at mass meetings, where the petition was read aloud and approved by acclamation before sheets were passed through the crowd, and by collectors who carried sheets from door to door and through workshops and public houses. A name might record conviction, but it might equally record a reluctance to be seen refusing a neighbor. Totals also confound opinion with opportunity. A collector in a crowded manufacturing district could reach hundreds of households in a day, while one working scattered rural parishes might reach a few dozen, so a town would yield far more signatures per day of canvassing than a village even if sympathy there were no greater.

The historian Margaret Ellery has proposed a way to draw from the petitions only what they can bear. Working from the town-by-town totals that Chartist newspapers printed, she expresses each locality’s signatures as a share of its adult male population, and she compares only localities alike in density and in how signatures were collected: meeting with meeting, house-to-house canvass with house-to-house canvass. Where two manufacturing towns of similar size, both canvassed door to door, differ sharply in the share of men who signed, the difference is unlikely to be an artifact of collection, and it becomes reasonable to read it as a difference in sympathy.

What the method yields is narrower than what either earlier reading claimed, and properly so. It cannot say how many Britons supported the Charter, and it cannot be applied wherever the manner of collection went unrecorded, which was often. Nor does it neutralize invented names: if these were commoner in some towns than in others, they would distort shares as surely as they distort totals. What it offers is a map of relative strength among comparable places, a kind of evidence that the totals, however large, could never have supplied.

passages.title: Funding research by lottery
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
Passage A

Most public research funding is allocated by peer review: panels of scientists score proposals, and those ranked highest are funded until the money runs out. When agencies could fund a third or more of the proposals they received, this system worked tolerably well. Some now fund fewer than one in seven, and the line between funded and unfunded proposals falls deep within a large group that reviewers regard as excellent.

Within that group, the evidence that panels can tell better proposals from worse is weak. When the same proposals have been scored independently by different panels, the panels have agreed reasonably well about which proposals were weak but scarcely better than chance about how to order the strong ones. Yet it is that ordering which now decides who is funded. The weeks scientists spend polishing each proposal, time taken from research itself, are thus spent on a contest whose outcome is close to random already.

A better system would admit the randomness openly. Panels would do what they do well, separating fundable proposals from unfundable ones, and grants would then be awarded by lot among the fundable, as New Zealand’s Health Research Council has done with its Explorer Grants since 2015. Because the present ordering carries so little information, nothing of value would be given up: science funded by lot would be as good as science funded by rank. A lottery would also free applicants from an arms race of presentation, and it cannot be swayed by a preference for familiar approaches or prestigious institutions, biases that, unlike merit, panels apply with great consistency.

Passage B

Advocates of funding research by lottery rest their case on the unreliability of peer review among strong proposals. The evidence for that unreliability is good; the inference drawn from it is not. A ranking that is unreliable for any single proposal can still be informative on average: if panels place truly stronger proposals in the upper half of the fundable group even modestly more often than chance, then funding by rank will, across thousands of grants, support somewhat better science than funding by lot.

There is also the matter of how applicants would respond. Under a lottery, a proposal that barely clears the threshold has the same chance as an outstanding one, and applicants who understand this will have reason to submit many adequate proposals rather than a few excellent ones. The volume of applications, already burdensome to reviewers, could rise sharply, and the threshold, now the only point at which merit would count, would have to bear the full weight of selection.

The Swiss National Science Foundation has taken a more cautious course, drawing lots only among proposals that its panels cannot separate at the funding line and ranking wherever rankings carry information. That reform is narrower than the advocates’ proposal, but its costs can be measured.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Les Liaisons dangereuses exposed as an illusion the sincerity that Richardson’s novels had attributed to letters, and in doing so it brought the vogue for the novel in letters to a close.
Because Valmont and Merteuil write chiefly to produce effects on their readers, no letter in Les Liaisons dangereuses can be taken as a reliable record of what its writer feels.
By giving its reader the same vantage as its libertines, Les Liaisons dangereuses implicates that reader in the corruption it depicts and thereby condemns the appeal of the epistolary form.
Rather than discarding the form’s promise of access to private feeling, Laclos’s novel moves that access from the single letter to the whole correspondence, on which its plot also turns.
Les Liaisons dangereuses suggests that letters reveal their writers’ feelings most fully when they reach readers for whom they were never intended, as Merteuil’s letters do at the novel’s end.
questions.explanation: The passage concedes that Laclos ‘emptied’ the form of the assumption that a letter is a confession (second paragraph), then argues that the form’s access to private feeling is ‘handed to someone else,’ the reader who holds the whole correspondence (third paragraph), and that the plot makes possession of the collection ‘the substance of power’ (fourth). D states that. B is the dominant trap: it is the second paragraph’s point, which the passage says the novel only ‘can seem at first’ to amount to. A and C overstate, and E distorts the ending.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall claim about how Laclos’s novel uses the letter form.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (‘emptied it of that assumption’), third paragraph (‘not abolished … so much as handed to someone else’), last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The passage has a fake-out built in. Paragraph 2 makes it look like the novel attacks the idea that letters reveal the heart. Then ‘Yet’: the access isn’t abolished, it moves, from the single letter to the whole set of letters, which only the reader (and, at the end, Merteuil’s enemies) can see. We need an answer that keeps both the move and the payoff in the plot.

choices.note: Too strong, twice. The passage never says the novel ended the vogue, and it denies that the novel simply exposes the form’s promise as an illusion: Laclos ‘does not repudiate the form’s promise of intimacy.’

Tempting, because this is exactly what the second paragraph says. But it’s the setup the author goes on to qualify: the novel only ‘can seem at first’ an assault on sincerity. A main point can’t stop at the part the author turns away from.

Overreach. Some readers find the reader’s position ‘uncomfortable’ and the author calls the resemblance ‘deliberate,’ but nothing says the novel condemns the form’s appeal. The author says the opposite: Laclos keeps its promise in a new place.

CORRECT. ‘Moves that access from the single letter to the whole correspondence’ is ‘handed to someone else’ and ‘kept by the collection rather than the single letter’; ‘on which its plot also turns’ is the fourth paragraph’s point that possession of the collection is power.

Distortion of the ending. The disaster for Merteuil is that others gain the reader’s vantage of setting letters side by side, not that misdirected letters are especially revealing. And this misses the passage’s central claim about the reader.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the letter that Valmont composes using a courtesan’s back as a writing desk
choices: is written on the same evening as a letter to Merteuil that describes his pursuit of Tourvel as an exercise in tactics
is read by Merteuil, at Valmont’s invitation, before it reaches the woman to whom it is addressed
is among the letters that Valmont hands to Danceny after being wounded in their duel
is the first letter in which Valmont’s growing attachment to Tourvel becomes evident to Merteuil
is taken by Tourvel as a sincere expression of the reverent passion that Valmont professes
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Valmont ‘forwards it through Merteuil, inviting her to read it first and savor its double meanings.’ B restates that. E is the most tempting trap: it may be true of the novel, but the passage never says how Tourvel received the letter. C borrows the duel from the fourth paragraph, where the packet contains Merteuil’s letters, not this one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about one specific letter.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: A plain detail question, so go back to the sentence. Valmont writes to Tourvel, sends the letter through Merteuil, and invites her to read it first. The right answer just restates the routing. Watch for answers that sound like the novel but aren’t in the passage.

choices.note: Not stated. The passage mentions no companion letter written that evening; it says only that Valmont uses ‘the language of reverent passion’ with Tourvel.
CORRECT. ‘Forwards it through Merteuil, inviting her to read it first’ = Merteuil reads it, at his invitation, before Tourvel gets it.
Wrong letters. The packet Valmont gives Danceny contains Merteuil’s letters, not his own letter to Tourvel.
Valmont’s defensiveness about Tourvel is mentioned in the third paragraph, but nothing ties it to this letter or calls any letter the first sign of it.
Tempting, because it fits what we’d guess about the plot. But the passage never says how Tourvel took the letter. True-sounding isn’t the same as stated.

questions.stem: In saying that the access to private feeling is “handed to someone else” (first sentence of the third paragraph), the author most likely means that
choices: Laclos gives Merteuil, rather than the letter writers themselves, the task of revealing what the novel’s characters feel
the private feelings that the novel discloses are ultimately those of its reader rather than those of any of its characters
the sincerity that Richardson located in the letter writer is located by Laclos in the recipients of the letters
Valmont’s feelings are disclosed less by his own letters than by the replies that Merteuil writes to him
what the characters leave unsaid can be discerned only by someone able to compare letters sent to different people
questions.explanation: The rest of the third paragraph explains the phrase: no character reads more than a portion of the letters, ‘only the reader holds the whole correspondence,’ and ‘the discrepancies among letters disclose what no single letter states.’ E paraphrases that. A is the dominant trap: Merteuil does see letters others don’t, but the passage assigns the disclosing vantage to the reader, and Merteuil is herself one of the writers being seen through. C moves sincerity to the recipients, who in fact see only part of the correspondence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Work out what ‘handed to someone else’ means from the sentences that follow it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, especially ‘Only the reader holds the whole correspondence’ and ‘the discrepancies among letters disclose what no single letter states.’

breakdown.analysis: Who is the ‘someone else’? Read on: no character sees more than a portion of the letters; the reader sees them all; the gaps between letters reveal what no letter says. So the access moves from the letter writer’s confession to whoever can compare letters to different people. The right answer will describe that vantage, probably without saying ‘reader’ outright.

choices.note: Tempting, because Merteuil sees letters others don’t and gets to read Valmont’s letter to Tourvel. But the passage says ‘only the reader holds the whole correspondence’; Merteuil is one of the writers whose letters the reader sees through.
Twists it. The feelings disclosed are still the characters’ (Valmont’s, for instance). What changes is who can see them, not whose feelings they are.
The recipients are the people who see only part. Tourvel and Cécile never learn what’s written about them. Moving the access to the recipients gets the passage backward.
Merteuil’s replies aren’t discussed as revealing Valmont. The example is his own reports growing defensive, visible when set beside other letters.
CORRECT. ‘Someone able to compare letters sent to different people’ is the reader who ‘holds the whole correspondence’; ‘what the characters leave unsaid’ is ‘what no single letter states.’

questions.stem: The passage attributes to some readers of Les Liaisons dangereuses which one of the following views?
choices: The novel places its reader in a position uncomfortably close to that of its scheming letter writers.
The resemblance between the reader’s position and that of the novel’s libertines was intended by Laclos.
The novel’s letters disclose, in their discrepancies, feelings that none of them states outright.
The novel is at bottom an assault on the very sincerity that had made the novel in letters popular.
The power of Valmont and Merteuil depends on their seeing letters that others do not see.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says ‘Some readers find this position uncomfortable, since it so resembles the libertines’ own.’ A paraphrases that view. B is the dominant trap: the next sentence, ‘The resemblance seems deliberate,’ is the author’s own claim, not the readers’. C and E are also the author’s claims, and D is the provisional impression the author raises in the second paragraph and then qualifies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Sort out which view belongs to ‘some readers’ rather than to the author.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: ‘Some readers’ get exactly one sentence: they find the reader’s position uncomfortable because it resembles the libertines’. Everything around that sentence is the author talking. So the trap answers will be true statements from the passage that belong to the wrong party. Classic wrong-party setup.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Uncomfortably close to that of its scheming letter writers’ = they find it ‘uncomfortable’ because it ‘so resembles the libertines’ own.’
Tempting, because it’s the very next sentence. But ‘The resemblance seems deliberate’ is the author’s judgment. The readers report discomfort; the passage never says they think Laclos meant it.
True in the passage, but it’s the author’s claim, made in the author’s voice. Wrong party.
This is how the novel ‘can seem at first,’ in the author’s framing, and the author goes on to deny it. It isn’t attributed to any group of readers.
The author’s claim, from the fourth paragraph. Wrong party again.

questions.stem: The author discusses the circulation of Merteuil’s letters (fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: illustrate the view, introduced in the second paragraph, that the novel is at bottom an attack on the sincerity of letters
suggest that the letters in the novel reveal the truth about their writers only once they have been made public
show that a principle governing how the novel discloses its characters’ feelings also governs the outcome of its story
argue that Merteuil’s downfall is a punishment for deception that the novel as a whole endorses
explain how Valmont’s growing attachment to Tourvel led to his fatal quarrel with Danceny
questions.explanation: The third paragraph argues that feeling is disclosed to whoever holds the whole correspondence; the fourth opens ‘The plot bears this out’ and uses Merteuil’s ruin to show that power, too, belongs to whoever sees the letters others don’t. C names that link between form and plot without echoing the passage’s words. D is the dominant trap, since Merteuil is a deceiver who is exposed, but the author says the catastrophe ‘is not simply that a deceiver is exposed.’ A attaches the episode to the reading the author sets aside.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings in the ending of the novel.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, first two sentences and ‘The catastrophe is not simply that a deceiver is exposed.’

breakdown.analysis: ‘The plot bears this out.’ Bears what out? The third paragraph’s claim: whoever holds the whole set of letters can see what no single letter says. In the ending, Merteuil falls when others finally get that vantage. So the episode shows the novel’s way of revealing feeling and its plot run on one principle. The trap is the moral reading (the liar gets punished), which the author explicitly sets aside.

choices.note: The second paragraph’s ‘assault on sincerity’ is the first impression the author corrects. The ending is used to support the correction, not that impression.
Overgeneralizes. The point isn’t that publicity reveals truth; it’s that whoever can compare letters gains power. And the reader sees through the letters long before any are made public.
CORRECT. The ‘principle’ is that whoever holds the collection sees what single letters hide; ‘The plot bears this out,’ since power passes with that vantage. Form and story run on the same rule.

Tempting, because Merteuil is a deceiver and she is ruined. But the author says the catastrophe ‘is not simply that a deceiver is exposed,’ noting that her deceptions went on for months without the novel treating them as a disaster. ‘Endorses’ adds a moral verdict the passage never gives.
The passage says Valmont’s reports grow defensive about Tourvel, but it never explains the duel, let alone traces it to that attachment.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A traditional view of a literary form is described; a critic’s objection to that view is presented; the objection is partly accepted; and an episode from a novel is cited in support of the resulting revision.
Two novelists’ uses of a literary form are contrasted; the later novelist’s innovations are enumerated; and the earlier novelist’s influence on the later one is assessed.
The premise behind a form’s appeal is set out; a work is shown to reject it in one respect; the work is said to honor the form’s promise otherwise; and its plot is read accordingly.
A novel’s notoriety is described; a reading that accounts for that notoriety is proposed; an objection to the reading is considered; and the objection is rejected on the basis of the novel’s ending.
A literary form is defined; a novel that ended the form’s popularity is identified; and the causes of the form’s decline are traced through that novel’s plot.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph sets out why letters appealed (each seemed a confession written ‘to the moment’); the second shows Laclos denying that letters can be taken at their word; the third says the promise of access survives in the whole correspondence; the fourth reads the plot accordingly. C tracks that. A is the dominant trap: it is the familiar critique template, but no critic objects to the traditional view here; it is Laclos’s novel that does. D misreads the ‘some readers’ remark as an objection to the author’s reading.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the passage’s structure paragraph by paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Topic sentences of all four paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: (1) why the letter form appealed: a letter seemed a confession; (2) Laclos’s letters are performances, so that premise fails; (3) ‘Yet’ the promise survives, moved to the reader; (4) the plot runs on the same idea. No named critic, no objection-and-reply. The right answer will be abstract; the trap will be the standard ‘view, critic, partial acceptance’ outline.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s the shape of many RC passages. But there is no critic’s objection here. The ‘traditional view’ is undercut by a novel, and the only other voices (‘some readers’) offer a reaction, not an objection the author partly accepts.
Richardson is background in a single sentence; nothing is said about his influence on Laclos, and the passage lists no catalog of innovations.

CORRECT. Premise: a letter is a confession (paragraph 1). Rejected in one respect: no letter can be taken at its word (2). Promise honored by other means: the whole correspondence discloses feeling (3). Plot read in that light (4).

Close but off. The ‘some readers’ who find the reader’s position uncomfortable aren’t objecting to the author’s reading, and the author doesn’t reject them; the author agrees the resemblance is real and ‘deliberate.’
The passage never says the novel ended the form’s popularity, and the plot is read for how it reflects the form, not for why the form declined.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about a novel consisting entirely of letters written by one character to a single correspondent?
choices: It would give readers more reliable access to its letter writer’s private feelings than Laclos’s novel does, since its writer would have only one reader to manipulate.
Its letters, unlike Valmont’s and Merteuil’s, could not properly be read as attempts to produce effects on their recipient.
It would be more likely than Laclos’s novel to achieve what Richardson described as writing to the moment.
Its letters would disclose more of their writer’s unstated feelings to its reader than to the correspondent who received them.
It could not reveal its letter writer’s unstated feelings by the means through which, on the author’s account, Laclos’s novel reveals those of its characters.
questions.explanation: On the author’s account, Laclos’s novel discloses feeling through ‘discrepancies among letters’ to different recipients, which only the reader, holding the whole correspondence, can compare (third paragraph). With one writer and one correspondent there are no letters to other recipients to set beside each other, so that means is unavailable: E. A is the dominant trap: it assumes fewer audiences means more sincerity, but the passage gives no reason to think a single addressee makes letters less of a performance. D carries the reader’s advantage over into a case where the correspondent sees every letter the reader sees.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply the author’s account of how Laclos’s novel reveals feeling to a novel with one writer and one recipient.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph (‘letters go to many recipients … discrepancies among letters disclose what no single letter states’).

breakdown.analysis: What makes disclosure work in Laclos? Many recipients, each seeing a part; the reader sees all and spots the gaps between versions. Strip that down to one writer and one recipient: the recipient sees everything the reader sees, and there are no differing versions for different audiences. So that particular mechanism is gone. The right answer should say exactly that, and no more. Don’t buy the intuitive idea that one audience means honesty; the passage never says so.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds intuitive: one audience, less manipulation. But the passage never says manipulation scales with the number of recipients, and in its account access to feeling comes from comparing letters, which this novel can’t offer.
Too strong. Any letter is written to someone; nothing in the passage suggests a single recipient makes a letter immune to being a performance.
‘Writing to the moment’ is about writing before one knows how events turn out. The number of correspondents has nothing to do with it.

Tempting if you carry over the idea that the reader always knows more. But here the correspondent receives every letter, so the reader holds nothing the correspondent lacks. The reader’s edge in Laclos comes from seeing letters to other people, and there are none.
CORRECT. Laclos’s means is the comparison of letters sent to different people. A single writer to a single correspondent produces no such set, so that route to unstated feeling is closed.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Looking-time differences cannot show whether young infants grasp that solid objects block one another, though a measure of where infants look before an outcome could.
Infants’ longer looking at impossible outcomes reflects the perceptual unfamiliarity of those outcomes rather than any expectation about how solid objects will behave.
That a difference in looking time survives careful matching of the two outcomes shows that young infants expect solid objects to stop when they meet a barrier.
Eye-tracking studies have now confirmed that infants of three or four months know that solid objects cannot pass through one another.
Developmental psychologists should abandon looking-time measures in favor of procedures that record where infants look before an event is complete.
questions.explanation: The passage presents a finding, two accounts of it, an argument that looking time cannot decide between them (third paragraph), and a measure that could (‘What would decide it’). A states both halves. C is the rich account’s reply, which the author says ‘cannot settle the matter’; B is the lean account, which the author never endorses. D treats a conditional (‘If they confirm…’) as a result, and E overstates: the author wants anticipatory measures added, not looking time abandoned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall conclusion about the looking-time debate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, last sentence; fourth paragraph, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Two accounts, one set of data. The author doesn’t pick a side on what infants know. The author’s claim is about evidence: looking time can’t decide it; anticipatory looking could. So the answer needs that ‘can’t / could’ pair and must stay neutral on which account is true.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Cannot show’ = ‘a surviving difference cannot settle the matter’; ‘a measure of where infants look before an outcome could’ = ‘What would decide it is a measure of expectation taken before there is anything new to see.’
This is the lean account. The author says it fits the data, not that it’s right, and allows that the rich account may ‘earn its conclusion.’

Tempting, since the passage says the difference ‘often survives.’ But the author says such a surviving difference ‘cannot settle the matter, since each account can claim it.’ This is the proponents’ position, not the author’s.
Possibility treated as fact. The passage says what eye-tracking could show and adds ‘If they confirm…’; no result is reported.
Too strong. The author says looking time can’t decide the question alone, not that it should be dropped. Anticipatory measures have ‘limits’ of their own.

questions.stem: According to the passage, infants who have been exposed only briefly to a display
choices: look longer at an impossible outcome only if that outcome is also perceptually novel
show no consistent preference between familiar displays and novel ones
often look longer at what they have already seen than at something new
look longer at novel displays, a preference that reverses after longer exposure
are less likely than other infants to look toward where a moving object should stop
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says ‘after brief exposure to a display they often look longer at what is familiar, and only with longer exposure does the preference reverse.’ C paraphrases the first half. D is the dominant trap: it keeps the passage’s words (‘preference,’ ‘reverses,’ ‘longer exposure’) but runs the sequence backward. B misreads the shifting preference as no preference at all.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about infants after brief exposure.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence gives an order: brief exposure → prefer the familiar; longer exposure → prefer the novel. A detail question built on a sequence is an invitation to a reversal trap, so check which end is which before you answer.

choices.note: Not stated. The passage says the impossible outcome is often also the less familiar one, but it never makes novelty a condition of looking longer.
The preference isn’t absent; it’s predictable from exposure. ‘Shifts’ is not ‘inconsistent.’
CORRECT. ‘Look longer at what they have already seen’ = ‘look longer at what is familiar.’
Tempting, because every word comes from the passage. But it reverses the order: after brief exposure infants prefer the familiar, and only later the novel.
Exposure and anticipatory glances are never connected in the passage.

questions.stem: The passage states that an infant who expects a ball rolling behind a screen to stop at a wall should
choices: look longer than other infants at the outcome in which the ball rests in front of the wall
look longer at the possible outcome after brief exposure and at the impossible one after longer exposure
shift its gaze beyond the wall once the screen has been removed
look ahead, while the ball is still moving, to the point just short of the barrier
show no difference in looking time once the outcomes have been matched in position, color, and timing
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says such an infant ‘should glance toward the near side of the wall, where it ought to come to rest,’ and the measurement is taken ‘just before the ball reaches the wall.’ D restates both points. A is the most tempting trap: it turns the passage’s prediction about where an expecting infant looks before the outcome into a claim about how long it looks afterward, compared with other infants. B splices in the familiarity sequence from the third paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the passage’s prediction for an infant who expects the ball to stop.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second and third sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Note the timing. The prediction is about where the infant looks before the ball arrives, which is the whole point of the eye-tracking proposal. Answers about how long infants look after the outcome come from the old method.

choices.note: Wrong measure and wrong comparison. The prediction is about where the infant glances before the outcome, not how long it looks afterward, and it doesn’t compare infants with one another.
That mixes in the third paragraph’s familiarity effect, which concerns any display, not an expecting infant.
Wrong place and wrong time: the expecting infant looks to the near side, before the screen comes off.
CORRECT. ‘While the ball is still moving’ = ‘just before the ball reaches the wall’; ‘the point just short of the barrier’ = ‘the near side of the wall, where it ought to come to rest.’
The passage says a difference ‘often survives’ matching, and in any case this describes no expecting infant.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the ball “comes to rest in a position the infant has not seen it occupy” (second sentence of the second paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: describe a flaw in the matching procedures by which proponents of the rich account later tried to control for perceptual differences
indicate how an impossible outcome can differ from a possible one in a respect unrelated to physical law
show that the impossible outcomes used in such studies are generally more complex visually than the possible ones
support the claim that, after only brief exposure to a display, infants tend to look longer at what is familiar
explain why critics concluded that infants lack any conception of solidity until they begin to search for hidden objects
questions.explanation: The sentence explains how ‘the impossible outcome is also the less familiar display’: the ball’s position is new as well as impossible, so longer looking could reflect novelty rather than a violated expectation. B states that role. A is the dominant trap: matching is the proponents’ later response to this very problem, not a flaw in it. E overstates the critics, who said the studies credited infants with knowledge a perceptual account ‘did not require,’ not that infants lack it.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author points out the ball’s unfamiliar resting place.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph’s claim: a second explanation fits the data. The example shows how: the impossible ending is also visually new (the ball sits somewhere the infant hasn’t seen it). So the impossible display differs from the possible one in a way that has nothing to do with physics. That’s the function.

choices.note: Tempting, because matching is about exactly this kind of difference. But the matching comes later, in the third paragraph, as the proponents’ answer to the problem this sentence describes. The sentence describes the original studies, not a flaw in the fix.
CORRECT. The ball’s new position makes the impossible outcome perceptually novel, a difference unrelated to whether the event obeys physical law.
‘More complex’ is never claimed; the point is that the display is unfamiliar, and it’s said of ‘many such studies,’ not ‘generally.’
The familiarity effect after brief exposure is a separate point in the third paragraph; this sentence is about novelty driving longer looking.
Too strong. The critics said the studies’ conclusion wasn’t required by the data, not that infants have no conception of solidity.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: present evidence that tells against the lean account by showing that looking-time differences survive careful matching of outcomes
defend the lean account against the charge that it can be made to fit any experimental result
describe a method of measurement that avoids the difficulty raised in the second paragraph
argue that the controls introduced by proponents of the rich account were in fact unnecessary
account for a continuing disagreement by showing that the available evidence fits both positions
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens ‘Neither side has dislodged the other, partly because of the measure itself,’ and explains why: matched studies still show a difference, but a perceptual account with both novelty and familiarity preferences can absorb it, so ‘each account can claim it.’ E states that function abstractly. A is the dominant trap: the paragraph does report surviving differences, but only to show they don’t decide the matter. C describes the fourth paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Identify what the third paragraph does in the passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Topic sentence: ‘Neither side has dislodged the other, partly because of the measure itself.’ The rest is the why: the proponents’ best evidence (surviving differences) and the critics’ flexibility (familiar vs. novel) leave the same data compatible with both. So the paragraph explains a stalemate. The trap is to grab the first piece of evidence and call it the point.

choices.note: Tempting, because the paragraph does say a difference ‘often survives.’ But the next sentences show why that doesn’t count against the lean account, which can accommodate a difference either way. Evidence mentioned to be neutralized isn’t the paragraph’s function.
Backward. The author notes that the lean account is ‘hard to refute’ as part of the stalemate, not to defend it; if anything that flexibility is a weakness.
That’s the fourth paragraph (eye-tracking). Right idea, wrong paragraph.
The passage says early studies didn’t think such controls necessary; it never says they really were unnecessary.
CORRECT. ‘A continuing disagreement’ = ‘Neither side has dislodged the other’; ‘the available evidence fits both positions’ = ‘each account can claim it.’

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the passage?
choices: A finding that infants looked longer at the possible outcome would not by itself count against the lean account.
Proponents of the rich account now acknowledge that a difference in looking time that survives careful matching cannot decide between the two accounts.
If possible and impossible outcomes were matched closely enough, the rich and lean accounts would predict different patterns of looking time.
A finding that looking-time differences disappeared after careful matching would be difficult for the lean account to explain.
Infants who look longer at familiar displays have not yet formed expectations about how solid objects behave.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says a perceptual account ‘armed with both tendencies can accommodate a difference in either direction’: after brief exposure infants prefer the familiar, so longer looking at the possible (familiar) outcome fits the lean account too. A applies that reasoning to a case the passage never mentions. B is the dominant trap: it is the author’s conclusion, attributed to the proponents, who instead keep matching outcomes. C is the natural assumption the paragraph undercuts, and D gets the lean account backward: a vanishing difference is just what it predicts once novelty is removed.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement the passage best supports. It will be an inference, not a quotation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph (novelty account) and third paragraph (familiarity preference; ‘a difference in either direction’).

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so think about what the third paragraph lets you derive. The lean account has two tools: infants prefer novel displays, and after brief exposure they prefer familiar ones. With both, it can explain longer looking at either outcome. So even a ‘backward’ result (longer looking at the possible outcome) wouldn’t embarrass it. Watch for the answer that puts the author’s conclusion in the proponents’ mouths.

choices.note: CORRECT. The lean account ‘can accommodate a difference in either direction’: the familiarity preference after brief exposure covers longer looking at the possible outcome. So such a finding wouldn’t refute it.

Tempting, because the claim is in the passage. But it’s the author’s claim. The proponents are described as continuing to match outcomes and citing surviving differences; nothing says they concede the point. Wrong party.
This is what one would hope matching does, and the paragraph says the opposite: even a difference that survives matching ‘cannot settle the matter, since each account can claim it.’
Backward. If matching removed the difference, the obvious reading is that perceptual novelty had been doing the work, which is just what the lean account says.
The familiarity preference is a general fact about attention after brief exposure; the passage never ties it to whether infants have expectations about objects.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the claim that infants of three or four months understand that solid objects cannot pass through one another is best described as
choices: receptive to its truth but unpersuaded that the evidence first offered for it suffices
provisionally accepting, on the grounds that looking-time differences have survived the controls proponents introduced
skeptical, since infants that young look longer at whatever is perceptually new to them
dismissive, since a perceptual account explains the looking-time data more economically
noncommittal, since the passage presents both accounts without evaluating the evidence for either
questions.explanation: The author allows that the rich account may ‘earn its conclusion’ if anticipatory measures confirm it, but insists ‘It will not have earned it from looking times alone,’ the evidence on which the claim originally rested. A captures both. B is the dominant trap: the passage does report surviving differences, but the author says they ‘cannot settle the matter.’ E is tempting because the author picks no winner, but the author plainly evaluates the evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author regards the claim about infants and solidity.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, last two sentences; third paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Two things are true at once: the author thinks the claim could turn out right (‘will have earned its conclusion’ if confirmed), and the author thinks the original evidence couldn’t prove it (‘not … from looking times alone’). Open on the claim, critical of the proof. Answers that pick a side on the claim itself are out; so is ‘no view at all.’

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Receptive to its truth’ = the rich account may ‘earn its conclusion’; ‘unpersuaded that the evidence first offered for it suffices’ = not ‘from looking times alone.’

Tempting, because surviving differences are reported. But the author says a surviving difference ‘cannot settle the matter, since each account can claim it.’ The author withholds acceptance until a different kind of evidence comes in.
The author reports the novelty effect as a rival explanation, not as a reason to doubt the claim; the author also allows the claim may be confirmed.
Too strong. The author never says the perceptual account is better; it’s ‘hard to refute,’ which the author presents as a problem, not a virtue.
The author does take a position on the evidence: looking times alone can’t establish the claim. That’s an evaluation, not neutrality.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Because the Chartist petitions recorded social pressure and ease of canvassing rather than opinion, they cannot serve as evidence of support for the Charter.
The fictitious names found in the 1848 petition show that the Chartists greatly exaggerated the extent of the support their movement enjoyed.
Read as shares of population and compared only among like places, the petitions yield evidence of where support for the Charter was relatively strong.
Even with fictitious names removed, the Chartist petitions show that the Charter commanded mass support among men who were unable to vote.
Historians should rely on signatures collected from door to door rather than on those gathered at mass meetings, where social pressure was greatest.
questions.explanation: The passage doubts that a signature was ‘something like a vote’ (second paragraph), describes Ellery’s method of comparing shares of population among like places (third), and concludes that it yields ‘a map of relative strength among comparable places’ though it cannot say ‘how many Britons supported the Charter’ (fourth). C states what the petitions can still show, in the method’s terms. A is the dominant trap: it keeps the second paragraph’s doubts but ignores the evidence the author says the petitions can still yield. B and D are the opponents’ and sympathetic historians’ readings, and E misdescribes Ellery’s method, which compares like with like rather than preferring one method.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author’s overall conclusion about what the Chartist petitions can show.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first sentence; fourth paragraph, first and last sentences.

breakdown.analysis: Three stages: (1) two readings of the totals; (2) both treat a signature as a vote, and that’s doubtful; (3) Ellery’s method salvages a narrower kind of evidence. The author ends on what the method offers and what it can’t do. So the main point needs the salvage and the limit, not just the doubt.

choices.note: Tempting, because the second paragraph supplies the reasons. But the passage goes on to show what the petitions can still show, ‘a map of relative strength.’ ‘Cannot serve as evidence’ is too strong.
That’s the opponents’ reading from the first paragraph, which the author says shares a mistaken premise.

CORRECT. ‘Read as shares of population and compared only among like places’ is Ellery’s method; ‘evidence of where support … was relatively strong’ is the fourth paragraph’s ‘map of relative strength among comparable places.’ The answer claims nothing about overall numbers, which fits the author’s limits.
That’s the sympathetic historians’ reading, which treats signatures as votes, the premise the author doubts.
Distortion. Ellery compares meeting with meeting and canvass with canvass; she doesn’t rank one method above the other.

questions.stem: The second paragraph indicates that at the mass meetings at which Chartist petitions were signed,
choices: only men who already supported the six points of the Charter were invited to sign
clerks of the House of Commons counted signatures as they were collected
collectors were paid according to the number of signatures they obtained
the petition was read aloud after the crowd had finished signing it
the crowd approved the petition before sheets were passed around for signing
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that at mass meetings ‘the petition was read aloud and approved by acclamation before sheets were passed through the crowd.’ E restates it. D is the dominant trap: it keeps ‘read aloud’ but puts it after the signing. The Commons clerks examined only the 1848 petition, after it was presented, and payment of collectors is never mentioned.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says happened at the mass meetings.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One sentence, with a sequence: read aloud → approved by acclamation → sheets passed through the crowd. Detail questions with a sequence invite a reversal, so check the order.

choices.note: The passage says nothing about who was invited; its point is that people may have signed without conviction.
The clerks appear only in the first paragraph, examining the 1848 petition after it reached the Commons.
Plausible, but never stated. The passage doesn’t say how collectors were paid.
Tempting, because ‘read aloud’ is right there. But the order is reversed: reading and approval came before the sheets went round.
CORRECT. ‘Approved by acclamation before sheets were passed through the crowd’ = the crowd approved it before the signing.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that historians sympathetic to the Chartist movement
choices: accepted the organizers’ claim that the third petition bore nearly 6 million signatures
took the petitions, even as reduced by official scrutiny, to show broad support among the unenfranchised
argued that the Commons rejected the first two petitions because many signatures were fictitious
compared the shares of men who signed in towns canvassed by similar means
held that many signatures gathered at mass meetings reflected social pressure rather than conviction
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says that for sympathetic historians ‘even the reduced figures recorded a mass demand in a country where few working men could vote.’ B paraphrases it. A is the dominant trap: ‘even the reduced figures’ shows they did not rely on the organizers’ claim. D is Ellery’s method, and E is the author’s doubt in the second paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the sympathetic historians.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First paragraph, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: One clause does it: ‘even the reduced figures recorded a mass demand.’ Note the word ‘even’: they granted the clerks’ smaller count and still saw mass support. Traps will hand them the organizers’ inflated number or someone else’s method.

choices.note: Tempting, but ‘even the reduced figures’ tells you they worked from the clerks’ lower count, not the organizers’ claim.
CORRECT. ‘Even as reduced by official scrutiny’ = ‘even the reduced figures’; ‘broad support among the unenfranchised’ = ‘a mass demand in a country where few working men could vote.’
Nobody in the passage explains the Commons’ rejections, and the fictitious names were found only in the 1848 petition.
That’s Ellery’s method, not the sympathetic historians’.
That’s the author’s point in the second paragraph, and it cuts against the sympathetic reading.

questions.stem: The author’s remark comparing a collector in a crowded manufacturing district with one working scattered rural parishes (second paragraph) serves primarily to
choices: support the claim that a signature might record a reluctance to be seen refusing a neighbor rather than conviction
explain why the 1848 petition contained so many signatures that the Commons clerks judged to be fictitious
suggest that support for the Charter was weaker in the countryside than in the manufacturing towns
illustrate how a factor unrelated to sympathy could make some places yield more signatures than others
show that a larger share of adult men signed in manufacturing towns than in rural parishes
questions.explanation: The remark follows ‘Totals also confound opinion with opportunity’ and ends ‘even if sympathy there were no greater’: ease of reaching households, not opinion, could explain why towns produced more signatures. D says that abstractly. A is the dominant trap: it is the adjacent sentence’s point, about why an individual signed, not about differences between places. C reverses the remark’s purpose, and E converts counts per day into shares of population, which the remark never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author contrasts town and rural collectors.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, fourth and fifth sentences.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence before it gives the job: ‘Totals also confound opinion with opportunity.’ The example shows ‘opportunity’: a town collector reaches hundreds of households a day, a rural one a few dozen, so towns pile up signatures ‘even if sympathy there were no greater.’ So the point is a non-opinion cause of differences between places. Note ‘also’: this is a second problem, separate from social pressure.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s the sentence right before. But that sentence is about why one person might sign; ‘Totals also confound…’ starts a separate problem about differences between places.
The fictitious names in 1848 are never explained, and the remark is about canvassing speed, not forgery.
Backward. The remark says towns would yield more ‘even if sympathy there were no greater.’ It warns against reading the gap as weaker rural support.
CORRECT. ‘A factor unrelated to sympathy’ = how easily collectors could reach households; ‘more signatures than others’ = towns yield far more per day ‘even if sympathy there were no greater.’
The remark concerns signatures per day of canvassing, not the share of men who signed. Shares of population come up only with Ellery’s method.

questions.stem: Which one of the following does the passage identify as a limitation that Ellery’s method shares with the use of raw petition totals?
choices: Its results would be skewed if invented names had been added more freely in some places.
It cannot be applied to places where the manner in which signatures were gathered went unrecorded.
It favors densely populated places, in which a collector could reach more households in a day.
It treats signatures gathered at mass meetings as equivalent to those gathered from door to door.
It relies on town-by-town figures from Chartist newspapers that the Commons clerks never verified.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says invented names, ‘if these were commoner in some towns than in others, … would distort shares as surely as they distort totals.’ ‘As surely as’ marks the shared weakness: A. B is the dominant trap: the passage does name it as a limitation of Ellery’s method, but it arises only because her method sorts places by how signatures were collected, which raw totals never require. C and D describe exactly what her method is designed to avoid, and E is not stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a weakness that, according to the passage, affects both Ellery’s method and raw totals.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second and third sentences; third paragraph for what the method does.

breakdown.analysis: The fourth paragraph lists two limits. (1) Unrecorded collection methods: a problem only for Ellery, because only she needs to know the method in order to compare like with like. (2) Invented names: ‘distort shares as surely as they distort totals,’ which is the shared one. The stem’s ‘shares with’ is the whole question. Most students pick the first limit because it is clearly stated; it fails because it isn’t shared.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘Distort shares as surely as they distort totals’: uneven invented names corrupt both measures.
Tempting, because the passage lists it as a limit of the method. But it isn’t shared: raw totals don’t require knowing how signatures were collected. Only Ellery’s like-with-like comparison does.
Backward. That bias belongs to raw totals; Ellery compares only ‘localities alike in density’ precisely to remove it.
Backward again. She compares ‘meeting with meeting, house-to-house canvass with house-to-house canvass.’
