The passage says she works from figures printed in Chartist newspapers, but it never calls their lack of verification a limitation.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: Two opposed readings of some evidence are described; a premise they share is questioned; a way of drawing more limited conclusions is outlined; and its reach is assessed.
A traditional interpretation of a body of evidence is presented; a historian’s challenge to it is described; and the traditional interpretation is defended against that challenge.
A traditional reading of some evidence is described; a challenge to it is presented and partly accepted; and the author proposes a narrower use of the evidence in its place.
A historical event is described; two explanations of its outcome are compared; and both explanations are rejected in favor of a third.
A body of evidence is described; a historian’s method of analyzing it is summarized; and the method is applied to show that support for a movement was concentrated in manufacturing towns.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives two readings of the petition counts (opponents’ and sympathetic historians’); the second questions what both assume, that a signature was ‘something like a vote’; the third outlines Ellery’s method; the fourth assesses what it can and cannot show. A tracks that. C is the dominant trap: it is the familiar critique outline, but the author fully endorses the doubts rather than partly accepting a challenge, and the narrower method is Ellery’s, not the author’s. E invents a result the passage never reports.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the passage’s structure paragraph by paragraph.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Topic sentences of all four paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Map it: (1) two readings of the counts; (2) ‘Both readings treat a signature as something like a vote’ — the shared premise, doubted; (3) Ellery’s procedure; (4) its limits and value. The tell is ‘Both readings’: the author goes after a premise two sides share, not one side’s view.

choices.note: CORRECT. Two opposed readings (paragraph 1); shared premise questioned (‘Both readings treat a signature as something like a vote,’ 2); a way of drawing more limited conclusions (Ellery’s, 3); its reach assessed (‘narrower,’ ‘cannot say,’ ‘a map of relative strength,’ 4).
The author never defends either reading of the totals; the second paragraph undercuts both.

Tempting, because it’s the shape of many passages. But there are two readings, not one; the author endorses the doubts outright; and the narrower use is Ellery’s proposal, which the author evaluates rather than proposes.
The passage isn’t about explaining an outcome (the Commons’ rejections go unexplained), and nothing is rejected in favor of a third explanation.
No application is reported. The passage never says where support was concentrated; it says the method could yield ‘a map of relative strength.’

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Why have peer-review panels become less able to distinguish strong research proposals from weak ones?
Should research grants be awarded by lot among the proposals that reviewers judge worthy of funding?
Can peer-review panels reliably determine the order of merit among proposals that they all regard as strong?
Would awarding grants by lot reduce the effort that applicants devote to polishing each of their proposals?
Would replacing the ranking of proposals with a lottery cause the number of grant applications to rise?
questions.explanation: Passage A argues that grants should be awarded by lot among fundable proposals; passage B argues that a full lottery has costs and endorses drawing lots only among proposals panels cannot separate. Both answer B. C is the dominant trap: both passages discuss it, but both treat the answer (no) as settled evidence on the way to the real question. E is passage B’s concern alone, D a side benefit in passage A, and A misstates both passages.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are mainly trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph; passage B, first and last paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: A says: award grants by lot among the fundable. B says: not across the board; draw lots only for ties. Same proposal, different verdicts. For a ‘both passages’ question, test every choice against both, and separate the question they argue about from the evidence they both accept.

choices.note: Neither passage says panels have become worse at anything. Passage A says they separate weak from strong ‘reasonably well’; what changed is the funding rate.
CORRECT. A says yes; B says only in part (for proposals panels cannot separate). Both are answering this question.

Tempting, because both passages talk about it. But they agree on the answer (A: ‘scarcely better than chance’; B: ‘The evidence for that unreliability is good’) and use it as a premise. The question they argue over is what follows for funding.
Passage A lists freeing applicants from ‘an arms race of presentation’ as one benefit of a lottery. A side point, not the question either passage is built to answer.
Passage B raises this in its second paragraph, but passage A never discusses the volume of applications. One passage’s concern, not both.

questions.stem: According to passage A, when the same proposals have been scored independently by different panels, the panels
choices: have agreed scarcely better than chance about which proposals deserved to be funded at all
have disagreed most often about proposals submitted by applicants from prestigious institutions
have agreed reasonably well about which proposals were strong but scarcely better than chance in ordering the weak ones
have agreed about how to order strong proposals only when they used the same scoring criteria
have been more consistent in picking out the proposals that fall short than in deciding which strong proposal should come first
questions.explanation: Passage A’s second paragraph says the panels ‘agreed reasonably well about which proposals were weak but scarcely better than chance about how to order the strong ones.’ E says the same in other words. C is the dominant trap: it reuses the passage’s phrases but swaps ‘weak’ and ‘strong.’ A moves the near-chance agreement to the basic fundable/unfundable judgment, and B and D are never stated.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says about different panels scoring the same proposals.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The sentence has two halves: good agreement on which proposals are weak, near-chance agreement on how to order the strong ones. Passage A’s whole proposal depends on that split (keep the panels for the threshold, use a lottery above it). The right answer restates the split in new words; the trap keeps the passage’s exact phrases and quietly swaps which group goes with which.

choices.note: The near-chance agreement was about ordering the strong proposals. On which proposals are weak, the panels agreed ‘reasonably well,’ which is why passage A trusts them with the threshold.
Bias toward prestigious institutions is mentioned later, but not as something the panel comparisons showed.

Tempting, because both of its phrases come straight from the passage. But it swaps the groups: the panels agreed on which proposals were weak and failed to agree on how to order the strong ones. Familiar words, reversed relationship.
Scoring criteria never come up.
CORRECT. ‘Proposals that fall short’ are the weak ones they agreed on; ‘which strong proposal should come first’ is the ordering they couldn’t agree on.

questions.stem: According to passage B, funding by rank would support better research overall than funding by lot if
choices: two panels scoring the same strong proposals agree on their order even modestly more often than chance would predict
applicants respond to the funding system by submitting only a few excellent, carefully prepared proposals rather than many merely adequate ones
reviewers are relieved of the task of separating fundable proposals from unfundable ones
panels’ rankings, though often mistaken about particular proposals, favor the better proposal slightly more often than a coin toss would
funding agencies continue to receive roughly the same number of applications each year as they receive under the present system
questions.explanation: Passage B’s first paragraph argues that a ranking ‘unreliable for any single proposal can still be informative on average’: if panels put truly stronger proposals higher even modestly more often than chance, ranking will, across thousands of grants, fund somewhat better science than a lottery. D restates that condition in other words. A is the dominant trap: it reuses ‘even modestly more often than chance’ but attaches it to agreement between two panels rather than to accuracy; two panels can agree on an order that doesn’t track which proposals are truly stronger. B and E concern passage B’s separate worry about applicants, and C describes nothing passage B proposes.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage B says would be enough for ranking to beat a lottery.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph, third sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B’s condition is about accuracy, and the bar is low: the ranking has to put the truly stronger proposal higher a bit more often than chance, even though it’s ‘unreliable for any single proposal.’ So the answer will sound weak and unimpressive (‘often mistaken,’ ‘slightly more often than a coin toss’), and that’s the point. Agreement between panels is a different thing: two panels can share the same blind spot and agree while both being wrong.

choices.note: Tempting, because it borrows passage B’s exact qualifier, ‘even modestly more often than chance.’ But passage B attaches that qualifier to placing ‘truly stronger proposals’ higher, which is accuracy. Panels agreeing with each other is passage A’s kind of evidence, and agreement doesn’t guarantee accuracy: two panels with the same bias would agree and still be wrong.
That’s from passage B’s second paragraph, about how applicants would behave under a lottery, not the condition for ranking to win.
Passage B never proposes this. In fact both passages keep the panels at the threshold.

CORRECT. ‘Often mistaken about particular proposals’ is ‘unreliable for any single proposal’; ‘slightly more often than a coin toss’ is ‘even modestly more often than chance.’ Passage B says that’s enough, across many grants.
Also from the applicant-behavior worry. Holding the number of applications steady isn’t the condition passage B gives for ranking to produce better science.

questions.stem: The attitude of the author of passage B toward passage A’s characterization of the competition among strong proposals as “a contest whose outcome is close to random already” (end of the second paragraph of passage A) can best be described as
choices: agreement that it holds for any given funding decision, coupled with denial that ranking therefore adds nothing in the aggregate
rejection of it, on the grounds that panels place stronger proposals in the upper half of the fundable group more often than chance
acceptance of it, together with agreement that a lottery would therefore cost nothing in the quality of the research funded
skepticism, since the studies in which proposals were scored by different panels examined only weak proposals
indifference, since passage B’s case against a full lottery rests entirely on how applicants would respond to it
questions.explanation: Passage B says ‘The evidence for that unreliability is good; the inference drawn from it is not,’ and adds that ‘a ranking that is unreliable for any single proposal can still be informative on average.’ A captures both halves. B is the dominant trap: passage B states its claim about the upper half only as a condition (‘if panels place…’), not as a fact, and it accepts the unreliability. C ignores passage B’s claim that ranking would ‘support somewhat better science,’ D misdescribes the panel studies, and E ignores passage B’s first paragraph.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down how passage B’s author regards passage A’s claim that the ranking of strong proposals is close to random.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage B splits passage A’s case in two: the evidence (good) and the inference (not). So B accepts A’s description case by case and denies what A draws from it, that ranking adds nothing. Watch the ‘if’ in B’s next sentence: B never asserts that panels beat chance; it says what follows if they do.

choices.note: CORRECT. Accepts the claim for single decisions (‘The evidence for that unreliability is good,’ ‘unreliable for any single proposal’) but denies that ranking is therefore worthless (‘informative on average’).

Tempting, because passage B does talk about panels beating chance. But it puts that as a condition (‘if panels place …’), not as a finding, and it calls the evidence of unreliability ‘good.’ It never rejects A’s description.
Half right. B accepts the unreliability, but says a weakly informative ranking would ‘support somewhat better science than funding by lot,’ so a lottery would cost something.
Passage A says the panels agreed on the weak proposals and not on ordering the strong ones, so the studies covered both. And passage B raises no doubts about them.
Passage B’s first paragraph is a direct response to this claim, so the author is hardly indifferent. Applicant behavior is a second, separate point.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of titles would be most appropriate for passage A and passage B, respectively?
choices: “Bias on the Funding Panel” / “Where Ranking Still Earns Its Keep”
“Admitting Chance into Research Funding” / “Why Rankings Fail Even on Average”
“The Lottery as Honest Reform” / “Where Ranking Still Earns Its Keep”
“The Lottery as Honest Reform” / “Gaming the Lottery: Why Applications Would Multiply”
“The Case for Randomness in Science Funding” / “The Case Against Randomness in Science Funding”
questions.explanation: Passage A proposes a lottery among fundable proposals that would ‘admit the randomness openly’; passage B argues that rankings carry information on average and should be kept wherever they do, with lots drawn only for ties. C fits both. D is the dominant trap: its passage B title names a real argument of passage B, but only its second paragraph, not its overall position. A’s first title shrinks passage A to one of its points, B reverses passage B’s claim, and E ignores that passage B endorses a limited lottery.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick a title pair that fits each passage’s overall point.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph; passage B, first and last paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Each title has to capture the whole passage. A: grant by lot among the fundable, openly admitting the randomness. B: rankings still carry information on average, so keep them where they do and draw lots only for ties. So we need ‘lottery’ for A and ‘ranking still matters, within limits’ for B. Check each half separately; most wrong pairs get one side right.

choices.note: Half right. The B title fits, but bias is only one point in passage A’s case (its ‘most important’ benefit, but still one), not its subject.
The A title fits, but the B title reverses passage B, which says a ranking ‘can still be informative on average.’
CORRECT. Passage A urges a lottery that would ‘admit the randomness openly’; passage B says rankings are worth keeping ‘wherever rankings carry information.’

Tempting, because passage B does argue that applications could ‘rise sharply.’ But that is one of its two objections; its main claim is that rankings are informative on average and its endorsement of a tie-breaking lottery. Too narrow for B.
Overshoot. Passage B isn’t against randomness; it endorses drawing lots among proposals panels can’t separate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage B identifies a drawback of the reform passage A proposes, a drawback that passage A anticipates but underestimates.
Passage B accepts both the premise and the conclusion of passage A’s argument but holds that the reform should be introduced gradually.
Passage B grants that the reform passage A proposes would reduce bias but argues that this benefit is outweighed by the reform’s costs.
Passage A reports the results of a funding lottery already in use; passage B questions whether those results can be generalized.
Passage B accepts the evidence for passage A’s proposal but denies that it warrants the full proposal, and favors a partial version.
questions.explanation: Passage B says ‘The evidence for that unreliability is good; the inference drawn from it is not,’ argues that ranking is informative on average, and endorses drawing lots only among proposals panels can’t separate. E describes that. A is the dominant trap: passage A does say a lottery would free applicants from ‘an arms race of presentation,’ which looks like anticipating B’s worry about applicants, but it never considers the volume of applications. D is tempting because passage A now mentions New Zealand’s lottery, but it reports no results. C credits passage B with a concession about bias it never makes, and B ignores B’s rejection of A’s conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A as a whole.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second and third paragraphs; passage B, all three paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: B’s move: evidence fine, inference not. B then offers reasons a full lottery costs something (lost information, more applications) and endorses a narrower use of lots. So: accept the premise, reject the full conclusion, back a partial version. The traps each misdescribe one piece: what A anticipated, what B concedes, or what A reports.

choices.note: Tempting, because passage A does talk about how a lottery affects applicants: it would end ‘an arms race of presentation.’ But that’s a benefit, and A never considers that applicants might submit more proposals. A doesn’t anticipate B’s drawback at all.
Passage B rejects A’s conclusion (a lottery among all fundable proposals) and favors a narrower reform, not a slower path to the same one.
Passage B never mentions bias, let alone grants that a lottery would reduce it. Its objections are lost information and more applications.
Tempting, since passage A mentions New Zealand’s Explorer Grants. But it cites them as an instance, reporting no results, and passage B never discusses them.

CORRECT. Accepts the evidence (‘The evidence for that unreliability is good’), denies the full inference (‘the inference drawn from it is not’), and favors a partial version (lots only among proposals panels cannot separate).

questions.stem: The authors of the passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: peer-review panels can reliably separate proposals that should not be funded from those that might be
the order in which panels rank the strong proposals is reliable for any individual proposal
the present method of allocating public research funding ought to be changed in at least some respect
a lottery among all fundable proposals would cost something in the quality of research funded
a lottery would lead applicants to submit more proposals than they submit under the present system
questions.explanation: Passage A says that under a lottery ‘nothing of value would be given up: science funded by lot would be as good as science funded by rank’; passage B says that if panels beat chance even modestly, ranking ‘will … support somewhat better science than funding by lot.’ They split on D. B is the dominant trap: both authors agree that the ranking is unreliable for individual proposals. A and C are points of agreement, and E is raised only by passage B.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a point on which one author would say yes and the other no.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph; passage B, first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. List what they share first: the ranking of strong proposals is unreliable case by case; panels can handle the threshold; the system should change. Then find the split: A says a full lottery gives up nothing of value. B says a weakly informative ranking still beats chance across thousands of grants, so a lottery would cost something.

choices.note: Both agree. Passage A says panels do this well; passage B keeps the threshold and gives it more weight.

Tempting, because it’s the central issue in both passages. But they agree on it: A says agreement is ‘scarcely better than chance,’ and B says the ranking is ‘unreliable for any single proposal.’ Same answer from both, so no disagreement.
Both say yes. A wants a full lottery; B endorses a tie-breaking lottery like the Swiss one.
CORRECT. A: no cost (‘nothing of value would be given up’). B: some cost (ranking would ‘support somewhat better science than funding by lot’).
Only passage B raises this. Passage A never addresses how many proposals applicants would submit, so we can’t say it disagrees.
